Tuition, retail sales, and space rentals generate reliable earned income that supports exhibitions, emerging artist programs, and free/low-cost community craft activities—illustrating a social enterprise approach that sustains accessible arts and cultural programming.

solutions.text: Accessible, Inclusive Programming and Supports: Design programming with barrier-reduction in mind (sliding-scale fees, childcare at events, accessible venues, transportation supports) to ensure diverse youth can participate and lead.

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op Community Access Program
resources.description: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op’s Community Access Program subsidizes venue rental fees for community groups, emerging artists, and youth-led events, enabling pay-what-you-can and low-cost programming. The theatre is an accessible venue with step-free entry and accessible washrooms and pairs rentals with technical mentorship, reducing financial and physical barriers so diverse youth can participate and lead on stage and behind the scenes.

resources.name: Canada Games Centre Inclusion & Fee Assistance Supports
resources.description: The Canada Games Centre provides inclusion support for children and youth in recreation programs, child-minding services for caregivers, and an accessible facility. Through partnerships with fee-assistance programs (such as Jumpstart and municipal subsidies), it reduces or eliminates program costs, ensuring youth from varied income levels can access year-round sport and recreation opportunities.
resources.address: 26 Thomas Raddall Drive, Halifax, NS B3S 0E2

resources.name: Ross Creek Arts Camps Bursary & Access Program
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts runs year-round youth arts camps and programs supported by bursaries and scholarships so cost is not a barrier. The Centre also hosts free or pay-what-you-can community arts events in accessible, supportive studios, enabling rural and urban youth to create, exhibit, and take on leadership roles in inclusive settings.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries – Free Youth Arts & Tech Programs (Central Library)
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries offers free, drop-in youth arts, music, and technology programs and provides creative labs and materials at no cost. The Central Library’s fully accessible spaces, evening/weekend scheduling, and youth-led advisory councils reduce financial and physical barriers, helping diverse youth participate, showcase work, and shape programming.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Neptune Theatre Pay-What-You-Can and Accessible Performances
resources.description: Neptune Theatre offers pay-what-you-can performances, relaxed performances, and ASL-interpreted shows, alongside discounted youth tickets, to make professional theatre accessible. By combining accessible pricing with an accessible downtown venue and youth-engagement initiatives, Neptune lowers cost and physical barriers so young people can attend, learn, and lead in the arts.

solutions.text: Local Digital Platform for Promotion and Sales: Build a community-run online marketplace and streaming/promo platform where local artists can sell work, advertise events and connect with audiences beyond physical venue limits.

resources.name: Art Gallery of Nova Scotia Online Shop
resources.description: The Art Gallery of Nova Scotia operates an e-commerce platform featuring work by Nova Scotian artists and artisans, complete with artist profiles and exhibition tie-ins. This extends sales and promotion beyond the museum’s physical shop, allowing creators to sell year-round while the Gallery’s site and channels advertise exhibitions and events to wider audiences.

resources.name: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design Online Shop
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: This juried online marketplace showcases Cape Breton artisans, providing secure online sales, artist profiles, and promotion for exhibitions and workshops. By aggregating local makers on a single platform, it helps creators reach customers year-round and beyond the island’s physical venues while advertising community programming.

resources.name: Argyle Fine Art Online Gallery & Virtual Events
resources.description: Argyle Fine Art maintains a robust online gallery with real-time inventory, enabling Nova Scotia artists to sell paintings, prints, and sculptures to buyers locally and internationally. The gallery also hosts virtual exhibitions and live-streamed studio visits, promoting events and connecting artists with audiences well beyond the brick-and-mortar space.

resources.name: HAT Online (Highland Arts Theatre)
resources.description: HAT Online offers live-streamed and on-demand performances by Cape Breton artists with digital ticketing and memberships, allowing creators to earn income without venue constraints. The platform also promotes upcoming shows and community events, helping local performers connect with province-wide and global audiences year-round.

obstacles.title: Inclusion and Discrimination
obstacles.description: Racism, homophobia, transphobia, ableism, and barriers faced by Indigenous and African Nova Scotian communities erode belonging.

solutions.text: Community-led Anti-racism and Inclusion Workshops: Organize regular workshops and training sessions led by local Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, and LGBTQ2S+ leaders for residents, businesses, schools, and municipal staff to teach local history, implicit bias, bystander intervention, and practical allyship strategies.

resources.name: Cultural Competency & Anti-Racism Training
resources.description: The Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre offers community-led cultural safety and anti-racism workshops for residents, schools, businesses, and public servants. Facilitated by local Mi'kmaw knowledge keepers and educators, sessions often include Mi'kmaw history of Kjipuktuk/Halifax, treaty education, implicit bias awareness, bystander intervention, and practical allyship strategies, with tools like the KAIROS Blanket Exercise to ground learning in local context.

resources.name: Education & Outreach Program
resources.organization: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia delivers anti-Black racism education, African Nova Scotian history presentations, and inclusion training to schools, workplaces, community groups, and government. Led by African Nova Scotian historians and community leaders, workshops cover local history, systemic and implicit bias, bystander strategies, and tangible allyship actions for participants.
resources.address: 10 Cherry Brook Road, Cherry Brook, NS B2Z 1A8

resources.name: Social Justice Education: Anti-Racism, Decolonization & Allyship Workshops
resources.description: Tatamagouche Centre convenes Indigenous elders, African Nova Scotian educators, and 2SLGBTQIA+ trainers to facilitate public and custom workshops across Nova Scotia. Sessions focus on local histories and lived experiences, implicit bias, bystander intervention, and practical allyship for residents, schools, municipalities, and businesses seeking community-led inclusion training.

resources.name: Race Relations, Cross-Cultural Understanding & Human Rights (RCH) Services
resources.description: HRCE’s RCH Services provide ongoing workshops and professional learning for students, educators, and staff to address racism and foster inclusion in schools. Delivered in collaboration with African Nova Scotian and Mi'kmaw Student Support Workers and community partners, sessions incorporate local histories, implicit bias awareness, bystander intervention, and actionable allyship practices.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

solutions.text: Cultural Centres and Celebration Festivals: Establish and support community-run cultural centres and annual festivals that showcase Mi'kmaq, African Nova Scotian and other cultural heritages through food, music, storytelling and art to build inter-community relationships and visibility.

resources.name: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.organization: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.description: A museum and cultural hub that preserves and promotes African Nova Scotian history and culture through exhibitions, educational programs, and year-round community events. It implements the solution by hosting cultural celebrations (e.g., African Heritage Month programming, Emancipation Day events) featuring music, dance, food, storytelling, and art that welcome all communities and build inter-cultural understanding across Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 10 Cherry Brook Road, Cherry Brook, NS B2Z 1A8

resources.name: Africville Museum and Emancipation Day Festival
resources.description: The Africville Museum serves as a cultural centre preserving the legacy of the Africville community and hosts public programs and exhibits year-round. Its annual Emancipation Day Festival and other gatherings feature gospel and contemporary music, traditional foods, storytelling, and art, creating welcoming spaces that increase visibility of African Nova Scotian heritage and foster inter-community relationships.

resources.name: Membertou Heritage Park
resources.description: An interpretive centre and museum offering exhibits, Elder-led storytelling, craft workshops, and cultural programming that share Mi’kmaw history and living traditions with visitors. By hosting cultural events and supporting community celebrations such as powwow gatherings in Membertou, it showcases Mi’kmaw foodways, music, dance, and art to connect diverse audiences and strengthen cross-cultural understanding.

resources.name: Nova Multifest
resources.description: An annual, community-run multicultural festival in Dartmouth featuring performance stages, cultural pavilions, and international food vendors. The festival regularly includes Mi’kmaq drumming and dance, African Nova Scotian music and storytelling, and showcases from many other cultural communities, creating an inclusive celebration that builds connections and visibility across Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Millbrook Cultural & Heritage Centre
resources.description: A Mi’kmaw cultural centre and museum offering exhibits, guided tours, cultural demonstrations, and community events. Through storytelling, art, drumming and dance presentations, and seasonal celebrations that welcome schools and the public, it elevates Mi’kmaw heritage, builds inter-community relationships, and advances understanding across the province.

solutions.text: Youth Mentorship and Career Pathways: Create mentorship programs pairing youth from Indigenous, African Nova Scotian and other marginalized communities with local employers, tradespeople, artists and entrepreneurs to build skills, internships, apprenticeship placements and clear career pathways.

resources.name: Pathways to Shipbuilding – African Nova Scotian and Indigenous Cohorts
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) in partnership with Irving Shipbuilding Inc.
resources.description: This NSCC program recruits African Nova Scotian and Mi’kmaw/Indigenous youth for pre-apprenticeship and trades training linked directly to Irving Shipbuilding and other marine-sector employers. Participants receive mentorship from journeypersons and industry professionals, academic and cultural supports, and paid work placements that lead to apprenticeship registrations and clear career pathways in the skilled trades.

resources.name: Imhotep’s Legacy Academy (ILA)
resources.description: ILA is a province-wide STEM mentorship program that pairs African Nova Scotian junior and senior high school students with university student mentors, scientists, engineers and tech professionals. Through after‑school programs, industry visits, internships and scholarships, ILA builds technical skills and connects youth to real employers and entrepreneurs, creating tangible pathways into post‑secondary STEM and related careers.

resources.name: Employment & Training (ISET/AYESS) Program
resources.description: The Native Council of Nova Scotia’s Employment & Training program supports off‑reserve Indigenous youth with career counselling, skills development and wage‑subsidized work placements. By matching participants with local employers and tradespeople for mentorship and on‑the‑job experience, the program removes barriers to employment, supports apprenticeship starts, and builds clear career pathways across sectors.
resources.address: 129 Truro Heights Road, Truro, NS B6L 1X1

resources.name: Pathways to Education – Spryfield
resources.description: This community‑based program supports youth in the Spryfield area with mentoring, tutoring and career exploration, and partners with local employers, trades, NSCC and arts organizations to create job shadowing, internships and summer employment. It specifically addresses barriers faced by marginalized youth, including African Nova Scotian and Indigenous students, and builds step‑by‑step pathways to graduation, post‑secondary, and meaningful careers.
resources.address: 531 Herring Cove Road, Halifax, NS B3R 1X3

solutions.text: Inclusive Local Hiring and Procurement Pledges: Encourage municipalities, school boards and local businesses to adopt public hiring and procurement commitments that prioritize equity, target barriers for underrepresented groups, and track/report progress transparently.

resources.name: Supplier Diversity and Social Procurement Program
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s supplier diversity and social procurement program embeds equity criteria in purchasing, encourages bids from diverse-owned businesses (including African Nova Scotian, Mi’kmaw/Indigenous, women, 2SLGBTQIA+, persons with disabilities, and newcomers), and provides outreach to reduce barriers to participation. The municipality includes community-benefit requirements on major contracts to create apprenticeships and jobs for underrepresented groups and publicly reports procurement outcomes, advancing transparent, inclusive local spending.

resources.name: Employment Equity and Diversity Hiring Initiative
resources.description: HRCE’s employment equity initiative designates certain roles for African Nova Scotian and Mi’kmaw/Indigenous candidates, runs targeted recruitment and mentorship to lower barriers, and uses self-identification to monitor representation. As one of Nova Scotia’s largest public-sector employers, HRCE’s transparent reporting and dedicated hiring pathways operationalize inclusive public hiring and create role-model representation for youth and families across the region.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

resources.name: Road to Economic Prosperity (ANREP) – Inclusive Hiring and Procurement Commitments
resources.description: ANREP convenes HRM, anchor institutions, and local businesses to adopt concrete commitments that grow employment and procurement opportunities for African Nova Scotians, including supplier diversity pledges, inclusive hiring pathways, and mentorship. The initiative sets measurable actions and publishes progress updates and scorecards, creating accountability for equitable hiring and local purchasing across Halifax.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

solutions.text: Accessible Community Spaces and Transit Improvements: Work with community groups and local government to audit and upgrade public spaces, recreational facilities and transit for physical accessibility, gender-inclusive facilities, sensory-friendly features and better route/service coverage in underserved neighbourhoods.

resources.name: Accessibility at Halifax Public Libraries
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries audits and upgrades branches for barrier-free access, including automatic doors, elevators, ramps, accessible computers, and hearing supports. Many locations provide gender-inclusive and universal washrooms, quiet/low-sensory spaces, and sensory kits to make programs and spaces welcoming for neurodivergent youth and families. These ongoing improvements directly implement the solution by enhancing physical accessibility and inclusive features across high-use community spaces, particularly in diverse neighbourhoods.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Sensory-Friendly Hours and Accessibility Program
resources.description: The Discovery Centre offers sensory-friendly hours with reduced noise and lighting, sensory maps, and quiet zones, while maintaining accessible entries, elevators, and universal washrooms. Staff receive inclusion training and the Centre works with community partners to reduce barriers for neurodivergent visitors and families. These measures implement the solution by embedding sensory-friendly features and inclusive facilities within a major public, youth-serving space.
resources.address: 1215 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: MusGo Rider Accessible Community Transit
resources.description: MusGo Rider operates community-based, wheelchair-accessible transportation on the Eastern Shore and Musquodoboit Valley, filling service gaps in rural, underserved parts of HRM. The co-operative offers door-to-door service, inclusive driver training, and coordinated routes to key community services, schools, jobs, and health care. By expanding coverage and prioritizing accessibility features, MusGo Rider advances the solution’s call for equitable, accessible transit in underserved neighbourhoods.
resources.address: 5228 Highway 7, Unit 6, Porters Lake, NS B3E 1J8

resources.name: Moving Forward Together Plan and Access-A-Bus
resources.description: Halifax Transit’s Moving Forward Together Plan improves route design and service frequency to better connect underserved communities, while its fleet features low-floor, ramp-equipped buses and audible/visual stop announcements. Access-A-Bus provides door-to-door, pre-booked accessible transportation for riders with disabilities across HRM. Together, these initiatives implement the solution by expanding equitable transit coverage and removing physical and sensory barriers to mobility.

resources.name: John W. Lindsay YMCA – Inclusive and Accessible Facilities
resources.description: The John W. Lindsay YMCA provides universally accessible recreation spaces, including barrier-free entries, elevators, adaptive fitness equipment, and gender-inclusive/universal change rooms. Staff receive inclusion training and the facility regularly updates accessibility features in line with Nova Scotia’s Accessibility Act and user feedback. These upgrades implement the solution by making a major community recreation hub welcoming and usable for people of all genders and abilities.

solutions.text: LGBTQ2S+ Safe Spaces and Peer-support Networks: Launch and fund local drop-in centres, peer-support groups and school-based alliances that provide confidential support, referrals, crisis resources and social programming for queer and trans youth and adults.

resources.name: The Youth Project (2SLGBTQIA+ Youth Services)
resources.description: The Youth Project provides confidential peer-support groups, social drop-ins, and one-on-one support for 2SLGBTQIA+ youth across Nova Scotia. They also help start and sustain school-based Gender and Sexuality Alliances (GSAs), offer referrals to crisis and mental health resources, and run inclusive social programming and workshops, directly implementing safe spaces and peer-support networks.

resources.name: South House Sexual and Gender Resource Centre
resources.organization: South House Sexual and Gender Resource Centre
resources.description: South House operates a safer-space drop-in centre that offers peer support, resources, and referrals for 2SLGBTQIA+ community members and allies. Through confidential one-on-one support, community-led groups, and social programming, they foster inclusion and reduce discrimination by providing welcoming spaces and connections to crisis and health services.

resources.name: Valley Youth Project (Annapolis Valley 2SLGBTQ+ Youth Group)
resources.description: The Valley Youth Project hosts free, confidential peer-support meetings and social programming for 2SLGBTQ+ youth and their allies in the Annapolis Valley. Meetings provide a welcoming drop-in environment with activities, discussion, and referrals to local supports, directly building community-based safe spaces for queer and trans youth.

resources.name: LGBTQ+ Newcomers Peer Support Group
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS’ LGBTQ+ Newcomers Peer Support Group provides a safe, confidential space for queer and trans immigrants and refugees to connect, share experiences, and access settlement and mental health referrals. Facilitated by staff, the group offers community-building activities, information sessions, and linkage to crisis resources, addressing inclusion while strengthening peer-support networks.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

solutions.text: School–Community Partnerships for Inclusive Curriculum: Collaborate with local Indigenous and African Nova Scotian knowledge-keepers to co-develop curriculum modules, classroom visits and teacher supports that reflect regional histories, languages and contributions, plus anti-bullying and inclusion programs.

resources.name: Education and School Programs
resources.description: The Africville Museum’s Education and School Programs offer curriculum-linked tours, classroom presentations, and teacher resources that centre African Nova Scotian histories and contributions. Knowledge-keepers and community educators collaborate with teachers to co-develop learning modules and classroom visits that deepen understanding of racism, resilience, and inclusion in Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Education & Outreach Programs
resources.description: The Black Loyalist Heritage Centre provides curriculum-aligned education programs, virtual and on-site school visits, and teacher guides focused on African Nova Scotian history and culture. Working with community historians and elders, they co-create classroom-ready materials and professional learning that foster inclusive practices and counter racism in school communities.
resources.address: 119 Old Birchtown Road, Shelburne, NS B0T 1W0

resources.name: Cultural Education and School Programs
resources.organization: Millbrook Cultural & Heritage Centre (Millbrook First Nation)
resources.description: The Millbrook Cultural & Heritage Centre delivers Mi’kmaq-led school programs, classroom visits, and teacher resources on Mi’kmaw language, culture, and regional history. Elders and cultural knowledge-keepers co-develop modules aligned with Nova Scotia curriculum, supporting inclusive classrooms and helping educators embed Indigenous perspectives and anti-discrimination learning.

resources.name: African Nova Scotian Student Support Workers (ANSSW) and Indigenous Education Support
resources.description: HRCE’s ANSSW and Indigenous Education teams partner with families, community elders, and knowledge-keepers to bring culturally responsive programming into classrooms, support teachers, and strengthen inclusive curriculum implementation. They coordinate classroom visits, mentorship, and staff professional learning that address anti-Black racism and support Mi’kmaw perspectives, advancing safe and welcoming school climates.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

resources.name: School Outreach and Education Program
resources.description: The Youth Project delivers workshops, classroom sessions, and teacher professional development across Nova Scotia to address homophobia, transphobia, and bullying, and to build inclusive school cultures. Their educators collaborate with schools to tailor content, provide resources for GSAs and staff, and integrate intersectional approaches that support 2SLGBTQIA+ students alongside broader equity initiatives.

solutions.text: Community Legal Clinics and Know-Your-Rights Campaigns: Set up or expand community legal clinics offering free or sliding-scale legal counsel, discrimination complaint assistance and 'know your rights' information sessions targeted to marginalized residents navigating housing, employment or policing issues.

resources.name: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service
resources.organization: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service (Schulich School of Law, Dalhousie University)
resources.description: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service is a community legal clinic providing free and sliding‑scale legal assistance in areas such as housing/tenancy, income assistance, employment issues, and human rights. The clinic also delivers community outreach and know‑your‑rights education sessions in partnership with community groups, helping marginalized residents navigate discrimination complaints and interactions with policing and public systems.

resources.name: Information Sessions and Workshops (Know Your Rights)
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS hosts regular information sessions and workshops for newcomers on tenant rights, employment standards, workplace discrimination, and navigating public systems. These know‑your‑rights sessions equip immigrants and refugees with practical legal information and referrals (including to legal clinics and human rights bodies), directly supporting marginalized residents facing housing, employment, or policing‑related barriers.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Indigenous Courtwork Program
resources.description: The Indigenous Courtwork Program supports off‑reserve and non‑status Indigenous people in Nova Scotia to navigate the justice system, including assistance with court processes, police interactions, and rights education. Courtworkers provide culturally informed advocacy, legal information, and referrals, offering community‑based, know‑your‑rights support that addresses discrimination and improves access to justice.
resources.address: 129 Truro Heights Road, Truro, NS B6L 1X1

solutions.text: Affordable, Accessible Housing Co-operatives: Support community-led housing co-ops and partnerships that prioritize affordable, accessible units for families, elders, persons with disabilities and returning residents, with policies to prevent displacement in gentrifying areas.

resources.name: Community Housing Growth Fund (Nova Scotia)
resources.organization: Community Housing Transformation Centre (in partnership with the Nova Scotia Department of Municipal Affairs and Housing)
resources.description: The Community Housing Growth Fund provides grants, planning assistance, and capacity-building supports to co-operative and non-profit housing providers across Nova Scotia to create, preserve, and expand affordable and accessible homes. Funding streams prioritize equity-denied groups (including Indigenous and African Nova Scotian communities) and support community-governed housing models—such as co-ops—that help prevent displacement in gentrifying areas by keeping housing under local, mission-driven control.

resources.name: Wije’winen Indigenous Housing and Community Hub
resources.description: Wije’winen is a community-led development that will deliver affordable, culturally safe, and accessible housing for urban Indigenous peoples in Halifax, including elders, families, and persons with disabilities, alongside wraparound services. By centering Indigenous governance and anchoring long-term affordability in the North End, the project advances partnerships that resist displacement and ensure residents can remain and thrive as the neighborhood changes.

resources.name: Affordable Homeownership Program (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia partners with communities to build affordable homes—often incorporating universal design features—to support families, elders, and persons with disabilities in putting down stable roots. While not a co-op, the program aligns with the solution by using community-driven partnerships to create permanently affordable pathways to housing, helping prevent displacement by enabling residents to remain in their home communities as costs rise.

solutions.text: Restorative Justice and Community Safety Circles: Develop restorative justice programs and community safety circles run by trained local facilitators as alternatives to punitive systems, emphasizing healing, accountability and community-based resolutions for youth and adults.

resources.name: Restorative Approaches in Schools (HRCE)
resources.description: HRCE implements restorative justice practices across its schools, training teachers and facilitators to lead restorative circles, conferences, and mediated dialogues to address harm, bias-based incidents, and conflicts. These practices prioritize accountability, healing, and relationship-building over punitive discipline, creating safer, more inclusive environments for diverse students, including Indigenous and African Nova Scotian youth, 2SLGBTQIA+ students, and students with disabilities.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

resources.name: Restorative Approaches in Schools (CCRCE)
resources.organization: Chignecto Central Regional Centre for Education
resources.description: CCRCE embeds restorative approaches in school culture by training staff to facilitate restorative circles and community conferences that repair harm and rebuild trust when incidents occur. The approach offers an alternative to suspensions and exclusions, centering student voice, accountability, and inclusion, and is used to respond to bullying, racism, homophobia/transphobia, and other harms in age-appropriate, community-based ways.

resources.name: Restorative Justice Program (ACRP)
resources.description: ACRP delivers restorative justice services that use facilitated restorative circles and conferences as alternatives to court processes for youth and adults referred by police, Crown, and community partners. Trained local facilitators bring together those who caused harm, those affected, families, and community members to craft accountability agreements and healing-focused resolutions, addressing harms including discrimination while strengthening community safety and belonging.

solutions.text: Mi'kmaq Language and Cultural Revitalization Programs: Invest in community-driven language nests, after-school programs, elder-mentorship, and public signage initiatives to revitalize Mi'kmaq language and cultural practices in neighbourhoods and schools.

resources.name: Unama'ki College – Mi'kmaq Language and Culture Programs
resources.description: Unama'ki College at Cape Breton University offers Mi'kmaw language courses, cultural programming, and partnerships with local schools that connect youth with Elders and Knowledge Keepers. The college hosts mentorship circles, community workshops, and on-campus initiatives that foreground Mi'kmaw language and culture, including visible Mi'kmaw signage and place names. These programs directly support language revitalization and belonging by creating welcoming, intergenerational learning spaces.
resources.address: 1250 Grand Lake Road, Sydney, NS B1M 1A2

resources.name: Mi’kmaw Interpretive and Language Programs at Kejimkujik National Park and National Historic Site
resources.description: Kejimkujik presents Mi’kmaw place names and bilingual public signage throughout the park and historic site, embedding the language into trails, exhibits, and wayfinding. The site regularly hosts Mi’kmaw interpreters, Elders, and Knowledge Keepers who lead cultural demonstrations and youth learning activities, strengthening intergenerational mentorship. These experiences connect families and schools to Mi’kmaw language and cultural practices in a widely accessible public setting.
resources.address: 3005 Kejimkujik Main Parkway, Maitland Bridge, NS B0T 1B0

resources.name: Indigenous Services and Mi’kmaw Language Programs
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries provides Mi’kmaw language learning circles, after-school activities for Indigenous youth, and regular sessions led by Elders and Knowledge Keepers across branches. Libraries also incorporate visible Mi’kmaw welcome messages and land-based acknowledgements on signage and displays, normalizing the language in community spaces. These programs create safe, inclusive hubs that support language revitalization and reduce barriers to belonging for Indigenous youth and families.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Cultural Education and Mi’kmaw Language Programs
resources.description: Membertou Heritage Park delivers school visits, youth workshops, and community events where Elders and Knowledge Keepers share Mi’kmaw language, stories, and cultural practices. Exhibits and on-site interpretive materials feature Mi’kmaw terminology and place names, reinforcing public visibility of the language. These intergenerational programs strengthen identity, build cultural pride, and create inclusive spaces for learning in the community.

solutions.text: Micro-grants and Business Supports for Black and Indigenous Entrepreneurs: Create local micro-grant funds, low-interest loans, business incubators and tailored training to remove barriers for African Nova Scotian and Indigenous entrepreneurs starting or scaling small businesses.

resources.name: Black Business Initiative — Loan Fund & Business Advisory Services
resources.description: The Black Business Initiative (BBI) offers tailored financing (including micro and small business loans), one-on-one advisory services, and entrepreneur training designed specifically for African Nova Scotians. By combining access to capital with mentorship, workshops, and networking, BBI reduces systemic barriers and helps Black entrepreneurs in Nova Scotia start and scale viable small businesses.
resources.address: 1660 Hollis Street, Suite 810, Halifax, NS B3J 1V7

resources.name: Aboriginal Business Financing Program (ABFP) — Ulnooweg
resources.description: Ulnooweg delivers the federal Aboriginal Business Financing Program across Atlantic Canada, providing non-repayable contributions (micro-grants and grants), business loans, and advisory supports to First Nations, Inuit, and Métis entrepreneurs. The program funds start-up and expansion costs and pairs capital with business planning assistance and mentorship, directly addressing access-to-finance and capacity barriers faced by Indigenous entrepreneurs in Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Black Start-Up Project
resources.description: Tribe Network’s Black Start-Up Project provides cohort-based incubator programming, mentorship, and tailored training for Black founders in Nova Scotia and Atlantic Canada. The initiative also connects entrepreneurs to micro-grant opportunities and capital partners while building networks that reduce barriers to financing, skills development, and market access.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: Black Entrepreneur Startup Program (BESP)
resources.description: Futurpreneur’s Black Entrepreneur Startup Program offers tailored business coaching, up to $60,000 in start-up financing (in partnership with BDC), and two years of mentorship for Black entrepreneurs aged 18–39. Operating in Nova Scotia through its Atlantic office, the program removes common barriers by combining accessible capital with training, planning tools, and community connections.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

solutions.text: Disability Employment and Skills Training Hubs: Establish community hubs offering supported employment programs, workplace accommodations consulting, job coaching and employer education to increase hiring and retention of people with disabilities.

resources.name: WorkBridge Employment Services
resources.description: WorkBridge is Easter Seals Nova Scotia’s supported employment hub that provides individualized career planning, job development, and on‑the‑job coaching for job seekers with disabilities. The team partners with employers to implement workplace accommodations, offers disability and inclusion training, and supports retention through ongoing employer and employee check‑ins—directly aligning with the solution’s focus on supported employment, accommodations consulting, and employer education.

resources.name: Prescott Employment Services
resources.description: Prescott Employment Services delivers supported employment for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, including skills development, job carving, placement, and intensive job coaching. They engage employers with guidance on accessible hiring, reasonable accommodations, and inclusive workplace practices, serving as a community hub that advances the solution’s goals of increasing hiring and retention through coaching and employer education.

resources.name: Come to Work (Nova Scotia)
resources.organization: CNIB (Canadian National Institute for the Blind) – Nova Scotia
resources.description: CNIB’s Come to Work program connects job seekers who are blind, partially sighted, or Deafblind with inclusive employers and provides job readiness training and one‑to‑one coaching. The program conducts workplace assessments, advises on accessible technology and accommodations, and delivers employer education to build inclusive hiring pipelines—embodying the solution’s supported employment and workplace accommodations consulting model.

resources.name: Supported Employment Services
resources.description: TEAM Work Cooperative (a Nova Scotia Works employment hub) offers specialized supported employment for people with disabilities, including career counseling, job development, and individualized job coaching and retention supports. The organization partners with employers to implement accommodations and hosts employer engagement and inclusion training—directly implementing the solution by operating as a community hub for supported employment and employer education.

resources.name: Employment Inclusion Services
resources.description: reachAbility provides barrier‑free employment readiness, job development, and supported employment for persons with disabilities, complemented by one‑to‑one job coaching and retention support. They deliver employer training on disability inclusion and accommodation best practices and advise on accessible recruitment—acting as a community hub that advances the solution’s goals of supported employment, accommodations consulting, and employer education.
resources.address: 3845 Joseph Howe Drive, Suite 201, Halifax, NS B3L 4H9

solutions.text: Local Storytelling and Public Awareness Campaigns: Produce community media projects (podcasts, murals, short films, local radio) that elevate lived experiences of marginalized Nova Scotians, challenge stereotypes, and promote positive local role models.

resources.name: Africville Museum
resources.description: A community museum that preserves and shares the lived experiences of the historic Africville community through exhibits, oral histories, film screenings, and public programs. By centering African Nova Scotian voices and narratives, the museum challenges stereotypes and builds public awareness, offering youth and the wider community positive local role models and a deeper sense of belonging.

resources.name: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.organization: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.description: A provincial museum and cultural hub that produces exhibitions, traveling displays, community talks, and digital storytelling projects highlighting African Nova Scotian history and contemporary leaders. These public-facing initiatives elevate underrepresented voices, counter discrimination through education, and offer positive role models for young people across Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 10 Cherry Brook Road, Cherry Brook, NS B2Z 1A8

resources.name: CKDU 88.1 FM
resources.description: Halifax’s campus–community radio station that trains volunteers to produce local programs and podcasts, including shows by and for African Nova Scotian, Mi’kmaw, LGBTQ2S+, immigrant, and disability communities. By broadcasting lived experiences and community news, CKDU amplifies marginalized voices, challenges stereotypes, and fosters a more inclusive public conversation province-wide.

resources.name: Centre for Art Tapes (CFAT)
resources.description: A media arts centre that provides gear, training, mentorship, and community residencies to help artists and community members produce short films, audio works, and digital media. CFAT’s public screenings, exhibitions, and community projects foreground underrepresented voices—including Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, and queer storytellers—building awareness and representation through locally made media.

resources.name: Anchor Archive Zine Library
resources.description: A community-run library and print resource that supports people—especially youth and marginalized residents—to create and distribute their own zines and print media. Through workshops, a risograph print studio, and public events and fairs, Anchor Archive elevates local stories and perspectives, building awareness and challenging stereotypes via accessible, DIY publishing.

solutions.text: Representative Community Advisory Councils: Form standing advisory councils composed of Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, disability and LGBTQ2S+ community members to consult with municipalities, schools and health services on policy, planning and budget decisions.

resources.name: 2SLGBTQIA+ Advisory Committee
resources.description: A standing advisory body of Halifax Regional Municipality composed of 2SLGBTQIA+ community members and allies that provides advice to Regional Council and municipal staff on policies, programs, services, and priorities. The committee brings lived experience to municipal planning and budget discussions to improve inclusion and reduce barriers for 2SLGBTQIA+ residents, implementing the representative community advisory model.

resources.name: African Descent Advisory Committee
resources.description: This HRM advisory council is made up of African Nova Scotian community members who advise Regional Council and staff on anti-Black racism, equity, service delivery, and community safety. By reviewing strategies and offering recommendations that inform policy, planning, and budget decisions, the committee operationalizes a representative advisory structure for African Nova Scotian voices in municipal decision-making.

resources.name: Accessibility Advisory Committee
resources.description: HRM’s Accessibility Advisory Committee, with a majority of members who are persons with disabilities, provides ongoing advice to Council and municipal departments on accessibility plans, capital projects, procurement, and policies. The committee’s recommendations shape planning and budget priorities to remove barriers and advance disability inclusion across municipal services.

resources.name: Chief’s Diversity Advisory Committee (CDAC)
resources.description: The Halifax Regional Police CDAC brings together leaders from Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, 2SLGBTQ+, disability, newcomer, and other communities to advise the Chief on policies, training, priorities, and community engagement. Meeting regularly, the committee informs policing strategies and resource allocation, ensuring municipal public safety planning reflects diverse community needs and reduces discrimination.

resources.name: African Nova Scotian Advisory Committee (ANSAC)
resources.description: ANSAC is a standing advisory body of the Halifax Regional Centre for Education composed of African Nova Scotian parents, elders, students, and community representatives. It advises HRCE leadership on policy, curriculum, school improvement, and resource allocation affecting African Nova Scotian learners, ensuring community perspectives directly inform education planning and decisions.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

solutions.text: Accessible Arts, Sports and Recreation Programs: Fund inclusive arts, sports and recreation programs with sliding-fee scales, adapted equipment, transit supports and outreach to marginalized neighbourhoods to broaden participation and community connection.

resources.name: KidSport Nova Scotia Fee Assistance Program
resources.description: KidSport Nova Scotia provides grants to help families cover registration fees for organized sport, ensuring cost isn’t a barrier to participation. Working through community chapters across the province, the program broadens access in marginalized and rural neighborhoods and complements clubs that offer inclusive or adapted programming. By removing financial barriers, more children and youth can join local teams and build community connections.
resources.address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

resources.name: Parasport Nova Scotia — Equipment Loan & Bridging to Sport
resources.description: Parasport Nova Scotia develops inclusive sport opportunities for people with disabilities and operates a province-wide adapted equipment loan program (e.g., sport wheelchairs, sit-skis) and Try-It events. The organization reduces or eliminates participant fees for many entry-level programs and connects athletes with accessible venues through community partners. This combination of adapted gear, fee support and outreach expands participation among youth facing ableism and other barriers.
resources.address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

resources.name: Affordable Access Program (Recreation & Transit)
resources.description: Halifax’s Affordable Access Program provides discounted recreation program fees at municipal facilities and reduced-cost Halifax Transit passes for eligible low-income residents. By lowering fees and transportation costs, the program makes arts, sports and recreation opportunities across HRM accessible to youth from marginalized neighborhoods. It is delivered in partnership with community centres that also offer inclusion supports.

resources.name: Community and Youth Recreation Programs
resources.description: The North Grove is a community hub in Dartmouth North offering free and low-cost youth arts, sports and recreation programs alongside meals, childcare and other supports. Programs are intentionally delivered in a historically marginalized neighborhood and include barrier-reduction measures such as on-site equipment and practical supports to help participants attend. This approach builds social connection while removing cost and access obstacles.

resources.name: HAT Academy (Pay-What-You-Can Arts Training)
resources.description: The HAT Academy offers inclusive theatre, music and dance training for children and youth in Cape Breton with a Pay-What-You-Can tuition model and bursaries so no one is turned away. The company partners with schools and community groups to reach youth in underserved neighborhoods and provides materials and supportive instruction to meet diverse needs. Sliding fees and outreach expand participation in the arts and foster a sense of belonging.

solutions.text: Community Mental Health and Peer-support Services: Expand culturally competent, trauma-informed mental health services and peer-support networks located in community hubs, with specific programming for survivors of racism, homophobia, transphobia and ableism.

resources.name: Health & Wellness Programs
resources.description: The Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre delivers culturally grounded, trauma-informed wellness supports for urban Indigenous community members, including access to Elders, talking circles, cultural programming, and navigation to counselling. These services are offered in a welcoming community hub that centers Mi’kmaw and other Indigenous ways of healing, reducing barriers created by racism and colonial trauma. Peer-support groups and cultural connections foster belonging and resilience for Indigenous youth and families.

resources.name: Wellness and Peer Support Programs
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS provides trauma-informed, culturally competent mental health and wellness supports for immigrants and refugees, including peer-support groups, community wellness workshops, and one-on-one navigation with interpretation as needed. Programming includes groups tailored for women, youth, and 2SLGBTQIA+ newcomers who have experienced homophobia/transphobia or racism, helping them access care and build supportive networks. Services are delivered from a community hub that reduces stigma and fosters belonging.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Phoenix Centre for Youth – Mental Health & Counselling
resources.description: Phoenix operates a community drop-in hub where youth can access trauma-informed mental health counselling, care coordination, and peer-support programming. The Centre intentionally creates safer, inclusive spaces for 2SLGBTQIA+ and racialized youth who have faced discrimination, offering groups, advocacy, and harm-reduction supports. By embedding mental health services in a welcoming community setting, Phoenix lowers barriers and builds belonging for young people.

resources.name: Counselling and Wellness Programs
resources.description: YWCA Halifax offers low-barrier, trauma-informed counselling and peer-support groups for women and gender-diverse people, including survivors of gender-based violence and discrimination. Programs use an intersectional, anti-racist and 2SLGBTQIA+-affirming approach, with specific supports for newcomers and African Nova Scotian communities. Services are delivered from a community hub that connects participants to housing, employment, and safety resources alongside mental health supports.
resources.address: 358 Herring Cove Road, Halifax, NS B3R 1V8

resources.name: Peer Support and Mentorship Programs
resources.description: Autism Nova Scotia provides peer-support groups, social connections, and one-to-one peer mentorship for autistic people and families across the province, grounded in neurodiversity-affirming and trauma-informed practice. Programming includes specialized groups (e.g., for 2SLGBTQIA+ autistic folks) and navigation to mental health resources, addressing barriers rooted in ableism. Services are coordinated through a community hub that fosters inclusion, self-advocacy, and mental well-being.
resources.address: 5945 Spring Garden Road, Suite 103, Halifax, NS B3H 3A7

solutions.text: Rapid-response Anti-discrimination Navigation Team: Create a local task team that provides immediate assistance for discrimination incidents — documenting cases, guiding people to remedies, liaising with employers/institutions and coordinating supports while tracking trends for systemic change.

resources.name: Dispute Resolution and Intake Services
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission provides immediate intake and navigation for people who experience discrimination under the Nova Scotia Human Rights Act. Staff help document incidents, explain options (e.g., early resolution, restorative approaches, and formal complaints), liaise with employers, landlords, and institutions to pursue remedies, coordinate referrals to supports, and track complaint trends to drive systemic change across the province.
resources.address: 5657 Spring Garden Road, Suite 305, Halifax, NS B3J 3S5

resources.name: Settlement Counselling and Anti-Discrimination Support
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS’ settlement counsellors provide rapid response when newcomers face racism or discrimination in employment, housing, education, or public services. They document incidents, guide clients through human rights and legal remedies, liaise with employers and institutions to resolve issues, coordinate interpretation and mental-health supports, and analyze trends to inform ISANS’ anti-racism initiatives and policy advocacy.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Hate Crime Unit and Victim Services
resources.description: Halifax Regional Police’s Hate Crime Unit provides specialized, rapid-response support for hate-motivated incidents, ensuring thorough documentation and guidance through reporting and justice-system options. The unit liaises with schools, employers, and community partners, connects victims to supports through Victim Services, and monitors local hate/bias trends to inform prevention, outreach, and policy responses.

resources.name: Human Rights & Equity Services
resources.description: Dalhousie’s Human Rights & Equity Services provides confidential intake and case management for students, staff, and faculty experiencing discrimination or harassment. The team documents incidents, advises on complaint and accommodation processes, liaises with academic and administrative units to secure remedies, coordinates counselling and safety supports, and reviews case data to address systemic barriers on campus.
resources.address: 6299 South Street, Henry Hicks Building, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2

resources.name: Advocacy & Support for 2SLGBTQIA+ Youth
resources.description: The Youth Project offers advocacy and case support for 2SLGBTQIA+ youth who encounter homophobia or transphobia at school, work, or in the community. Staff help document incidents, navigate school board and Nova Scotia Human Rights complaint pathways, liaise with educators and employers to secure accommodations or remedies, coordinate wraparound supports, and use emerging trends to inform policy and education efforts.

solutions.text: Intercultural Community Exchanges and Shared Projects: Facilitate regular intercultural dialogues, community arts collaborations, and neighbourhood improvement projects that bring diverse groups together to build relationships, reduce prejudice and co-create solutions.

resources.name: Community Connections Program
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS’ Community Connections Program matches newcomers with local volunteers and hosts group activities, conversation circles, and community events that foster meaningful interactions across cultures. By creating ongoing spaces for dialogue and shared experiences, the program reduces prejudice and helps participants co-create solutions to everyday settlement and neighbourhood challenges.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Community Presents
resources.organization: Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21
resources.description: Community Presents is a museum-led series that partners with cultural and community groups to co-host performances, talks, festivals, and exhibits. These public events create regular intercultural dialogue and shared arts experiences, building relationships among diverse communities and deepening understanding through collaborative programming.

resources.name: Open Studio
resources.description: Wonder’neath’s Open Studio invites neighbours of all ages and backgrounds to create art together in a free, welcoming space. Through collaborative projects like community murals and shared art-making sessions, the program builds relationships across differences, encourages dialogue, and uses the arts to co-create solutions that reflect local voices.

resources.name: Community Greenhouse & Urban Farm
resources.description: Hope Blooms’ youth-led urban farm and greenhouse bring residents together to grow food, cook, and host community dinners that welcome people from many cultures and identities. These shared projects improve the neighbourhood’s green space, build cross-cultural relationships, and empower young people to co-create solutions to food security and inclusion.

resources.name: Education and Outreach Program
resources.organization: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Black Cultural Centre’s Education and Outreach Program delivers exhibits, workshops, and dialogues that highlight African Nova Scotian history and culture while engaging diverse audiences. By partnering with schools and community groups—especially during African Heritage Month—the program facilitates intercultural learning and shared projects that reduce prejudice and strengthen community connections.
resources.address: 10 Cherry Brook Road, Cherry Brook, NS B2Z 1A8

obstacles.title: Youth Voice and Civic Influence
obstacles.description: Young people often lack meaningful roles in decision-making, leading to policies that miss their needs and aspirations.

solutions.text: Municipal Youth Advisory Councils: Create local youth advisory councils in towns and municipalities that meet regularly, receive formal mandates, and provide recommendations to councils and school boards; ensure representation from rural, urban, Mi'kmaq and newcomer youth.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Youth Advisory Committee (YAC)
resources.description: HRM’s Youth Advisory Committee is a formal advisory body of Regional Council that meets regularly to provide recommendations on municipal policies, programs, and services impacting young people. Members, aged 15–24, are appointed to reflect HRM’s urban, suburban, and rural areas and submit advice through established council and standing committee processes. Its terms emphasize equitable recruitment and inclusion, seeking representation from Mi’kmaw, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, and other underrepresented youth—aligning directly with the solution’s call for diverse, mandated youth voice in municipal decision-making.

resources.name: Wolfville Youth Council
resources.description: The Wolfville Youth Council is a standing advisory committee to the Town of Wolfville that convenes local youth to discuss community priorities and make formal recommendations to Town Council and municipal departments. The council holds regular meetings, engages peers through schools and community partners, and submits advice on issues such as recreation, active transportation, and community safety. Recruitment emphasizes broad inclusion and welcomes participation from rural-area youth, Mi’kmaw youth, and newcomer and international youth connected to the town—fulfilling the solution’s focus on diverse, formally mandated youth input at the municipal level.

solutions.text: Paid Youth Representation on Committees: Allocate paid seats and honoraria for youth on municipal committees, planning boards and nonprofit boards so young people have voting roles and financial support to participate.

resources.name: Town of Bridgewater Youth Advisory Committee
resources.description: The Town of Bridgewater’s Youth Advisory Committee embeds young people directly in municipal decision-making by appointing them as voting members of an advisory body to Council. Youth members receive the same per‑meeting honoraria and expense supports that apply to other citizen appointees, reducing financial barriers to participation. The committee’s recommendations inform Council and staff, and members may also be appointed to other Town committees and projects to extend youth influence across municipal files.

resources.name: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg Youth Council
resources.organization: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
resources.description: MODL’s Youth Council gives local youth a formal, voting role advising municipal staff and Council on priorities like recreation, planning, and community development. Members are provided an honorarium per meeting and supports such as transportation, mirroring compensation for other citizen appointments so participation is accessible. The Youth Council forwards motions and recommendations directly to Council and may place youth on standing committees, ensuring paid youth representation influences municipal policy.

resources.name: Municipality of the County of Kings Youth Council
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
resources.description: Kings County’s Youth Council formalizes youth participation in municipal governance, with youth serving as voting members on the council and, where applicable, on other municipal committees. The municipality provides per‑meeting honoraria and related supports to Youth Council members in line with its citizen committee compensation policies. This structure ensures young people have paid seats and real influence over recommendations that go forward to Council.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: IWK Health Centre Youth Advisory Council
resources.description: The IWK Youth Advisory Council engages young people as partners in hospital planning and service design, with members serving on committees and working groups that shape policies and programs. The IWK provides honoraria/stipends and reimburses expenses to recognize youth expertise and remove financial barriers to participation. By placing paid youth partners in decision-making forums, the YAC ensures youth perspectives carry weight in institutional decisions that affect them.

solutions.text: Community Participatory Budgeting Pilot: Run participatory budgeting processes at the neighbourhood or municipal level where youth design, pitch and vote on small community projects funded by a dedicated public pot.

resources.name: Participatory Budgeting – District 9 (Halifax West Armdale)
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality – Office of Councillor Shawn Cleary (District 9)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s District 9 runs a participatory budgeting process where residents—including youth who live, work, or attend school in the district—submit ideas, develop proposals, pitch them at a public event, and vote to allocate a portion of the District Capital Fund to winning community projects. The format directly empowers young people to co-design and select small-scale improvements (e.g., youth spaces, recreation, arts) funded from a dedicated public pot, giving them a concrete voice in local spending decisions.

resources.name: Participatory Budgeting – District 7 (Halifax South Downtown)
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality – Office of Councillor Waye Mason (District 7)
resources.description: District 7’s participatory budgeting invites community groups and youth teams to propose and publicly pitch small capital projects, after which residents vote to determine which projects receive funding from the councillor’s District Capital Fund. By opening proposal development and balloting to young residents and student groups, the process creates a recurring, structured channel for youth to influence municipal investments in their neighbourhoods.

resources.name: Participatory Budgeting – District 8 (Halifax Peninsula North)
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality – Office of Councillor Lindell Smith (District 8)
resources.description: District 8 implements participatory budgeting where residents, including youth and youth-led groups, co-create proposals and pitch them at a community event, followed by a public vote that allocates a set amount of district capital funds. The approach emphasizes outreach to young people and provides a practical avenue for them to decide which small-scale community projects—from recreation to arts and safety—receive municipal dollars.

solutions.text: Youth Civic Internship Program: Partner municipalities, provincial offices, school boards and local NGOs to offer paid internships that rotate youth through planning, parks, economic development and cultural departments.

resources.name: Co-op Student and Internship Opportunities
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality (HRM) runs a centralized program that hires paid co-op students and interns across civic business units including Planning & Development, Parks & Recreation, Culture & Events, and Public Works/Economic Development. Placements can be arranged across multiple terms and units, giving youth exposure to different municipal functions and practical input into projects, which mirrors the solution’s goal of rotating interns through planning, parks, economic development and cultural departments.

resources.name: Clean Leadership Summer Internship
resources.description: This province-wide paid internship program places youth with municipalities, Mi’kmaw communities, provincial offices, and local NGOs to work on climate adaptation planning, parks and trail stewardship, community energy, waste reduction, and related projects. By rotating host sites and roles across terms, interns gain hands-on experience in civic planning, parks, economic development, and community/cultural programming while contributing youth perspectives to public-sector decisions.

resources.name: Co-operative Education Incentive (CEI)
resources.organization: Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration (Government of Nova Scotia)
resources.description: CEI provides a provincial wage subsidy to create paid co-op positions for post-secondary students with eligible employers, including municipalities, school boards, and non-profit organizations across Nova Scotia. Many funded placements are in planning, parks and recreation, culture/heritage, and local economic development, enabling employers to offer multi-term or sequential rotations that expose students to different civic functions and amplify youth voice in public projects.

resources.name: Student and Co-op Employment
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Municipality hires paid students and co-op interns across Planning & Development, Recreation/Parks, Engineering & Public Works, Communications, and Culture & Events. Students can complete sequential placements in different units, effectively rotating through planning, parks, economic development, and cultural areas while contributing youth insight to municipal initiatives and services.

solutions.text: Youth Co‑Design Labs: Host recurring co-design workshops where young people work with officials and service providers to redesign programs (transit, housing, recreation) affecting them, with prototypes and follow-through commitments.

resources.name: Youth Advisory Council (YAC)
resources.description: IWK Health’s Youth Advisory Council brings young people together with hospital leaders, clinicians, and service designers in recurring co-design sessions to improve youth-facing care and supports. Youth members help map pain points and prototype solutions (e.g., youth-friendly clinic spaces, intake forms, communication tools), and staff commit to testing and implementing changes across programs, with regular feedback loops to track what is adopted.

resources.name: Teen Advisory Group (TAG) – Halifax Central Library
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries’ Teen Advisory Group convenes youth and library staff in ongoing co-design meetings to shape services that affect young people—program schedules, study/maker spaces, and inclusive collections. Teens generate and test prototypes (pop-up events, space layouts, resource guides), and the Library commits staff time and budgets to refine and roll out successful ideas branch-wide.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Teen Arts Group (TAG)
resources.description: AGNS’s Teen Arts Group is a standing youth council that collaborates with curators, educators, and program staff to co-design exhibitions, events, and learning programs relevant to young people. Participants run design workshops, develop and prototype interactive installations and teen nights, and the Gallery follows through by resourcing and implementing the ideas in public programming.

resources.name: Youth Advisory Committee (YAC)
resources.description: HRM’s Youth Advisory Committee is a formal mechanism for young people to co-design municipal initiatives with staff from departments such as Parks & Recreation, Planning & Development, and HalifACT. The committee hosts recurring working sessions to surface youth needs, prototype engagement and program ideas (e.g., rec access, public space use), and advance recommendations that departments commit to report on and integrate into Council-directed work.

solutions.text: Micro‑grants for Youth‑Led Civic Projects: Create a community fund that awards small, rapid-turnaround grants to youth-led civic initiatives (public art, pop-up services, neighbourhood improvements) with light reporting requirements.

resources.name: #RisingYouth Community Service Grants
resources.description: A national micro‑grant program that funds youth (ages 15–30) to design and lead community service projects, including public art, pop‑up services, mutual aid, and neighbourhood improvements. It operates in Nova Scotia and offers $250–$1,500 micro‑grants with quick turnaround, mentorship, and light reporting so youth can rapidly implement civic ideas in their communities.
resources.address: 117 Peter Street, Suite 312, Toronto, ON M5V 0M3

resources.name: Project/Action Grants
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Public Interest Research Group (NSPIRG)
resources.description: NSPIRG provides small, rapid‑turnaround grants to student and youth‑led initiatives that advance social and environmental justice on campus and in the broader Halifax community. Funding typically supports civic‑minded projects such as public education events, pop‑up services, mutual aid efforts, and public art, with a simple application and light reporting that make it easy for youth to lead.
resources.address: Room 314, Dalhousie Student Union Building, 6136 University Avenue, Halifax, NS B3H 4J2

resources.name: Community Action Fund
resources.organization: South House Sexual and Gender Resource Centre
resources.description: South House offers small grants to student‑ and youth‑led projects that build inclusive, safer, and more equitable communities in Halifax. Funds support civic activities such as community workshops, public art/awareness campaigns, mutual aid pop‑ups, and neighbourhood initiatives, using a simple application process and minimal reporting so youth can act quickly.

solutions.text: School‑to‑Community Civic Curriculum and Service Learning: Work with school boards to embed community-based civic projects and local governance simulations into the curriculum that connect students directly to municipal needs and decision-makers.

resources.name: Student Vote Nova Scotia
resources.organization: CIVIX (in partnership with Elections Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Student Vote is a parallel election program that runs in Nova Scotia schools during real election periods, providing teachers with curriculum-aligned lesson plans, activities, and materials so students can learn about government, issues, and candidates before participating in a school-wide mock vote. By mirroring the official election process and encouraging classroom Q&As or forums with local candidates and representatives, it provides a hands-on simulation of democratic decision-making. This embeds civic learning directly into the school experience and connects students to real decision-makers and current public policy debates.
resources.address: 202 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 101, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1T5

resources.name: Service Learning Program
resources.description: Saint Mary’s University integrates community-based projects into for-credit courses across disciplines, partnering with municipal departments and community organizations in Halifax to address real needs such as planning, environment, and inclusion. Students apply course concepts to solve identified challenges, produce deliverables for partners, and present findings to staff and stakeholders. This embeds civic engagement in the curriculum and gives students direct exposure to municipal decision-making processes.

resources.name: Service Learning Program
resources.description: St. Francis Xavier University’s Service Learning integrates structured community projects into academic courses, linking students with local governments and community organizations in Antigonish and across Nova Scotia. Through semester-long placements and reflective assignments, students work on policy, planning, and community development initiatives and share results with partners and officials. This approach embeds civic practice within curricula and builds students’ capacity to influence local decision-making.

resources.name: Community-Engaged Service Learning (SUST 3003)
resources.description: Dalhousie University’s College of Sustainability offers a for-credit Community-Engaged Service Learning course that places students with municipal and community partners to co-create solutions on sustainability and policy challenges. Coursework includes scoping with partners (e.g., HRM units and local NGOs), applied research, and public-facing presentations or briefs that inform decision-makers. This directly embeds civic, place-based problem solving and governance literacy into the academic curriculum.

solutions.text: Digital Engagement Platform with Local Focus: Develop an accessible online platform and mobile app where youth can propose ideas, comment on consultations, track decisions, and receive updates on how their input influenced outcomes.

resources.name: Shape Your City Halifax
resources.description: Shape Your City Halifax is HRM’s digital engagement hub where residents—including youth—can propose ideas, respond to surveys, join discussions, and ask questions on municipal projects. The platform lets users follow specific projects, receive email updates, and view “What We Heard” and decision summaries so they can track how their input influenced outcomes.

resources.name: Let’s Talk CBRM
resources.description: Let’s Talk CBRM is the Cape Breton Regional Municipality’s online engagement platform, offering idea boards, discussion forums, polls, and surveys so youth and other residents can share feedback on municipal plans and bylaws. Participants can subscribe to projects to receive updates and see posted reports and council outcomes, clearly linking community input to decisions.

resources.name: Have Your Say Lunenburg
resources.description: Have Your Say Lunenburg is the Town’s mobile-friendly engagement site where community members, including youth, can submit ideas, comment on draft policies, and participate in Q&As about local initiatives. The platform publishes project timelines, updates, and “What We Heard” summaries, enabling users to track decisions and understand how their feedback shaped municipal actions.

resources.name: Get Involved Yarmouth
resources.description: Get Involved Yarmouth is the Town’s digital consultation portal that invites youth and residents to propose ideas, complete surveys, and comment on local projects such as waterfront and mobility initiatives. Users can follow projects for notifications and access result summaries and council decisions, creating a clear feedback loop that shows how public input informs outcomes.

solutions.text: Mobile and Pop‑Up Engagement in Rural Areas: Organize pop-up forums, listening tours and mobile buses that bring engagement events to rural and remote communities, reducing travel barriers for youth participation.

resources.name: Shape Your City HFX Pop-Up Engagement
resources.description: HRM’s engagement team runs mobile, pop-up booths and travelling open houses across the municipality—including rural and remote communities on the Eastern Shore and Musquodoboit Valley—to collect resident input. They intentionally set up at youth-heavy locations (schools, libraries, community events) so young people can share feedback on municipal plans (parks, transit, planning) without needing to travel downtown, directly strengthening youth voice in civic decision-making.

resources.name: CBRM Forward Public Engagement Pop-Ups
resources.description: CBRM uses pop-up engagement stations and community listening sessions across communities like North Sydney, Glace Bay, New Waterford, and Louisbourg to gather public input. Youth are engaged where they are—at markets, libraries, schools, and recreation facilities—so their perspectives inform municipal strategies (strategic planning, active transportation, recreation) while reducing travel barriers for rural youth.

resources.name: Get Involved Kings – Community Pop-Up Engagement
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
resources.description: The Municipality of the County of Kings deploys pop-up engagement tables and travelling workshops across rural villages and small towns to meet residents where they live. Staff frequently visit youth-centered spaces (high schools, NSCC Kingstec, community centres) to host listening sessions, enabling young people to shape municipal priorities on topics like economic development, recreation, and community planning without needing to travel long distances.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: Provincial Outreach and School Tours
resources.description: The Youth Project’s educators and facilitators travel to rural and remote communities across Nova Scotia to run pop-up workshops, discussion circles, and youth forums in schools and community spaces. These mobile sessions gather youth perspectives to inform local service delivery and advocacy efforts, ensuring 2SLGBTQ+ youth voices influence policies and practices while removing the need for youth to travel to urban centres.

solutions.text: Mentorship Network Linking Youth and Local Leaders: Establish mentorship pairings between youth and local elected officials, Indigenous leaders, entrepreneurs and tradespeople to transfer skills, networks and civic knowledge.

resources.name: Connector Program
resources.description: The Connector Program matches post-secondary students and recent graduates with established local business and community leaders (“Connectors”) for one-on-one informational interviews and guided networking. These mentor meetings transfer practical career insights, civic and labour‑market knowledge, and result in referrals to the Connector’s network—directly implementing a mentorship model that links youth with entrepreneurs and civic leaders.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Business Is Jammin’ (BIJ) Mentorship Program
resources.organization: Business Is Jammin’ (a program of the Black Business Initiative)
resources.description: BIJ pairs Black youth in Nova Scotia with Black entrepreneurs, professionals, and community leaders for coaching, job-shadowing, and project-based learning. Through these mentor relationships, youth build business skills, confidence, and local networks while gaining exposure to community leadership and entrepreneurship—fulfilling the solution’s goal of linking young people with local leaders to transfer skills and civic knowledge.
resources.address: 1660 Hollis Street, Suite 1301, Halifax, NS B3J 1V7

resources.name: Youth Programs (Elder and Knowledge Keeper Mentorship)
