resources.description: The Mi’kmaw Native Friendship Centre’s youth programs connect Indigenous youth with Elders, Knowledge Keepers, and Indigenous community leaders through cultural teachings, leadership workshops, and mentorship circles. This intergenerational model transfers cultural, civic, and community knowledge while building life and leadership skills—directly aligning with the solution’s emphasis on linking youth with Indigenous leaders.

resources.name: CEED Startup and Mentorship Programs
resources.organization: Centre for Entrepreneurship Education and Development (CEED)
resources.description: CEED provides coaching, advisory services, and mentorship circles that connect aspiring young entrepreneurs with experienced founders, small business owners, and tradespeople across Nova Scotia. Through one-on-one advising, workshops, and mentor introductions, youth gain practical skills, access to local networks, and insight into the regional business ecosystem—implementing the solution’s mentorship approach with entrepreneurs and trades leaders.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 225, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: 4-H Nova Scotia Clubs and Mentorship
resources.description: 4-H Nova Scotia places youth in club-based mentorship with trained volunteer leaders—local farmers, artisans, and tradespeople—through hands-on projects (e.g., agriculture, welding, small engines, public speaking) and community service. Youth develop technical and leadership skills, take on elected club roles, and work with local agricultural societies and municipal partners, strengthening civic knowledge and community connections consistent with the mentorship network solution.
resources.address: 60 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

solutions.text: Youth‑Led Cultural and Storytelling Projects: Support youth in producing community storytelling, festivals, zines and digital media that surface local issues and recommendations to decision-makers and the broader public.

resources.name: Teen Advisory Group (TAG) - Youth Zine & Storytelling
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries’ Teen Advisory Group (TAG) empowers youth to design programs, curate zines, and create digital stories that reflect local issues like housing, climate, and transit. Youth plan and lead public showcases, pop-up exhibits, and library events where their work is shared with community members and municipal staff, and their feedback informs library and community priorities.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Youth Media & Storytelling Camps
resources.description: The Deanery Project runs seasonal camps and labs where rural youth learn filmmaking, podcasting, and zine-making to document community stories on topics like coastal change, transportation, and rural livelihoods. Youth-led projects are screened at community festivals and town halls attended by residents and local officials, helping surface recommendations from young people to decision-makers.
resources.address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

resources.name: Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre - Youth Program
resources.description: The MNFC Youth Program supports urban Indigenous youth to lead cultural storytelling through drumming, spoken word, video, and digital media grounded in Mi'kmaw culture and language. Youth produce short films, zines, and public events on issues like education, reconciliation, and housing, and present their work at community gatherings and meetings with service providers and HRM/NS representatives to inform policy and programs.

resources.name: Phoenix Centre for Youth - Creative Expression & Storytelling
resources.description: Phoenix engages youth to co-create zines, photo essays, exhibitions, and digital media that elevate their lived experiences and community solutions. These youth-led projects culminate in public showcases and dialogues where service providers and government partners are invited, ensuring young people’s recommendations shape local services and decision-making.

solutions.text: Inclusive Meeting Supports: Provide transportation stipends, childcare, honoraria, meeting-time flexibility, language support and accessible venues so youth from all backgrounds can meaningfully attend and contribute.

resources.name: IWK Youth Advisory Council
resources.description: The IWK Youth Advisory Council brings together diverse young people to advise IWK Health on policies, programs, and services that affect youth, especially in mental health and addictions. To reduce barriers to participation, the council offers honoraria/gift cards, covers transportation (bus fare/parking), schedules meetings at youth-friendly times with hybrid options, and uses accessible hospital or community venues with interpretation available on request—ensuring youth from varied backgrounds can attend and contribute meaningfully.

resources.name: Phoenix Youth Advisory Council (YAC)
resources.description: Phoenix’s Youth Advisory Council engages young people with lived experience to shape programs, services, and advocacy across the organization. The YAC provides honoraria, transit tickets and meals, flexible meeting times and hybrid options, and holds sessions in accessible, youth-centered spaces; staff also accommodate language needs and parenting responsibilities so youth can participate without financial or logistical barriers.
resources.address: 5880 Spring Garden Road, Suite 401, Halifax, NS B3H 4S4

resources.name: Youth Harbour Advisory Council
resources.description: Youth Harbour, an initiative supporting youth-led climate action, convenes a provincial Youth Advisory Council that co-designs grants and engagement activities. Advisors receive stipends/honoraria, transportation support (e.g., bus fare or gas cards), accessible meeting locations or virtual participation, and language/ASL support as needed—practical measures that enable diverse youth to attend and influence decisions.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Youth Advisory Committee
resources.description: The HRM Youth Advisory Committee provides a formal channel for young people to advise Regional Council on municipal policies and services. To make involvement accessible, HRM hosts meetings in accessible civic facilities with hybrid options, schedules sessions outside school hours, and offers travel/parking reimbursements consistent with municipal volunteer policies—practical supports that lower the cost and time barriers to youth participation.

solutions.text: Training for Co‑Governance and Facilitation: Offer short community workshops for youth and adult allies on facilitation, policy literacy, negotiation and power-sharing so both sides can engage in equitable co‑decision processes.

resources.name: School Advisory Council (SAC) Training and Support
resources.description: HRCE equips students and adult allies on School Advisory Councils with orientation sessions and short workshops covering meeting facilitation, consensus-building, and roles and responsibilities under Nova Scotia’s Education Act (policy literacy). The training helps youth and adults share power in co-decision processes on school improvement planning, budgeting, and policy, ensuring young people have an equitable voice in school governance.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

resources.name: Workshops & Skillshares
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Public Interest Research Group (NSPIRG)
resources.description: NSPIRG runs free, short, skills-based workshops for students and community members on facilitation, consensus decision-making, conflict navigation, power analysis, and advocacy/policy literacy. These trainings prepare youth and adult allies to co-facilitate meetings, negotiate with decision-makers, and design equitable, shared-power processes for campus and community change.
resources.address: Room 314, Student Union Building, 6136 University Avenue, Halifax, NS B3H 4J2

resources.name: Workshops & GSA Leadership Training
resources.description: The Youth Project delivers province-wide workshops for students and adult allies (educators, service providers) on inclusive facilitation, anti-oppression, and policy literacy related to 2SLGBTQIA+ rights in schools and communities. By training youth and adults to co-facilitate GSAs, run effective meetings, and negotiate with school administrators, the program builds shared-power structures that embed youth voice in policy and program decisions.

resources.name: Leadership & Communications Program
resources.description: 4-H Nova Scotia offers practical workshops for youth on chairing meetings, parliamentary procedure, public speaking, and negotiation through its Communications and Leadership streams. Complementary leader training for adult volunteers emphasizes youth–adult partnership and shared governance in clubs, enabling intergenerational teams to facilitate, make decisions together, and influence policies within their organizations and communities.
resources.address: 60 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

resources.name: Facilitation and Participatory Leadership Workshops
resources.description: Tatamagouche Centre hosts short, open-enrolment courses on participatory facilitation, consensus-building, restorative practices, and conflict transformation that bring together youth and adult allies from across Nova Scotia. These trainings provide concrete tools for power-sharing, co-design, and equitable decision-making in community and organizational settings, directly supporting youth–adult co-governance.

solutions.text: Partnerships with Mi'kmaq and Indigenous Youth Councils: Co-create formal pathways for Indigenous youth voice by partnering with Mi'kmaq communities and organizations to ensure culturally appropriate roles in local decision-making.

resources.name: Native Council of Nova Scotia Youth Council
resources.description: The NCNS Youth Council represents off‑reserve and non‑status Mi’kmaq/Indigenous youth across Nova Scotia and provides a formal voice into the Council’s governance and advocacy. Youth leaders advise NCNS leadership and participate in consultations with municipal, provincial, and community partners to shape programs and policy, ensuring culturally grounded youth perspectives inform local decision‑making.
resources.address: 129 Truro Heights Road, Truro, NS B6L 1X1

resources.name: Atlantic First Nations Youth Council on Water (AFNYCW)
resources.organization: Atlantic Policy Congress of First Nations Chiefs Secretariat
resources.description: AFNYCW brings together Mi’kmaq and other Indigenous youth from Atlantic communities, including Nova Scotia, to advise Chiefs, planners, and governments on water and environmental decisions. Through APC’s environment programs, the council co-develops recommendations and community engagement processes, creating a structured, culturally appropriate pathway for youth voices to shape local water stewardship and related policy.

resources.name: Eskasoni Youth Council
resources.description: The Eskasoni Youth Council provides a formal mechanism for Mi’kmaq youth in Eskasoni to advise Chief and Council, participate on community committees, and co-design initiatives affecting young people. By embedding youth representatives within local governance, the council ensures culturally relevant youth perspectives inform decisions on education, recreation, health, and community development.
resources.address: 63 Mini Mall Drive, Eskasoni, NS B1W 1A0

solutions.text: Youth Impact Dashboard and Annual Report: Publish an easy-to-read local dashboard and yearly report that tracks youth engagement activities, decisions influenced, funded projects and outcomes to increase transparency and accountability.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Youth Advisory Committee (YAC)
resources.description: YAC advises Regional Council on policies and services affecting youth, with meetings, recommendations, and motions recorded publicly. HRM publishes YAC agendas, minutes, and an annual committee report to Council summarizing activities, recommendations, and outcomes; together with the Shape Your City Halifax engagement dashboard that shows participation statistics (including youth demographics) and how feedback influenced municipal decisions, this provides an easy-to-read, transparent record of youth engagement and impacts.

resources.name: IWK Health Youth Advisory Council
resources.description: The Youth Advisory Council brings young people into decision-making on hospital policies, programs, and spaces at IWK Health. IWK publishes annual Patient and Family Engagement/Family Leadership reports that track YAC meetings, priorities, recommendations, and actions taken by hospital leaders; paired with public-facing scorecards and experience measures, this functions as a youth impact dashboard and yearly report demonstrating how youth input shaped decisions and program outcomes.

resources.name: Clean Leadership (Nova Scotia Youth Conservation Corps)
resources.description: Clean Foundation’s Clean Leadership/NSYCC program places youth in paid roles across Nova Scotia to deliver community environmental projects and public education. The organization publishes an annual impact report and program “by the numbers” summaries that track youth participants, host sites, funded projects, and measurable outcomes; project pages and case studies document recommendations adopted by host municipalities and partners, providing a transparent dashboard-style view of youth engagement and decisions influenced.

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries Teen Advisory Group (TAG) and Annual Impact Reporting
resources.description: TAG gives teens structured roles to co-design programs, collections, and spaces across Halifax Public Libraries, with recommendations captured in branch reports and Board updates. The Library publishes easy-to-read annual reports and “by the numbers” summaries that track teen participation, initiatives delivered, and changes implemented based on youth input—providing transparent, dashboard-style reporting on youth engagement activities, outcomes, and how feedback influenced library decisions.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

obstacles.title: Policy Fragmentation and Short-Term Funding
obstacles.description: Programs are siloed, pilot-heavy, and unpredictable across governments and regions, making long-term planning difficult.

solutions.text: Community Multi-Year Fund: Create a locally managed multi-year pooled fund supported by municipalities, businesses, foundations and citizen donations to provide predictable, long-term operating grants to community programs and reduce reliance on short pilots.

resources.name: United Way Halifax Community Fund
resources.description: United Way Halifax pools donations from individual residents, workplace campaigns, corporate partners, and local philanthropic supporters into a community-wide fund that invests in frontline agencies tackling poverty, homelessness, and social exclusion. Through multi-year Community Impact funding agreements (often 2–3 years), it provides predictable operating support so organizations can plan long-term, retain staff, and scale proven services instead of relying on short pilot projects—directly addressing funding fragmentation.
resources.address: 46 Portland Street, 7th Floor, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1H4

resources.name: Community Funds Program (Place-Based Endowments)
resources.description: The Community Foundation of Nova Scotia establishes locally governed, place-based community funds (e.g., county and regional funds) that pool contributions from residents, businesses, service clubs, and, in many cases, municipal or foundation partners into permanent endowments. Investment earnings are granted to local nonprofits—often through multi-year commitments set by local advisory committees—creating a predictable, long-term operating funding stream that stabilizes community programs and reduces dependence on short-term pilots.
resources.address: 1888 Brunswick Street, Suite 202, Halifax, NS B3J 3J8

solutions.text: Regional Service Councils: Establish cross-municipal councils of community organizations, local governments and service providers to coordinate priorities, share resources, align timelines and present unified proposals to provincial or federal funders.

resources.name: Kings Transit Authority
resources.description: Kings Transit Authority is a jointly governed, multi-municipal public transit service for the Annapolis Valley, coordinating routes and investments across partner municipalities. Its board structure brings together local governments and service stakeholders to align priorities, pool operating and capital resources, and coordinate project timelines. The Authority routinely submits unified funding proposals to provincial and federal programs (e.g., Public Transit and ICIP streams), directly addressing fragmentation by presenting a single regional plan.
resources.address: 29 Crescent Drive, New Minas, NS B4N 3G7

resources.name: Annapolis Valley Regional Library (AVRL)
resources.description: AVRL is a regional library board serving multiple municipalities in the Annapolis Valley, using a cross-municipal governance model that includes municipal and community representatives to set shared service priorities. It coordinates programming, staffing, and infrastructure across branches, aligning timelines and budgets so that initiatives scale regionally rather than siloed by town. AVRL consolidates and submits joint applications for provincial public library funding and federal project grants, ensuring a unified regional case to funders.

resources.name: South Shore Public Libraries (SSPL)
resources.description: SSPL is the regional public library system for Lunenburg and Queens Counties, governed by a cross-municipal board that brings together local governments and community stakeholders to coordinate priorities and services. It aligns programming, collections, staffing, and capital planning across multiple communities, sharing resources and synchronizing timelines for maximum regional impact. SSPL develops unified proposals to provincial and federal funders for literacy, digital inclusion, and infrastructure projects, reducing fragmentation and stabilizing multi-year planning.
resources.address: 135 North Park Street, Bridgewater, NS B4V 9B3

solutions.text: Shared Program Incubator: Develop a community-run incubator that hosts new pilots on a standardized, transferable platform with common evaluation metrics so successful initiatives can scale across towns without restarting funding cycles.

resources.name: Start-Up Yard at COVE
resources.organization: Centre for Ocean Ventures and Entrepreneurship (COVE)
resources.description: Start-Up Yard at COVE is an ocean-focused incubator that provides shared lab, prototyping, and on-water test infrastructure for startups and partners across Nova Scotia. By running cohorts on a common platform with standardized milestones and measurement (e.g., technical validation, sea-trial KPIs, customer discovery metrics), it enables pilots to be evaluated consistently and scaled to other coastal communities without restarting funding and approval cycles. The shared facilities and evaluation frameworks allow successful initiatives to transfer learnings and models across towns and ports in the province.

resources.name: ShiftKey Labs (Nova Scotia Sandbox)
resources.organization: Dalhousie University – Faculty of Computer Science (Nova Scotia Sandbox Initiative)
resources.description: ShiftKey Labs is a node of the Nova Scotia Sandbox network hosted at Dalhousie University that incubates student- and community-led tech pilots using shared challenge formats, toolkits, and mentorship models. Through the Sandbox network’s standardized curricula and evaluation rubrics (e.g., common venture-readiness and impact indicators), pilots can be replicated or scaled across campuses and communities in the province without rebuilding programs or funding from scratch. This community-oriented, transferable platform helps reduce policy and program fragmentation by aligning partners around shared metrics and delivery.

resources.name: Navigate Startup Ecosystem (Navigate Startup House)
resources.organization: Navigate Startup Ecosystem (Cape Breton University & NSCC Marconi Campus Partnership)
resources.description: Navigate supports entrepreneurship across Cape Breton by operating a shared incubator space and coordinated programs delivered in partnership with Cape Breton University and NSCC. Using common programming structures (bootcamps, mentorship sprints) and consistent outcome tracking across cohorts and communities, Navigate enables pilots to be tested, measured, and then transferred to other towns on the island without restarting funding or program design. This networked approach reduces siloing and creates a standardized pathway for scaling successful community initiatives.

resources.name: Acadia Entrepreneurship Centre
resources.description: The Acadia Entrepreneurship Centre delivers incubator-style programming and advisory services across multiple municipalities in Nova Scotia, using shared curricula, tools, and reporting frameworks. By standardizing program design and evaluation (e.g., venture milestones, client outcomes, and community impact indicators), AEC helps pilots move between towns and partners without rebuilding contracts or funding cycles. This transferable platform enables communities to adopt proven initiatives quickly while aligning stakeholders on common metrics.

solutions.text: Local Match Partnership Program: Build partnerships with local businesses and credit unions to offer matching funds for community projects that secure shorter-term grants, extending program horizons and encouraging private co-investment.

resources.name: Façade Improvement Program
resources.description: The Town of Truro provides 50/50 matching grants to downtown property and business owners for storefront and building upgrades. By requiring a private match, the program directly mobilizes local business co-investment and can be stacked alongside short-term provincial or federal grants, effectively extending project timelines and impact in line with the Local Match Partnership approach.

resources.name: Façade & Commercial Building Improvement Program
resources.description: Bridgewater offers cost-shared (typically 50/50) funding to commercial property owners for façade and building improvements in the downtown core. The matching structure incentivizes private co-investment and is often paired with short-term grants or low-cost financing (including from local credit unions), extending project horizons and stabilizing local revitalization efforts.

resources.name: Small Business Loan Guarantee Program
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Co-operative Council (in partnership with Nova Scotia Credit Unions and the Province of Nova Scotia)
resources.description: This province-wide program partners the Government of Nova Scotia with local credit unions to provide loans (with a government guarantee) to small businesses and social enterprises. Organizations frequently use these loans to match short-term grants, creating blended financing that extends program timelines and encourages private co-investment consistent with the Local Match Partnership model.
resources.address: 111 Provost Street, Suite 31, New Glasgow, NS B2H 2P9

resources.name: Community Investment & Sponsorship Program
resources.organization: Community Credit Union of Cumberland Colchester
resources.description: Community Credit Union provides grants and sponsorships to local initiatives, frequently structured to match community fundraising or to complement short-term grants from municipalities or foundations. This approach leverages credit union capital to co-invest with local businesses and extend the life and scope of community projects, directly implementing the Local Match Partnership concept.

solutions.text: Community Knowledge Hub: Create an online and in-person hub that centralizes program outcomes, evaluation templates, funding calendars and best practices so organizations can plan ahead and avoid duplicated pilot efforts.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Open Data Portal
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Open Data Portal centralizes datasets and published program outcomes from across provincial departments, providing standardized data and metadata that organizations use for planning and evaluation. By making results, indicators, and historical datasets accessible in one place, it supports shared measurement, reduces duplicated pilots, and enables nonprofits and communities to adopt consistent evaluation templates and evidence-based best practices.
resources.address: One Government Place, 1700 Granville Street, Halifax, NS B3J 1X5

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries – Community Organizations Support
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries serves as an in-person and online hub where community groups can access grant directories, program design and evaluation resources, and staff support for finding templates and best-practice guides. The Central Library hosts workshops, meeting spaces, and calendars of funding-related events, helping organizations plan ahead, adopt consistent evaluation approaches, and avoid duplicating pilot projects.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic – Community & Startup Hub
resources.description: IGNITE Atlantic operates physical hubs and an online resource library that centralize funding opportunities, program calendars, and practical templates (e.g., validation and impact measurement tools) for startups, social enterprises, and community innovators. By convening cross-sector partners and sharing best practices and outcomes from pilot initiatives, IGNITE helps organizations coordinate efforts, plan multi-year projects, and reduce duplicated experimentation across regions.

resources.name: Ecology Action Centre – Community Climate Action Hub
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre curates toolkits, case studies, and evaluation frameworks from community climate projects, and shares funding calls and timelines through its programs and communications, acting as a province-wide knowledge hub. By consolidating lessons learned and outcomes from pilots and facilitating communities of practice, EAC enables local organizations to adopt proven approaches, align on measurement, and avoid duplicating short-term efforts.

solutions.text: Cross-Sector Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs): Encourage local organizations and municipalities to sign MOUs that guarantee shared commitments (space, staff time, data sharing) across multiple years to reduce fragmentation when external funding changes.

resources.name: SchoolsPlus (Halifax Regional Centre for Education)
resources.description: SchoolsPlus embeds facilitators and outreach workers in schools to coordinate services with Nova Scotia Health, Community Services, Justice, and local nonprofits. The model operates under formal interdepartmental MOUs and information‑sharing agreements that secure shared school space, staff time, and data protocols over multiple years, reducing siloed, pilot‑style programming even when external funding shifts.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

resources.name: 211 Nova Scotia
resources.description: 211 Nova Scotia is a province‑wide navigation and referral service that maintains an integrated database of community, social, health, and government programs. It uses formal data‑sharing MOUs/agency agreements with service providers and multi‑year funding agreements with the Province to guarantee shared commitments (information, staff time for updates, and standardized data) across sectors, minimizing fragmentation as program funding and governments change.

resources.name: ISANS–Halifax Public Libraries Settlement Partnership
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS co‑locates settlement practitioners and employment staff at Halifax Public Libraries branches, including the Central Library, to deliver newcomer services where people already gather. The partners use formal partnership agreements/MOUs that guarantee shared space, scheduled staff time, and consent‑based referral and data‑sharing protocols over multiple years, ensuring continuity of services even when specific project funding changes.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Our Health Centre (Community Health Hub)
resources.description: Our Health Centre is a multi‑tenant community health hub that co‑locates primary care, mental health, public health, and community services under one roof. The centre relies on MOUs/service agreements and long‑term leases with Nova Scotia Health, the Municipality of Chester, and nonprofit partners to share space, coordinate staff time, and enable appropriate data‑sharing, reducing fragmented service delivery for families and youth across funding cycles.

solutions.text: Participatory Budgeting Initiatives: Use local participatory budgeting to allocate a portion of municipal or community foundation funds to multi-year community priorities chosen by residents, increasing predictability and local ownership.

resources.name: District 7 Participatory Budgeting (Halifax South Downtown)
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality – Office of the Councillor, District 7
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s District 7 has run recurring participatory budgeting assemblies where residents propose and vote on how a defined portion of the District Capital Fund is allocated to community projects. By committing a regular slice of capital funds to priorities chosen directly by residents, the process builds predictability across years and enables multi‑year community improvements (e.g., parks, arts, youth spaces) to advance with local ownership.

resources.name: Town of Antigonish Participatory Budgeting
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish hosts participatory budgeting rounds where community members submit proposals and vote to allocate a set portion of municipal funds to local projects. This resident‑driven process is repeated, creating a predictable pathway for funding multi‑year, community‑identified priorities and reducing reliance on short‑term, siloed grants while strengthening local ownership of outcomes.

resources.name: District 8 Participatory Budgeting (Halifax Peninsula North)
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality – Office of the Councillor, District 8
resources.description: HRM’s District 8 has organized participatory budgeting events in which residents present ideas and vote to direct a portion of the District Capital Fund to community priorities. By repeating the process, the district provides a consistent, resident‑led mechanism to fund projects that can span multiple years—supporting youth, public spaces, and local services with clear, community‑set priorities.

solutions.text: Youth & Community Advisory Panels: Form standing advisory panels of youth, Indigenous and diverse community members that feed consistent priorities into funding proposals and provincial engagement processes to reduce short-term, fragmented programming.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Youth Advisory Committee
resources.description: A standing committee of HRM that brings together diverse youth (ages 15–24) from across the municipality to advise Regional Council on policies, programs, budgets, and engagement. By providing ongoing, structured input into municipal strategies and grant priorities—and aligning with intergovernmental initiatives—the committee helps ensure youth priorities are consistently reflected in funding proposals and reduces fragmented, short-term programming across departments.

resources.name: CBRM Youth Council
resources.description: The Cape Breton Regional Municipality Youth Council is a permanent advisory body that engages diverse youth voices to inform municipal policy, services, and partnerships. The council channels youth priorities into municipal planning and funding decisions and supports CBRM’s collaboration with provincial programs, helping align efforts and reduce siloed or short-term initiatives affecting young people across the region.

resources.name: Immigrant Advisory Table (IAT)
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS’ Immigrant Advisory Table is a standing group of newcomers—including youth and representatives of diverse communities—that co-designs programs and provides continuous feedback on services, partnerships, and policy engagement. The IAT’s input informs funding applications and government consultations, ensuring immigrant and youth priorities are embedded consistently over time and helping curb fragmented, pilot-style programming.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Native Council of Nova Scotia Youth Council
resources.description: The NCNS Youth Council engages off-reserve Mi’kmaq/Indigenous youth in a formal advisory role to guide NCNS programming, partnerships, and advocacy. By shaping organizational priorities and informing proposals and engagement with provincial and federal partners, the council ensures Indigenous youth perspectives are consistently reflected and helps move funding and services away from short-term, fragmented approaches.
resources.address: 129 Truro Heights Road, Truro, NS B6L 1X1

resources.name: IWK Health Youth Advisory Council (YAC)
resources.description: The IWK Youth Advisory Council is a standing group of youth with lived experience who advise on service design, research, and engagement across mental health, addictions, and family health programs. Their ongoing input shapes priorities for grants, partnerships, and provincial system initiatives, helping align youth-centered goals across departments and reducing one-off or fragmented projects that affect young people’s care and supports.

solutions.text: Shared Measurement Framework: Agree on a simple set of community impact indicators among local organizations so funders see comparable results across projects, making longer-term funding and scaling more attractive and less fragmented.

resources.name: Community Health Boards – Community Health Plan Indicators
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Health (Community Health Boards Program)
resources.description: Nova Scotia’s Community Health Boards (CHBs) use a province-wide set of indicators drawn from the Nova Scotia Quality of Life Survey and health/public health data to set local priorities and report progress consistently across regions. By requiring Wellness Fund projects and community partners to align to these common indicators (e.g., mental well-being, social connection, food security), CHBs implement a shared measurement framework that lets funders compare outcomes across communities, reduce duplication, and support longer-term investment in what works.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Works – Performance Measurement Framework (LaMPSS)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration
resources.description: The province funds a network of Nova Scotia Works employment service providers and requires them to track standardized client and outcome metrics through the Labour Market Program Support System (LaMPSS). This shared measurement approach—covering indicators like job placements, retention, skills gains, and credential attainment—creates comparable results across agencies and regions, enabling funders to identify effective models, reduce fragmented pilots, and scale proven youth employment supports over multiple years.

resources.name: Community Wellbeing Survey (with Canadian Urban Institute)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality participates in a standardized Community Wellbeing Survey framework used across multiple Canadian cities, enabling consistent measurement of quality-of-life indicators such as belonging, safety, housing, and access to services. HRM integrates these shared indicators into strategic planning and community grants, letting local organizations report on common metrics so funders can compare results across projects and prioritize long-term, system-wide investments that benefit youth and communities.

solutions.text: Local Social Bond or Community Investment Notes: Mobilize local investors through social bonds or community investment notes to fund capital and operating needs for multi-year social initiatives, repaid through cost-savings or community revenues.

resources.name: Community Economic Development Investment Funds (CEDIF) Program
resources.organization: Government of Nova Scotia – Nova Scotia Securities Commission
resources.description: The Province of Nova Scotia’s CEDIF program enables communities to raise capital locally by selling RRSP/TFSA-eligible shares to Nova Scotians, channeling patient, multi-year investment into local enterprises and initiatives. Functionally similar to community investment notes, CEDIFs mobilize residents as impact investors and repay them through enterprise revenues, reducing reliance on short-term grants and addressing policy fragmentation by creating stable, community-driven financing.
resources.address: 5251 Duke Street, Suite 400, Halifax, NS B3J 1P3

resources.name: FarmWorks Investment Co-operative Limited (CEDIF)
resources.description: FarmWorks raises capital from Nova Scotians through recurring CEDIF share offerings and invests that pooled community capital in farms, food processors, and local food enterprises across the province. Acting like a community investment note, these offerings provide multi-year, patient financing that is repaid from business revenues, building resilient local food systems and reducing dependence on short-term, siloed funding.

resources.name: New Dawn Community Investment (CEDIF)
resources.description: New Dawn raises local capital through CEDIF share offerings to finance community-focused ventures in Cape Breton, including enterprises that generate employment and services for young people and diverse communities. By mobilizing residents as investors and repaying them from enterprise and community revenue streams, the fund provides predictable, multi-year financing akin to community investment notes, countering short-term, pilot-style funding cycles.

solutions.text: Pilot Reciprocity Agreement: Create agreements among neighbouring municipalities to accept and continue successful pilots from one jurisdiction, reducing the need to re-prove impact and enabling sustained program delivery across regions.

resources.name: National Connector Program (Nova Scotia Network)
resources.description: Originally piloted by Halifax Partnership, the Connector Program links job-ready newcomers and recent graduates with local business leaders for networking and referrals. In Nova Scotia it operates through formal agreements with neighbouring municipalities and regional partners (e.g., Western REN, Cape Breton Partnership, Truro/Colchester), which accept the proven Halifax model and recognize client intake and employer engagement standards across jurisdictions. This reciprocity reduces the need to re‑prove impact in each municipality and enables seamless continuation of participant support as people move within the province.
resources.address: 1800 Argyle Street, Suite 810, Halifax, NS B3J 3N8

resources.name: Regional Solid Waste Program (Inter-Municipal Service Agreement)
resources.description: Valley Waste-Resource Management delivers integrated solid waste services for multiple neighbouring municipalities in the Annapolis Valley under a standing inter-municipal agreement. When pilots such as clear bag policies, organics enhancements, or curbside textile recycling prove successful within one member area, the board structure enables rapid acceptance and roll-out across all participating municipalities without each having to re‑prove outcomes. This reciprocity mechanism sustains region-wide program delivery and reduces fragmentation of local policies.
resources.address: 90 Donald E. Hiltz Connector Road, Kentville, NS B4N 3V7

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) – South Shore Cluster
resources.description: The Town of Bridgewater’s Clean Energy Financing program uses a proven Local Improvement Charge (PACE) model first piloted in Nova Scotia and extends it through standardized bylaws and shared delivery partners so neighbouring municipalities can adopt and continue the same program design. Through reciprocal agreements and aligned eligibility/contractor standards, nearby municipalities accept the results of the pilot and deliver identical financing to residents without recreating assessments or proof-of-impact. This approach sustains home‑energy upgrades across the region and reduces policy fragmentation between municipal units.

solutions.text: Volunteer Continuity & Knowledge Team: Assemble a trained volunteer cadre to preserve institutional knowledge (archives, contacts, evaluation records) and provide short-term operational support when funding gaps threaten continuity.

resources.name: Ecology Action Centre Volunteer Program
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre engages trained volunteers in office administration, digital archiving, CRM/contact list maintenance, research, and program evaluation support. By documenting processes, organizing records, and keeping data current, volunteers preserve institutional knowledge and provide short-term operational capacity when funding cycles create staffing gaps, helping programs continue without interruption.

resources.name: Pro Bono Students Canada – Dalhousie Chapter
resources.organization: Schulich School of Law, Dalhousie University
resources.description: PBSC’s Dalhousie chapter places supervised law student volunteers with nonprofits and community groups across Nova Scotia to draft bylaws and policies, build governance binders, standardize MOUs, and organize compliance checklists—formalizing and preserving institutional knowledge. These short-term, well-scoped volunteer projects deliver critical documentation and administrative support at no cost, bridging capacity and continuity when organizations face funding uncertainty.

resources.name: HRM Volunteer Services
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Volunteer Services trains and equips community organizations with volunteer management, record-keeping, and governance tools, helping them build reliable volunteer cadres that maintain archives, contact lists, procedures, and evaluation files. The team also assists with recruitment and mobilization so trained volunteers can step into administrative and event roles, sustaining operations through funding or staffing gaps.

resources.name: Nature Trust Volunteer Program (Land Stewards & Office Volunteers)
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Nature Trust trains volunteer land stewards and office volunteers to collect and file monitoring reports, GIS notes, species observations, and stewardship records, and to maintain internal databases and contact lists—safeguarding institutional knowledge about conserved lands. Volunteers also support reception and short-term admin projects, providing surge capacity that keeps stewardship and outreach running when funding is tight.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 231, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Feed Nova Scotia Volunteer Program
resources.description: Feed Nova Scotia engages skilled volunteers in data entry for donor and client systems, file organization, and reporting support, which preserves institutional knowledge and ensures accurate, up-to-date records. Volunteers are also mobilized for short-term operational needs—such as reception, logistics, and warehouse coordination—helping maintain service continuity during periods of funding or staffing fluctuation.

obstacles.title: Climate Risks and Infrastructure Resilience
obstacles.description: Storms, flooding, and coastal erosion threaten homes, jobs, and insurance affordability, especially in rural/coastal areas.

solutions.text: Community Coastal Monitoring and Mapping: Organize volunteer teams to monitor shoreline change, flooding incidents and erosion, and maintain a community-accessible map/database to inform planning, early warning and grant applications.

resources.name: CoastSnap Nova Scotia
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: CoastSnap Nova Scotia engages volunteers to take repeat photos from fixed smartphone brackets installed at beaches and dunes to track shoreline change over time. Submitted images are processed to extract shoreline position and are shared through public web maps and dashboards, providing communities and municipalities with evidence to guide coastal planning, early warnings for erosion hotspots, and stronger grant applications for adaptation projects.

resources.name: Living Shorelines Nova Scotia
resources.description: Living Shorelines supports communities in stabilizing eroding coasts with nature-based methods and trains local volunteers to monitor beach profiles, photo-points, and storm/flood impacts. Monitoring results and site maps are published via project dashboards and GIS story maps, informing municipal planning, permit and grant applications, and timely public communications during severe weather.

resources.name: Joint Emergency Management (JEM) Program
resources.description: JEM organizes neighbourhood-level volunteer teams across Halifax to monitor and report coastal storm impacts—such as flooding, erosion, and road washouts—using standardized forms and geotagged photos. Reports feed into the municipal Emergency Management Office for situational awareness, public alerts, and the maintenance of community hazard maps used in resilience planning and funding applications.

resources.name: Nova Scotia King Tides Project
resources.description: This citizen-science initiative invites residents to document extreme high tides and storm surges at set times and locations by submitting geotagged photos and observations. The data are compiled into public maps and visual reports that reveal flood pathways and erosion-prone areas, supporting municipal planning, early-warning outreach, and evidence for coastal adaptation grant applications.

solutions.text: Local Natural Infrastructure Projects: Restore and protect salt marshes, dunes, wetlands and riparian buffers through community planting days and stewardship agreements to reduce storm surge, absorb flood waters and stabilize shorelines.

resources.name: Living Shorelines Nova Scotia
resources.description: Living Shorelines Nova Scotia designs and installs nature-based shoreline protection such as salt marsh plantings, dune restoration, coir logs, and native shrub buffers. The program hosts community planting days and works with landowners and municipalities to create stewardship agreements that maintain riparian buffers and stabilize eroding coasts, reducing storm surge and flooding risks.

resources.name: Making Room for Wetlands – Salt Marsh and Dune Restoration
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-based Solutions, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: This initiative restores tidal flow and re-establishes salt marshes and protective dunes at priority coastal sites across Nova Scotia, using native vegetation plantings and natural materials to absorb floodwaters and buffer storm surge. It engages communities through volunteer planting days and partners with municipalities, Mi’kmaq communities, and landowners to develop long-term stewardship for riparian buffers and marsh corridors.

resources.name: Coastal and Water Program – Dune and Coastal Habitat Restoration
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre coordinates community-led dune restoration at beaches such as Lawrencetown and Rainbow Haven, planting native beach grasses and installing sand fencing to rebuild dunes that reduce wave energy and storm impacts. The program also supports living shoreline pilots and wetland protection, and helps local groups and municipalities establish stewardship of riparian buffers and coastal wetlands.

resources.name: Riparian Restoration and Stewardship Program
resources.description: Clean Annapolis River Project restores riparian buffers and adjacent wetlands along the Annapolis River watershed by organizing community planting days with schools, volunteers, and landowners to plant native trees, shrubs, and marsh vegetation. Through landowner outreach and stewardship agreements, the program improves bank stability, reduces flood risk, and enhances natural infrastructure that absorbs stormwater.
resources.address: 314 St. George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

solutions.text: Neighbourhood Resilience Hubs: Create local hubs (in community centres, libraries, or churches) stocked with emergency supplies, communications equipment and information; train volunteers to operate them during storms or power outages.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Comfort Centres Program
resources.description: HRM Emergency Management designates and supports Comfort Centres and Warming Centres in community centres, libraries, churches, and fire halls across the municipality. These neighbourhood hubs provide heat, device charging, Wi-Fi, information updates, and basic supplies during storms and extended power outages, operated by municipal staff and trained community volunteers. HRM coordinates activation, provides guidance and communications support, and shares real-time status so residents can access nearby hubs.

resources.name: Cape Breton Regional Municipality Comfort Centres
resources.organization: Cape Breton Regional Municipality Emergency Management Organization
resources.description: CBRM’s Emergency Management Organization maintains a network of designated Comfort Centres in community halls, churches, and fire stations equipped with generators throughout the municipality. Local volunteers open and operate these hubs during severe weather or power interruptions to provide warmth, device charging, internet access, emergency information, and basic supplies. CBRM EMO coordinates readiness, offers training support, and communicates openings and locations to residents.

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries – Community Comfort Centres and Storm Response
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries functions as a system of neighbourhood resilience hubs, with multiple branches designated as Comfort Centres during storms and outages. Locations such as Halifax Central Library offer backup power, public Wi-Fi, device charging, washrooms, and curated emergency information, with staff coordinating alongside HRM Emergency Management and community volunteers to maintain services. The library system also hosts preparedness workshops and shares recovery resources to strengthen local resilience before and after events.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Canadian Red Cross – Nova Scotia Emergency Management
resources.description: The Canadian Red Cross in Nova Scotia trains and equips volunteer teams to operate reception centres, warming/comfort centres, and emergency shelters during hurricanes, winter storms, and other outages. Working with municipalities and community partners, it pre-positions supplies such as cots, blankets, and registration tools, and deploys personnel to support or staff local hubs when needed. This program directly enables neighbourhood resilience hubs to open quickly with trained volunteers, essential supplies, and coordinated communications.

solutions.text: Home Resilience Retrofit Program: Run a community-supported retrofit initiative offering group discounts, volunteer labour swaps and how-to workshops for flood-proofing basements, elevating utilities, improving drainage and sealing buildings.

resources.name: Depave Paradise (Halifax)
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre delivers Depave Paradise volunteer events to remove excess pavement and replace it with rain gardens and permeable landscaping, which helps infiltrate stormwater and reduce overland flow into basements. They pair these hands-on builds with homeowner workshops on practices like downspout disconnection, grading, and native planting, giving residents the skills to improve drainage and seal problem areas around their homes.

resources.name: Rainscaping Program
resources.description: ACAP Cape Breton runs community rainscaping initiatives that include public workshops and demonstration installs of rain gardens, swales, and downspout redirection to keep stormwater away from foundations. Through hands-on volunteer planting days and homeowner training, the program helps residents improve lot drainage and reduce flood risk to basements and lower levels.

resources.name: Workshops and Tool Lending
resources.description: Halifax Tool Library equips residents to undertake DIY resilience retrofits by lending tools and teaching practical skills in workshops (e.g., sealing foundation cracks, installing window wells, redirecting downspouts, and regrading to shed water). Members commonly organize neighbour work parties and volunteer ‘fix-it’ events, lowering costs and enabling group retrofit days that improve drainage and reduce basement flood risk.

resources.name: Living Shorelines Program
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions (Saint Mary’s University)
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations works with coastal property owners and communities to design and install nature-based living shorelines that stabilize banks, dissipate wave energy, and reduce erosion and coastal flooding. They host training sessions and community build days, enabling volunteer crews to implement site-specific measures that protect homes and outbuildings and complement lot-level drainage improvements.

resources.name: Home Repair Program
resources.description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia mobilizes volunteer crews to help low-income homeowners complete essential repairs that can include weatherproofing, addressing water ingress, and restoring storm-damaged elements of the home. By coordinating donated materials and supplier partnerships, the program reduces costs and provides the labour support needed to seal buildings and improve resilience to heavy rain and flooding.

solutions.text: Community Emergency Response Teams (CERT): Train local volunteers in first response, search and rescue basics, sandbagging, and neighborhood check-ins to reduce immediate storm damage and support vulnerable residents.

resources.name: Joint Emergency Management (JEM) Program
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality Emergency Management Office
resources.description: Halifax’s JEM program organizes neighborhood-based volunteer teams that support communities before, during, and after storms. Volunteers are trained in basic emergency response, damage assessment, door-to-door wellness checks, opening comfort centres, and practical tasks like debris clearing and sandbagging to reduce flood impacts, all coordinated under the Halifax Regional Municipality Emergency Management Office.

resources.name: Canadian Red Cross – Nova Scotia Disaster Management Program
resources.description: The Canadian Red Cross recruits and trains volunteers across Nova Scotia to prepare for and respond to floods, hurricanes, and severe storms. Volunteer teams receive training in first-response support, wellness checks, sheltering and evacuations, needs assessments, and hands-on tasks such as sandbagging and distributing relief supplies to protect vulnerable residents in coastal and rural communities.

resources.name: East Hants Emergency Management (EMO)
resources.description: East Hants EMO coordinates community-based preparedness and response efforts and organizes local volunteers to assist during severe weather and flooding. The program trains residents to operate comfort centres, conduct neighborhood wellness checks, provide basic first-aid support, and perform sandbagging and water-diversion work to reduce immediate storm damage for at-risk households.

solutions.text: Local Stormwater and Low-Impact Development (LID) Projects: Install rain gardens, permeable pavement, bioswales and roadside infiltration basins through community-led design and build days to reduce runoff and urban flooding.

resources.name: Depave Paradise – Halifax
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre delivers Depave Paradise events that mobilize residents to remove sections of unnecessary pavement and replace them with rain gardens and native plant beds that infiltrate stormwater. Through community design workshops and hands-on build days at schools, faith sites, and street edges, the initiative installs bioretention features that reduce runoff, mitigate urban flooding, and improve water quality. The program demonstrates low-impact development (LID) practices and builds local skills for ongoing maintenance.

resources.name: Stormwater and LID Projects (Coasts & Watersheds)
resources.description: Clean Foundation partners with municipalities, schools, and community groups across Nova Scotia to co-design and install rain gardens, bioswales, and other green stormwater infrastructure. Their teams host volunteer planting and maintenance days, provide technical guidance on site selection and native plants, and deliver public workshops that help residents retrofit properties with permeable surfaces and downspout disconnection. These projects reduce peak flows, improve infiltration, and lessen localized flooding risks.

resources.name: South Shore Stormwater Management and Green Infrastructure
resources.description: Bluenose Coastal Action Foundation works with towns and communities on Nova Scotia’s South Shore to design and implement LID features such as rain gardens, bioswales, and shoreline infiltration plantings that capture and filter runoff before it reaches harbours and streams. The initiative frequently organizes community planting events and youth education sessions, building local capacity to plan, install, and care for green infrastructure. These projects reduce flooding and erosion while improving water quality and habitat.

resources.name: Non-Residential Stormwater Credit Program
resources.description: Halifax Water provides bill credits to non-residential customers that install and maintain approved LID practices—such as permeable pavement, rain gardens/bioretention, and infiltration galleries—that reduce runoff to the municipal system. The utility offers technical guidelines and a review process that encourages property owners to retrofit sites with green infrastructure, decreasing peak flows and urban flooding. This incentive accelerates widespread adoption of LID across commercial, institutional, and industrial properties.
resources.address: 450 Cowie Hill Road, Halifax, NS B3P 2V3

solutions.text: Community-Owned Microgrids and Backup Power: Develop small-scale renewable energy plus battery storage projects (solar co-ops, microgrids) to keep critical services running during outages and lower energy costs for residents and businesses.

resources.name: Smart Grid Nova Scotia
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s Smart Grid Nova Scotia pilot deploys distributed energy resources such as residential battery storage (e.g., Tesla Powerwall), smart inverters, and advanced controls to form a virtual power plant across participating communities. The batteries provide backup power during storms and outages while coordinated operation lowers peak demand and overall energy costs, improving grid resilience for residents and small businesses.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Mahone Bay Solar Garden Project
resources.organization: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility
resources.description: The Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility is developing a subscriber-based community solar garden that enables residents and businesses to purchase a share of local solar generation and receive bill credits. As part of the town’s broader grid-modernization work with AREA, the project supports local resilience by laying the groundwork to pair solar with battery storage so critical municipal services can remain powered during outages while lowering electricity costs for participants.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Antigonish Community Solar Garden
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish Electric Utility is implementing a community solar garden that lets customers subscribe to locally produced solar power and receive credits on their bills. Integrated with municipal utility operations and AREA’s community energy platform, the project advances a distributed, community-owned approach that can be complemented by battery storage to maintain essential services during outages and cut energy costs for residents and small businesses.

resources.name: AREA (Alternative Resource Energy Authority) Community Renewables
resources.description: AREA is a joint venture of the municipal electric utilities of Antigonish, Berwick, and Mahone Bay that develops and operates community-owned clean energy projects, including the Ellershouse Wind Farm and community solar initiatives. By coordinating local generation with planned battery storage and smart grid controls, AREA enables its member towns to enhance outage resilience for critical services and deliver more affordable, locally owned electricity to customers.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

solutions.text: Local Insurance and Affordability Workshops: Host sessions with insurance experts and municipal staff to explain coverage options, government programs, mitigation discounts and steps homeowners can take to lower premiums.

resources.name: Community Insurance Information Sessions (Nova Scotia)
resources.organization: Insurance Bureau of Canada – Atlantic Region
resources.description: The Insurance Bureau of Canada’s Atlantic office partners with Nova Scotia municipalities to host town halls and workshops that explain home insurance coverage, including overland flood and sewer backup, and how mitigation measures can reduce risk and premiums. Sessions often include Q&A with insurance experts, guidance on discounts and endorsements, and information on how provincial Disaster Financial Assistance (DFA) interacts with private insurance.
resources.address: Suite 802, 1801 Hollis Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3N4

resources.name: Disaster Financial Assistance and Insurance Information Sessions
resources.description: Nova Scotia Emergency Management Office (NSEMO) coordinates community information sessions with municipal emergency coordinators and insurance experts to help residents understand coverage options, the DFA program, and steps to reduce household risk. These workshops explain how mitigation (e.g., sump pumps, backflow valves, fire‑smarting) can improve insurability and lower premiums while clarifying what losses are insurable versus eligible for government assistance.
resources.address: 21 Mount Hope Avenue, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 4R4

resources.name: Flood Preparedness and Insurance Workshops
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality hosts public workshops and open houses—often in partnership with Halifax Water and the Insurance Bureau of Canada—to explain flood risks, home insurance options (overland flood, sewer backup), and practical mitigation steps that can reduce claims and premiums. Municipal staff and insurance professionals jointly outline available programs, rebates, and discounts tied to risk-reduction improvements, helping homeowners make informed, affordability-focused decisions.

resources.name: Community Insurance and Recovery Information Sessions
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Municipality collaborates with provincial officials and the Insurance Bureau of Canada to deliver public information sessions that walk residents through insurance coverage, claims processes, and DFA supports following severe storms. These events include practical guidance on property-level mitigation—such as drainage, backwater valves, and wildfire risk reduction—and how such actions can improve eligibility and help lower premiums.

solutions.text: Managed Retreat & Land-Use Dialogues: Facilitate community-led conversations and planning tools about voluntary buyouts, relocation incentives, and future land use to create fair, transparent managed-retreat strategies for high-risk areas.

resources.name: Regional Plan Review – Coastal Resilience and Flood Hazard Policies
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Regional Plan Review engages residents through open houses, surveys, and mapping tools to update land-use rules for areas at high risk of sea-level rise, storm surge, and river flooding. The review advances coastal elevation and floodplain overlays, development setbacks, and restrictions on rebuilding in the highest-risk floodways, and it explores policy pathways that enable voluntary relocation and property acquisition, helping create fair, transparent managed-retreat strategies for at-risk communities.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations – Community Coastal Adaptation Workshops & Decision-Support Tools
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-based Solutions, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations works with Nova Scotia municipalities and Mi’kmaw communities to facilitate community-led conversations about adapting to sea-level rise and erosion, using participatory mapping, flood/erosion scenarios, and cost–benefit tools. Their workshops compare protection, accommodation, and managed retreat options (including voluntary buyouts and relocation incentives) and translate outcomes into land-use policies and plans to support equitable, transparent managed-retreat strategies.

resources.name: Coastal Adaptation Program
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre convenes community forums and participatory mapping sessions across coastal Nova Scotia to help residents and municipalities understand flood and erosion risks and evaluate future land-use choices. The program provides guidance on voluntary retreat and property acquisition, and promotes planning tools such as rolling easements and coastal setbacks to build fair, community-driven managed-retreat strategies in high-risk areas.

resources.name: Climate Change Working Group & Coastal Adaptation Dialogues
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Federation of Municipalities brings municipalities together with planners, provincial partners, and the public to share best practices on managing development in flood- and erosion-prone areas. Through webinars, workshops, and policy guidance, the initiative supports local governments to design transparent managed-retreat approaches—covering voluntary buyouts, relocation assistance, and land-use bylaw updates—that reflect community input and equity considerations.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1304, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

solutions.text: Youth Resilience and Green Trades Training: Develop apprenticeships and short courses for young people in resilient construction, coastal restoration, flood-proofing and renewable energy to create local jobs tied to adaptation needs.

resources.name: Clean Leadership Summer Internship
resources.description: A paid summer internship program placing high school and post-secondary youth with host organizations across Nova Scotia in roles such as coastal restoration crews, energy efficiency outreach, and green construction support. Interns receive mentorship, safety training, and workplace skills that prepare them for careers in climate adaptation, flood resilience projects, and renewable energy.

resources.name: Coastal Training and Living Shorelines Workshops
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-based Solutions (Saint Mary’s University)
resources.description: Hands-on training for students, early-career practitioners, and trades on designing and building nature-based coastal protection, including living shorelines and salt marsh restoration that reduce flood and erosion risks. Participants gain field skills in site assessment, design, installation, and monitoring, directly supporting local adaptation projects and creating pathways into coastal restoration jobs.

resources.name: Solar Electricity (PV) Design and Installation – Continuing Education
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) – Ivany Campus, Centre for the Built Environment
resources.description: A short, practical course that trains learners to design and install solar PV systems safely and in compliance with codes, including system sizing, wiring, and commissioning. Delivered through NSCC’s Centre for the Built Environment, it builds green trades capacity and supports community resilience by expanding local renewable energy skills and employment.

resources.name: Contractor and Energy Advisor Training & Certification Support
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia provides training, workshops, and certification support for contractors and energy advisors on heat pumps, building envelope upgrades, air sealing, and EnerGuide assessments. These short courses align with provincial rebate programs, creating immediate work opportunities in resilient retrofits and flood- and storm-ready home improvements across the province.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Living Shorelines and Coastal Restoration Program
resources.description: Coastal Action designs and delivers living shoreline and salt marsh restoration projects on Nova Scotia’s South Shore, including training days and seasonal technician roles for youth. Participants learn erosion control, bioengineering, and shoreline monitoring that directly enhance community resilience while building local coastal restoration career pathways.

solutions.text: Local Materials and Labour Exchange: Set up a platform for sharing building materials, tools and skilled volunteers for resilience projects so small communities can carry out repairs and upgrades affordably.

resources.name: Halifax Tool Library
resources.description: A community lending library that provides members access to hundreds of hand and power tools for home repair, construction, and weatherization projects, so people can borrow what they need rather than purchase. It also runs volunteer-led skill-shares and Repair Cafés that connect experienced tradespeople with neighbours to fix and upgrade homes, directly enabling a local exchange of tools and skilled labour for affordable resilience work such as storm repairs, sealing, and flood preparedness.

resources.name: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia ReStore – Dartmouth
resources.description: The ReStore accepts donations of new and gently used building materials, tools, fixtures, and furniture, and sells them at low cost to the public. By making construction supplies and hardware affordable and locally available, it operates as a materials exchange that helps small communities source what they need for repairs, retrofits, and resilience upgrades after storms and flooding.

resources.name: Lunenburg Regional Community Recycling Centre – Reuse Centre
resources.organization: Lunenburg Regional Community Recycling Centre (Municipality of the District of Lunenburg)
resources.description: An on-site Reuse Centre where residents drop off and pick up usable items including doors, windows, lumber, hardware, and small tools at little or no cost. This local exchange of building materials reduces waste and lowers project costs, enabling households and volunteer groups to carry out repairs and resilience improvements across Lunenburg County.
resources.address: 908 Mullock Road, Whynott's Settlement, NS B4V 5T9

resources.name: Waste Check Region 10 – Reuse Centre (Yarmouth Waste Park)
resources.description: The Yarmouth Waste Park operates a Reuse Centre where community members can donate and take household and home-improvement items, including surplus building materials and tools, often free or at very low cost. By facilitating the local circulation of materials, it supports affordable home repairs and upgrades that strengthen resilience in rural coastal communities.

solutions.text: Small-Scale Coastal Protection Demonstration Projects: Pilot community-led living shorelines, breakwaters or hybrid nature-based hardening projects to demonstrate cost-effective protection and build local capacity for larger interventions.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations – Living Shorelines Demonstration Projects
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations – Centre for Nature-Based Solutions, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations (TCA) designs and implements community-led living shoreline pilot sites across Nova Scotia, installing hybrid nature-based measures such as low-crested rock sills/offshore breakwaters, coir logs, and salt marsh/cordgrass plantings to reduce wave energy and erosion. The team partners with municipalities, Indigenous communities, and local groups to co-develop small-scale projects, provide hands-on training to contractors and volunteers, and monitor performance to prove cost-effectiveness. These demonstrations build local capacity and inform scaling up to larger coastal protection interventions province-wide.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Living Shoreline Project
resources.description: The Town of Mahone Bay is piloting living shoreline installations along vulnerable sections of its waterfront (e.g., near the Three Churches and Edgewater Street), combining low-crested rock sills/breakwaters with marsh bench creation and native vegetation plantings. The project reduces wave energy, limits flooding and erosion, and showcases practical, cost-effective alternatives to traditional seawalls. Community partners and volunteers participate in design and planting, building local skills and experience that can be applied to larger coastal resilience efforts on the South Shore.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Coastal Restoration and Living Shorelines
resources.description: Coastal Action leads small-scale coastal protection and restoration projects on Nova Scotia’s South Shore, including living shoreline demonstrations that integrate rock sills, coir fiber stabilization, dune enhancement, and salt marsh plantings. These pilots are implemented with municipal and community partners at priority erosion sites to test nature-based and hybrid solutions, gather monitoring data, and refine best practices. Coastal Action also trains youth, volunteers, and local contractors through workshops and field days, growing regional capacity for larger future interventions.
resources.address: 37 Tannery Road, Unit 3, Lunenburg, NS B0J 2C0

resources.name: Sir Sandford Fleming Park (Dingle) Living Shoreline Pilot
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality is piloting a living shoreline at Sir Sandford Fleming Park on the Northwest Arm, where a failing seawall is being replaced with a hybrid nature-based design featuring rock sills, cobble/gravel berms, and vegetated marsh benches. The pilot reduces wave energy and shoreline erosion while maintaining public access, and serves as a demonstration site for future municipal coastal protection projects. Implemented with partners and community engagement, the project builds local knowledge and technical capacity for scaling nature-based shoreline solutions across HRM.

solutions.text: Community Resilience Fund and Microgrants: Establish a locally governed resilience fund (seeded by donations, municipal contributions and fundraisers) that provides microgrants for household flood mitigation, small business preparedness and local adaptation pilots.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Sustainable Communities Challenge Fund
resources.description: A province-wide fund administered by Clean Foundation that provides grants to municipalities, Mi’kmaw communities, and non-profits for climate adaptation and mitigation projects, including flood resilience and nature-based coastal protection. By offering small to mid-sized grants that seed local pilots and preparedness initiatives, it functions as a community resilience fund that enables neighbourhood-scale adaptation and supports locally governed solutions.

resources.name: Community Grants Program (Environment & Emergency Services categories)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s annual Community Grants Program provides small project grants to local non-profits, including for environmental stewardship and emergency preparedness initiatives such as flood-readiness workshops, rain gardens, and neighbourhood resilience projects. Funded by the municipality and governed locally, these microgrants enable community-led pilots and preparedness activities that reduce flood risk and build climate resilience at the neighbourhood level.

resources.name: Living Shorelines and Stormwater Resilience Program
resources.description: Coastal Action partners with communities and property owners to design and implement nature-based flood and erosion solutions—such as living shorelines, rain gardens, and stormwater retrofits—and provides technical assistance along with small, cost-share support when available. By channeling government grants, donations, and partner contributions into homeowner and community pilot projects, the program operates like a local microgrant mechanism for household flood mitigation and adaptation demonstrations.
resources.address: 37 Tannery Road, Unit 1, Lunenburg, NS B0J 2C0

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations – Living Shorelines Program
resources.organization: Saint Mary’s University – TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-based Solutions
resources.description: Based at Saint Mary’s University, TransCoastal Adaptations supports municipalities, community groups, and property owners with technical expertise and small seed funding for pilot living shoreline and wetland restoration projects that reduce coastal flooding and erosion. By leveraging philanthropic and public funds to catalyze locally governed adaptation pilots, the program advances a community resilience fund model that helps scale practical, site-specific flood mitigation solutions.

solutions.text: Data-Sharing Partnerships with Universities and First Responders: Partner with regional universities, Indigenous knowledge holders and emergency services to share modelling, historical flood data and traditional shoreline knowledge to guide community decisions.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions
resources.description: Based at Saint Mary’s University, TransCoastal Adaptations (TCA) convenes partnerships among university researchers, Mi’kmaw communities, municipalities, and emergency managers to co-develop flood and storm-surge models and living shoreline projects. They share geospatial data, monitoring results, and traditional shoreline knowledge through workshops and decision-support tools so planners and first responders can prioritize infrastructure upgrades, evacuation routes, and coastal resilience actions.

resources.name: Applied Geomatics Research Group (AGRG) – Coastal Flood and Storm-Surge Mapping
