Housing is prioritized for Mi’kmaq and urban Indigenous community members experiencing homelessness or discrimination, and resident voice is embedded through Indigenous governance and tenant advisory mechanisms. These efforts advance shared-living and resident-directed models that reduce barriers and foster inclusion and belonging.

resources.name: New Dawn Community Housing
resources.description: New Dawn develops and manages community-owned affordable housing in Sydney/Cape Breton, offering small-scale apartment buildings and shared-living arrangements that include barrier-free, accessible units. Placement focuses on local residents with low and moderate incomes, newcomers, seniors, and people with disabilities, and tenant input informs building operations and community programming. This community-governed approach expands inclusive, affordable housing while fostering resident leadership and belonging.

solutions.text: Community Allyship and Bystander Intervention Campaigns: Run neighbourhood campaigns and short workshops that teach practical allyship behaviours, safe bystander interventions, and how to support people experiencing racism, homophobia, transphobia, or ableism.

resources.name: Disrupting Racism: Learning
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission delivers the Disrupting Racism learning series and community workshops that build practical skills to recognize, interrupt, and report racism. Sessions include concrete allyship behaviours and safe bystander strategies so participants can intervene without escalating harm and better support those experiencing anti-Black and anti-Indigenous racism and other discrimination in public and workplace settings.
resources.address: 5657 Spring Garden Road, Suite 305, Halifax, NS B3J 3R4

resources.name: Anti-Racism and Anti-Oppression Training for Workplaces and Communities
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS provides interactive workshops that equip employers, service providers, and community members with allyship skills and safe bystander intervention techniques to address racism and xenophobia. Training covers how to recognize microaggressions, safely step in when harm occurs, and support newcomers and racialized people who experience discrimination in neighbourhoods and workplaces.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: 2SLGBTQ+ Inclusion Workshops
resources.description: The Youth Project offers province-wide education sessions that teach practical allyship, inclusive language, and safe bystander responses to homophobia and transphobia in schools, youth programs, and community organizations. Workshops provide concrete tools for supporting 2SLGBTQ+ youth experiencing harassment, including how to de-escalate situations and follow up with impacted individuals.

resources.name: Bystander Intervention Training
resources.organization: Dalhousie University, Human Rights & Equity Services
resources.description: Dalhousie University’s Human Rights & Equity Services delivers bystander intervention and anti-oppression sessions that help students, staff, and community members recognize and interrupt racism, ableism, homophobia, transphobia, and other forms of discrimination. The training emphasizes practical, scenario-based techniques (e.g., the 5 D’s) so participants can intervene safely and support people who have experienced harm on campus and in surrounding communities.

resources.name: Anti-Black Racism Education Workshops
resources.organization: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia provides community and school-based workshops that build historical understanding and practical allyship to address anti-Black racism. Sessions include guidance on being an effective ally and safe bystander, with strategies for interrupting harm, supporting those targeted, and fostering inclusive neighbourhood and workplace cultures.
resources.address: 10 Cherry Brook Road, Cherry Brook, NS B2Z 1A8

solutions.text: Local Procurement Equity Initiative: Encourage municipal and institutional procurement policies that earmark a percentage of contracts for Mi'kmaq-led, African Nova Scotian, newcomer-owned, 2SLGBTQ+-led, and disability-run businesses and co-ops.

resources.name: Social Procurement Program
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Social Procurement Program embeds supplier diversity and community benefits into municipal purchasing. The program uses weighted evaluation criteria and contract requirements that encourage and, in major projects, set targets for subcontracting and spending with Mi’kmaq-led, African Nova Scotian, newcomer-owned, 2SLGBTQ+-led, and disability-run businesses and co-ops. This directs a share of municipal contract value to equity-deserving suppliers and requires reporting on outcomes.

resources.name: Supplier Diversity and Inclusive Procurement (Set-Aside Pilot)
resources.description: The Province of Nova Scotia’s procurement program includes a supplier diversity strategy and a set-aside pilot that reserves select low-value purchases for Mi’kmaw and African Nova Scotian businesses. The program also promotes inclusive evaluation criteria and outreach so provincial departments, health authorities, and Crown entities can increase the percentage of spend awarded to diverse suppliers, including newcomer-owned, 2SLGBTQ+-led, and disability-run businesses.

resources.name: Supplier Diversity Program
resources.description: Halifax Port Authority’s Supplier Diversity Program encourages participation and spending with underrepresented businesses in the Port’s procurement and capital projects. Through targeted outreach, inclusive vendor registration, and social value criteria for tenders, the Port increases opportunities for Mi’kmaq-led, African Nova Scotian, newcomer-owned, 2SLGBTQ+-led, and disability-run firms, and encourages prime contractors to allocate a share of subcontracts to these suppliers.

solutions.text: Community Mental Health Peer Support Network: Train peer-support volunteers from diverse backgrounds to provide culturally safe mental-health drop-in hours, referral navigation, and trauma-informed support for people facing discrimination.

resources.name: Peer Support Nova Scotia (Provincial Peer Support Program)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Health, Mental Health & Addictions Program
resources.description: Peer Support Nova Scotia recruits and trains peer-support workers and volunteers with lived experience to deliver trauma-informed, culturally safe mental health support across the province. They offer one-on-one peer support, group sessions, Recovery College workshops, and a warm line, and they help people navigate and get referrals to appropriate health and community services, including supports for 2SLGBTQ+, Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, and disabled communities.

resources.name: Urban Indigenous Peer Outreach and Wellness Supports
resources.description: The Mi’kmaw Native Friendship Centre provides culturally safe, trauma-informed drop-in supports where Indigenous peer workers and volunteers offer wellness check-ins, traditional cultural activities, and navigation to mental health and community services. The program centers Mi’kmaw worldviews and lived experience to reduce barriers for people facing racism, homelessness, and discrimination, and provides warm referrals to specialized care.

resources.name: Peer-Led Drop-in and Harm Reduction Mental Health Supports
resources.description: Stepping Stone’s sex worker–led drop-in offers trauma-informed, judgment-free peer support where trained peer staff and volunteers provide mental health check-ins, crisis de-escalation, and navigation to counselling, health, and community resources. The space is intentionally low-barrier and culturally safer for people who experience discrimination, including 2SLGBTQ+, Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, migrant, and disabled community members.

resources.name: Newcomer Wellness and Peer Support Groups
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS runs culturally responsive wellness and peer support groups where trained facilitators and community volunteers with lived newcomer experience provide mental health psychoeducation, mutual-aid peer circles, and warm navigation to primary care, counselling, and settlement services. These supports address stigma, language, and system-navigation barriers so immigrants and refugees can access trauma-informed care and community resources.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Peer Outreach and Community Drop-in Mental Health Supports
resources.description: The Ally Centre of Cape Breton operates a low-barrier drop-in where peer workers and volunteers with lived experience provide trauma-informed mental health support, harm reduction, and navigation to housing, addictions, and clinical services. The program prioritizes culturally safe care for people who face discrimination, including Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, and 2SLGBTQ+ community members, and makes warm referrals to local health providers.

solutions.text: Inclusive School and After-School Programs: Partner with schools to expand inclusive after-school clubs and curriculum supplements that reflect Mi'kmaq history, African Nova Scotian contributions, newcomer experiences, LGBTQ+ inclusion, and disability awareness.

resources.name: Imhotep's Legacy Academy
resources.description: Imhotep's Legacy Academy runs after-school STEM clubs, tutoring, and mentorship programs for African Nova Scotian junior high and high school students in partnership with schools across Nova Scotia. By combining culturally relevant curriculum supplements with hands-on clubs led by university mentors, the program affirms African Nova Scotian contributions and builds belonging and academic confidence.

resources.name: The Youth Project Education Program
resources.description: The Youth Project partners with schools to deliver workshops on 2SLGBTQ+ inclusion, supports Gender-Sexuality Alliances (GSAs), and offers after-school drop-ins and leadership programs for youth. These education sessions and clubs equip students and educators with inclusive practices, reduce discrimination, and create safer, affirming school environments.

resources.name: ISANS Youth Program
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS partners with schools to support newcomer youth through school settlement workers, homework clubs, leadership development, and after-school activities. The program builds welcoming school communities by addressing language, cultural transition, and social integration, while co-developing curriculum supports and workshops that reflect newcomer experiences.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre Youth & Cultural Programs
resources.description: The Mi’kmaw Native Friendship Centre offers after-school homework help, cultural workshops, and school outreach that connect Indigenous youth with Mi’kmaq language, history, and traditions. By partnering with local schools, the programs deliver culturally grounded activities and curriculum enhancements that foster Indigenous identity, pride, and belonging.

resources.name: CNIB Beyond the Classroom (Nova Scotia)
resources.organization: CNIB – Canadian National Institute for the Blind
resources.description: CNIB’s Beyond the Classroom and youth programs collaborate with schools to provide blindness and accessibility awareness presentations, assistive technology training, and after-school skill-building clubs for students with sight loss. These activities advance disability awareness in classrooms while creating inclusive, participatory spaces for youth to thrive academically and socially.

obstacles.title: Regional disparities between HRM and rural communities
obstacles.description: Opportunities, amenities, and services are concentrated in urban centres, leaving rural areas with fewer pathways and weaker community infrastructure.

solutions.text: Rural Remote-Work Hubs: Convert underused municipal buildings, libraries or community centres into high‑quality co‑working spaces with reliable internet, meeting rooms and hot desks to attract remote workers and support local entrepreneurs.

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic – Yarmouth Innovation Hub
resources.description: IGNITE operates a rural co-working and innovation hub in downtown Yarmouth that offers high-speed internet, hot desks, meeting rooms, and community programming for startups, small businesses, and remote workers. By providing professional workspace and amenities in a rural town, the hub attracts remote talent and supports local entrepreneurs, directly addressing the urban–rural opportunity gap.

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic – New Glasgow Innovation Hub
resources.description: IGNITE’s Pictou County hub provides a co-working environment with reliable internet, bookable meeting rooms, and shared workspaces for entrepreneurs, students, and remote professionals. The space cultivates a rural innovation ecosystem outside HRM, enabling people to live and work locally while accessing the infrastructure and community typically found in urban centres.
resources.address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

resources.name: Navigate Startup House
resources.organization: Navigate (Cape Breton University and NSCC partnership)
resources.description: Navigate runs a downtown Sydney co-working and incubation space featuring hot desks, private offices, high-speed internet, and meeting rooms for startups, freelancers, and remote workers. By offering professional facilities and programming in Cape Breton, it functions as a rural remote-work hub that anchors talent and entrepreneurial activity outside the Halifax region.

resources.name: Antigonish Town and County Library (The People’s Place) – Community Work and Meeting Spaces
resources.description: The People’s Place library offers free high-speed Wi‑Fi, quiet study areas, and bookable meeting rooms that residents, students, and remote workers use as co-working style space. As a modern municipal library in a rural university town, it effectively serves as a local remote‑work hub, providing the infrastructure and community environment needed for professional work outside major urban centres.

solutions.text: Community Broadband Partnerships: Form local consortia (municipalities, businesses, co‑ops) to co‑fund last‑mile broadband upgrades, apply for provincial/federal grants, and negotiate bulk service agreements to improve internet access across rural areas.

resources.name: Internet for Nova Scotia Initiative (IFNSI)
resources.description: Led by Build Nova Scotia, IFNSI structures partnerships among municipalities, First Nations, community groups, and internet service providers to deliver last‑mile fibre and fixed‑wireless in underserved rural communities. The program blends provincial funds with federal grants (e.g., Universal Broadband Fund/CRTC) and local contributions, and uses bulk procurement and master service agreements to secure long‑term, affordable 50/10+ service across rural Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 1875 Upper Water Street, Suite 300, Halifax, NS B3J 1S9

resources.name: Kings County Rural Internet Project
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
resources.description: The Municipality of the County of Kings convenes municipal units, local businesses, and ISPs to co‑fund and deliver fibre and fixed‑wireless expansions to unserved and underserved communities. By issuing joint RFPs, committing municipal capital to leverage provincial and federal grants through IFNSI/UBF, and negotiating area‑wide build and service agreements, the project reduces costs and accelerates last‑mile deployment for rural residents.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: Cumberland County Rural Internet Initiative
resources.description: The Municipality of Cumberland partners with private ISPs and neighbouring communities to co‑fund fibre and fixed‑wireless builds in sparsely populated areas. The initiative aggregates local demand, applies for provincial/federal broadband grants, and negotiates bulk build and service terms, enabling affordable last‑mile upgrades that bring reliable high‑speed internet to rural residents and businesses.
resources.address: 1395 Blair Lake Road, Upper Nappan, NS B4H 3Y4

resources.name: CBRM Rural Broadband Upgrade Program
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Municipality collaborates with local ISPs and community stakeholders to extend fibre and fixed‑wireless coverage to rural and exurban areas of the municipality. By coordinating community sign‑ups, contributing municipal resources and rights‑of‑way, leveraging IFNSI and federal funding, and negotiating bulk service agreements, the program reduces per‑premise costs and accelerates last‑mile upgrades across rural Cape Breton.

solutions.text: Mobile Service Units: Operate mobile buses or pop‑up clinics that deliver services (health screenings, mental health supports, library services, business advising, skills training) on a rotating schedule to smaller communities.

resources.name: Mobile Primary Care Clinics
resources.description: Nova Scotia Health operates mobile and pop-up primary care clinics that rotate through small towns and rural communities across the province. These clinics set up in community venues and provide same-day assessment for non-urgent concerns, prescription refills, screening, vaccinations, and referrals/attachment to ongoing care—bringing essential health services closer to residents who live far from urban centres.
resources.address: 1276 South Park Street, Halifax, NS B3H 2Y9

resources.name: Nova Scotia Breast Screening Program – Mobile Mammography
resources.description: The Breast Screening Program runs mobile mammography coaches that visit rural and remote communities on a published rotation, offering digital breast cancer screening without requiring travel to urban hospitals. By bringing equipment and technologists directly to community sites, the program reduces access barriers and ensures timely preventive care for residents outside major centres.

resources.name: Pop-Up Library Service
resources.description: Eastern Counties Regional Library delivers pop-up library stops in smaller communities across Guysborough, Richmond, and Inverness counties. Staff bring a mobile collection, library card sign-up, technology help, and programming to community halls and local hubs on a rotating schedule, extending library access and services to places without a permanent branch.

resources.name: Mobile Blood Donation Clinics (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Canadian Blood Services runs mobile donor clinics that regularly travel to community centres and arenas throughout rural Nova Scotia, bringing the full blood donation experience outside Halifax. These pop-up clinics follow a rotating calendar and provide on-site screening, donation, and post-donation care, enabling residents in smaller communities to participate without long-distance travel.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 130, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

solutions.text: Local Skills and Apprenticeship Hubs: Partner with community colleges, tradespeople and employers to host short courses, apprenticeships and micro‑credentials locally, aligning training with nearby industry needs to keep youth employed in region.

resources.name: NSCC Strait Area Campus – Nautical Institute and Marine Training
resources.description: NSCC’s Nautical Institute in Port Hawkesbury delivers Transport Canada-approved certificates, short courses, and micro-credentials in marine navigation and engineering that are aligned with the Strait area’s fishing, shipping, and offshore sectors. The campus partners with local employers and tradespeople to offer work placements and apprenticeship pathways, ensuring residents can train and transition into marine careers without leaving the region.
resources.address: 226 Reeves Street, Port Hawkesbury, NS B9A 2A2

resources.name: NSCC Shelburne Campus – School of Fisheries and Marine Trades
resources.description: NSCC’s Shelburne Campus offers industry-responsive training for the South Shore, including fisheries and aquaculture programs, marine safety tickets, and trades short courses and micro-credentials relevant to local boatbuilding and seafood processing. Working with nearby employers and journeypersons, the campus provides practical learning and apprenticeship connections that help youth gain skills and secure jobs close to home.

resources.name: Building Futures for Youth (BFY)
resources.description: BFY places high school students in paid, local construction work terms with vetted employers across Nova Scotia, introducing them to skilled trades through mentorship and hands-on experience. In partnership with NSCC, the Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency, and industry, the program creates clear pathways to apprenticeship and short, industry-aligned training that help young people start trades careers in their home communities.
resources.address: 134 Eileen Stubbs Avenue, Unit 103, Dartmouth, NS B3B 2C4

resources.name: Apprenticeship START Program
resources.description: The START Program provides financial incentives to employers—especially in rural and small communities—to hire and train first-year apprentices in Red Seal and designated trades. By pairing on-the-job mentorship with block training at nearby NSCC campuses and trade training centres, it expands local apprenticeship seats and aligns skills development with regional labour market needs so youth can stay and work where they live.

solutions.text: Community Business Incubators: Create small business incubator programs providing mentorship, low‑cost shared workspace, startup microgrants and market access support aimed at agriculture, fisheries, crafts, tourism and tech micro‑enterprises.

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic – Yarmouth Hub (Incubator & Coworking)
resources.description: IGNITE Atlantic operates a rural innovation hub in Yarmouth that provides low‑cost shared workspace, incubation programming, mentorship, and hands‑on workshops for founders in sectors such as fisheries, agri‑food, tourism, crafts, and tech. The hub connects entrepreneurs to startup funding and microgrant opportunities through partner programs and competitions, and facilitates market access via industry networks and regional showcases. This directly implements the solution by anchoring mentorship, shared space, and growth supports in a rural community outside HRM.

resources.name: Navigate Startup House
resources.organization: Navigate (Cape Breton Partnership & Cape Breton University)
resources.description: Navigate Startup House in Sydney provides subsidized co‑working desks and offices, one‑on‑one mentorship, workshops, and accelerator-style programming for early‑stage companies and micro‑enterprises across Cape Breton. It supports diverse sectors—tech, tourism, crafts, and food—by helping founders validate ideas, access microgrants and funding programs through partners, and connect with buyers and investors via regional networks and events. This places incubator services and shared workspace in a rural region, closing gaps with HRM.

resources.name: Launchpad Craft Business Incubator
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: Launchpad is a craft‑focused business incubator that offers affordable studio/workspace, equipment access, business training, and tailored mentorship to emerging artisans. Participants gain market access through the Centre’s gallery and retail channels, juried shows, and export/readiness supports, while receiving guidance on pricing, e‑commerce, and wholesaling. This delivers low‑cost shared space, mentorship, and direct pathways to markets for craft micro‑enterprises in rural Nova Scotia.

resources.name: North Queens Business Hub
resources.description: The North Queens Business Hub provides low‑cost shared offices, co‑working space, meeting rooms, and on‑site advisory supports for entrepreneurs and remote workers in Caledonia and surrounding rural communities. The Hub convenes mentorship clinics and training with partners (e.g., CBDC, NSCC), helps startups navigate grants and procurement opportunities, and showcases local products and services along a key tourism corridor. It implements the solution by strengthening rural business infrastructure with workspace, coaching, and market‑access support for small enterprises.

solutions.text: Local Investment & Microfinance Funds: Establish community loan funds or social finance vehicles to provide seed capital and low‑interest loans for local startups, social enterprises and housing projects that traditional lenders overlook.

resources.name: CEED Microloan Program
resources.organization: Centre for Entrepreneurship Education and Development (CEED)
resources.description: CEED provides microloans to startups and early-stage small businesses that may not qualify for traditional bank financing, paired with coaching and training to improve success. By offering accessible, lower-barrier capital province-wide, CEED acts as a local social finance vehicle that seeds new ventures and supports community-based entrepreneurs, including those outside major urban centres.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 225, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: ISANS Business Loan Program
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS partners with local credit unions to offer microloans to immigrant and newcomer entrepreneurs, providing capital alongside business planning and mentorship supports. This program expands access to seed and working capital for under-served founders across Nova Scotia, implementing a community-focused microfinance model that helps launch and grow local enterprises traditional lenders may overlook.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Nova Scotia Small Business Loan Guarantee Program
resources.description: Delivered through credit unions across the province, this program provides loans backed by a provincial guarantee, enabling financing for startups, expansions, and social enterprises that face collateral or credit-history barriers. By leveraging local financial co-operatives, it channels community capital into small businesses in rural and urban Nova Scotia, directly addressing gaps in traditional lending and supporting regionally distributed economic growth.
resources.address: 111 Ilsley Avenue, Unit 204, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1S8

solutions.text: Rural Transit and Community Shuttle Programs: Develop flexible, demand‑responsive shuttle services linking rural communities to regional hubs and institutions, coordinated by municipalities or community organizations to improve access to jobs and services.

resources.name: Kings Transit Authority
resources.description: Kings Transit operates public transit across the Annapolis Valley, linking rural towns and villages with regional hubs like Wolfville, Kentville, Berwick, and Middleton where jobs, colleges, health care, and services are concentrated. In addition to fixed routes, it provides route-deviated and connector services coordinated with municipalities, improving access for residents in dispersed communities. This directly implements rural shuttle connectivity by reducing transportation barriers between smaller communities and key urban amenities.
resources.address: 29 Crescent Drive, New Minas, NS B4N 3G7

resources.name: MusGo Rider Co-operative Ltd.
resources.description: MusGo Rider provides demand-responsive, door-to-door and community shuttle transportation across the Eastern Shore and Musquodoboit Valley, connecting rural residents to shopping, employment, health care, and post-secondary services in regional hubs. As a community co-operative, it coordinates rides and scheduled shuttles based on local demand, ensuring flexible, reliable links where fixed-route transit is not viable. This model directly advances rural mobility by bridging gaps between small communities and larger service centres.

solutions.text: Affordable and Flexible Housing Initiatives: Repurpose vacant buildings, support secondary suites and co‑housing projects, and offer renovation grants or tax incentives for landlords to expand affordable, youth‑friendly housing options.

resources.name: Affordable Housing Grants Program
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality provides capital grants to non-profit and co-operative housing providers to create or preserve affordable rental units, including the adaptive re-use of vacant or underutilized buildings. The program helps projects that expand youth-friendly, affordable options across both urban and rural parts of HRM by offsetting development and renovation costs.

resources.name: Secondary and Backyard Suites
resources.description: HRM’s land-use rules enable secondary and backyard suites by-right in many zones, making it easier for homeowners to add small rental units on existing properties. This expands affordable, youth-friendly housing choices throughout HRM, including suburban and rural communities, by increasing gentle-density options without requiring large new developments.

resources.name: Secondary and Garden Suites (Accessory Dwelling Units)
resources.description: The Town of Kentville permits secondary and garden suites (ADUs) in residential areas, providing homeowners with a clear pathway to add small rental units. By supporting gentle-density and infill, the initiative increases affordable options for young people and newcomers in a rural town setting while using existing infrastructure efficiently.

resources.name: Rental Property Repair Program
resources.organization: Housing Nova Scotia (Department of Municipal Affairs and Housing)
resources.description: Housing Nova Scotia offers forgivable loans to landlords to repair and upgrade rental properties in exchange for maintaining affordable rents. This renovation support keeps existing units safe and accessible, expands affordable supply in smaller and rural communities, and helps preserve youth-friendly housing close to work and services.

resources.name: New Dawn Community Housing and Adaptive Reuse Initiatives
resources.description: New Dawn repurposes and renovates existing buildings in Cape Breton Regional Municipality to create and manage affordable rental housing. By adaptively reusing underutilized properties and maintaining modest rents, the organization adds stable, youth-friendly homes in a rural region, supporting community revitalization outside the Halifax area.

solutions.text: Youth Engagement and Return‑Home Campaigns: Run local mentoring, internships, and career‑shadowing programs plus targeted marketing and relocation supports to encourage young people to stay, return, or start businesses in their home communities.

resources.name: Connector Program (ISANS)
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS’ Connector Program matches recent graduates and internationally trained youth with local professionals for short, structured mentorship meetings that build networks and open doors to work experience in Nova Scotia. By combining mentoring, employer introductions, and access to settlement/relocation support, the program helps young people establish careers and community ties that encourage them to stay or move to Nova Scotian communities, including those outside HRM.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Saint Mary’s University Entrepreneurship Centre – Student Consulting & Work-Integrated Learning
resources.description: SMUEC places students with businesses and non-profits across Nova Scotia for paid consulting projects, internships, and mentorship with local entrepreneurs. These work-integrated learning experiences and founder supports help young people gain practical skills, build local networks, and launch ventures in their home communities—encouraging them to stay in or return to rural areas after graduation.

resources.name: Acadia University Co-operative Education Program
resources.description: Acadia’s Co-op program arranges paid, supervised work terms with employers across Nova Scotia—including many in rural communities throughout the Annapolis Valley and beyond. Through career coaching, employer mentorship, and local placements (including entrepreneurship co-op terms), students build lasting ties with regional businesses and services, often leading to full-time opportunities that encourage them to stay or return after graduation.

resources.name: In.Business: A Mentorship Program for Indigenous Youth (Atlantic Region)
resources.organization: Cape Breton University – Shannon School of Business
resources.description: In.Business connects Indigenous high school students with Indigenous business mentors through a blend of in-person events and virtual mentorship led from Cape Breton University. The program nurtures entrepreneurial skills, career exploration, and community-rooted pathways that encourage participants to pursue education, start ventures, and build careers in their home communities across Nova Scotia and the Atlantic region.
resources.address: 1250 Grand Lake Road, Sydney, NS B1M 1A2

solutions.text: Place‑Making and Cultural Activation: Invest in festivals, public art, performance spaces and markets to boost local identity, attract visitors and create creative economy pathways for youth in the arts and culture sectors.

resources.name: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts – Community Arts and Festivals
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts operates a rural arts campus that hosts festivals, exhibitions, outdoor performances, and community arts events that activate public spaces in the Annapolis Valley. Through youth camps, mentorships, and production opportunities with partners, the Centre creates pathways into the creative economy while drawing visitors to a rural cultural hub and strengthening local identity.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

resources.name: Ship's Company Theatre – Summer Festival and Waterfront Performance Space
resources.description: Ship's Company Theatre presents a summer festival of new and established works in a signature waterfront performance space that anchors Parrsboro’s cultural life. The theatre attracts visitors to the Fundy coast, offers youth and emerging artist programming, and stimulates downtown businesses—demonstrating place‑making through live performance, community events, and creative employment in a rural setting.
resources.address: 18 Lower Main Street, Parrsboro, NS B0M 1S0

resources.name: King’s Theatre – Performing Arts and Community Presentations
resources.description: King’s Theatre is a historic venue in Annapolis Royal that programs film, music, theatre, and community events year‑round, animating the town’s main street and waterfront. By presenting local and touring artists, providing youth workshops and volunteer opportunities, and partnering with community groups, it builds cultural identity, draws cultural tourism, and creates on‑ramps to arts employment in a rural area.
resources.address: 209 St George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

resources.name: KitchenFest! Traditional Music Festival
resources.organization: Colaisde na Gàidhlig / The Gaelic College
resources.description: KitchenFest! is a Gaelic music and culture festival that activates venues across rural Cape Breton communities with concerts, sessions, and community celebrations. Run by the Gaelic College, it showcases local talent, provides performance and mentorship opportunities for young musicians, and brings visitors into community halls and small businesses—advancing place‑making and creative economy pathways outside urban centres.
resources.address: 51779 Cabot Trail, St. Ann’s, NS B0E 1B0

resources.name: Celtic Music Interpretive Centre – Live Music, Education and Community Events
resources.description: The Celtic Music Interpretive Centre in Judique offers daily live music, ceilidhs, educational programs, and seasonal events that celebrate and sustain local culture. Its performances, workshops, and youth programming activate community space, attract cultural tourists to rural Inverness County, and create training and employment opportunities in music and event production.

solutions.text: Shared Service Centers for Small Businesses: Provide centralized back‑office supports (accounting, HR, procurement, online sales support) so micro and small rural businesses can scale without duplicating costly infrastructure.

resources.name: Consultant Advisory Services (CAS) Program
resources.organization: CBDC NOBL (Northern Opportunities for Business Limited)
resources.description: CBDC NOBL’s CAS program gives rural micro and small businesses subsidized access to professional consultants for bookkeeping/accounting systems, human resources policies and recruitment, procurement readiness, and digital marketing/e‑commerce. By centralizing specialized expertise and making it affordable, CAS lets firms plug into back‑office functions they cannot staff in‑house, helping them scale without duplicating costly infrastructure.
resources.address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

resources.name: Perennia Innovation Centre and Advisory Services
resources.description: Perennia provides centralized technical and business advisory services for Nova Scotia’s agri‑food and seafood SMEs, including food safety/QA system implementation (e.g., HACCP), product development labs, packaging/label guidance, and market development and e‑commerce readiness. These shared services function as an external back office for producers and processors across rural communities, reducing the need to invest in their own specialized staff and facilities.
resources.address: 75 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

resources.name: Advisory and Training Services for Entrepreneurs
resources.organization: Centre for Women in Business (Mount Saint Vincent University)
resources.description: The Centre for Women in Business delivers province‑wide advisory and training that help entrepreneurs implement and improve back‑office functions such as accounting systems, HR policies and recruitment, supplier diversity/procurement readiness, and online sales/digital marketing. Acting as a shared support hub with workshops, one‑on‑one advising, and connections to vetted service providers, it enables small and rural women‑owned businesses to access the systems and expertise they need without building them internally.

resources.name: Business Advisory and Training Services
resources.description: Acadia Entrepreneurship Centre offers hands‑on advising, training, and project support that help small businesses implement bookkeeping/accounting systems, HR practices, procurement readiness, and digital commerce. As a regional hub housed at Acadia University, it centralizes expertise and tools so rural entrepreneurs in the Annapolis Valley and across Nova Scotia can access back‑office capabilities and scale efficiently.

solutions.text: Local Food and Value‑Added Processing: Support community kitchens, shared processing facilities and cooperative marketing for farmers and fishers to add value locally, increase year‑round jobs and create new exportable products.

resources.name: Perennia Food and Beverage Innovation Centre
resources.description: Perennia operates shared pilot-scale processing spaces, labs, and product development services that help farms and fisheries turn raw commodities into shelf-stable, branded foods and beverages. By providing equipment, technical expertise, and food-safety/commercialization support, the centre lowers barriers for rural producers to create value-added products, sustain year-round operations, and prepare for new export markets.
resources.address: 199 Innovation Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2H5

resources.name: WFM2Go Online Food Hub
resources.description: WFM2Go aggregates, packs, and delivers products from farmers and fishers through a province-wide online marketplace with multiple rural pickup points. The platform provides cooperative marketing, e‑commerce, and shared logistics so producers can reach customers year‑round without building their own retail or distribution systems, keeping more of the value and jobs in rural communities.

resources.name: Scotian Gold Cooperative – Packing and Processing Operations
resources.description: This grower-owned cooperative operates large-scale controlled-atmosphere storage, grading, packing, and processing facilities that transform apples into premium, branded, and export-ready products. By providing shared infrastructure and cooperative marketing, Scotian Gold helps member farms add value locally, stabilize year-round employment in the Annapolis Valley, and expand into national and international markets.

resources.name: Deanery Community Kitchen and Food Lab
resources.description: The Deanery Project offers a licensed, affordable community kitchen and food lab that local producers and startups can rent to develop, test, and package value‑added foods. Through shared equipment, training, and events that connect makers to markets, the facility strengthens the Eastern Shore’s local food economy and creates pathways for rural entrepreneurs outside HRM.
resources.address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

solutions.text: Volunteer Childcare Cooperatives: Organize parent‑run or cooperative childcare hubs that reduce costs and increase flexible childcare options, enabling parents and youth to pursue training and work locally.

resources.name: Co-operative Development Services (Childcare Co‑ops Support)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Co-operative Council provides hands-on development support to communities that want to start and run co-operatives, including parent-run childcare co-ops. They help groups incorporate, design governance where parents share duties, develop sustainable budgets and policies, and access credit union financing—reducing costs and enabling flexible, community-based childcare so parents and youth can pursue work and training locally, especially in rural areas.
resources.address: 90 Research Drive, Suite 203, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

resources.name: Co-operative Playgroups and Childminding
resources.organization: Home of the Guardian Angel (Chebucto Family Centre)
resources.description: Chebucto Family Centre supports parent-led, cooperative playgroups where caregivers rotate volunteer supervision and share responsibilities, lowering childcare costs for families. The centre provides space, coordination, and resources so parents can attend training, employment supports, and appointments—creating flexible, community-run childcare options that align with the volunteer childcare cooperative model.

resources.name: Parent Co‑operative Childcare & Playgroup Support
resources.description: New Ross Family Resource Centre facilitates parent co‑op playgroups and childminding exchanges in a rural community setting, helping families share care duties and reduce childcare costs. By organizing volunteer rosters, providing safe space and materials, and aligning sessions with skills programs and community services, the centre enables parents and youth to pursue local training and work with flexible, community-run childcare.

solutions.text: Community Energy and Climate Projects: Develop small‑scale renewable projects (solar co‑ops, biomass) that create local jobs, lower energy costs and generate revenue that can be reinvested in community services.

resources.name: Ellershouse Wind Farm
resources.description: Owned by the Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA) — a partnership of the Towns of Antigonish, Berwick, and Mahone Bay — the Ellershouse Wind Farm supplies renewable electricity to their community-owned utilities. The project creates local operations and maintenance jobs, lowers power costs for residents served by the municipal utilities, and keeps energy revenues within the towns, enabling reinvestment in community services and local infrastructure.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Mahone Bay Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility
resources.description: The Town of Mahone Bay’s municipal electric utility developed a community solar garden that allows residents and businesses to subscribe and receive bill credits from locally generated solar power. This small-scale, community-owned project reduces participants’ energy costs, supports local installers and maintenance jobs, and keeps revenues within the municipal utility so savings can be reinvested into community energy infrastructure and services.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: HRM’s Solar City provides property-assessed financing and turnkey support for solar PV and solar hot water installations across urban and rural parts of the municipality, using local contractors and trades. By enabling hundreds of small-scale systems that lower households’ energy bills, the program’s revolving loan model keeps repayments in a municipal fund to finance additional projects, effectively reinvesting benefits back into a community-run energy service.

resources.name: Energize Bridgewater (Clean Energy Financing and Community Projects)
resources.description: Energize Bridgewater helps residents and local businesses adopt rooftop solar and other clean energy upgrades through a PACE-style financing program and community partnerships, creating steady work for local installers and trades. The initiative lowers energy costs for participants and uses a revolving fund approach so repayments and municipal energy savings can be directed into further clean-energy projects and community services that benefit the town.

obstacles.title: Underinvestment in arts, culture, and recreation
obstacles.description: Limited funding, venue scarcity, and unstable support for creative spaces and community programming reduce vibrancy and retention in the arts and beyond.

solutions.text: Community Arts Microgrants: Small, locally administered grants (e.g., $250–$5,000) funded by municipal seed money, businesses, and citizen donations to support pop-up shows, youth projects, community murals, and emerging artists. Local review panels allocate funds quickly and provide simple reporting to lower barriers.

resources.name: Community Grants Program
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Community Grants Program provides small, locally administered operating grants (typically up to $5,000) to non-profit groups, including arts and culture organizations. Funds can support pop-up performances, youth-led arts projects, community murals, and other creative activations, with local review and straightforward reporting designed to lower barriers and move money quickly into community projects.

resources.name: Neighbourhood Placemaking Program
resources.description: HRM’s Neighbourhood Placemaking Program offers micro-grants and materials support to resident-led groups to create quick, low-cost public art and gathering spaces such as street murals, pop-up installations, and youth projects. A local review process and simple application/reporting help emerging artists and community volunteers access small amounts of funding and implement art-in-place projects across neighbourhoods.

resources.name: Public Art and Placemaking Grants
resources.description: The Downtown Dartmouth Business Commission provides small grants to support community murals, storefront activations, pop-up arts events, and youth or emerging-artist projects that animate public space. Funded by local businesses and administered by a local review panel, these micro-grants enable quick turnarounds and low barriers to entry, catalyzing arts-led vibrancy in the downtown core.

resources.name: Public Art & Placemaking Grants
resources.description: Downtown Truro Partnership offers small, community-driven grants for murals, pop-up shows, window galleries, and other creative placemaking led by local and emerging artists. With funding sourced from the local business community and a streamlined local review, the program moves modest grants quickly to projects that build vibrancy and accessibility in Truro’s downtown.

solutions.text: Shared Creative Spaces and Maker Hubs: Convert underused rooms, storefronts, or municipal buildings into low-cost shared studios and maker spaces with pooled tools and bench time. Managed by community boards, these hubs offer affordable workspace, equipment access, and meeting space for collaborations.

resources.name: Lou Duggan Creative Studio
resources.description: A bookable, public makerspace inside Halifax Central Library offering free or low-cost access to creative tools, supplies, and guided programming. It provides shared bench space and equipment (e.g., sewing and craft tools) plus meeting and workshop capacity, enabling community groups and individuals to prototype, create, and collaborate without the expense of owning gear.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: The Lunenburg Makery
resources.description: A community studio and sewing lounge that transforms a Main Street storefront into shared creative workspace with sewing machines, cutting tables, and craft tools. It offers affordable drop-in bench time, classes, and collaborative projects, giving makers and artists low-cost access to equipment and a supportive, community-managed environment.

resources.name: Open Studio Access (Studios Program)
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: Membership-based access to fully equipped craft studios in ceramics, textiles, metal/jewelry, and printmaking, including benches, kilns, looms, wheels, and presses. By pooling specialized tools and offering supervised, low-cost studio time, the program enables artists, youth, and community members to produce work and collaborate without high startup costs.

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic – Yarmouth Innovation Hub
resources.description: A community innovation hub providing shared prototyping labs and collaboration spaces, including access to maker tools like 3D printers and electronics benches alongside meeting rooms and coworking. Through programs and memberships, entrepreneurs, students, and community groups gain low- or no-cost access to equipment and space that supports building, testing, and collaborative projects.

resources.name: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: A cooperatively run arts venue offering affordable rehearsal, performance, and meeting space for theatre, music, dance, and community arts. Governed by a member-elected board, it functions as a shared creative hub where artists can access space, pooled production resources, and collaborative opportunities at community rates.

solutions.text: Pop-up and Mobile Venues: Organize short-term pop-up theatres, galleries, and performance stages using vacant storefronts, community centres, parks, and trailers. Rotate locations to activate neighbourhoods, reduce venue scarcity, and give emerging artists exposure without long-term overhead.

resources.name: Halifax Fringe Festival
resources.description: An annual multi-venue theatre and performance festival that converts bars, storefronts, galleries, churches, and parks into short-term stages across Halifax-Dartmouth. By activating dozens of non-traditional and rotating pop-up venues, Halifax Fringe lowers overhead for artists and expands access to audiences, giving emerging creators vital exposure without the need for long-term venue rentals.

resources.name: STAGES Theatre Festival
resources.description: Eastern Front Theatre’s annual festival presents new and experimental work in a mix of theatres, community hubs, and unconventional spaces around Dartmouth and Halifax. The program frequently stages site-specific and pop-up performances—using libraries, cafés, waterfront plazas, and outdoor areas—to rotate cultural activity through neighbourhoods and offer emerging artists low-barrier platforms.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Program
resources.description: A Downtown Halifax Business Commission grant program that funds temporary activations, including pop-up art installations, micro-galleries, and small performance stages in vacant or underused spaces. By seeding rotating, short-term projects in storefronts, laneways, and public squares, it reduces venue scarcity and creates low-cost opportunities for local and emerging artists to showcase work.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 2A2

resources.name: Lumière: Cape Breton’s Art-at-Night Festival
resources.description: This annual festival transforms downtown Sydney and surrounding communities with pop-up galleries, performances, and installations in storefronts, parks, and other public spaces—often reanimating vacant or unconventional locations for one night and related events. By dispersing programming across rotating sites, Lumière creates accessible, temporary venues that spotlight emerging and established artists without long-term overhead.

resources.name: Neptune TourCo
resources.description: Neptune Theatre’s touring program brings professional productions to schools, community centres, and rural halls across Nova Scotia, setting up temporary performance spaces in gyms and multi-use rooms. This mobile model rotates locations, expands access to live theatre, and supports emerging performers while avoiding the cost and limitations of permanent venues.

solutions.text: Artist Co-ops and Collective Galleries: Form artist-run cooperatives to share rent, marketing, administration, and exhibition costs. Co-ops stabilize income through membership fees, shared sales commissions, and rotating exhibitions that keep local art visible and affordable.

resources.name: ART 1274 Hollis Gallery
resources.description: An artist-run cooperative gallery in downtown Halifax where member artists pay dues, staff the gallery, and share operating responsibilities to keep rent, marketing, and administration affordable. The co-op runs rotating solo and group exhibitions and sells members’ work on commission, stabilizing income while keeping local art visible and accessible year-round.

resources.name: Lunenburg Art Gallery
resources.description: A volunteer, artist-run gallery operated by a membership of local creators who share staffing and administrative duties and contribute fees that support rent, promotions, and programming. The gallery presents rotating juried and member exhibitions and sells work on commission, reinvesting proceeds to sustain a cooperative space for affordable, year-round visibility of local art.

resources.name: Tidewater Art Gallery & Studio
resources.description: An artist cooperative in Pictou showcasing work by member artists from northeastern Nova Scotia. Members pay annual fees, staff the gallery, and pool resources for rent, marketing, and administration, while shared sales commissions and rotating exhibitions sustain operations and keep regional art visible and affordable for the community.

resources.name: ARTsPLACE (Artist-Run Centre)
resources.description: ARTsPLACE is an artist-run centre where artists share governance and volunteer roles, with membership fees and commissions helping cover rent, exhibitions, and marketing. The centre hosts multiple rotating shows and a members’ retail gallery, spreading administrative and promotional costs across the collective while keeping local art consistently in view.
resources.address: 396 St George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

solutions.text: Creative Placemaking and Public Art Projects: Community-led placemaking initiatives that fund and install murals, pocket parks, performance squares, and wayfinding art. Projects are planned with neighbourhood input, employ local artists, and make public space more attractive to residents and visitors.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Program
resources.description: Gritty to Pretty provides grants to create murals, public art installations, parklets, and streetscape enhancements throughout downtown Halifax. The program engages local artists and property owners through a community application process, resulting in neighbourhood-driven art, wayfinding, and small public spaces that animate streets and attract residents and visitors.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 3X7

resources.name: Public Art & Placemaking Program
resources.description: The Downtown Dartmouth Business Commission supports murals, utility box art, seasonal streetscape features, and small public space activations in the downtown core. Projects are developed with input from local businesses and residents and employ Nova Scotia artists to improve wayfinding, beautify public areas, and create vibrant gathering spots.

resources.name: Placemaking Program
resources.description: Downtown Truro Partnership’s Placemaking Program funds and delivers community-led projects like murals, parklets, planters, lighting, and wayfinding that enhance downtown public spaces. By commissioning local artists and collaborating with residents and businesses, the program animates streets and squares to make downtown Truro more welcoming for everyday use and events.

resources.name: Public Art Program
resources.description: HRM’s Public Art Program commissions permanent and temporary public artworks, supports community-led art projects, and integrates artist engagement into civic spaces and wayfinding. Through open calls and neighbourhood collaboration, the program hires local artists to create murals, installations, and site-specific works that enliven parks, plazas, and streets across the municipality.

resources.name: Halifax Waterfront Public Art and Placemaking
resources.description: Build Nova Scotia curates and delivers public art, event spaces, seating areas, and wayfinding along the Halifax waterfront through year-round placemaking. Working with local and Mi’kmaw artists and engaging the community, the initiative installs temporary and permanent artworks, pocket parks, and performance zones that draw visitors and create inviting public spaces.
resources.address: 1875 Upper Water Street, Suite 301, Halifax, NS B3J 1S9

solutions.text: Volunteer-run Festivals and Event Series: Local volunteers, businesses, and artists co-produce annual or seasonal festivals, street fairs, and concert series. Shared volunteer structures, sponsorship tiers, and in-kind contributions reduce costs while creating recurring cultural draws.

resources.name: Paint the Town
resources.description: Paint the Town is an annual plein air art festival and auction where artists paint throughout Annapolis Royal and volunteers coordinate logistics, sales, and community outreach. Local businesses provide sponsorships and in-kind support (e.g., hosting sites, materials, and services), keeping costs low while creating a recurring cultural draw that fills streets and venues each summer.
resources.address: 396 St George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

resources.name: Lunenburg Folk Harbour Festival
resources.description: This multi-day summer music festival is produced by a volunteer-driven society that partners with local venues, artists, and sponsors to present concerts and community events across Lunenburg. With hundreds of volunteers, tiered sponsorships, and in-kind contributions (such as billeting performers and donated services), the festival reduces operating costs while creating an annual cultural anchor for the town.

resources.name: Halifax Lebanese Festival
resources.organization: Our Lady of Lebanon Maronite Catholic Church
resources.description: An annual, volunteer-run cultural festival featuring music, dance, food, and artisan vendors on the church grounds, produced in partnership with community members and local sponsors. The event relies on sponsorship tiers and extensive in-kind contributions (equipment, food preparation, and services) to keep expenses manageable while drawing large, recurring audiences to celebrate arts and culture.
resources.address: 111 Clayton Park Drive, Halifax, NS B3M 1M6

resources.name: Music at the Barn Summer Concert Series
resources.description: This seasonal, volunteer-led concert series brings local and touring musicians to a community-run venue in Hubbards, with operations supported by sponsorships and in-kind help from area businesses and residents. Low overhead and shared volunteer structures keep the series sustainable while creating a reliable, recurring cultural gathering that activates the community each summer.

solutions.text: Artist-in-School and Community Residency Programs: Partner schools, libraries, and community centres with artists for temporary residencies that deliver workshops, co-created public works, and skill-building for youth. Funding comes from microgrants, parent councils, and local foundations.

resources.name: ArtsSmarts Nova Scotia
resources.description: ArtsSmarts Nova Scotia funds collaborative artist–teacher projects in K–12 schools across the province, supporting short-term residencies where artists co-plan curriculum-linked activities and lead hands-on workshops with students. Projects commonly culminate in public showcases—exhibitions, performances, or installations—co-created by youth, building creative skills and confidence. The microgrant model encourages cost-sharing with school budgets, parent/guardian councils, and community partners to leverage local support.
resources.address: 1741 Brunswick Street, 3rd Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 3X8

resources.name: Writers in the Schools (WITS)
resources.description: WITS places professional authors, poets, and spoken-word artists in classrooms and school libraries to deliver multi-session workshops and mentorship for youth. Residencies often culminate in co-created chapbooks, readings, or zines that showcase student work while building literacy, storytelling, and creative career skills. Program fees are subsidized by the federation and local sponsors, with additional support frequently provided by school budgets and parent councils.

resources.name: ArtsReach
resources.organization: The Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: ArtsReach sends Ross Creek’s resident and visiting artists into schools and community centres across rural Nova Scotia for short-term residencies. Artists lead hands-on workshops and co-create murals, performances, and other public artworks with youth, building skills in visual and performing arts while engaging local communities. The initiative is sustained through grants, foundation support, and contributions from local partners to keep programming accessible.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

resources.name: ArtReach (Education & Outreach)
resources.description: AGNS’s ArtReach program brings artist-educators into schools, libraries, and community venues across Nova Scotia to deliver workshops and collaborative projects with children and youth. Activities often culminate in shared exhibitions or community art displays that reflect local stories, strengthening skills and connections among participants. Programming is supported by the Gallery’s donors, sponsors, and foundation partners to reduce barriers to access.

solutions.text: Business-Artist Partnerships and Buy-Local Campaigns: Encourage local businesses to commission artists, host exhibits, or sponsor events. Launch buy-local promotions that spotlight creative products and experiences, creating income streams while strengthening local supply chains.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Grants
resources.description: Gritty to Pretty is a placemaking grants program that funds murals, storefront art, and public installations by local artists on or near downtown businesses. By commissioning artists and supporting business-led beautification, it forges direct partnerships between merchants and creatives. The commission also runs recurring Shop Downtown Halifax buy-local promotions that spotlight creative retailers and cultural experiences, channeling spending to local artists and the downtown supply chain.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 3X7

resources.name: Centre for Craft Nova Scotia & Mary E. Black Gallery
resources.description: The Centre for Craft Nova Scotia and its Mary E. Black Gallery present exhibitions, a retail shop, and programs that connect craftspeople with buyers and corporate clients. They collaborate with local businesses for commissions, retail partnerships, and sponsorships, and run seasonal buy-local craft promotions that highlight Nova Scotia–made work. This creates steady income streams for artists while keeping purchasing within the provincial creative economy.

resources.name: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design — Retail Shop and Exhibitions
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design operates a retail gallery and year-round exhibitions that feature Cape Breton artisans. The Centre brokers partnerships with local businesses and tourism operators for corporate gifts, commissions, and pop-up showcases, and promotes buy-local craft through campaigns and events. These activities link artists directly with buyers and business sponsors, strengthening local cultural supply chains.

resources.name: Alderney Landing Seaside Farmers’ Market & Cultural Events
resources.description: Alderney Landing runs The Craig Gallery and the Seaside Farmers’ Market, providing businesses with opportunities to sponsor and host exhibits while showcasing local artists and makers. Its festivals and markets are explicit buy-local platforms, drawing residents to purchase creative products and experiences from Nova Scotia vendors. The venue’s programming creates mutually beneficial ties between merchants and artists across downtown Dartmouth.

resources.name: Paint the Town
resources.description: Paint the Town is a live art-making and auction weekend where artists create works across Annapolis Royal, often hosted or sponsored by local businesses. Finished pieces are auctioned to the public the same day, generating income for artists and the arts council while activating shops, restaurants, and public spaces. The event is a proven business–artist partnership and a buy-local celebration that keeps arts spending in the community.
resources.address: 396 St. George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

solutions.text: Timebanking and Equipment Libraries: Create a community timebank where volunteers trade skills (e.g., event planning for rehearsal time) and a tool/equipment library where sound, lighting, and art supplies can be borrowed, lowering barriers for small-scale productions.

resources.name: Halifax Tool Library
resources.description: A member-run library that lends hand and power tools for woodworking, home repair, set building, and creative projects. By providing affordable access to tools and workshops, it lowers costs for small-scale arts and culture productions that need equipment for staging, props, and installation builds.

resources.name: Library of Things: Musical Instruments & Recording Kits
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries lends instruments (e.g., guitars, ukuleles) and portable recording gear, and provides in-branch studios for audio production. This equipment access model functions as an arts-focused lending library, reducing financial barriers for emerging artists and youth to create music, podcasts, and performance-ready material.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: AFCOOP Equipment Rentals
resources.description: AFCOOP maintains a comprehensive pool of film and media gear—cameras, lighting, grip, and audio—available to members at subsidized rates. By operating a cooperative equipment library and offering training, AFCOOP enables low-budget and emerging creators to mount small-scale productions without the prohibitive cost of owning gear.

resources.name: Centre for Art Tapes Equipment Access
resources.description: CFAT provides members with access to media-arts equipment including cameras, audio recorders, lighting, and post-production resources. This shared-equipment model functions as an equipment library for experimental and community media projects, lowering the cost of producing installations, video art, and small film works.

solutions.text: Community Cultural Space Acquisition Fund: A pooled community fund, supplemented by municipal incentives and local donors, to purchase or secure long-term leases on affordable cultural spaces. Managed transparently by a community trust to protect venues from market volatility.

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op purchased its building at 2203 Gottingen Street through a blended financing model that combined community bonds and donations with municipal and provincial/federal cultural-space grants. As a member-owned cooperative with transparent governance, it functions like a community trust, holding the asset in perpetuity and offering affordable, long-term access to rehearsal and performance space protected from market volatility.

resources.name: Eltuek Arts Centre
resources.description: Eltuek Arts Centre, a project of New Dawn Enterprises, acquired and redeveloped the former Holy Angels Convent as a community-owned arts hub using a mix of philanthropic gifts, community fundraising, and government cultural-infrastructure support. By providing below-market, long-term studios and creative workspaces under community ownership and governance, Eltuek implements a pooled, community-anchored model that secures cultural space and shields it from real estate pressures.

resources.name: deCoste Performing Arts Centre
resources.description: The deCoste Performing Arts Centre is a community-owned venue that has undertaken multi-year capital campaigns to renew and expand its facility using pooled community donations alongside municipal, provincial, and federal grants. This blended financing and non-profit stewardship model secures an affordable, long-term cultural space for northern Nova Scotia, protecting the venue from market volatility while supporting year-round arts programming.

resources.name: Chester Playhouse
resources.description: The Chester Playhouse Theatre Society owns and operates the Chester Playhouse and has rebuilt and modernized the venue through pooled community fundraising augmented by municipal, provincial, and federal support. Community ownership and transparent non-profit governance keep rental rates affordable and ensure the space is held for public benefit over the long term, insulating the venue from commercial real estate pressures.

solutions.text: Mentorship, Training, and Small-Business Support for Creatives: Peer mentorship networks and short training series on entrepreneurship, grant-writing, marketing, and digital sales, run by experienced local artists and business owners. Provide templates, shared accounting resources, and co-op buying power.

resources.name: VANS Mentorship Program
resources.description: Visual Arts Nova Scotia’s year-long Mentorship Program pairs emerging artists with established local mentors for one-on-one guidance on portfolio development, grant-writing, pricing, and marketing. VANS also delivers short professional development workshops on taxes for artists, contracts, social media, and e-commerce, and shares practical templates (CVs, budgets, invoices) and peer networks that help creatives run sustainable small businesses.
resources.address: 1113 Marginal Road, Suite 141, Halifax, NS B3H 4P7

resources.name: Craft Business Skills Workshops
resources.organization: Craft Nova Scotia (Nova Scotia Centre for Craft and Design)
resources.description: Through the Centre for Craft Nova Scotia, this workshop series provides short, practical training for craft artists on entrepreneurship, including pricing, wholesale readiness, branding, digital sales, and marketing. Participants also access mentorship from experienced makers, shared resources such as line sheet and contract templates, and collective marketing/retail opportunities that increase market reach and reduce individual costs.
resources.address: 1061 Marginal Road, Suite 140, Halifax, NS B3H 4P7

resources.name: Creative Entrepreneurship Program
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design’s entrepreneurship programming helps artisans build viable businesses through training on business planning, bookkeeping, grant-writing, product pricing, and online sales. The Centre connects participants with established local craft entrepreneurs as mentors, offers shared studios and retail/gallery channels, and provides templates and bookkeeping resources that lower barriers for small creative enterprises.

resources.name: Business Affairs Workshop Series
resources.description: Screen Nova Scotia delivers producer-focused training and mentorship led by experienced local producers and business affairs professionals, covering financing, budgeting, contracting, tax credits, marketing, and distribution. It also shares production guides and template resources, facilitates peer mentorship and networking, and provides member supports that function as shared resources for creative small businesses in the screen sector.
resources.address: 1800 Argyle Street, Suite 802, Halifax, NS B3J 3N8

solutions.text: Youth-led Arts Councils and Advisory Boards: Establish youth advisory bodies that plan programming, allocate microgrants, and advise municipal cultural policy. Empowering youth builds leadership, ensures relevant programming, and improves retention of young creatives.

resources.name: Youth Advisory Committee (YAC)
resources.description: The Halifax Regional Municipality’s Youth Advisory Committee provides direct advice to Regional Council on policies, programs, and services affecting young people, including arts, culture, and recreation. By elevating youth voices in municipal cultural planning and community programming, the YAC helps ensure initiatives are relevant to young creatives and strengthens youth leadership in local decision-making.

resources.name: Teen Advisory Groups (TAG)
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries’ Teen Advisory Groups are youth-led councils at multiple branches that co-design and lead arts and culture programming such as open mics, zines, exhibits, and creative workshops. TAG members advise staff on services and spaces for teens and help steward branch-level resources for youth-led events, building leadership while keeping programming relevant to local youth.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Teen Arts Council (TAC)
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: Ross Creek’s Teen Arts Council is a youth leadership body that plans and curates youth-led arts programming, exhibitions, and special events at the centre and in surrounding communities. TAC members advise organizational staff on youth engagement and help direct resources like space, materials, and promotional support to peer-led creative projects, nurturing young creative leaders in rural Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

resources.name: Youth Advisory Council (YAC)
resources.description: The MacPhee Centre’s Youth Advisory Council engages teens and young adults in shaping the centre’s creative programming, from designing workshops and exhibitions to hosting community arts events. Through ongoing advising and co-creation with staff, the council ensures programs reflect youth priorities and helps guide how resources like space, materials, and artist stipends are used for youth-led initiatives.

solutions.text: Advocacy for Flexible Zoning and Fast-track Permits: Community coalitions lobby municipal governments to create flexible zoning for pop-up venues, affordable studio conversions, and simplified permitting for neighbourhood arts events to reduce bureaucratic barriers.

resources.name: Halifax Music Advisory Committee
resources.description: A citizen advisory body to Halifax Regional Council that brings together artists, venue operators, and industry stakeholders to remove red tape for live music and community arts programming. The committee recommends policy changes such as venue-compatible zoning, agent-of-change principles, and streamlined temporary event permits, advocating directly to HRM staff and Council for faster approvals of pop-up shows and neighbourhood performances.

resources.name: ArtsHalifax Advisory Committee
resources.description: An HRM advisory committee that consults the arts sector and advises Council on policies that improve access to creative space and simplify permitting for community arts events. Through recommendations on cultural spaces planning, interim use of vacant buildings, and special event processes, the committee advocates for flexible zoning and faster, clearer approvals for pop-up galleries, affordable studio conversions, and neighbourhood arts activations.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Program
resources.description: A placemaking program that funds and coordinates murals, parklets, pop-up installations, and micro-festivals in downtown Halifax while advocating for simpler approvals to make them possible. The program regularly works with HRM to pilot and streamline right-of-way, encroachment, and event permits and helps artists and businesses navigate or consolidate applications—advancing flexible rules for temporary venues and creative use of underused spaces.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 3X7

resources.name: Open Street Sundays Dartmouth
resources.description: Recurring street-activation events that transform Portland Street and surrounding areas into pedestrian-first arts and culture spaces with pop-up performances and vendors. The organizers coordinate with HRM to secure road closures and advocate for predictable, faster special-event permitting and temporary occupancy for creative pop-ups—reducing barriers for neighbourhood arts programming and encouraging flexible use of public and storefront spaces.

solutions.text: Community Crowdfunding and Local Investment Campaigns: Organize crowdfunding drives and community investment shares to finance specific spaces, festivals, or artist incubators. Combine small citizen contributions with matching municipal or business funds to build sustainable capital.

resources.name: Save the Bus Stop Theatre (Community Ownership Campaign)
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op organized a multi-year community crowdfunding and ownership drive to purchase and renovate its permanent venue on Gottingen Street. Hundreds of small citizen donations and co-op memberships/shares were combined with municipal and provincial capital support to secure and improve an affordable, multi-use arts hub.
