resources.description: IGNITE Atlantic operates collaborative innovation hubs that provide community workshops in digital skills, robotics, prototyping, and entrepreneurship, along with access to maker tools such as 3D printers and electronics kits. Its programs bring together youth, postsecondary students, startups, and industry to develop practical skills and prototype marketable solutions. By mentoring teams and connecting them with regional companies and investors, IGNITE turns community learning into a pipeline for local commercialization projects.

resources.name: NSCC Continuing Education (Ivany Campus)
resources.description: NSCC’s Ivany Campus offers short-format Continuing Education courses and workshops in trades refreshers (e.g., welding, machining, carpentry), digital media, and fabrication, alongside access to campus labs and applied research supports. These practical, community-accessible offerings help residents upgrade skills and prototype ideas aligned with local industry needs. Through industry-partnered projects, co-ops, and entrepreneurship supports, NSCC provides a direct pathway from skills training to employment and commercialization in the region.

resources.name: The People’s Place: Antigonish Town & County Library (Makerspace Programs)
resources.description: The People’s Place Library hosts community makerspace programming with 3D printing, coding clubs, robotics kits, and digital media tools that are free or low-cost to use. Workshops build practical fabrication and tech skills for youth and adults, enabling residents to prototype, test, and showcase ideas. By partnering with schools, local groups, and entrepreneurs, the library helps convert community learning into pathways for local projects, startups, and employment.

solutions.text: Community Angel and Investor Network: Organize local informal investor groups and pitch nights that prioritize community impact, keeping early-stage capital and mentorship focused on regional ventures.

resources.name: Volta Cohort
resources.description: Volta Cohort is a recurring pitch competition that provides early-stage Atlantic Canadian startups with investment (typically $25,000), mentorship, and access to Volta’s community. By hosting public pitch nights and engaging local partners and investors, the program keeps early-stage capital and guidance focused on regional ventures and strengthens the local founder–investor network.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: Creative Destruction Lab – Atlantic
resources.organization: Rowe School of Business, Dalhousie University
resources.description: CDL-Atlantic runs a mentorship-driven program at Dalhousie University where founders present in a series of objective-based sessions to a group of seasoned entrepreneurs and active angel/VC investors. These sessions function as structured pitch and decision meetings that connect local companies with capital and hands-on mentorship, helping translate regional research and ideas into scalable ventures.

resources.name: New Dawn Community Economic Development Investment Fund (CEDIF)
resources.description: New Dawn’s CEDIF mobilizes community investors in Cape Breton to pool capital and invest in local businesses, often engaging entrepreneurs through information sessions and community pitch-style presentations. This keeps investment dollars and mentorship rooted in the region, aligning investor interests with community impact and job creation.

resources.name: Atlantic Venture Forum
resources.description: The Atlantic Venture Forum is an annual Halifax event where startups and scale-ups pitch to panels of angel investors, venture capitalists, and industry leaders. By convening investors and founders for curated pitch sessions and networking in Nova Scotia, it channels early-stage capital and mentorship to regional companies and strengthens the local commercialization pipeline.
resources.address: Halifax Convention Centre, 1650 Argyle Street, Halifax, NS B3J 0E6

resources.name: Ocean Startup Challenge
resources.description: The Ocean Startup Challenge is a pan-Atlantic program led from Nova Scotia that runs competitive pitch rounds offering non-dilutive funding, mentorship, and investor exposure for ocean-tech startups. Through pitch events, investor showcases, and ongoing guidance anchored at COVE, it directs early-stage resources and relationships to regional ventures tackling ocean-industry problems.
resources.address: COVE, 27 Parker Street, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 4T5

solutions.text: Business Incubation Exchanges: Coordinate short-term exchanges where postsecondary commercialization staff and industry practitioners co-locate in community incubators to fast-track tech transfer and product-market fit activities.

resources.name: Start-Up Yard at COVE
resources.organization: Invest Nova Scotia in partnership with the Centre for Ocean Ventures & Entrepreneurship (COVE)
resources.description: Start-Up Yard at COVE is an ocean-technology incubator that co-locates startups, established marine companies, and postsecondary partners to accelerate commercialization. Through regular on-site programming and office hours with university/college commercialization teams (e.g., Dalhousie, NSCC, and Springboard Atlantic members), industry practitioners and academic staff work side-by-side in shared labs and workshops to advance tech transfer and validate product–market fit with real users. The facility’s proximity to naval, port, and offshore partners enables rapid prototyping, testing, and procurement-informed feedback loops.

resources.name: Volta Residency Program
resources.description: Volta’s Residency Program provides startups with dedicated space inside a community incubator where corporate innovation teams and postsecondary commercialization staff frequently run embedded office hours and pop-up clinics. Dal Innovates, Mitacs, and Springboard Atlantic members regularly engage on-site, enabling short-term exchanges that connect researchers and tech-transfer professionals with founders and industry mentors to pressure-test market needs and accelerate commercialization. This co-location model supports rapid product–market fit discovery and streamlines pathways from research to procurement-ready solutions.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Unit 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic Community Innovation Hubs
resources.description: IGNITE operates rural innovation hubs that intentionally co-locate founders, industry practitioners, and postsecondary partners (NSCC, StFX LaunchBox, Dal Innovates and others) through rotating office hours, embedded residencies, and challenge sprints. These short-term exchanges bring commercialization staff into the community incubator to work alongside companies on customer discovery, prototyping, and pilot projects with local industry, speeding up tech transfer and product–market fit. The hubs also facilitate procurement-focused collaborations with municipal and regional partners to help ventures land first customers.
resources.address: Unit 2, 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

resources.name: Navigate Startup House
resources.organization: Cape Breton University and Nova Scotia Community College, in partnership with the Cape Breton Partnership
resources.description: Navigate Startup House is a community incubator jointly driven by Cape Breton University and Nova Scotia Community College that co-locates student and faculty-led ventures with industry mentors and regional partners. By bringing postsecondary entrepreneurship and commercialization supports into a shared space with local businesses, Navigate facilitates short-term exchanges, advisor-in-residence hours, and collaborative sprints that translate research and prototypes into market-validated products. This setup strengthens university–industry linkages in Cape Breton and accelerates commercialization pathways for local talent.
resources.address: New Dawn Centre for Social Innovation, 37 Nepean Street, Sydney, NS B1P 1K4

solutions.text: Open Data and Procurement Opportunity Portal: Maintain a community-run online portal that lists local procurement opportunities, research partnership requests, available facilities and equipment, and talent seeking projects to reduce silos.

resources.name: Halifax eProcurement (bids&tenders)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s eProcurement portal publicly lists municipal RFPs, RFQs, tenders, and contract awards, making local procurement opportunities transparent and easy to discover for startups, SMEs, postsecondary researchers, and nonprofits. By centralizing opportunities and supplier registration in one online portal, it reduces silos and lowers barriers for local innovators to partner with the city and win work.

resources.name: COVE Careers & Opportunities
resources.organization: Centre for Ocean Ventures and Entrepreneurship (COVE)
resources.description: COVE’s online portal aggregates ocean-sector job postings, collaboration calls, startup programs, and supplier opportunities from across Nova Scotia’s marine innovation community. Combined with COVE’s member directory and shared test facilities, the portal connects industry, researchers, and talent—making equipment access and partnership requests visible in one place to break down ecosystem silos.

resources.name: Dalhousie Core Research Facilities
resources.description: Dalhousie maintains an online directory of core research facilities and shared equipment that are available to external partners, with technical descriptions, access details, and contacts for collaboration. This open facilities listing helps industry and community organizations find the tools and expertise they need, facilitating research partnerships and commercialization pathways within Nova Scotia.

resources.name: NSCC Applied Research: Facilities & Equipment
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) Applied Research
resources.description: NSCC’s applied research site showcases labs, specialized equipment, and technical services across its campuses, with pathways for companies and community groups to propose projects and access college resources. By openly listing capabilities and partnership contacts, it enables industry–postsecondary collaboration and gives local firms and talent a centralized view of available facilities and expertise.

solutions.text: Place-Based Innovation Challenges: Run annual community challenges that invite cross-sector teams to solve local problems (housing, fisheries, tourism) with seed funding, mentorship, and guaranteed pilot sites with municipal support.

resources.name: Civic Innovation Outpost
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality (in partnership with Volta)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Civic Innovation Outpost, hosted at Volta, runs recurring challenge calls where HRM departments publish problem statements (e.g., mobility, housing services, permitting, public safety) and invite startups, students, and industry partners to co-develop solutions. Selected teams receive mentorship and workspace support through Volta and work with HRM staff to run real-world pilots inside municipal operations, creating a procurement pathway and de-risking commercialization in a place-based setting.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: Municipal Innovation Program (MIP)
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Federation of Municipalities’ MIP provides competitive, challenge-style funding to collaborative municipal projects that test new solutions in areas like housing, infrastructure, climate adaptation, and service delivery. Cross-sector teams—often including municipalities, private firms, and postsecondary researchers—receive seed funding and support to run pilots within participating municipalities, overcoming procurement barriers and accelerating commercialization in a local, place-based context.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1304, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: COVE Ocean Challenges
resources.description: COVE organizes challenge competitions that invite cross-disciplinary teams to solve ocean-sector problems relevant to Nova Scotia’s fisheries, marine transportation, and offshore industries. Winners receive mentorship, access to COVE’s testbeds and waterfront facilities, and opportunities to pilot and demonstrate solutions in Halifax Harbour and with local industry partners—providing place-based validation and pathways to commercialization.

resources.name: Ocean Startup Challenge
resources.description: This annual competition invites startups and research teams to develop solutions for ocean challenges spanning fisheries, aquaculture, shipping, and marine monitoring. Teams receive seed funding, mentorship, and connections to Nova Scotia-based test sites and industry partners (including ports, seafood companies, and research facilities), enabling place-based pilots that speed up commercialization and job creation in the province’s ocean economy.

resources.name: IGNITE Reverse Pitch: Municipal Innovation Challenges
resources.description: IGNITE works with rural municipalities and community partners to run reverse-pitch challenges where local governments articulate pressing problems (e.g., waste management, tourism seasonality, coastal resilience) and invite cross-sector teams to propose solutions. Selected teams receive mentorship, micro-grants, and facilitated access to municipal departments to pilot in the host communities—creating a supported, place-based pathway from prototype to adoption.
resources.address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

solutions.text: Cultural-Tech Collaboration Labs: Create programs that bring artists together with technologists and small businesses to co-create products and experiences, broadening commercialization pathways beyond traditional tech sectors.

resources.name: FabLab at Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: FabLab is a digital fabrication studio where artists, craftspeople, technologists, and local businesses co-create products using tools like laser cutters, CNC routers, and 3D printers. The program supports prototyping, small-batch manufacturing, and product development, pairing creative practitioners with technical mentors and entrepreneurs to commercialize new craft-tech offerings beyond traditional software sectors.

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic Makerspace and Innovation Programs
resources.description: IGNITE operates community makerspaces and runs cross-disciplinary programming that brings together artists, designers, technologists, and small businesses to build prototypes, interactive installations, and market-ready products. Through mentorship, equipment access (e.g., 3D printing, laser cutting, electronics), and industry challenges, the programs create commercialization pathways for creative-tech collaborations across rural and urban Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries Creation Spaces (Media Studio and 3D Printing)
resources.description: The Creation Spaces provide public access to media production studios, 3D printers, and digital tools that enable artists, technologists, and entrepreneurs to co-develop content, prototypes, and immersive experiences. Workshops and open labs foster collaboration between creatives and small businesses, lowering barriers to experimentation and helping cultural-tech ideas move toward marketable products and services.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: ShiftKey Labs (Nova Scotia Sandbox Program)
resources.organization: Faculty of Computer Science, Dalhousie University
resources.description: ShiftKey Labs convenes interdisciplinary teams through hackathons, design sprints, and industry projects that pair developers and technologists with designers, artists, and local firms to create new digital experiences and products. By connecting creative talent with small-business challenges and mentorship, the lab accelerates commercialization of cultural-tech solutions outside traditional tech-only pipelines.
resources.address: Goldberg Computer Science Building, 6050 University Avenue, Halifax, NS B3H 1W5

resources.name: The Spark Zone (Nova Scotia Sandbox)
resources.description: The Spark Zone is a multi-institution innovation sandbox that includes NSCAD University and brings students and community members from arts, design, technology, and business together to co-create products and creative services with local companies. Through client-driven projects, mentorship, and venture support, it translates cultural and design ideas into market-ready offerings, broadening commercialization beyond traditional tech sectors.

solutions.text: Local Success Stories Campaign: Promote returning and staying talent by storytelling—sharing profiles of local entrepreneurs, apprentices, and innovators to inspire youth and signal that viable careers can be built here.

resources.name: CEED Client Success Stories
resources.organization: Centre for Entrepreneurship Education and Development (CEED)
resources.description: CEED regularly publishes client success stories and founder spotlights featuring Nova Scotia entrepreneurs from diverse sectors. By showcasing how local founders started and scaled here—and mapping supports like training, financing, and mentorship—these narratives inspire youth and returnees to see viable careers and ventures in the province, advancing a culture of staying and building locally.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 225, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: NSCC Alumni Success Stories
resources.description: NSCC’s Alumni Success Stories highlight graduates—from skilled trades apprentices to tech developers and social entrepreneurs—who built careers and businesses in communities across Nova Scotia. Through detailed profiles and videos shared with students, employers, and partners, NSCC demonstrates clear local career pathways and role models, encouraging youth to stay, study, and work in the province while showcasing collaboration with industry.

resources.name: ISANS Client Success Stories
resources.organization: Immigration Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS publishes client success stories profiling newcomer entrepreneurs, skilled workers, and innovators who have established careers and companies in Nova Scotia. These stories, shared online and at events, illustrate tangible pathways—mentorship, training, networking, and procurement navigation—signaling that newcomers can thrive and contribute to local industries while inspiring others to settle and stay.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: IGNITE Stories
resources.description: IGNITE Atlantic spotlights founders, students, and innovators from rural Nova Scotia through articles, videos, and events that celebrate homegrown success. By telling the journeys of local companies and youth-led projects—and pointing to ecosystem supports that helped them—IGNITE’s storytelling inspires students and returnees to pursue careers and startups in their home communities and fosters cross-sector collaboration.
resources.address: 208 Main Street, Unit 101, Yarmouth, NS B5A 1C8

resources.name: Entrepreneur Spotlights
resources.description: The Saint Mary’s University Entrepreneurship Centre (SMUEC) shares entrepreneur spotlights and student-led venture profiles that feature alumni and founders building companies in Halifax and across Nova Scotia. These narratives highlight accessible supports—consulting programs, mentors, and funding—showing concrete local career and startup pathways that encourage students and recent grads to stay or return.

obstacles.title: Energy affordability and reliability
obstacles.description: High electricity costs and grid capacity constraints challenge households and deter energy-intensive or advanced manufacturing investments.

solutions.text: Community-owned solar co‑ops (community solar gardens): Neighbourhood or municipal co‑ops develop shared solar arrays where households, small businesses and local manufacturers buy or subscribe to generation capacity, lowering electricity costs, keeping revenue local and improving grid resilience.

resources.name: Berwick Community Solar Garden
resources.description: The Berwick Community Solar Garden allows customers of the Berwick Electric Commission to subscribe to blocks of solar generation and receive on-bill credits tied to the output of the shared array. By pooling investment in a municipally managed solar site, households and small businesses lower electricity costs while revenues stay in the community and local grid resilience is strengthened.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility
resources.description: Mahone Bay’s municipal electric utility operates a community solar garden that offers residents and businesses the option to purchase subscriptions to the array’s capacity and receive bill credits based on actual production. This shared-ownership model reduces barriers to solar, keeps energy dollars local, and diversifies the local supply mix to support a more reliable community grid.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Antigonish Community Solar Garden
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish Electric Utility operates a community solar garden that enables utility customers to subscribe to shares of a centralized solar array and earn credits on their electricity bills for the power generated. This utility-led, community-owned approach lowers energy costs for participants, keeps investment in the local economy, and enhances grid reliability by adding distributed renewable generation.

solutions.text: Neighborhood microgrids with shared battery storage: Community-scale microgrids pair local generation (solar, wind) with batteries to stabilize supply, shave peak demand, and provide backup during outages — improving reliability for homes and energy‑intensive local employers.

resources.name: Smart Grid Nova Scotia – Community Energy Storage Pilot
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s Smart Grid Nova Scotia pilot deploys utility-owned, neighborhood-scale battery systems on distribution feeders in communities such as Elmsdale and Amherst. These shared batteries charge from local renewables when available and discharge to shave peak demand, stabilize feeder voltage, and provide backup support during outages—functioning as community microgrids that enhance reliability and affordability for nearby homes and businesses.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Onslow Grid Innovation Zone
resources.description: The Onslow Grid Innovation Zone integrates a utility-scale battery energy storage system with advanced distribution controls to form a microgrid capable of islanding local feeders near Truro. By pairing storage with local generation on the circuit, it smooths renewable intermittency, reduces peak loads, and keeps critical community loads energized during transmission outages—demonstrating neighborhood-scale resilience and improved reliability for customers.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

solutions.text: Bulk procurement programs for heat pumps, solar and insulation: Community-organized bulk-buy campaigns reduce unit costs and installation time for home and business upgrades (heat pumps, panels, insulation), accelerating uptake, cutting bills and creating local installer work.

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: Halifax’s Solar City aggregates homeowner and business demand for rooftop solar and secures standardized pricing through competitive procurement with pre-qualified installers, reducing unit costs and streamlining installation timelines. The municipality also provides streamlined permitting and program coordination, allowing installations to be scheduled in batches. This accelerates solar adoption, lowers energy bills, and supports steady local installer work.

resources.name: HomeWarming
resources.organization: EfficiencyOne (operating as Efficiency Nova Scotia) in partnership with Clean Foundation
resources.description: HomeWarming delivers no-cost energy efficiency upgrades—including insulation, air sealing, and often heat pumps—to qualifying low-income households across Nova Scotia, bundling many homes into coordinated work packages. By aggregating demand and working with a network of vetted contractors, the program leverages bulk purchasing and standardized scopes to lower per-home costs and compress installation timelines, while creating steady work for local trades.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Mi'kmaw Home Energy Efficiency Project (MHEEP)
resources.organization: Clean Foundation (in collaboration with Mi'kmaw communities)
resources.description: MHEEP works with Mi'kmaw communities across Nova Scotia to deliver coordinated home energy retrofits—such as insulation, air sealing, and heat pumps—using aggregated procurement and standardized installation practices. By bundling upgrades across many homes, the program reduces unit costs, shortens project timelines, and supports local workforce development through training and ongoing work for community-based installers.

solutions.text: Local retrofit and energy‑efficiency volunteer/program grants: Neighbourhood teams plus municipal grants deliver low-cost retrofits (draft sealing, LED lighting, thermostats) for low‑income households, lowering bills immediately and increasing disposable income and housing attractiveness for young residents.

resources.name: HomeWarming (Income-Qualified Home Energy Upgrades)
resources.organization: HomeWarming (delivered by Clean Foundation and Efficiency Nova Scotia/EfficiencyOne)
resources.description: HomeWarming provides no-cost energy-efficiency retrofits to income-qualified households across Nova Scotia. Trained neighborhood teams conduct in-home assessments and install draft sealing, insulation, LED lighting, and smart thermostats, immediately lowering electricity and heating costs for low-income residents and improving comfort—supporting affordability that helps young people stay and thrive.

resources.name: Mi’kmaw Home Energy Efficiency Project (MHEEP)
resources.description: MHEEP works with Mi’kmaw communities across Nova Scotia to deliver community-based, no-cost home energy retrofits in band-owned and member homes. Local teams and contractors complete air sealing, insulation, LED lighting, and programmable thermostat installs, cutting bills for low-income households while building local skills and jobs that strengthen community resilience and opportunity for youth.

resources.name: Affordable Multifamily Housing Program
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia supports non-profit and affordable housing providers with incentives and direct-install measures that reduce tenant energy bills. The program funds upgrades such as draft-proofing, high-efficiency lighting (LEDs), heating controls/thermostats, and building envelope improvements in multi-unit buildings—lowering operating costs that flow to low-income residents and improving the quality and attractiveness of housing for young families.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) – Town of Bridgewater
resources.description: Bridgewater’s Property Assessed Clean Energy program helps homeowners finance energy retrofits—such as insulation, draft sealing, LED lighting, and smart thermostats—with low-interest, on-property tax repayment that can be paired with provincial incentives. By lowering up-front costs and coordinating vetted contractors, the program enables immediate bill savings and improves home comfort, supporting affordability that attracts and retains young residents.

solutions.text: Community demand‑response and load‑flex programs: Organize local demand‑response clusters (smart thermostats, timed EV charging, coordinated industrial loads) so the community can reduce peak demand, earn incentives, and ease grid constraints during critical periods.

resources.name: Smart Grid Nova Scotia
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s Smart Grid Nova Scotia is a virtual power plant pilot that enrolls households with devices like smart thermostats, connected electric water heaters, EV chargers, and home batteries to respond to peak events. During grid-critical periods, the utility coordinates participating devices to reduce or shift load, providing bill credits or incentives to customers while easing local feeder constraints and lowering system peak demand.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Time-of-Day (TOD) Rate for Electric Thermal Storage (ETS)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s Time-of-Day rate encourages customers to use Electric Thermal Storage heaters and other controllable loads to charge or operate primarily during off‑peak hours. By shifting heating and other electricity use away from peak periods—often coordinated with programmable thermostats and timers—communities collectively reduce peak demand, mitigating grid constraints and improving affordability through lower bills and system cost savings.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Strategic Energy Management (SEM) for Business and Industry
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia’s SEM program works with commercial and industrial facilities to monitor demand, implement controls, and adopt operating procedures that curtail or shift loads during peak periods. Through coaching, metering, and controls optimization (e.g., HVAC scheduling, process staging, demand limiters), cohorts of local businesses reduce coincident peak demand, cut demand charges, and provide flexible load that supports community-level grid reliability.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

solutions.text: Local workforce training and apprenticeships in clean energy: Partner with colleges, trades and employers to run training programs and apprenticeships for solar installers, battery technicians and energy managers — creating jobs that keep young people in the region.

resources.name: Energy Sustainability Engineering Technology (ESET)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) – Ivany Campus
resources.description: NSCC’s two-year ESET diploma trains technologists to design, integrate, and manage clean energy systems including solar PV, battery storage, and building energy management. The program combines labs, field projects, and an industry work placement that connects students with Nova Scotia employers, creating a direct pipeline into local roles such as solar installer, energy technologist, and energy manager.

resources.name: On-site Energy Manager Program
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia co-funds and embeds trained energy managers within large organizations (e.g., municipalities, hospitals, campuses) to deliver energy savings projects and demand management, while providing professional development toward credentials like Certified Energy Manager. This creates in-province, employer-linked roles that reduce energy costs and improve reliability, and builds a sustained career pathway in energy management for Nova Scotians.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Clean Leadership Internship Program
resources.description: This paid internship program places youth and early-career professionals with Nova Scotia employers in clean energy and climate-related roles, including solar installers, energy efficiency firms, and community energy projects. Interns receive training, mentorship, and professional development while gaining on-the-job experience that often leads to full-time employment, helping retain young talent in the province’s clean energy sector.

resources.name: Solar School (hands-on solar PV training)
resources.description: The Deanery Project delivers hands-on workshops in solar PV design, safety, and installation—often in partnership with Solar Nova Scotia and local contractors—giving participants practical skills to work on grid-tied and battery-backed systems. By linking learners to community projects and regional installers, the program builds a local talent pipeline for solar installation and related clean energy jobs in rural and urban Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

solutions.text: Community green financing (on‑bill loans, credit union products): Local credit unions and municipalities offer low‑interest loans or on‑bill financing for energy upgrades and clean equipment for households and small manufacturers, lowering upfront barriers and spreading costs over time.

resources.name: Solar City Program (Local Improvement Charge Financing)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Solar City offers low-interest Local Improvement Charge (LIC) financing that is repaid on the property tax bill, enabling homeowners to install solar photovoltaic (PV) systems with no large upfront payment. By spreading costs over up to 10 years on the municipal bill, the program reduces affordability barriers and helps households manage energy costs while improving grid resilience through distributed generation.

resources.name: Small Business Energy Solutions — On-Bill Financing
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia’s Small Business Energy Solutions provides incentives and interest-free on-bill financing for eligible upgrades such as lighting, HVAC, and controls, with repayments made directly on the Nova Scotia Power electricity bill. This model allows small businesses and light manufacturers to undertake energy improvements without major upfront capital, smoothing cash flow and improving energy affordability and reliability.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing Program (PACE) — Town of Wolfville
resources.description: Wolfville’s Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) program offers homeowners low-interest financing for energy upgrades such as heat pumps, insulation, and solar PV, with repayment attached to the property and collected via the property tax bill. This municipal on-bill mechanism lowers upfront costs and spreads payments over time, enabling residents to reduce energy expenses and improve home comfort.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing Program (PACE) — Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
resources.organization: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
resources.description: The Municipality of the District of Lunenburg provides Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) financing that lets homeowners undertake efficiency and clean energy upgrades and repay the cost through their property tax bill over a set term. By converting upfront capital into affordable, predictable payments, the program increases access to heat pumps, insulation, and solar, supporting household energy affordability and local economic activity.

solutions.text: District heating and shared thermal systems: Develop small-scale district heating (biomass, waste heat recovery, geo) in dense communities or industrial parks to reduce reliance on electrical heating, lower per‑unit energy costs and capture local fuel resources.

resources.name: Alderney 5 Energy Project
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality operates a shared thermal loop in downtown Dartmouth that captures and redistributes recovered heat to multiple civic buildings at Alderney Landing. By using heat recovery and centralized heating/cooling for a cluster of dense municipal facilities, the project functions as a small district energy system that reduces reliance on electric resistance heating and lowers per‑unit energy costs.

resources.name: St. Francis Xavier University Biomass District Heating Upgrade
resources.description: StFX added a biomass boiler to its central heating plant and distributes steam/hot water through an on‑campus network to multiple buildings, creating a campus‑scale district energy system. The project leverages locally sourced biomass to displace electric and oil heating, cutting energy costs and peak grid demand while using a shared thermal backbone.

resources.name: Dalhousie University Central Heating Plant (District Energy System)
resources.description: Dalhousie operates a central thermal plant that distributes steam and hot water via tunnels and piping to dozens of campus buildings, functioning as a district heating network. This shared system consolidates heating loads, reduces the need for individual electric heating equipment, and enables efficiency improvements and heat recovery across a dense urban campus.

resources.name: Port Hawkesbury Biomass Combined Heat and Power (CHP)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s biomass CHP facility at Point Tupper generates electricity while delivering process steam to the adjacent Port Hawkesbury Paper mill, a shared thermal application across an industrial site. By using locally sourced biomass and capturing thermal energy for on‑site industry, it exemplifies district/industrial park heating that cuts reliance on separate electric heating and improves overall energy efficiency.
resources.address: 120 Pulp Mill Road, Port Hawkesbury, NS B9A 1A1

solutions.text: Aggregated procurement and energy parks for manufacturers: Communities aggregate demand from multiple small manufacturers to negotiate better electricity/renewable contracts or create shared energy parks (co‑located generation and storage) to attract advanced manufacturing.

resources.name: Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA) – Aggregated Renewable Procurement
resources.description: AREA is a joint venture of the municipal electric utilities of Berwick, Mahone Bay, and Antigonish that aggregates their communities’ electricity demand to develop and procure shared renewable resources. Through projects like the Ellershouse Wind Farm and additional community-scale renewables, AREA uses joint, long-term contracts to secure stable pricing and improve reliability for local customers, including small manufacturers in member towns’ industrial parks. By pooling demand, these communities achieve economies of scale that individual firms could not, directly implementing the aggregated procurement model.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Green Choice Program
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Department of Natural Resources and Renewables
resources.description: Nova Scotia’s Green Choice Program enables eligible large customers—municipalities, institutions, and businesses including manufacturers—to collectively procure electricity from new wind and solar projects through a competitive, aggregated process run with Nova Scotia Power. Participants lock in long-term renewable supply and pricing, while new capacity is added to the provincial grid to improve reliability. The program operationalizes aggregated demand from multiple customers so smaller manufacturers can access utility-scale renewables and better contract terms than they could secure alone.

resources.name: Springhill Geothermal Industrial Park
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Cumberland
resources.description: The Springhill Industrial Park uses a shared geothermal district energy system that circulates warm water from flooded mine workings to provide heating and cooling to multiple tenants. This co-located, common energy infrastructure lowers operating costs and improves reliability for manufacturers and warehouses in the park, acting as an energy park that helps attract and retain industry. By sharing energy assets across many firms, the park demonstrates the community energy-park model tailored to industrial users.
resources.address: 1395 Blair Lake Road, Upper Nappan, NS B4H 3Y4

solutions.text: Public EV charging network and V2G pilot projects: Install community EV chargers and run vehicle‑to‑grid pilots so parked EVs supply grid services and revenue, smoothing peaks, increasing asset utilization and supporting low‑cost transport for young people.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Power EV Fast-Charging Network
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power operates a province-wide network of public DC fast chargers and Level 2 stations at community hubs and along key travel corridors. By expanding public charging access and integrating chargers with utility demand-management programs, the network helps shift charging to off-peak periods, easing grid constraints and lowering transportation energy costs for residents, including young people.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Public EV Charging
resources.description: HRM installs and manages public Level 2 and DC fast EV chargers at libraries, arenas, park-and-ride lots, and municipal parking facilities across the city. The program expands low-cost, shared charging access and coordinates siting and load management with the local grid to smooth peaks, supporting reliable service while enabling affordable transportation options.

resources.name: Antigonish Electric Utility Public EV Charging
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish’s municipal utility has deployed public Level 2 EV charging stations in downtown and municipal lots, with additional sites supported by federal-provincial funding. Networked chargers provide community access to affordable transportation while enabling the utility to monitor usage and plan charging to align with local grid capacity and peak-management needs.

resources.name: NSCC–Nova Scotia Power Vehicle-to-Grid Demonstration (Ivany Campus)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (in partnership with Nova Scotia Power Inc.)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Community College, in partnership with Nova Scotia Power, operates a bidirectional charging pilot that uses V2G-capable chargers and campus EVs to provide grid services. Parked EVs discharge to the building/grid during peak events and recharge off-peak, testing revenue models and demonstrating how V2G can smooth demand, increase asset utilization, and support lower-cost electric mobility.

solutions.text: Energy literacy, advisory clinics and peer mentors: Run community workshops, one‑on‑one advisory clinics and peer mentor programs to help residents and small businesses identify cost‑effective upgrades, access incentives, and adopt demand‑flex behaviors.

resources.name: Small Business Energy Solutions
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia’s advisors provide on-site energy assessments for small businesses, offer tailored advice on cost-effective upgrades (lighting, HVAC, controls), and connect owners to available rebates and financing. They also run webinars and clinics that build energy literacy, help participants understand their bills and time-of-day options, and coach staff on demand-flex behaviors like load shifting and smart control scheduling to reduce peak demand.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Energy Assist
resources.description: Energy Assist provides in-home energy education and one-on-one navigation for income‑qualified households, including basic efficiency upgrades, personalized advice on reducing consumption, and referrals to programs like HomeWarming and Efficiency Nova Scotia rebates. Trained navigators act as mentors, helping participants plan cost‑effective upgrades, apply for incentives, and adopt demand‑flex habits such as shifting appliance use to off‑peak times.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing Program (PACE)
resources.description: Bridgewater’s Clean Energy Financing program offers group information sessions and one‑on‑one guidance to help homeowners identify practical upgrades through EnerGuide home evaluations and connect with municipal financing plus provincial/federal incentives. Program staff and contractors provide advisory support throughout the project, building energy literacy and encouraging adoption of demand‑flex measures like smart thermostats, heat pump optimization, and load shifting to manage energy costs.

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: HRM’s Solar City runs public workshops and offers one‑on‑one advisory support to help residents and small businesses evaluate solar options, understand lifecycle costs, and access municipal financing alongside provincial rebates. Advisors provide site assessments and coaching on energy literacy and demand‑flex practices, such as aligning major loads with daytime solar production and using smart controls to reduce peak grid demand.

solutions.text: Local permitting assistance and fast‑track for distributed energy: Municipal teams offer step‑by‑step permitting help, standard permit packages and fast‑track approvals for rooftop solar, batteries and small generation to reduce soft costs and speed deployment.

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: Solar City helps property owners install rooftop solar PV (and solar hot water) by pairing financing with hands-on project management. The municipal team provides step-by-step permitting assistance, standardized application packages, and direct coordination of building/electrical permits and Nova Scotia Power interconnection, effectively fast-tracking approvals to cut soft costs and speed distributed energy deployment.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing Program (PACE)
resources.description: Bridgewater’s PACE program supports rooftop solar and related home energy upgrades with financing and concierge-style support. Staff guide participants through permitting and inspections using standardized scopes and contractor packages, and they coordinate with municipal permitting and Nova Scotia Power to fast-track approvals and interconnections, reducing soft costs and accelerating small-scale clean energy adoption.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing Program (PACE)
resources.organization: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
resources.description: MODL’s program enables residents to install rooftop solar PV, solar hot water, and other upgrades with structured support. The municipality assists with permit requirements, provides template documents and pre-approved work scopes, and coordinates with building/electrical inspectors and Nova Scotia Power to streamline and fast‑track approvals, cutting administrative time and costs to speed distributed energy deployment.

solutions.text: Partnerships with utilities for community tariffs and peak sharing: Collaborate with the local utility to pilot community tariffs, aggregated meter arrangements or neighborhood peak‑sharing, so residents and small businesses benefit from lower rates tied to measured community performance.

resources.name: Berwick Solar Utility (Community Solar Garden)
resources.organization: Town of Berwick Electric Utility (Berwick Electric Commission)
resources.description: The Town of Berwick’s municipal electric utility operates a community solar garden that residents and small businesses can subscribe to, receiving on‑bill credits based on the garden’s measured output. This functions as an aggregated, community‑level arrangement where participants benefit from a shared asset and a utility‑administered crediting mechanism, effectively creating a community tariff. By generating power locally and crediting participants collectively, the program helps lower community demand from the grid during peak periods and improves affordability.
resources.address: 236 Commercial Street, Suite 1, Berwick, NS B0P 1E0

resources.name: Mahone Bay Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility
resources.description: Mahone Bay’s municipal electric utility runs a subscription‑based community solar garden that provides bill credits to customers according to the project’s metered generation. This shared, utility‑managed model aggregates participants under one community asset, aligning with community tariff concepts and enabling residents and small businesses to benefit from performance‑based credits. The local generation and coordinated utility operations also contribute to reducing neighborhood peak demand and enhancing grid capacity.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Antigonish Community Solar Garden
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish Electric Utility offers a community solar garden that allows customers to subscribe and receive on‑bill credits tied to the project’s measured production. This aggregated arrangement leverages the municipal utility’s billing to distribute benefits across multiple accounts, functioning similarly to a community tariff. By serving local load with shared solar output and coordinated operations, the program supports peak reduction and improves electricity affordability for participants.

resources.name: Domestic Service Time-of-Day (TOD) Rate for Electric Thermal Storage
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s TOD rate offers significantly lower off‑peak electricity prices for customers with qualifying electric thermal storage and related equipment, encouraging load shifting away from peak hours. While applied at individual meters, this utility tariff reduces coincident community peaks when adopted across neighborhoods, improving affordability and grid reliability. The structure supports aggregated peak‑sharing outcomes by aligning customer bills with measured off‑peak usage and community‑level peak reduction goals.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

solutions.text: Resilience hubs and community backup power: Equip schools, libraries or community centres with solar + battery microgrids to serve as resilience hubs during outages, providing critical services and protecting vulnerable residents while demonstrating local reliability solutions.

resources.name: HalifACT – Resilient Community Hubs
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality is implementing resilience hubs under its HalifACT climate plan by equipping select municipal facilities—such as libraries, recreation centres, and community halls—with rooftop solar and battery storage so they can operate during grid outages. These hubs provide critical services like device charging, refrigeration for medications, and safe warming/cooling spaces while reducing utility costs in normal operations and demonstrating local solar-plus-storage reliability solutions.

resources.name: Energize Bridgewater – Community Energy Resilience
resources.description: Through its Smart Cities initiative and Community Energy Investment Plan, the Town of Bridgewater is deploying solar PV and battery storage at priority municipal and community facilities to create resilience hubs that can remain operational during power outages. These sites are designed to support residents with essential services—like heating/cooling, charging, and communications—while lowering operating costs and showcasing practical, local microgrid reliability solutions.

resources.name: Community Energy Resilience Projects
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre works with municipalities and community organizations across Nova Scotia to design and implement solar-plus-battery systems at community buildings—such as halls and libraries—so they can serve as resilience hubs during outages. The projects reduce energy costs year-round, provide critical services to vulnerable residents when the grid is down, and build local capacity by demonstrating scalable microgrid solutions.

obstacles.title: Nonprofit and community-service capacity strain
obstacles.description: Chronic underfunding, volunteer burnout, and thin philanthropy limit the social supports and community life that make places sticky for young people.

solutions.text: Community Micro-Grant Pool: Create a locally governed micro-grant fund seeded by small donations from residents, businesses, and events to provide rapid, flexible funding for neighborhood projects, arts initiatives, and pilot programs that help sustain community services.

resources.name: Neighbourhood Fund
resources.description: United Way Halifax’s Neighbourhood Fund offers small, rapid-response grants to resident-led groups, grassroots organizers, and community organizations to run neighbourhood projects, pop-up arts and culture activities, and service pilots. The fund is sustained by pooled local donations from individuals, workplace campaigns, and business sponsors, and is governed locally to keep decisions close to community needs—implementing a flexible micro-grant pool that relieves volunteer strain and helps sustain community services.
resources.address: 46 Portland Street, 7th Floor, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1H4

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Grants
resources.description: Gritty to Pretty provides micro-grants and mid-sized grants to local artists, nonprofits, and community groups for murals, public art, pop-ups, and small-scale public realm improvements in Downtown Halifax. Funded by a pool created through business levy contributions and local sponsors, the program quickly deploys flexible dollars to grassroots initiatives—mirroring a community micro-grant model that activates neighbourhood spaces and supports the creative sector.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 2A2

resources.name: Events and Placemaking Grants
resources.description: The Events and Placemaking Grants program supports small, community-led projects—such as street activations, public art, festivals, and pilot ideas—that enhance the Downtown Dartmouth area. It operates as a local micro-grant pool funded through member business levies and community sponsorships, providing nimble, low-barrier funding that helps volunteer-led groups and nonprofits sustain programming and improve neighbourhood vibrancy.

resources.name: Community Grants and Event Partnership Program
resources.description: Downtown Truro Partnership offers small grants and event partnerships for resident-led projects, arts activations, and placemaking pilots that animate the downtown core. The program is supported by a locally governed pool of funds sourced from member levies, local sponsors, and community contributions, enabling quick, flexible micro-grants that bolster nonprofit capacity and sustain community life.

resources.name: Goodwill Bot Community Micro‑Grants
resources.description: Good Robot Brewing’s Goodwill Bot program provides small, fast-turnaround micro-grants and in-kind support to grassroots community groups, arts initiatives, and neighbourhood projects in HRM. Funded by a pool created from customer donations, fundraising events, and business contributions, it exemplifies a locally governed micro-grant model that channels many small gifts into flexible support for community services and creative placemaking.

solutions.text: Volunteer Co-op and Shift-Sharing: Form a cooperative of nearby nonprofits and community groups to share volunteers, coordinate schedules, and rotate responsibilities so individuals can contribute without burnout and organizations cover core hours without over-reliance on a few people.

resources.name: Kings Volunteer Resource Centre (KVRC)
resources.organization: Kings Volunteer Resource Centre (a program of the Valley Community Learning Association)
resources.description: KVRC serves as a county-wide hub that recruits, trains, and shares volunteers among community halls, festivals, food programs, and nonprofits across Kings County. By maintaining a shared volunteer pool and coordinating centralized sign‑ups and shift schedules for multi‑organization events and ongoing programs, KVRC enables groups to rotate responsibilities and cover core hours without over‑relying on the same people.
resources.address: 118 Oakdene Avenue, Suite 201, Kentville, NS B4N 2T5

resources.name: Volunteer Antigonish
resources.organization: Volunteer Antigonish (hosted at People’s Place: Antigonish Town & County Library)
resources.description: Volunteer Antigonish operates a community-wide volunteer hub that matches residents with multiple local nonprofits and coordinates joint sign‑ups for events, food security initiatives, arts, and social services. The hub helps partner organizations share trained volunteers and build rotating shift rosters, reducing burnout while ensuring reliable coverage for core hours across groups.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Volunteer Services
resources.description: HRM’s Volunteer Services supports dozens of community associations, centres, and event committees by running centralized volunteer recruitment, screening supports, and shared scheduling tools. Through pooled volunteer lists and coordinated shift planning for multi‑organization programs and events, the service enables partners to rotate duties and share coverage, easing pressure on individual groups.

resources.name: Volunteer Nova Scotia (provincial volunteer-sharing platform)
resources.organization: 211 Nova Scotia (in partnership with community and government partners)
resources.description: Volunteer Nova Scotia provides a province‑wide online hub where nonprofits and community groups post opportunities and draw from a shared pool of volunteers using common tools for scheduling and shift management. By enabling cross‑organization recruitment and coordinated rosters, the platform helps partners rotate volunteers to cover core hours and reduces over‑reliance on a small number of people.
resources.address: 46 Portland Street, Suite 100, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1H4

solutions.text: Local Time Bank / Skills Exchange: Set up a time-banking system where community members earn credits by helping with events, mentorship, or repairs and spend credits on services (childcare, tutoring, tech help), increasing reciprocity and reducing volunteer pressure.

resources.name: Work-Trade and Skill-Share Program
resources.description: The Deanery Project runs a work-trade system where community members earn credits by contributing time to events, facility maintenance, and program support, and then redeem those hours for workshop fees, space use, and accommodations. This reciprocal model functions like a local time bank, channeling community skills (e.g., carpentry, eco-building, arts facilitation) into shared benefits and reducing reliance on cash while easing pressure on a small staff and core volunteers.
resources.address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

resources.name: Working Member Program (Volunteer-for-Access)
resources.description: Radstorm Halifax operates a working-member program where people contribute set volunteer hours toward tasks like event support, studio maintenance, and mentorship/skill-shares, and in return receive access to its community-run resources (music venue, rehearsal rooms, screenprinting studio, zine library). This is a practical time-credit model that swaps hours for services and space, spreading workloads across many contributors and building a sustainable, peer-supported arts and community hub.

solutions.text: Shared Administrative Services: Develop a shared-services hub offering pooled accounting, fundraising, HR, and grant-writing support for small nonprofits to reduce overhead, professionalize operations, and free frontline staff for mission work.

resources.name: Health Association Nova Scotia Shared Services
resources.description: Health Association Nova Scotia provides pooled administrative services to nonprofit health and community-care organizations across the province, including centralized payroll, group benefits administration, HR advisory, and labour relations support. By consolidating these back-office functions, small nonprofits reduce overhead, improve compliance and professionalize operations, freeing frontline teams to focus on client care and community programming.

resources.name: Member Agency Support
resources.description: FEED Nova Scotia centrally raises funds, manages donor receipting, and distributes resources and training to a network of small, community-based food banks and meal programs. This shared platform reduces the administrative and fundraising burden on local agencies—many volunteer-run—so they can focus on frontline food security work while benefiting from coordinated grants, logistics, and capacity-building.

resources.name: Clean Leadership
resources.description: Clean Foundation’s Clean Leadership program acts as an employer-of-record and administrative backbone for youth placements hosted by small nonprofits and community groups across Nova Scotia. The program centralizes HR, payroll, insurance, and grant compliance, easing administrative load for host organizations and allowing them to expand services while maintaining professional standards.

solutions.text: Community Volunteer Wellness Program: Implement supports for volunteers including regular check-ins, debrief groups, mental-health resources, small appreciation stipends, and respite slots to prevent burnout and retain long-term contributors.

resources.name: Hospice Halifax Volunteer Program
resources.description: Hospice Halifax trains and supports volunteers who provide companionship, respite, and practical help to people at end of life and their families. The program builds in regular check-ins with coordinators, structured debrief circles after difficult shifts or deaths, access to grief and mental-health resources, and flexible respite-style scheduling to prevent burnout; volunteers are also recognized with appreciation events and small tokens to sustain long-term engagement.

resources.name: Canadian Red Cross Nova Scotia Volunteer Program
resources.description: The Canadian Red Cross in Nova Scotia supports emergency management and community health volunteers with Psychological First Aid training, post-activation debriefs, and access to wellness and mental-health supports. Supervisors conduct regular check-ins, offer peer-support networks and Critical Incident Stress Management resources, provide flexible scheduling and rest rotations during responses, and recognize service with appreciation events to reduce burnout and retain volunteers.

resources.name: ISANS Volunteer Program
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS engages volunteers as language tutors, mentors, and settlement supporters and backs them with structured orientation, ongoing staff check-ins, and facilitated group debriefs for challenging situations. Volunteers receive resource guides and referrals for mental-health and trauma-informed practice, flexible scheduling and the option to pause/rotate roles for respite, plus recognition and appreciation activities that help sustain long-term volunteer participation.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 1020, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: IWK Health Volunteer Resources
resources.description: IWK Health’s Volunteer Resources supports volunteers across women’s and children’s health programs with role-specific training, scheduled check-ins with coordinators, and access to debriefing and psychosocial supports after difficult patient encounters. The program emphasizes flexible shift options and respite coverage to prevent overload, and it recognizes volunteer contributions through appreciation activities to encourage long-term retention.

solutions.text: Youth-Led Mini-Grants and Project Funds: Allocate a portion of community funds to youth juries that select and manage small grants for projects by and for young people, boosting leadership, relevance of services, and youth investment in staying local.

resources.name: Bridgewater Youth Action Council (YAC) Micro‑Grants
resources.description: The Bridgewater Youth Action Council allocates a small grants pool that local young people can apply to for youth-led projects such as community events, arts, and wellness initiatives. Youth council members review applications, select recipients, and help steward the projects, directly implementing a youth-jury model that builds leadership and keeps programming relevant to local youth.

resources.name: DSU Society and Project Grants
resources.description: The Dalhousie Student Union dedicates a portion of student activity fees to a student-led grants committee that adjudicates funding for student societies and youth-led projects on campus and in the community. These micro-grants are selected and managed by students themselves, functioning as a youth jury that cultivates leadership, strengthens student services, and supports youth-driven initiatives in Halifax.

resources.name: SMUSA Society Funding and Project Grants
resources.description: Saint Mary’s University Students’ Association allocates part of its student fee revenue to a student-run funding program that awards small grants to student societies and youth-led projects. A committee of student peers evaluates applications and distributes funds, providing a youth-jury model that empowers emerging leaders and supports relevant services and events that keep students engaged locally.

resources.name: ASU Society Funding and Initiatives Grants
resources.description: The Acadia Students’ Union administers student-fee–supported grants that fund youth-led societies and projects benefiting students and the broader Wolfville community. Funding decisions are made by student committees, creating a youth-led mini-grant process that develops leadership skills, sustains student-centered services, and encourages young people to build community where they study and live.

solutions.text: Business–Community Partnership Network: Organize a local employer network for in-kind support, payroll-giving, pro bono services, employee volunteer days, and sponsorship of capacity-building efforts for nonprofits.

resources.name: Workplace Campaigns and Day of Caring
resources.description: United Way Halifax convenes local employers to run Workplace Campaigns that enable payroll giving and corporate donations, channeling sustained funding to frontline nonprofits. Through Day of Caring, they organize employer-led volunteer days to complete hands‑on projects for community agencies, and they broker in‑kind and pro bono support from business partners. Corporate sponsorships also help fund community capacity‑building initiatives, training, and grants that strengthen nonprofit operations across HRM.

resources.name: Team Build
resources.description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia’s Team Build program engages companies in structured employee volunteer days on construction sites, combining hands‑on service with safety training and team development. Businesses also provide in‑kind materials, skilled pro bono labour, and sponsorships that underwrite tools, training, and operational improvements. This integrated employer partnership model strengthens Habitat’s capacity and the broader community housing ecosystem to deliver lasting social impact.

resources.name: Corporate Partnerships and Workplace Giving
resources.description: Feed Nova Scotia partners with employers to run workplace giving campaigns, corporate fund and food drives, and group volunteer shifts in its Dartmouth warehouse. Companies also contribute in‑kind logistics support, pro bono services, and sponsorships that help strengthen distribution systems and training for the network of food banks and meal programs across the province. This coordinated business–community approach boosts nonprofit capacity and stabilizes essential social supports for families and youth.

resources.name: Corporate and Group Volunteering & In‑Kind Giving
resources.description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank engages local employers in organized volunteer days to sort food, refurbish furniture, and support warehouse operations, while also coordinating in‑kind donations of goods and services. Businesses provide pro bono expertise (e.g., logistics, marketing, IT) and sponsorships that bolster infrastructure and program delivery. These partnerships directly expand Parker Street’s capacity to serve low‑income residents and reduce strain on community‑service nonprofits.

solutions.text: Neighbourhood Membership and Patron Models: Encourage community organizations to offer low-cost membership tiers or patron circles that provide reliable, recurring revenue from residents in exchange for modest benefits and stronger community ties.

resources.name: Art Gallery of Nova Scotia Membership Program
resources.description: AGNS offers tiered annual memberships (including student, individual, family, and patron levels) that provide benefits like free admission, discounts, and previews. These low-cost and patron-tier memberships generate predictable, recurring revenue that supports exhibitions, education, and community programs, strengthening the cultural fabric that helps retain and attract young people.

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op Membership
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre operates as a co-operative with accessible individual, organizational, and supporter memberships that include benefits like discounted rentals, voting rights, and member events. These recurring dues and patron-tier contributions provide steady operating income, helping the venue subsidize community arts access and combat burnout in Halifax’s independent arts scene.

resources.name: Ecology Action Centre Membership
resources.description: EAC offers annual and monthly donor memberships at accessible levels, with benefits such as newsletters, event invitations, and member updates. This membership model creates reliable, recurring revenue that sustains community programs, volunteer coordination, and advocacy—reducing capacity strain and supporting a healthier, more livable Nova Scotia for young people.

resources.name: Neptune Theatre Patron & Membership Programs
resources.description: Neptune maintains donor and patron circles, alongside season memberships/subscriptions, offering benefits such as early access, special events, and recognition. Monthly and annual patron support delivers dependable revenue that underwrites productions and education/outreach initiatives, helping stabilize a key cultural institution that engages and retains young talent in Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts Membership & Donor Program
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: Ross Creek offers supporter memberships and patron giving options that provide modest benefits like event invitations and program updates, with opportunities for monthly giving. These recurring contributions help fund year-round arts education, camps, and community programming in rural Nova Scotia, easing funding volatility and sustaining creative opportunities for youth.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

solutions.text: Community Endowment Building: Launch a long-term endowment campaign managed by a local community foundation to provide steady, sustainable funding for core community services and relieve year-to-year fundraising pressure.

resources.name: Community Funds (Endowment Program)
resources.description: The Community Foundation of Nova Scotia helps local leaders and charities establish permanent, locally branded endowment funds whose investment earnings provide annual grants to community services across the province. By pooling donations into long-term funds and handling investment, stewardship, and grant administration, the program creates steady, sustainable funding that reduces year-to-year fundraising pressure on nonprofits and volunteers.
resources.address: Suite 806, 1888 Brunswick Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3J8

resources.name: Lunenburg County Community Fund
resources.description: A locally led endowment, managed by the Community Foundation of Nova Scotia, that builds a permanent fund for charities and community groups in Lunenburg County. The fund’s investment income is granted annually to core community services (e.g., youth programs, arts and culture, community health and inclusion), providing predictable support that eases annual fundraising demands and helps reduce volunteer burnout.
resources.address: Suite 806, 1888 Brunswick Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3J8

solutions.text: Pop-up Community Hubs and Shared Spaces: Activate underused civic and commercial spaces as rotating community hubs where multiple groups can share meeting rooms, equipment, and front-desk support, reducing overhead and increasing visibility.

resources.name: Halifax Central Library
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries’ flagship branch acts as a large-scale community hub with extensive bookable public spaces—meeting rooms, media labs, and performance/program areas—available at no or low cost to nonprofits, youth groups, and community organizers. Library staff provide front-desk support, A/V equipment, and promotional channels, enabling multiple groups to rotate through shared spaces without maintaining their own facilities. This shared-use model lowers overhead and increases visibility for community services that support young people.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op is a member-owned venue offering an affordable black box theatre, lobby, and meeting rooms to dozens of arts, youth, and community organizations on a rotating rental basis. The co-op provides front-of-house/box office, technical gear, and staff support so groups can deliver programs and events without carrying facility overhead. By pooling space and equipment, it strengthens community programming capacity and visibility in Halifax’s North End.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Centre
resources.description: A repurposed former school now operating as a multi-tenant community hub, the Mahone Bay Centre offers shared offices, classrooms, studios, and meeting rooms for local nonprofits, clubs, and service providers. Central reception and facility staff manage bookings, utilities, and common equipment, allowing multiple groups to host rotating programs and services without maintaining standalone premises. This shared-space model reduces overhead and creates a visible focal point for youth and community life on the South Shore.
resources.address: 45 School Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Eltuek Arts Centre
resources.description: Eltuek Arts Centre, a project of New Dawn Enterprises, transformed a former convent/school into a multi-use arts and community facility with co-working, studios, galleries, and bookable meeting and event spaces. Onsite staff provide reception, communications, and technical support while numerous organizations and artists rotate through shared rooms for workshops, programs, and community events. By centralizing services and resources, the Centre lowers operational burdens for small groups and broadens public access to creative and social programming in Sydney.

solutions.text: Coordinated Grant-Writing Consortium: Form a consortium where several small organizations pool staff time or hire a shared grant writer to pursue larger grants they could not access alone, improving success rates and funding stability.

resources.name: Clean Leaders
resources.description: Clean Leaders is a province-wide youth employment program that places participants with dozens of small nonprofits and municipalities to deliver environmental projects. Clean Foundation serves as the lead applicant and administrator, writing and managing large, multi-partner grants and handling reporting and compliance for all host sites. By centralizing grant writing and administration, the program functions as a shared grants office that enables smaller organizations to pool capacity and access funding they could not secure alone.

resources.name: Living Shorelines Nova Scotia
resources.description: Living Shorelines Nova Scotia is a collaborative initiative that supports nature-based coastal protection projects with community groups and municipalities across the province. The Ecology Action Centre convenes partners and develops multi-year, multi-partner funding proposals to federal and provincial programs, acting as the lead applicant and managing reporting. This coordinated approach effectively provides shared grant-writing capacity for smaller partners, improving success rates and bringing stable resources to rural and coastal communities.

resources.name: Habitat Restoration Program (Multi-Partner Grants)
resources.description: Coastal Action’s Habitat Restoration Program brings together watershed associations and community groups to co-design restoration projects on the South Shore. Acting as the consortium’s lead, Coastal Action prepares and submits composite grant applications to programs such as the Habitat Stewardship Program and other federal/provincial funds, then subgrants resources and provides technical/reporting support to partners. This model serves as a shared grant-writing and grants-management hub that increases funding access and stability for small, volunteer-led organizations.

resources.name: Sydney Harbour Watershed Health Program (Collaborative Grants)
resources.description: ACAP Cape Breton convenes community associations, schools, and local governments around Sydney Harbour and regional watersheds to deliver restoration and education projects. As the lead applicant, ACAP develops large, multi-partner grant proposals and centralizes grant writing, reporting, and compliance, enabling smaller community groups to pool capacity and participate in projects funded by federal/provincial and foundation grants. This coordinated approach mirrors a shared grant-writing consortium that raises success rates and stabilizes funding for participating organizations.

solutions.text: Local Crowdfunding and Storytelling Campaigns: Run community crowdfunding drives that pair personal stories with small matching gifts from local businesses to mobilize resident giving and spotlight underfunded programs.

resources.name: NSCC Giving Day
resources.description: A 24-hour, province-wide crowdfunding campaign led by the NSCC Foundation that highlights student and alumni stories to inspire small, local donations. The campaign frequently includes matching challenges from local businesses and alumni sponsors, doubling gifts during set hours to mobilize resident giving for bursaries and underfunded student supports.

resources.name: IWK Telethon for Children
resources.description: An annual community fundraising broadcast that shares powerful patient and family stories from across Atlantic Canada to inspire broad-based, small-donor giving. Local businesses and media partners provide sponsorships and matching gift segments, turning personal storytelling into community crowdfunding that supports underfunded pediatric care and family programs at the IWK.
resources.address: 5855 Spring Garden Road, Suite 302, Halifax, NS B3H 4N1

resources.name: Giving Tuesday Halifax (United Way Halifax)
resources.description: United Way Halifax activates the global Giving Tuesday movement locally through online crowdfunding appeals that spotlight resident and neighborhood stories tied to priority community programs.
