Funding can be applied to site/venue rental, production and PA rentals, security, and permitting, with guidance on best practices for managing noise and late-night operations to keep activations youth-friendly and neighbourhood-compatible.

resources.name: Community Access Program (Rental Subsidies)
resources.description: The Community Access Program reduces or waives rental fees for non-profit and grassroots arts groups using the Bus Stop Theatre for performances and events, most of which occur in the evening. By directly lowering venue rental costs and providing a professionally equipped, acoustically treated space, the program enables affordable night events and helps minimize neighbourhood noise concerns while supporting young artists and promoters.

solutions.text: Local Bylaw Reform Working Group: Form a citizen task force of artists, business owners, youth and municipal staff to audit restrictive bylaws and propose practical reforms (e.g., noise buffers, flexible licensing windows, arts overlay zones) supported by case studies and petitions.

resources.name: ArtsHalifax Advisory Committee
resources.description: ArtsHalifax is a citizen advisory committee of artists, cultural leaders, and community representatives that works with municipal staff and Council to improve policies affecting the arts sector. Through consultations and reports, the committee identifies regulatory barriers (e.g., noise rules, temporary event permits, use definitions for studios/venues) and recommends practical bylaw and policy reforms that support affordable creation, rehearsal, and performance spaces. This implements the solution by convening a local, multi-stakeholder working group to audit restrictions and propose reforms such as clearer cultural-use zoning and more flexible licensing windows.

resources.name: Halifax Centre Plan – Community Design Advisory Committee (CDAC)
resources.description: The CDAC was a citizen–staff working group that helped audit and modernize Halifax’s land-use bylaw and zoning under the Centre Plan, with strong attention to enabling cultural and nightlife uses. By bringing together residents, business owners, design/arts voices, and municipal planners, the committee informed reforms that permit live/work artist spaces, streamline temporary event licensing, and better site entertainment uses to mitigate noise conflicts. This directly implements the solution by using case studies and public input to craft zoning tools and flexible licensing that protect and grow arts and performance space.

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op – Policy and Community Advocacy
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op convenes artists, nearby businesses, youth, and HRM staff to address municipal rules affecting small performance venues, including noise, occupancy, and event permitting. Through research briefs, petitions, and meetings with city officials, the co-op has advocated for zoning flexibility, clearer cultural-use definitions, and more workable licensing windows that keep independent venues viable. This implements the solution by operating as a grassroots working group that audits restrictive bylaws and proposes practical reforms to support affordable creation and performance space.

solutions.text: Noise Mitigation Toolkit and Subsidies: Develop community-led guidance and small subsidy programs for soundproofing and acoustic treatments for small venues and rehearsal rooms, along with local installers' directory and volunteer retrofit teams.

resources.name: Community Grants Program
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Community Grants Program provides small project and capital grants to non-profit organizations for facility upgrades, equipment, and building improvements. Small venues, rehearsal rooms, and community arts spaces can use these funds to add soundproofing, acoustic panels, and other noise-mitigation features, directly offsetting costs and reducing conflict with nearby residents.

resources.name: Business Energy Solutions (Small Business & Commercial Rebates)
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia offers rebates and on-site support that subsidize insulation, window/door upgrades, and HVAC improvements, all of which provide meaningful sound attenuation in addition to energy savings. The program maintains a directory of registered contractors/installers, giving small venues and rehearsal spaces a vetted list of local professionals who can implement acoustic treatments as part of building upgrades.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Halifax Tool Library – Community Build & Repair Programs
resources.description: The Halifax Tool Library lends specialized tools and offers skills workshops and volunteer fix-it/build events that community groups and small venues can leverage to construct DIY acoustic panels, bass traps, and door/window treatments at low cost. This community-led approach helps rehearsal rooms and performance spaces implement practical noise-mitigation upgrades while coordinating volunteer retrofit teams and sharing guidance on materials and methods.

resources.name: The Deanery Project – Community Retrofit & Hands-on Building Workshops
resources.description: The Deanery Project delivers hands-on building workshops and community retrofit initiatives that guide groups through designing and constructing practical building improvements, including acoustic treatments using affordable and sustainable materials. Small venues and community halls can tap into staff expertise and volunteer cohorts to plan and carry out sound-dampening upgrades, making rehearsal and performance spaces more viable in rural and coastal communities.
resources.address: 751 West Ship Harbour Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

solutions.text: Rehearsal Space Time‑Bank or Swap Platform: Build a local online platform or time-bank where bands, theatre groups and venue owners exchange rehearsal hours, volunteer labour or small payments for discounted access to rooms and equipment.

resources.name: Membership and Work‑Trade Access
resources.organization: Radstorm Halifax (Ink Storm, SADRAD, Halifax Zine Library)
resources.description: Radstorm operates a volunteer‑run arts and music space that offers rehearsal rooms, show space, and shared equipment to members on a sliding‑scale basis. Members can contribute volunteer labour (work‑trade) to earn or reduce fees for booking rehearsal time and using gear, and they schedule time through Radstorm’s online systems—functioning like a local time‑bank that trades labour for space and equipment access.

resources.name: Community Access Program
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co‑op provides a community‑owned black‑box theatre that local bands and theatre groups can book at subsidized, sliding‑scale rates. Through an online booking system and a co‑operative model supported by member labour and community fundraising, the program lowers costs for rehearsal and performance time and includes access to in‑house equipment—delivering the ‘small‑payments for discounted access’ component of the solution.

resources.name: Membership and Volunteer Credit Program
resources.description: AFCOOP runs a cooperative platform where members can earn volunteer credits that reduce the cost of renting production gear, editing suites, and studio facilities. Bookings are managed online, and artists exchange volunteer labour for discounted access to rooms and equipment—directly mirroring a time‑bank model that keeps creative space affordable.

resources.name: Access Program (Membership, Equipment, and Studios)
resources.description: CFAT offers members discounted access to media‑arts equipment, edit suites, and production spaces, with online booking and periodic work‑exchange or subsidized initiatives that further lower costs for emerging artists. By combining small payment models with opportunities to offset fees, CFAT enables a practical exchange system for space and equipment aligned with the time‑bank/swap approach.

solutions.text: Partnerships with Developers for Cultural Floors: Negotiate community-benefit agreements with residential and commercial developers to include dedicated affordable cultural spaces (studios, micro-theatres) or in-lieu contributions to a municipal arts space fund.

resources.name: Downtown Halifax Bonus Zoning Public Benefit Program (HRM by Design)
resources.description: Halifax’s downtown planning framework uses negotiated development agreements and density bonusing to secure public benefits from private projects. Eligible public benefits include on-site cultural/community uses and public art, allowing the municipality to require developers to deliver dedicated cultural space (e.g., studios, rehearsal or small performance space) in new buildings or to provide cash-in-lieu contributions to municipal public benefit reserves (including the Public Art Reserve) when on-site space is not feasible.

resources.name: Halifax Centre Plan – Density Bonusing & Public Benefits
resources.description: The Centre Plan extends incentive zoning across the Regional Centre, enabling extra height/floor area in exchange for negotiated public benefits. Through development agreements, benefits can include cultural amenities (such as public art and community-serving spaces) or cash-in-lieu contributions to municipal reserve funds when on-site space cannot be provided—mechanisms that support affordable cultural infrastructure and programming tied to private development.

resources.name: Halifax Waterfront Development Agreements for Cultural Public Realm
resources.description: Build Nova Scotia negotiates ground leases and development agreements with private developers on the Halifax waterfront that require publicly accessible cultural spaces and year‑round programming. Agreements secure cultural floors in mixed-use projects (e.g., event plazas, gallery and exhibition areas, performance locations) or require financial contributions that help program and maintain cultural public spaces—linking private development to affordable, publicly available arts venues.
resources.address: 1751 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 1S5

solutions.text: Business-Embedded Artist Residencies: Encourage local restaurants, cafés and shops to host short-term artist residencies or small-scale performances that bring art into commercial spaces, share revenue, and create regular low-cost stages for emerging talent.

resources.name: Open Mic Mondays at The Carleton
resources.description: A weekly, hosted open-mic night inside The Carleton’s restaurant-bar gives emerging musicians a no- or low-cost stage embedded in a commercial dining space. The venue also programs frequent small-ticket shows where artists are paid via ticket/cover splits and guarantees, bringing performance directly into a revenue-sharing hospitality setting and building regular opportunities for new talent.

resources.name: New Scotland Brewing Taproom Live Music Series
resources.description: New Scotland Brewing hosts near-daily small-scale concerts and jam nights in its downtown Dartmouth taproom, turning a commercial brewery into an accessible performance space. Artists often play ticketed, tip-based, or revenue-shared sets, creating recurring, low-cost stages and informal residencies that support emerging and local talent.

resources.name: The Old Triangle Halifax Live Music & Sessions
resources.description: The Old Triangle’s Halifax location presents daily live music and traditional sessions directly in its pub dining rooms, blending performance with food-and-beverage service. Musicians are booked for recurring weekly slots and special sets, with compensation through guarantees, tips, and bar-driven revenue, providing a reliable, low-barrier stage for emerging and folk artists.

resources.name: The Union Street Live Music Series
resources.description: This community-rooted restaurant and pub in Berwick regularly hosts intimate concerts and songwriter nights in its dining space, integrating arts into a commercial venue. Artists benefit from ticket or door splits alongside food-and-beverage revenue, creating repeatable, affordable performance opportunities and informal residencies for emerging talent in the Annapolis Valley.

solutions.text: Festival and Block-Party Licensing Simplification: Create a community-led guide and liaison service that helps organizers navigate licensing, insurance and noise rules and negotiates streamlined temporary permits for neighbourhood festivals and late-night cultural events.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Event Services
resources.description: HRM’s Event Services provides a single point of contact and a step-by-step guide for organizing community festivals, block parties, and late-night cultural events. The team coordinates noise by-law exemptions, street and sidewalk closures, temporary occupancy permits, insurance and risk requirements, and connections with Police, Fire, and Transportation—streamlining approvals so organizers don’t have to navigate multiple departments on their own.

resources.name: CBRM Special Event Application
resources.organization: Cape Breton Regional Municipality Recreation Department
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Municipality’s Recreation Department offers an event application and liaison service that helps community organizers secure required permissions for festivals and neighbourhood events. Staff guide applicants through noise by-law exemptions, street closures, insurance coverage, and safety plans, coordinating with municipal services to simplify and speed up temporary permits.

resources.name: Town of Truro Special Event Application
resources.organization: Town of Truro Parks, Recreation & Culture
resources.description: Truro’s Parks, Recreation & Culture team supports organizers with a centralized special event application for festivals, block parties, and cultural activations. They advise on insurance, noise by-law exemptions, street/park use, and coordinate across municipal departments (police, public works, fire) to streamline temporary permits and ensure events meet local regulations.

resources.name: Town of Wolfville Host an Event
resources.description: Wolfville provides a ‘Host an Event’ service that walks community groups through permitting for neighbourhood festivals and block parties, including noise considerations, street closures, and use of public spaces. Staff offer templates and guidance for insurance and safety plans and act as liaisons with municipal departments to consolidate approvals into a coordinated, temporary permit process.

solutions.text: Venue Management Training and Volunteer Network: Run regular training for volunteers and small venue operators on programming, safety, book-keeping, grant writing and community outreach; establish a shared pool of trained volunteers to staff shows and reduce operating costs.

resources.name: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op Workshops & Volunteer Roster
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co‑op provides regular professional development for emerging producers and small venue operators, including sessions on production planning, technical safety, grant writing, budgeting, and community outreach. The co‑op also coordinates a roster of trained members and volunteers who staff shows and community events at the theatre, creating a shared pool that reduces labour costs for grassroots presenters.

resources.name: CFAT Workshop Series & Volunteer Program
resources.description: Centre For Art Tapes delivers year‑round workshops and mentorships covering project budgeting/book‑keeping, grant writing, tech skills (camera, sound, projection), and safety and accessibility for public presentations. They maintain a volunteer program that trains and schedules community members to support screenings, installations, and partner events, providing a shared pool of skilled helpers that keeps small media‑arts presentations affordable.

resources.name: King’s Theatre Volunteer Program
resources.description: King’s Theatre recruits, trains, and schedules volunteers for front‑of‑house, ticketing, concessions, ushering, and basic technical support, with clear safety and accessibility protocols. This creates a reliable pool of trained community volunteers to staff live shows and film screenings, lowering operating costs for the non‑profit venue and enabling more community programming.
resources.address: 209 St George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

resources.name: Al Whittle Theatre Volunteer Program
resources.description: Operated by the Acadia Cinema Cooperative, the Al Whittle Theatre runs a comprehensive volunteer program with orientation and role‑specific training for ushers, box office, projection, and event support, including emergency and audience safety procedures. As a co‑operative community venue, the trained volunteer pool is shared across a range of presenters using the theatre, helping reduce labour costs and sustain affordable, year‑round arts programming.

obstacles.title: Regulatory Burden and Slow Permitting
obstacles.description: Complex, lengthy processes for housing, business start-ups, and professional licensing delay projects and deter investment.

solutions.text: Community Permit Navigation Hubs: Volunteer-run or nonprofit-staffed centers that help residents and small businesses complete permit and licensing applications, collect required documents, and track submission status to reduce errors and rework.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Business Navigators
resources.organization: Service Nova Scotia and Internal Services (Government of Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Province-wide advisors who provide one-on-one guidance to entrepreneurs and small businesses on what permits and licences they need at the municipal, provincial, and federal levels. They help clients complete applications correctly, identify and gather required documents, liaise with regulatory offices, and track submissions to reduce errors, rework, and delays.

resources.name: Access Nova Scotia – Halifax (Bayers Lake) Service Centre
resources.organization: Access Nova Scotia (Service Nova Scotia, Government of Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Front-counter and appointment-based support that helps residents and small businesses register with the Registry of Joint Stock Companies, obtain business-related licences, and complete associated applications. Staff review forms for completeness, verify identification and required documents, submit applications on behalf of clients, and provide status updates or next steps to reduce processing delays.
resources.address: 300 Horseshoe Lake Drive, Unit 100, Halifax, NS B3S 0B7

resources.name: HRM Planning & Development Permit Centre (Bayers Road)
resources.description: In-person customer service hub where homeowners, contractors, and small businesses receive help preparing and submitting building, development, sign, and occupancy permit applications. Staff advise on required drawings and documents, pre-screen submissions for completeness, accept applications, and guide clients on tracking through HRM’s permitting system to reduce rework and turnaround times.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, 2nd Floor, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Licensing and Credential Recognition Support
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: Advisors work with internationally trained individuals and immigrant entrepreneurs to navigate professional licensing, trade certification, and business registration requirements in Nova Scotia. They help complete application forms, compile and certify required documents and translations, and communicate with regulatory bodies to track progress and resolve issues, reducing delays and errors in the process.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 1W8

solutions.text: Pre-Application Community Consultations: Organize regular community-led forums where project proposers meet neighbours and municipal staff early to identify concerns and align proposals with local guidelines, shortening formal review cycles.

resources.name: Shape Your City Halifax (Planning Case Engagement)
resources.description: HRM’s Shape Your City Halifax platform hosts early engagement sessions and project pages where applicants present concepts and meet neighbours alongside municipal planning staff before formal hearings. These forums capture local concerns and clarify policy requirements so proponents can adjust proposals early, which helps align with municipal guidelines and shortens later review and approval cycles.

resources.name: Public Information Meetings (Planning Applications)
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings – Planning & Development
resources.description: Kings County conducts Public Information Meetings near the start of many development agreement and rezoning applications. Applicants present to nearby residents with municipal planners facilitating, documenting feedback, and advising on policy alignment so proposals can be refined before Planning Advisory Committee and Council review, reducing back-and-forth and expediting formal approvals.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: Public Information Meetings (Planning & Development)
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Colchester – Planning & Development
resources.description: Colchester’s Planning Department holds Public Information Meetings early in the application process for planning amendments and development agreements. Proponents meet neighbours and municipal staff to discuss site plans, compliance, and mitigation strategies; feedback is incorporated into submissions and staff reports, resolving issues before formal hearings and helping shorten permitting timelines.

resources.name: Public Information Sessions for Planning Applications
resources.organization: Cape Breton Regional Municipality – Planning & Development
resources.description: CBRM Planning organizes Public Information Sessions at the outset of rezoning and development agreement applications. Developers share preliminary concepts with community members while planning staff explain applicable policies and gather input, enabling proponents to revise proposals prior to formal Council processes and reducing delays in the review cycle.

resources.name: Pre-Application Consultation and Public Information Meetings (Development Agreements)
resources.description: Wolfville’s planning process requires a pre-application meeting with municipal planners and typically a Public Information Meeting early in development agreement applications. These forums bring applicants together with neighbours and staff to identify concerns and align proposals with the Municipal Planning Strategy and Land Use By-law, allowing revisions before formal submission and helping to streamline approvals.

solutions.text: Standardized Application Templates and Checklists: Develop and distribute clear, localized templates and step-by-step checklists for common permits (home renovations, pop-up shops, food trucks, home-based businesses) so applicants submit complete, consistent files.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Business Navigator Service
resources.organization: Government of Nova Scotia — Service Nova Scotia
resources.description: A provincial service that provides one-on-one guidance to entrepreneurs on permits and licenses with practical, step-by-step checklists and document templates. Navigators supply tailored application packages for common scenarios (e.g., food trucks, home-based businesses, pop-up retail), ensuring applicants submit complete, consistent files that reduce back-and-forth and speed up approvals.
resources.address: Maritime Centre, 1505 Barrington Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: BizPaL Nova Scotia
resources.organization: Government of Nova Scotia — Service Nova Scotia (in partnership with ISED Canada and municipalities)
resources.description: An online tool that generates a customized list of all permits and licences required for a specific business activity and location in Nova Scotia, with direct links to standardized application forms and guidance. By consolidating requirements from provincial and municipal authorities into clear, user-friendly checklists (including for home-based businesses, food trucks, and pop-up shops), BizPaL helps applicants assemble complete submissions and avoid delays.
resources.address: Maritime Centre, 1505 Barrington Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: Planning & Development Permit Applications and Checklists
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality provides standardized application packages and detailed checklists for residential renovations, building and development permits, patios/pop-up retail, signage, and business licensing. Clear, localized forms specify required drawings, documents, and inspections so applicants can submit complete, consistent files that move through permitting more quickly.
resources.address: Alderney Gate Customer Service Centre, 40 Alderney Drive, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 2N5

resources.name: CBRM Planning & Development — Permits, Forms and Checklists
resources.organization: Cape Breton Regional Municipality — Planning & Development
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Municipality publishes standardized permit applications and checklists for building and development (including renovations, accessory structures, signage, and occupancy), along with clear instructions on required plans and approvals. These templates guide residents and businesses to prepare complete, consistent submissions, reducing processing times and follow-up requests.

solutions.text: Local 'Pre-Approval' Design Guides: Create community-backed design standards (for modest infill, signage, storefronts) that, when met, allow expedited approval through a fast-track municipal review based on pre-agreed criteria.

resources.name: Downtown Halifax Site Plan Approval (HRM by Design)
resources.description: Using the Downtown Halifax Land Use By-law and Design Manual (HRM by Design), development that meets pre-set urban design criteria for building form, massing, signage, and storefronts can be approved by a Development Officer through Site Plan Approval, avoiding lengthier development agreements or Council hearings. This operates as a pre-approval design guide: applicants who demonstrate compliance with the manual’s scorecard and checklists receive expedited, as-of-right approvals, enabling faster infill and facade projects in the downtown.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 2005, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Halifax Centre Plan – Site Plan Approval
resources.description: Under the Halifax Centre Plan (Packages A and B), the Regional Centre Land Use By-law and associated Design Manual set clear, form-based standards and qualitative objectives for corridors, centers, and mixed-use areas. Projects that meet these pre-agreed design requirements are eligible for streamlined Site Plan Approval by staff, fast-tracking compliant infill, small multi-unit housing, signage, and storefront changes without discretionary Council processes.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 2005, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Core Area Design Guidelines and Site Plan Approval
resources.description: Wolfville’s Core Area Design Guidelines establish architectural, storefront, signage, and public-realm standards for the downtown and adjoining mixed-use streets. When proposals conform to these standards, the Town issues approvals through staff-administered Site Plan Approval, effectively pre-approving modest infill, facade improvements, and signage to speed permitting and reduce regulatory delays.

solutions.text: One-Stop Permit Pilot Partnership: Partner with the municipality to run a time-limited one-stop shop pilot that co-locates staff from planning, building, business licensing and health to issue combined decisions within set timelines.

resources.name: Festival & Event Application (One-Stop Event Permitting)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality runs a single, one-stop application for festivals and events that coordinates all required municipal permits and reviews through one intake. Staff from parks, right-of-way/traffic, planning (site permissions), building (tents/stages), fire, and police review files together and liaise with Nova Scotia Public Health for food vendor requirements, issuing coordinated decisions within published timelines. This co-located, cross-department workflow functions as a practical one-stop permitting model that reduces regulatory burden for organizers and businesses tied to events.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Business Navigators
resources.organization: Government of Nova Scotia – Service Nova Scotia
resources.description: Business Navigators provide a one-window point of contact that helps entrepreneurs obtain multiple permits and licences by coordinating with municipal planning/building officials and provincial regulators (e.g., Environment/Public Health) on parallel timelines. While permits are issued by the competent authorities, Navigators streamline the process by organizing the right reviewers, clarifying requirements up front, and driving concurrent reviews so clients receive combined decisions within predictable timeframes. This reduces regulatory burden and mirrors a one-stop permitting pilot by centralizing staff coordination through a single service.

resources.name: Planning & Inspections – One-Window Counter
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
resources.description: At the County municipal complex, planning, development engineering, building inspection, and by-law staff are co-located to provide a single intake for development and building permits. The team coordinates required external approvals (e.g., Nova Scotia Environment/Public Health for on-site sewage or food premises) and applies published service standards, delivering consolidated comments and decisions to applicants. This one-stop, co-located service shortens permitting timelines and reduces back-and-forth for housing and business projects.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: Community Development – Planning & Building Inspection (One-Stop Permit Counter)
resources.description: Bridgewater’s Community Development team co-locates planning, development, and building inspection services at Town Hall, offering a single counter where applicants can initiate and track all approvals. Staff coordinate related municipal licences (e.g., signage, patios) and bring in fire/engineering and provincial health/environmental reviewers as needed to run parallel reviews, providing applicants with consolidated decisions within target timelines. This one-stop approach streamlines housing and business permitting and reduces regulatory delays.

solutions.text: Community Data & Impact Reports: Collect and publish local data on delayed projects' economic and social impacts to build evidence for municipal reform and prioritize permits that drive jobs and housing.

resources.name: Halifax Open Data Program – Planning & Development Datasets and Application Tracker
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality maintains an open data portal and an online development application tracker that publish detailed information on planning applications, building permits, timelines, locations, and permit values. By making application statuses and permitting data public, the program enables communities, researchers, and businesses to quantify backlogs and assess the economic and housing impacts of delays. This evidence supports municipal reform efforts and helps prioritize permits that drive jobs and new housing supply.

resources.name: Halifax Index
resources.description: The Halifax Index is an annual, data-rich report that consolidates local indicators on population, labour, business climate, housing supply, construction activity, and affordability. It highlights bottlenecks in development and the costs of delayed growth, providing a clear evidence base for municipal policy and process improvements. These insights inform prioritization of approvals that unlock jobs and housing, aligning stakeholders around measurable outcomes.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1300, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Municipal Report Card
resources.description: The Halifax Chamber of Commerce publishes an annual Municipal Report Card and related advocacy briefs that compile data and business feedback on permitting timelines, planning performance, and regulatory burden in HRM. By quantifying the economic impacts of delays and benchmarking service standards, the reports build evidence for municipal reform. This helps focus attention on streamlining approvals and prioritizing permits that enable investment, jobs, and housing development.

resources.name: CBRM Planning & Development – Building Permit Reports
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Municipality publishes monthly and annual building permit summaries detailing permit counts, construction values, and types across communities, alongside development application information. This local reporting enables residents, builders, and policymakers to track construction momentum, identify bottlenecks in approvals, and assess the jobs and housing impacts of delays. The data supports evidence-based reforms to permitting processes and prioritization of projects with strong economic and social returns.

solutions.text: Peer Mentoring for New Entrepreneurs: Match experienced local business owners with new entrepreneurs to guide them through licensing, inspections, and compliance requirements, reducing time lost to trial-and-error.

resources.name: Business Mentorship Program
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS’ Business Mentorship Program matches newcomer and immigrant entrepreneurs with experienced Nova Scotia business owners in their sector for one-on-one guidance. Mentors provide practical advice on navigating local requirements such as business registration, municipal permits, inspections, and provincial/federal compliance, and make introductions to regulators and service providers. This peer-to-peer support reduces trial-and-error and helps new entrepreneurs move through licensing and compliance steps more efficiently.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Advisory and Mentorship Services
resources.description: CEED connects new founders with a network of experienced local entrepreneurs and Advisors-in-Residence who provide targeted mentorship. These mentors help startups understand and complete key regulatory steps—such as registering with the Nova Scotia Registry of Joint Stock Companies, securing municipal permits and inspections, and meeting sector-specific compliance—while sharing proven checklists and contacts. The peer mentoring reduces delays and uncertainty so entrepreneurs can launch and grow more quickly.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 225, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Mentorship and Advisory Circles
resources.organization: Centre for Women in Business (Mount Saint Vincent University)
resources.description: The Centre for Women in Business pairs women and gender-diverse entrepreneurs with seasoned Nova Scotia business owners through one-on-one mentorship and small advisory circles. Mentors guide mentees through practical compliance tasks—business registration, municipal occupancy and signage permits, health and safety requirements, CRA payroll/GST accounts, and WCB/OH&S obligations—sharing templates and local contacts. This structured peer support shortens the learning curve and minimizes delays caused by regulatory uncertainty.

resources.name: Connector Program – Entrepreneur Stream
resources.description: Halifax Partnership’s Connector Program includes an entrepreneur stream that matches early-stage and newcomer entrepreneurs with established local business owners and executives for guided, one-on-one conversations. Connectors provide real-world advice on Halifax and Nova Scotia permitting and compliance processes—who to contact at the municipality, what applications and inspections are required, and how to sequence steps—while offering warm referrals to inspectors, accountants, and lawyers. This peer mentoring helps new entrepreneurs avoid common regulatory pitfalls and accelerate startup timelines.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1201, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

solutions.text: Volunteer Review Panels for Low‑Risk Projects: Establish trained community review panels to assess and endorse very low-risk applications (temporary events, small home-based businesses) so municipalities can accept those endorsements for faster approval.

resources.name: Design Advisory Committee
resources.description: Halifax’s Design Advisory Committee is a volunteer panel of trained design, architecture, and planning professionals that reviews qualifying site plan applications against established qualitative design criteria. By providing an expert endorsement on compliant, as-of-right proposals, the committee enables municipal staff to issue approvals without Council hearings, expediting lower-risk applications and reducing regulatory delays.

resources.name: Heritage Advisory Committee
resources.description: Lunenburg’s Heritage Advisory Committee is a citizen volunteer panel trained in the town’s Heritage Conservation District guidelines that reviews Heritage Permit applications for minor exterior alterations, storefront changes, and signage. When applications align with the standards, the committee’s recommendation allows municipal staff or Council to issue permits quickly, streamlining low-risk approvals for homeowners and small businesses in the historic district.

resources.name: Heritage Advisory Committee
resources.description: Annapolis Royal’s Heritage Advisory Committee is a volunteer community panel that assesses Heritage Alteration Permit applications using the town’s conservation guidelines. Their endorsements on compliant, low-risk changes—such as minor façade updates or signage—allow municipal approvals to proceed more quickly, reducing permitting timelines for small projects and local enterprises in the heritage district.
resources.address: 285 St. George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

resources.name: Heritage Advisory Committee
resources.description: Truro’s Heritage Advisory Committee is a committee of trained citizen volunteers who review applications for heritage properties and districts against established local standards. By issuing recommendations on minor, low-risk alterations and signage, the panel enables staff and Council to process permits faster, easing regulatory burden for residents and small businesses operating in heritage areas.

solutions.text: Community Legal Clinic for Licensing: Provide pro bono or low-cost legal/administrative help focused on professional licensing, zoning appeals, and regulatory interpretation to speed resolution of hold-ups and appeals.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Business Navigators
resources.organization: Office of Regulatory Affairs and Service Effectiveness, Government of Nova Scotia
resources.description: A free, province-wide service that provides one-on-one guidance to entrepreneurs and small businesses on permits, licenses, inspections, and zoning. Navigators interpret regulatory requirements, help complete applications correctly, liaise with provincial and municipal departments, and troubleshoot delays—speeding up approvals and resolving permitting hold-ups.

resources.name: SmartBusiness Program
resources.description: SmartBusiness works directly with local companies to identify and remove red-tape barriers, including challenges with permits, business licensing, and municipal planning/zoning processes. The team connects businesses to the right decision-makers, interprets regulatory requirements, and escalates stalled files to speed up approvals and resolve permitting issues.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1101, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Regulated Professions and Trades Support
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS provides individualized advising and workshops to help internationally trained professionals navigate licensing and certification pathways in Nova Scotia. Staff explain regulatory requirements, assist with documentation and applications, and liaise with licensing bodies—reducing delays and resolving credentialing hold-ups so clients can work in their fields sooner.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service (Clinic)
resources.organization: Dalhousie University, Schulich School of Law
resources.description: A community legal clinic that offers free legal services and advocacy to low-income residents, including assistance with administrative and regulatory matters affecting work and housing. The clinic helps clients understand and challenge government and bylaw decisions, prepares submissions for administrative tribunals, and negotiates with authorities—providing pro bono representation that can resolve permitting, bylaw, or licensing-related disputes more quickly.

solutions.text: Regulatory Feedback and Red‑Tape Reduction Campaigns: Coordinate structured community feedback to municipal councils identifying the most burdensome rules and proposing simpler, local solutions (e.g., fee waivers, timeline caps).

resources.name: Business Navigator Service
resources.organization: Government of Nova Scotia – Office of Regulatory Affairs and Service Effectiveness
resources.description: The Province’s Business Navigator Service provides one-on-one guidance to entrepreneurs on licensing, permitting, and regulatory requirements at the provincial and municipal levels. Navigators document recurring barriers (e.g., long permit timelines, duplicative paperwork, excessive fees) and feed structured feedback to the Office of Regulatory Affairs and Service Effectiveness, which then works with municipalities to streamline processes, set service standards, and pursue simpler local solutions such as fee relief and clearer checklists.
resources.address: Maritime Centre, 1505 Barrington Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3Y6

resources.name: Red Tape Reduction Advocacy
resources.description: The Halifax Chamber of Commerce runs ongoing policy and advocacy efforts that survey businesses, host roundtables, and compile evidence on the most burdensome municipal rules affecting permits, licensing, and development. The Chamber delivers formal submissions and delegations to Halifax Regional Council, pressing for timeline caps, digital permitting, simplified application requirements, and targeted fee relief to reduce red tape and speed up investment.

resources.name: Municipal Advocacy & Policy
resources.description: The Downtown Dartmouth Business Commission gathers structured feedback from local businesses on permitting, signage, patios, and inspections, and regularly presents this input to HRM Council and staff. Through letters, committee participation, and public submissions, the Commission has advocated for streamlined approvals, seasonal fee waivers (e.g., sidewalk café/patio fees), clearer guidelines, and predictable service timelines to reduce municipal red tape.

resources.name: Government Relations & Regulatory Affairs
resources.description: CANS convenes contractors, developers, and suppliers to identify bottlenecks in municipal planning, permitting, and inspection processes across Nova Scotia. The association aggregates member feedback into policy briefs and presentations to municipal councils and staff, advocating for standardized checklists, fixed review timelines, transparent fees, and simplified local rules that cut red tape and accelerate construction and housing delivery.

solutions.text: Micro-Grant Program for Fast-Track Compliance: Fund small grants to help applicants meet regulatory requirements quickly (e.g., paying for a required inspection, engineering memo, or minor retrofits) so projects aren't stalled for lack of cash.

resources.name: Heritage Incentives Program
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality provides matching grants to owners of registered heritage properties for conservation and code-related upgrades. Eligible costs include professional engineering assessments, required permits/fees, and life-safety or structural retrofits needed to meet building and fire code. By covering these compliance expenses up front, the program helps applicants satisfy regulatory requirements quickly so projects can proceed without cash-related delays.

resources.name: Façade Improvement Program
resources.description: The Downtown Dartmouth Business Commission offers micro-grants to help small businesses upgrade storefronts and signage in compliance with municipal bylaws and design standards. Funds can be used for design drawings, permit fees, signage that meets code, and minor code-related repairs, enabling applicants to clear permitting requirements quickly and avoid project slowdowns due to lack of immediate cash.

resources.name: Façade Improvement Program
resources.description: Downtown Truro Partnership provides matching grants to commercial property owners and tenants to complete storefront improvements that comply with municipal permitting and design guidelines. Eligible expenses often include design/engineering drawings, required inspections, permit fees, and minor accessibility or safety upgrades, helping businesses meet regulatory conditions faster and continue renovations without financial bottlenecks.

resources.name: SCAP Food Safety and Quality Program (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Under the Sustainable Canadian Agricultural Partnership, Nova Scotia offers cost-shared funding to farms and agri-food businesses for regulatory compliance, including HACCP/CanadaGAP development, third-party food safety audits/inspections, and minor equipment or facility upgrades required by regulators. By offsetting the immediate costs of audits, engineering/consulting memos, and compliance retrofits, the program enables applicants to obtain licenses and approvals more quickly and keep projects moving.
resources.address: 74 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

solutions.text: Youth-Led Policy Labs and Hackathons: Host community design sprints where youth, designers, business owners and municipal staff prototype streamlined permitting workflows or digital tools that simplify submission and tracking.

resources.name: ShiftKey Labs Civic & GovTech Hackathons
resources.organization: Dalhousie University – ShiftKey Labs (Nova Scotia Sandbox)
resources.description: ShiftKey Labs runs student- and youth-led design sprints and hackathons with public-sector partners to improve government services. Multidisciplinary teams of students, designers, entrepreneurs, and municipal/provincial staff co-design and prototype digital tools and workflows—such as simplified permit/licence applications and application-tracking dashboards—then demo them for feedback and potential pilot adoption.

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic Innovation Challenges & Hackathons
resources.description: IGNITE convenes youth, local businesses, and municipal staff in rural Nova Scotia for challenge sprints and hackathons focused on solving real public-service bottlenecks. Teams rapidly prototype practical digital tools (e.g., intake portals, status trackers) and reworked workflows that can streamline small-business licensing and development-permit processes in partnership with municipal departments.
resources.address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

resources.name: Volta Civic Innovation Hackathons
resources.description: Volta hosts hackathons and design sprints that bring together youth talent, startup founders, designers, and public-sector partners to co-create civic tech solutions. Using open data and user-centred design, teams prototype apps and service blueprints that simplify how residents and businesses navigate municipal processes—including permitting and licensing—and present them to municipal staff for iteration and pilots.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Unit 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: Digital Nova Scotia Hackathons & Policy Design Sprints
resources.description: Digital Nova Scotia partners with industry and government to run hackathons and problem-solving sprints that engage students, early-career technologists, and civic stakeholders. These events focus on prototyping user-friendly digital tools and service improvements—such as clearer licensing pathways and permit application trackers—to reduce regulatory friction for startups and small businesses.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 309, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

obstacles.title: Public Safety, Housing Insecurity, and Substance Use Harms
obstacles.description: Homelessness, toxic drug supply, and community safety concerns strain services and affect perceptions of livability and inclusion.

solutions.text: Peer-led outreach and navigation teams: Train and fund people with lived/living experience to run outreach teams that build trust, deliver harm-reduction supplies, connect individuals to services (housing, health care, income supports), and accompany clients through appointments.

resources.name: Harm Reduction Outreach Program
resources.description: Northern Healthy Connections Society (NHCS) operates peer-driven street outreach across northern Nova Scotia, distributing harm-reduction supplies (safer use kits, naloxone), providing education, and making low-barrier connections to housing, health care, and income supports. The program trains and employs people with lived/living experience as peer outreach workers who build trust, offer navigation support, and accompany clients to appointments and services when requested.

resources.name: Sharp Advice Needle Exchange (Peer Outreach)
resources.description: The Ally Centre of Cape Breton’s Sharp Advice Needle Exchange runs peer-led street outreach that provides harm-reduction supplies, overdose education and naloxone, and on-the-spot referrals to housing, health, and income supports. Trained peer navigators with lived/living experience accompany clients to appointments and help them navigate systems, building trust with people who use substances and those experiencing homelessness.

resources.name: Stepping Stone Street Outreach Program
resources.description: Stepping Stone’s peer-led outreach team, comprised of current and former sex workers and people with lived experience, conducts regular street-based outreach in Halifax providing harm-reduction supplies, safer-sex materials, and overdose prevention education. Peer navigators build trust, connect participants to housing, health care, legal and income supports, and accompany clients to appointments to reduce barriers and improve safety.

resources.name: Mobile Outreach Street Health (MOSH)
resources.description: MOSH is a mobile outreach program that meets people where they are—on the street, in shelters, and encampments—offering harm-reduction supplies, primary health care, and social-navigation supports. The team partners with and employs peer support workers with lived experience to build trust, provide system navigation, and accompany clients to health, housing, and income-support appointments across HRM.

solutions.text: Community naloxone distribution and training: Organize regular public naloxone training sessions and free kit distribution at community centres, libraries, faith groups, events and shelters, and create a local map of kit locations.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Take Home Naloxone (THN) Program
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Health – Mental Health & Addictions Program (in partnership with Nova Scotia Department of Health and Wellness)
resources.description: The provincial Take Home Naloxone (THN) Program provides free naloxone kits and brief overdose response training through a network of community partners including shelters, libraries, community health centres, and pharmacies across Nova Scotia. The program also maintains an online site locator map showing where kits are available and partners on pop-up trainings at community venues, directly aligning with community naloxone distribution, training, and public mapping.

resources.name: Mobile Outreach Street Health (MOSH) – Harm Reduction & Naloxone
resources.description: MOSH teams provide on-the-spot naloxone training and free kits to people in shelters, encampments, drop-ins, and at community events throughout Halifax, reducing barriers for people experiencing homelessness or substance-use harms. As a Take Home Naloxone distribution site, they also host regular harm-reduction sessions at the clinic and connect people to nearby kit locations featured on the provincial map.

resources.name: Public Naloxone Training and Kit Distribution at Halifax Public Libraries
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries hosts recurring public naloxone trainings in partnership with Nova Scotia Health and local harm-reduction organizations, and many branches keep free Take Home Naloxone kits for patrons. Through branch events, staff education, and outreach, libraries help community members learn overdose response and direct them to the provincial site locator map to find kit locations across HRM.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

solutions.text: Drug-checking and early warning networks: Partner with public-health labs or mobile service providers to host local drug-checking events and create a community alert system (text, social media, posters) to warn about toxic supplies and trends.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Health Public Drug Alerts
resources.description: Nova Scotia Health Public Health operates a province-wide early warning system that tracks toxic drug trends using information from hospital toxicology, Emergency Health Services, harm reduction partners, and public-health laboratories. They issue real-time community alerts through their website and social media and provide printable advisories for shelters, clinics, and community services; they also support partner agencies to offer local drug-checking with fentanyl/xylazine test strips and to share timely alerts back to people who use drugs.

resources.name: MOSH (Mobile Outreach Street Health) Harm Reduction Program
resources.description: MOSH brings mobile harm-reduction services to encampments, shelters, and street-involved communities in Halifax, including on-the-spot drug checking using fentanyl and other test strips and safer-use education. The team relays Nova Scotia Health drug alerts directly to clients during outreach and via social media and printed posters, and feeds anonymized information about concerning samples back to Public Health to strengthen the local early-warning network.

solutions.text: Local supervised consumption advocacy and site support: Form community coalitions to advocate for and support low-barrier supervised consumption or overdose prevention sites, including volunteer support, fundraising, and hosting space where appropriate.

resources.name: Mainline Needle Exchange
resources.description: Mainline Needle Exchange is a community harm reduction program that provides safer-use supplies, peer outreach, naloxone training, and overdose response education in Halifax. The organization actively advocates for sanctioned, low-barrier overdose prevention/supervised consumption services and supports community-led OPS efforts by coordinating peers, providing supplies and technical guidance, and assisting with volunteer mobilization and fundraising. By partnering with local service providers and people who use drugs, Mainline helps plan and sustain safer consumption spaces that reduce overdose deaths and improve public safety.

resources.name: Mobile Outreach Street Health (MOSH)
resources.description: MOSH is the North End Community Health Centre’s harm reduction and primary care outreach team serving people experiencing homelessness and substance use-related harms in Halifax. The team and NECHC have been key advocates for establishing low-barrier overdose prevention/supervised consumption services, leveraging clinic and outreach infrastructure to support planning, staffing, and integration of health and social supports for prospective OPS. They coordinate with peers, community partners, and public authorities to align volunteers, training, and operational supports that an OPS requires.

resources.name: Northern Healthy Connections Society – Harm Reduction Program
resources.description: NHCS provides fixed-site harm reduction services and outreach in Truro, including safer-use supplies, naloxone distribution, peer support, and overdose education. The organization convenes local partners and people with lived/living experience to advocate for low-barrier overdose prevention/supervised consumption services in northern Nova Scotia, and offers to support or host space as feasible when an OPS is approved. NHCS contributes volunteers, training, supplies, and coalition-building to help communities prepare for and sustain supervised consumption options that improve health and public safety.

solutions.text: Tiny-house villages and housing co-ops: Develop community-led tiny-house villages and tenant-run housing co-ops that provide safe, affordable transitional housing plus on-site supports and pathways to permanent housing.

resources.name: The Sunflower Rapid Housing Community
resources.description: The Sunflower is a community of small, rapidly built homes operated by Adsum for Women & Children that provides safe, affordable, and supported housing for women, gender-diverse people, and families exiting homelessness. The village model includes on-site staff, case management, and wraparound services that help residents stabilize, access health and social supports, and transition along a pathway from interim housing toward long-term, permanent housing options.

resources.name: LakeCity Tiny Homes
resources.description: LakeCity Works designs and builds energy-efficient tiny homes in Dartmouth as part of a social enterprise that supports people living with mental illness. By partnering with municipalities and community housing providers, LakeCity’s tiny homes are used to create small, community-led clusters of dwellings that serve as transitional and supportive housing, with residents connected to on-site or partner-delivered services and clear pathways into longer-term, permanent housing.

solutions.text: Low-barrier mobile health and wraparound services: Coordinate volunteer staffing and local fundraising for mobile units offering wound care, primary care, mental-health supports, vaccinations, and on-the-spot referral to housing and treatment.

resources.name: Mobile Outreach Street Health (MOSH)
resources.description: MOSH is a low-barrier, mobile health service that brings primary care to people who are homeless or under-housed across Halifax. Its interdisciplinary team provides on-the-street wound care, primary care, foot care, mental-health supports, harm-reduction supplies, and vaccinations, and makes on-the-spot referrals to housing workers, detox/OAT treatment, and social services. The program leverages community volunteers and local fundraising through the North End Community Health Centre to staff outreach and keep the MOSH van stocked and on the road.

resources.name: Street Outreach (Mobile Services)
resources.description: Northern Healthy Connections Society operates a mobile, low-threshold outreach program serving people who use substances and those experiencing homelessness in northern Nova Scotia. The team provides harm-reduction supplies, nursing-led primary care and wound care, STI/HIV/HCV testing, immunizations when available, mental-health navigation, and immediate referrals to detox/OAT, housing supports, and other wraparound services. The program is sustained by community partnerships, volunteers, and local donations to keep outreach vehicles and pop-up clinics active.

solutions.text: Supportive tenancy and landlord mediation program: Create a community mediation hub to work with landlords and tenants, offering incentives, damage mitigation funds, tenancy coaching and rapid-response support to keep people housed.

resources.name: Residential Tenancies Program
resources.organization: Government of Nova Scotia – Service Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Government of Nova Scotia’s Residential Tenancies Program provides dispute resolution and mediation-style services between landlords and tenants, helping resolve issues such as non-payment of rent, repairs, or lease terms before they escalate to eviction. By offering information, early resolution options, and formal hearings, the program supports housing stability and keeps people housed through conflict resolution rather than displacement.
resources.address: 300 Horseshoe Lake Drive, Halifax, NS B3S 0B7

resources.name: Phoenix Housing Support
resources.description: Phoenix provides housing support for youth, including tenancy coaching (rights, responsibilities, budgeting), help navigating leases/utilities, and rapid-response eviction prevention. Staff actively mediate with landlords, secure rent supplements or damage-deposit assistance through community and provincial programs, and build landlord relationships to keep young people safely housed.

resources.name: Eviction Prevention Program
resources.description: Brunswick Street Mission’s Eviction Prevention Program works directly with tenants and landlords to prevent evictions by mediating payment plans and resolving conflicts early. The program also provides emergency financial assistance for rent arrears, utilities, or damage deposits and offers tenancy coaching to stabilize housing and reduce repeat crises.

resources.name: Housing Support Program
resources.description: Open Arms’ Housing Support Program engages landlords across the Annapolis Valley to secure and sustain housing for people at risk of homelessness, mediating tenancy issues and arranging practical supports. The team provides rapid-response outreach, tenancy coaching, and access to emergency funds for rent/utility arrears or damage deposits to prevent evictions and keep people stably housed.

solutions.text: Employment and skills programs for people with lived experience: Partner with local businesses and trades to create apprenticeship, micro-employment, and stipended work opportunities for people exiting homelessness or treatment, with supports for retention.

resources.name: LakeCity Woodworkers
resources.description: LakeCity Woodworkers is a social enterprise that provides paid employment, skill-building, and on-the-job training in woodworking and furniture manufacturing for people living with mental illness and those in recovery. The program partners with local contractors, retailers, and customers to fulfill real work orders, offering transitional and supported employment, wage subsidies, and job-coaching to help participants retain work and move into community jobs. This directly creates micro-employment and apprenticeship-style opportunities for people exiting treatment or homelessness with wraparound supports.

resources.name: MetroWorks Employment Programs and Social Enterprises
resources.description: MetroWorks runs employment training and wage-subsidized placements for people facing multiple barriers—including homelessness and recovery from substance use—through employer partnerships and in-house social enterprises (e.g., culinary and catering, landscaping, and other project-based work). Participants receive paid work experience, certifications, and job coaching, with retention supports that include case management and connections to community services. By collaborating with local businesses and trades, MetroWorks creates micro-employment and supported pathways into longer-term jobs.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 501, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Peer Outreach Employment Program
resources.description: Mainline engages people with lived and living experience of substance use and homelessness as paid peer outreach workers who provide harm reduction education, naloxone distribution, and street-level support. These stipended, shift-based roles come with training, mentorship, and ongoing wraparound supports that stabilize participants and build workplace skills. The program creates micro-employment opportunities that can bridge to further training or community jobs while prioritizing retention through peer supervision and supportive case management.

resources.name: Peer Harm Reduction Employment
resources.description: The Ally Centre employs people with lived experience of homelessness and substance use as paid peer workers to support outreach, education, and client navigation across Cape Breton. Roles are stipended or waged and include training, supervision, and ongoing supports to promote stability and workplace retention, with referrals to treatment, housing, and community services. This model creates micro-employment and supported work experience that can lead to longer-term opportunities with local partners.

solutions.text: Non-police crisis response teams: Train volunteers, peer responders, social workers and nurses to form community crisis teams that respond to mental-health and substance-related calls without police, emphasizing de-escalation and service linkage.

resources.name: Mobile Outreach Street Health (MOSH)
resources.description: MOSH deploys nurses, outreach workers, and peer supporters into the community to meet people where they are, responding to homelessness, mental-health crises, and substance-related harms on the street and in shelters. The team provides on-the-spot assessment, de-escalation, overdose prevention and basic medical care, and makes warm connections to primary care, detox/OAT, housing, and social supports. As a health-led community team, they attend without police unless safety requires, offering a non-judgmental, trauma-informed alternative to law-enforcement responses.

resources.name: Mainline Needle Exchange (Outreach Program)
resources.description: Mainline operates a peer-based harm reduction outreach team across HRM that responds to people who use drugs, including during moments of crisis, in encampments and public spaces. Staff and trained peers provide crisis de-escalation, naloxone and overdose response, safer-use supplies, and immediate referrals/warm handoffs to shelter, detox, opioid agonist therapy, and mental-health care. The service is community-led and non-police, diverting crises from 911 and linking people directly to supports.

resources.name: Ally Centre of Cape Breton – Outreach & Harm Reduction
resources.description: The Ally Centre’s outreach and harm reduction team provides street-level crisis response in Sydney, supporting people who use drugs and those experiencing homelessness. Peer workers and nurses intervene in overdoses, offer de-escalation and supportive counselling, and connect individuals to housing, primary care, mental-health services, and opioid agonist treatment; they also operate sanctioned harm reduction programming. This is a non-police, peer-informed approach that builds trust and reduces the need for law-enforcement involvement in mental-health and substance-related calls.

resources.name: Harm Reduction Outreach Program
resources.description: Northern Healthy Connections Society runs a mobile harm reduction outreach team in Truro and surrounding communities that responds to mental-health and substance-related crises without police. Outreach workers and peers conduct welfare checks, provide overdose prevention and reversal, de-escalate conflicts, and offer transportation/support with warm referrals to Nova Scotia Health services, shelters, detox, and social supports. The team provides a community-first, trauma-informed alternative to law-enforcement responses.

solutions.text: Community respite spaces and warming centres: Establish short-term daytime respite centres offering warm space, showers, laundry, food, phone access and referrals, run in partnership with community groups and churches.

resources.name: Halifax Centre of Hope – Community Services & Drop‑In
resources.organization: The Salvation Army – Halifax Centre of Hope
resources.description: The Salvation Army’s Halifax Centre of Hope operates a daytime community services and drop-in space that provides warm respite, hot meals, showers, laundry, phone and internet access, mail service, and referrals to housing, health, and substance-use supports. As a church-based provider, it directly implements community respite and warming supports and coordinates with local agencies to connect people experiencing homelessness or housing instability with needed services.

resources.name: Phoenix Centre for Youth (PCFY)
resources.description: PCFY is a daytime drop‑in for youth that offers a safe, warm space with access to showers, laundry, hot meals/snacks, phones, internet, and a mailing address, alongside on‑site staff who provide referrals to housing, health, and harm‑reduction services. By meeting immediate respite needs and offering practical amenities and navigation supports, PCFY advances the community warming-centre model for young people at risk of or experiencing homelessness.

resources.name: Open Arms Resource Centre (Daytime Drop‑In & Warming Space)
resources.description: Open Arms operates a downtown Kentville daytime drop‑in that provides warm space, showers, laundry, food, phone/charging, and on‑site support with referrals to housing, health care, and addictions services. The organization partners with local churches and community volunteers and also activates church‑hosted warming spaces during extreme weather, directly aligning with the respite and warming‑centre solution.

solutions.text: Public education and anti-stigma campaigns: Run local campaigns, school programs and community dialogues that humanize people who use drugs, correct myths about addiction, and promote inclusive neighbourhoods to improve perceptions of livability.

resources.name: Harm Reduction 101 and Community Presentations
resources.description: Mainline delivers Harm Reduction 101 workshops and tailored presentations to schools, service providers, neighbourhood groups, and workplaces across HRM to correct myths about drug use and promote people-first, non-stigmatizing language. Sessions are often co-led by peers with lived/living experience, humanizing people who use drugs while covering safer use, overdose prevention, and community inclusion to improve neighbourhood perceptions of safety and livability.
resources.address: 5511 Nora Bernard Street, Halifax, NS B3K 1B6

resources.name: Overdose Prevention & Stigma Reduction Education
resources.description: The Ally Centre of Cape Breton provides community training on overdose recognition and response (including naloxone), harm reduction basics, and respectful language, delivered to schools, service providers, and the general public. Through peer-informed talks, public awareness events, and dialogue sessions, the initiative challenges myths about addiction and homelessness, humanizes people who use drugs, and builds more compassionate and inclusive communities in Cape Breton.

resources.name: MOSH (Mobile Outreach Street Health) – Community Education
resources.description: North End Community Health Centre’s MOSH team provides community education on harm reduction, trauma-informed care, and supportive responses to homelessness and substance use for local residents, businesses, landlords, and schools. Using lived-experience perspectives and practical guidance, these sessions reduce stigma, address safety concerns with evidence, and promote inclusive neighbourhoods where people who use drugs are treated with dignity.

resources.name: CHOICES: Substance Use and Gambling Program – School & Community Education
resources.description: IWK’s CHOICES program offers prevention and early-intervention education for youth, families, and educators, including school presentations and community workshops that provide accurate information about substances, normalize help-seeking, and counter stigma. By centering youth voices and evidence-based harm reduction, CHOICES helps create welcoming, informed school and community environments that improve perceptions of safety and quality of life.

solutions.text: Community-based overdose prevention hubs: Where regulation allows, support local, peer-operated overdose prevention hubs that provide supervised use, harm-reduction supplies, health checks and rapid connection to treatment and housing services.

resources.name: Overdose Prevention Site (OPS)
resources.description: The Ally Centre’s OPS provides a supervised space where people can use pre-obtained substances under the observation of trained, peer-informed staff, reducing the risk of fatal overdose. The site distributes harm-reduction supplies (sterile consumption equipment, naloxone), offers basic health checks and wound care, and rapidly connects participants to opioid agonist treatment, detox, primary care, and housing/navigation supports.

resources.name: Overdose Prevention Site (OPS)
resources.description: Northern Healthy Connections Society operates a community-based OPS where people can consume pre-obtained drugs in a supervised setting, with peers and staff monitoring for overdose and providing immediate response. The hub offers harm-reduction supplies, on-site health assessments and naloxone training, and facilitates fast referrals to addiction treatment, mental health care, and local housing/homelessness services.

solutions.text: Partnerships with pharmacies and primary care for rapid OAT access: Work with local pharmacies and clinics to create walk-in slots and fast-track pathways to opioid agonist treatment (OAT), including community funding for first doses or transportation.

resources.name: Rapid Access to Addictions Medicine (RAAM) Clinic – Central Zone (Halifax)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Health’s RAAM Clinic provides low-barrier, walk-in assessment and same/next-day initiation of opioid agonist treatment (OAT), including buprenorphine/naloxone. Clinic prescribers coordinate directly with local community pharmacies for rapid first doses and ongoing witnessed dispensing, and they collaborate with primary care to fast-track follow-up and continuity of care. Staff also help patients navigate practical barriers (e.g., transportation supports available through health or community partners) to make rapid access feasible for people experiencing homelessness or instability.

resources.name: Rapid Access to Addictions Medicine (RAAM) Clinic – Western Zone (Kentville/Annapolis Valley)
resources.description: This RAAM site offers walk-in, no-referral access to OAT with quick induction and stabilization, then links clients to family physicians or nurse practitioners for ongoing care. The team partners with community pharmacies in the Valley to arrange same-day witnessed doses and streamlined dispensing, reducing delays for people at risk due to toxic drug supply. Care coordinators also work with local services to mitigate transportation barriers when possible.

resources.name: Rapid Access to Addictions Medicine (RAAM) Clinic – Northern Zone (New Glasgow/Pictou County)
resources.description: The Northern Zone RAAM clinic provides rapid, walk-in OAT starts and stabilization, prioritizing people without a primary care provider or those facing housing instability. Clinicians coordinate with nearby community pharmacies for immediate buprenorphine/naloxone induction and daily observed dosing, and establish fast-track pathways back to primary care for follow-up. Staff help clients address access issues, including transportation logistics through local supports.
resources.address: 835 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3S6

resources.name: Rapid Access to Addictions Medicine (RAAM) Clinic – Western Zone (Yarmouth)
resources.description: The Yarmouth RAAM clinic delivers same-day or rapid-start OAT and harm-reduction supports through a walk-in model, minimizing barriers for people affected by homelessness and toxic drug supply. Providers partner with local pharmacies to initiate first doses quickly and arrange ongoing dispensing, while coordinating with primary care to transition patients for longer-term management. The team also connects clients with community resources that can assist with transportation and other practical needs.

solutions.text: Local data-sharing and coordinated service navigation: Create a secure, community-led data-sharing forum for service providers and peer organizations to coordinate referrals, track system gaps, and rapidly respond to emerging hot spots of need.

resources.name: Halifax Situation Table (Collaborative Risk-Driven Intervention)
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality — Public Safety Office
resources.description: A multi-agency problem-solving table convened by the Public Safety Office that brings together housing, health, policing, justice, and community organizations to share limited client information under strict privacy protocols and coordinated consent. The table enables rapid, cross-agency referrals and jointly monitors patterns (e.g., encampment risks, overdose clusters) to identify system gaps and respond quickly to emerging hot spots in homelessness, substance use, and public safety.

resources.name: Navigator Street Outreach Program
resources.description: A street-level service navigation program that coordinates referrals among shelters, housing supports, income assistance, health and addictions care, and justice partners for people who are unsheltered or at risk. The Navigator collaborates through community case conferencing and shares outreach data and trends with partners to spot service gaps and hot spots, improving real-time responses across the downtown Halifax and Dartmouth areas.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 2A2

resources.name: Coordinated Access and By-Name List (participation via shelters and housing programs)
resources.description: Shelter Nova Scotia participates in Halifax’s Coordinated Access system and maintains client information in HIFIS (a secure, shared homelessness information system) to streamline referrals and track inflow/outflow on the community’s By-Name List. Through case conferencing and data-sharing agreements, the organization and its partners identify system bottlenecks, prioritize housing matches, and respond to emerging needs like encampments and drug-poisoning risks.

resources.name: Wije’winen Housing and Support Navigation
resources.description: The Mi’kmaw Native Friendship Centre operates a culturally grounded housing and wraparound support hub that coordinates referrals among Indigenous and mainstream service providers. Through participation in community coordinated access processes and shared case management, the team securely tracks client needs and service gaps, and collaborates with partners to respond quickly to hot spots impacting urban Indigenous community members.

resources.name: Phoenix Centre for Youth — Coordinated Service Navigation
