resources.description: Volta Academy is a skills-focused program that pairs students and early-stage founders with experienced entrepreneurs, investors, and industry experts for regular mentorship and coaching. Participants receive guidance on validating ideas, building ventures, and growing careers in Nova Scotia’s startup ecosystem, creating structured mentorship circles that connect youth with local business leaders.

resources.name: Business Advisory & Mentorship
resources.organization: Centre for Entrepreneurship Education and Development (CEED)
resources.description: CEED’s advisory and mentorship services connect aspiring and young entrepreneurs with seasoned local business owners and subject-matter experts for regular coaching, skills development, and peer-to-peer learning. Through workshops, one-on-one advising, and mentor networks, youth gain practical insights and contacts needed to start and grow ventures in communities across Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 225, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: IGNITE Mentorship & Coaching
resources.description: IGNITE Atlantic facilitates mentorship for students and early-stage entrepreneurs by connecting them with local business owners, tradespeople, and community leaders in rural regions of Nova Scotia. Through cohort programming, office hours with advisors, and community events at its innovation hubs, youth receive ongoing skills-sharing and entrepreneurship coaching that strengthens local opportunity outside HRM.

solutions.text: Inter‑Municipal Coordination Table: Form a regular council of neighbouring towns, First Nations and rural communities to align investment priorities, share services and jointly pursue regional funding.

resources.name: Eastern District Planning Commission (EDPC)
resources.description: EDPC is a shared municipal planning, development, and building inspection service governed by a board of representatives from multiple neighbouring municipalities in eastern Nova Scotia. It functions as an inter‑municipal coordination table by aligning land‑use priorities, transportation and infrastructure planning, and service standards across member towns and rural counties, reducing duplication and improving regional outcomes. The commission also helps communities jointly pursue provincial and federal funding for regional projects by presenting unified, prioritized plans.
resources.address: 606 Reeves Street, Unit 104, Port Hawkesbury, NS B9A 2R7

resources.name: Western Regional Enterprise Network (Western REN)
resources.description: Western REN is a collaborative regional economic development body created by municipalities in Southwest Nova Scotia and the Province, with a board that brings together municipal, business, and community leaders. It acts as a standing inter‑municipal council to set shared investment priorities, coordinate sector strategies (e.g., fisheries, tourism, clean energy), and align infrastructure and workforce initiatives across rural communities. The REN regularly develops joint proposals and leverages regional partnerships to secure funding for projects that benefit multiple member municipalities.

resources.name: Cape Breton Regional Enterprise Network (via Cape Breton Partnership)
resources.description: Delivered by the Cape Breton Partnership, the regional enterprise network convenes municipalities and Mi’kmaw communities across Unama’ki–Cape Breton to coordinate economic development, investment attraction, and workforce initiatives. It operates as an inter‑municipal table where local governments and First Nations align regional priorities, share services such as investment readiness and business outreach, and jointly pursue provincial and federal funding. This coordinated approach helps balance opportunities between the urban centre and rural communities across the island.
resources.address: 275 Charlotte Street, Suite 204, Sydney, NS B1P 1C6

resources.name: Kings Transit Authority — Inter‑Municipal Transit Service
resources.description: Kings Transit is a public transit system jointly governed and funded by neighbouring municipalities in the Annapolis Valley, providing region‑wide mobility that connects towns and rural communities. Its board structure serves as an inter‑municipal coordination table to prioritize route investments, pool resources, and submit joint applications for senior‑government funding to expand and modernize service. By coordinating transit across jurisdictions, it supports equitable access to jobs, education, and services outside larger urban centres.
resources.address: 29 Crescent Drive, New Minas, NS B4N 3G7

solutions.text: Community Renewable Energy Projects: Develop community‑owned solar, wind or biomass projects that lower local energy costs, create jobs and generate revenue for community initiatives.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility
resources.description: The Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility operates a subscription-based community solar garden that lets residents and businesses buy shares and receive bill credits, keeping energy dollars local. As a municipally owned project, savings and revenues flow back into the community to stabilize rates and support local services, while construction and maintenance create local jobs. This directly advances community-owned clean energy generation in a small rural town.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Berwick Community Solar Garden
resources.description: Berwick Electric Commission’s community solar garden produces locally owned renewable electricity and offers residents the ability to participate and receive credits on their municipal power bills. Revenues and cost savings remain in Berwick, helping to fund community priorities and keep electricity rates stable for a rural customer base. The project also supports local employment through installation and ongoing operations.

resources.name: Antigonish Community Solar Garden
resources.description: The Antigonish Electric Utility operates a community solar garden that allows utility customers to subscribe to locally generated solar power and receive bill credits, cutting energy costs. Because it is municipally owned, revenues are reinvested in local services and grid improvements, helping a university town and surrounding rural area share in the benefits. The project supports local contractors and clean energy jobs while building community energy resilience.

resources.name: Ellershouse Wind Farm (AREA Municipal Partnership)
resources.description: The Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA)—a partnership of the Towns of Berwick, Mahone Bay, and Antigonish—owns and operates the Ellershouse Wind Farm, supplying clean power to three small municipal electric utilities. Community ownership keeps profits and cost savings within these towns, lowering long-term electricity costs and generating revenue for local priorities. Development and ongoing operations support skilled jobs across rural Nova Scotia and strengthen local energy independence.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

obstacles.title: Cost of Living and Student Debt Burden
obstacles.description: Rising prices and debt loads delay home ownership, entrepreneurship, and family formation.

solutions.text: Community Land Trusts and Affordable Housing Co-ops: Establish community land trusts and housing co-ops to acquire land and preserve long‑term affordable rental and ownership options for young households, preventing market speculation from pricing locals out.

resources.name: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia – Affordable Homeownership Program
resources.description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia acquires land and builds homes that are sold to qualifying families through affordable, non-profit stewardship models (e.g., geared-to-income mortgages and resale restrictions) that preserve long-term affordability. By holding land and homes within a community-oriented framework and controlling resale conditions, the program prevents speculative price escalation and keeps ownership opportunities within reach for young households.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Co-operative Council – Co-operative Development Services
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Co-operative Council provides hands-on support to establish and sustain housing co-operatives across the province, including incorporation, governance training, and financing guidance. By helping groups acquire land collectively and structure it under member-owned housing co-ops, the program locks in affordability over the long term and shields homes from market speculation that can price out local young families.

solutions.text: Rent-to-Own and Shared‑Equity Home Programs: Create locally administered rent‑to‑own and shared‑equity models that let young people build equity with lower up‑front costs, with municipal or non‑profit partners guaranteeing transparency and resale rules.

resources.name: Affordable Homeownership Program
resources.description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia’s Affordable Homeownership Program enables modest-income households to purchase a home with significantly lower up‑front costs and transparent terms. Homes are sold using an affordable first mortgage paired with a deferred, zero‑interest second mortgage that acts as shared equity; clear buy‑back and resale rules ensure long‑term affordability while allowing purchasers to build equity as they pay down their mortgage. The model mirrors the solution’s shared‑equity approach by using nonprofit administration, standardized eligibility, homeowner education, and covenants that preserve community benefit.

resources.name: Indigenous Housing Partnership (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: This Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia initiative adapts the organization’s shared‑equity homeownership model for Indigenous families living on- and off‑reserve, reducing barriers to ownership with lower up‑front costs and sweat‑equity in place of a traditional down payment. Purchasers receive an affordable first mortgage and a deferred shared‑equity second mortgage, with transparent resale and buy‑back provisions that protect long‑term affordability while allowing families to build equity over time. The program partners with Indigenous communities and local nonprofits, aligning with the solution’s call for locally administered, transparent shared‑equity pathways.

solutions.text: Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) & Secondary Suite Support: Promote and streamline permits, design templates, and low‑interest loans for homeowners to build ADUs/secondary suites to increase affordable rental supply and allow multi‑generational household support.

resources.name: Secondary and Backyard Suites (HRM)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality allows secondary suites and backyard suites as-of-right in many zones and provides step-by-step permitting guidance, checklists, and FAQs to help homeowners legalize or build new ADUs. By clarifying rules, streamlining approvals, and offering homeowner-facing resources, HRM reduces red tape and soft costs, directly supporting more accessory rental supply and multigenerational living options.

resources.name: Secondary and Backyard Suite Program
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Provincial Housing Agency (Housing Nova Scotia)
resources.description: This provincial program provides financial assistance to homeowners to create a new secondary or backyard suite, with forgivable or low-interest loan options tied to affordability and accessibility criteria. By offsetting upfront construction costs and setting clear eligibility and design requirements, the program expands affordable ADU supply and enables families to support seniors, students, and intergenerational living.

resources.name: Backyard and Secondary Suites (Town of Wolfville)
resources.description: Wolfville’s planning framework permits both secondary and backyard suites and provides homeowner guidance on permits, design standards, and servicing. The town’s clear rules and application support streamline approvals and reduce uncertainty, helping residents add small rental units or family suites that increase local affordable housing options.

resources.name: Secondary and Garden Suites (Municipality of the County of Kings)
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings — Planning & Inspections
resources.description: Kings County permits secondary suites and garden suites and offers guidance through its planning office on zoning, building permits, and code-compliant designs. By making ADUs permissible across more areas and providing a clear approvals path, the municipality supports homeowners to add long-term rental supply and flexible, multigenerational housing.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

solutions.text: Local Microgrant and Seed Funds for Young Entrepreneurs: Set up community‑run microgrant programs and matching seed funds, administered by local business associations or foundations, to reduce startup capital barriers for young founders.

resources.name: Spark Nova Scotia
resources.description: Spark Nova Scotia is a province-wide, non-dilutive funding competition that awards cash grants to early-stage founders to validate and launch innovative startups. Administered by Invest Nova Scotia in partnership with regional ecosystem organizations, Spark directly reduces startup capital barriers by providing microgrant-style awards plus mentorship and training. Young founders are a core participant group, benefiting from seed-stage funds that help them move from idea to traction without taking on debt.
resources.address: 1871 Hollis Street, Suite 1100, Halifax, NS B3J 0C3

resources.name: Volta Cohort
resources.description: Volta Cohort is a biannual pitch program that provides seed funding, mentorship, and network access to early-stage Atlantic Canadian startups, with many participants and winners being young founders. Administered by Volta, the program offers investment-based seed funding and wraparound support that lowers the upfront capital hurdle and accelerates business launch and growth. This community-run initiative helps founders secure early financing before they can access traditional loans or venture capital.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Unit 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: Ready2Launch
resources.description: Ready2Launch is Dal Innovates’ summer accelerator that provides non-dilutive funding, coaching, and resources to student and recent graduate teams building startups. The program functions as a microgrant and pre-seed support mechanism, giving young founders a stipend and structured mentorship so they can focus on validating their business without taking on debt. This reduces the initial capital burden and helps youth-led ventures reach key early milestones.

resources.name: Black Start-Up Project
resources.description: The Black Start-Up Project, led by Tribe Network, provides non-dilutive microgrants and entrepreneurial support to Black founders across Atlantic Canada, with a strong presence in Nova Scotia. By offering small cash grants alongside mentorship and community connections, the program helps young entrepreneurs overcome early capital barriers and build sustainable ventures. Funds are administered by a local community organization, aligning with a community-run microgrant model.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Unit 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

solutions.text: Community‑Run Student Debt Advisory Clinics: Offer free clinics (in partnership with universities, credit unions, and legal clinics) that provide budgeting support, debt‑management plans, and guidance on provincial/national repayment programs.

resources.name: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service
resources.organization: Schulich School of Law, Dalhousie University
resources.description: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service offers free legal information and summary advice clinics to low‑income community members and students, including support on debt, consumer issues, and credit problems. Advisors help clients understand and navigate provincial and federal student‑loan repayment options (e.g., Repayment Assistance Plan and Nova Scotia Student Assistance programs), provide budgeting guidance, and connect individuals to community credit‑counselling partners for debt‑management plans when appropriate.

resources.name: Financial Literacy Workshops (Halifax Public Libraries)
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries hosts free community workshops and drop‑in sessions on budgeting, credit management, and student‑loan repayment, often delivered in partnership with local credit unions, non‑profits, and legal information providers. These sessions help students and recent graduates understand Nova Scotia and Canada student‑loan programs, build realistic budgets, and access debt‑management strategies, mirroring the community‑run clinic model.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Financial Aid & Awards
resources.description: Saint Mary’s University’s Financial Aid & Awards office provides free one‑on‑one advising and group clinics on budgeting, student‑loan management, and post‑graduation repayment planning. Staff guide students and alumni through Nova Scotia and Canada Student Loans processes (including RAP and interest relief), help create repayment timelines, and partner with community financial experts for sessions on debt‑management options.

resources.name: Student Awards and Financial Aid (Ivany Campus)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) – Ivany Campus
resources.description: NSCC’s Student Awards and Financial Aid team offers free budgeting support, financial coaching, and student‑loan advising to learners and recent graduates, delivered through appointments and periodic clinics at campus. Advisors explain provincial and federal repayment programs, help prepare repayment plans, and refer individuals to accredited community credit‑counselling partners for debt‑management plans when needed.

solutions.text: Employer‑Community Tuition Repayment Partnerships: Encourage local employers to co‑fund tuition repayment or loan forgiveness in exchange for commitments to work locally, coordinated through chambers of commerce or industry councils.

resources.name: EHS Nova Scotia Paramedic Tuition Reimbursement Program
resources.organization: Medavie Health Services Nova Scotia (Emergency Medical Care Inc.)
resources.description: Medavie Health Services Nova Scotia (which operates EHS ambulance services) reimburses tuition for new Primary Care and Advanced Care Paramedic graduates who commit to multi‑year return‑of‑service employment in Nova Scotia. The employer co-funds tuition repayment with the Province and administers agreements in partnership with local training institutions, directly reducing graduates’ debt and tying financial support to sustained local work.
resources.address: 100 Eileen Stubbs Avenue, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1Y6

resources.name: Tuition Relief for Nurses (TRN)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Health’s TRN program provides tuition relief and student-loan repayment to nurses who sign return‑of‑service agreements to work in eligible roles and communities across the province. The incentive is employer-backed and coordinated with the Department of Health and Wellness, functioning as a co‑funded tuition repayment mechanism that lowers debt burdens while ensuring nurses remain employed locally.

resources.name: Tuition Relief for Doctors Program
resources.description: Coordinated by Nova Scotia Health’s Physician Recruitment team with the Office of Healthcare Professionals Recruitment, this program offers substantial tuition relief to family physicians who enter formal return‑of‑service agreements to practice in Nova Scotia communities. The incentive offsets medical school debt in exchange for multi‑year commitments to work locally, aligning employer recruitment with community retention goals.

resources.name: Pathways to Shipbuilding
resources.description: Irving Shipbuilding partners with NSCC, unions and community groups to sponsor tuition and training for cohorts in shipbuilding trades, with graduates moving into guaranteed jobs at the Halifax Shipyard under employer-set return‑of‑service expectations. By covering or offsetting tuition and linking funding to local employment commitments through industry partnerships, the program reduces debt loads and anchors skilled workers in Nova Scotia.

solutions.text: Apprenticeship, Trades and Placement Hubs: Develop community hubs that connect youth with trades training, paid apprenticeships, and employer placements (including wraparound supports like transportation and childcare).

resources.name: Women Unlimited
resources.description: Women Unlimited is a province-wide program that recruits, trains, and supports diverse women to enter skilled trades and technology careers. Working in partnership with NSCC and unions/industry, it delivers pre-apprenticeship cohort programs that combine college-based trades training with employer exposure and paid work placements, and then connects graduates into registered apprenticeships. The program provides wraparound supports—such as transportation assistance, childcare referrals, PPE/tools, and coaching—to reduce financial barriers and improve completion and retention.

resources.name: Pathways to Shipbuilding
resources.description: Pathways to Shipbuilding is a cohort-based initiative led by NSCC with Irving Shipbuilding and community partners that prepares underrepresented Nova Scotians for marine trades careers. Participants complete foundational and trade-specific training at NSCC followed by paid work terms at Halifax Shipyard, progressing directly into apprenticeship roles with employer sponsors. The model includes academic upgrading, mentoring, and barrier-reduction supports (e.g., transportation assistance and childcare referrals) to enable participation and long-term success.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Works Employment Services – TEAM Work Cooperative
resources.description: TEAM Work Cooperative operates a Nova Scotia Works employment centre that serves as a hub connecting youth and jobseekers to skilled trades training, apprenticeships, and employer placements across HRM. Through job developers and partnerships with NSCC, the Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency, unions, and local contractors, clients are matched to paid roles, wage-subsidized placements, and apprenticeship starts. Case managers help remove barriers with eligible wraparound supports such as transit passes, work gear, short-term training funds, and childcare subsidies, addressing cost-of-living pressures during training and early employment.
resources.address: 7051 Bayers Road, Suite 501, Halifax, NS B3L 4V2

solutions.text: Childcare Co‑ops and Sliding‑Scale Childcare Programs: Support parent and community childcare co‑ops and partner with municipalities to expand sliding‑scale childcare subsidies, reducing one of the primary costs that delays family formation.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Child Care Subsidy Program
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Department of Education and Early Childhood Development
resources.description: The province’s income-tested Child Care Subsidy reduces out-of-pocket fees for eligible families using licensed child care, functioning as a sliding-scale subsidy based on household income and need. By lowering monthly child care costs, the program directly addresses cost-of-living pressures that can delay family formation and career decisions for young people.

resources.name: Canada-Wide Early Learning and Child Care (CWELCC) in Nova Scotia
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Department of Education and Early Childhood Development (in partnership with the Government of Canada)
resources.description: Nova Scotia’s CWELCC implementation reduces parent fees at licensed centres and family home child care, with the goal of reaching an average of $10/day care, substantially lowering the cost burden on families. This system-wide fee reduction complements targeted subsidies and makes licensed child care more affordable across municipalities, supporting family formation and workforce participation.

resources.name: YMCA of Greater Halifax/Dartmouth – Early Learning & Child Care (with Financial Assistance)
resources.description: The YMCA operates licensed early learning and school-age programs and provides need-based financial assistance while also accepting provincial child care subsidies, effectively creating a sliding-scale fee structure for eligible families. By combining internal assistance with government supports, the YMCA lowers child care costs for working parents and students, easing cost-of-living pressures that affect family planning and career choices.

resources.name: Pre-primary Program (HRCE)
resources.description: HRCE delivers Nova Scotia’s free, universal pre-primary program for four-year-olds in public schools, eliminating fees for a year of early learning that often substitutes for paid child care. By removing costs for this age group across communities, the program reduces overall child care expenses for families and supports parents’ ability to work or train.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

solutions.text: Community Energy Efficiency and Bulk Purchasing: Organize group bulk purchases for insulation, heat pumps, and energy retrofits, plus community programs to help low‑income young households reduce utility bills long term.

resources.name: HomeWarming
resources.organization: Efficiency Nova Scotia and Clean Foundation
resources.description: HomeWarming provides no-cost home energy assessments and free upgrades like insulation, air sealing, and other efficiency measures for income-qualified households across Nova Scotia. Delivered jointly by Efficiency Nova Scotia and Clean Foundation, it reduces utility bills long term for low-income families and young households by installing proven efficiency retrofits through vetted local contractors and standardized measures at scale.

resources.name: Heat Pump Affordability Program
resources.description: This provincial program provides fully funded or deeply subsidized cold-climate heat pumps to income-qualified Nova Scotians, covering assessment, equipment, and installation. Administered by Efficiency Nova Scotia, it leverages a network of approved contractors and bulk procurement to lower costs, helping low-income and younger households cut heating expenses and improve home comfort for the long term.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) Program
resources.description: Clean Energy Financing enables homeowners in participating Nova Scotia municipalities to complete energy retrofits—such as insulation, heat pumps, and air sealing—and repay the cost over time via their property tax bill. Operated by Clean Foundation in partnership with municipalities, the program coordinates vetted contractors and streamlined project delivery to reduce per‑project costs and help households lower their energy bills sustainably.

resources.name: Bridgewater Clean Energy Financing Program
resources.description: Through the Town of Bridgewater’s PACE-based Clean Energy Financing, residents can bundle energy upgrades—like insulation and heat pumps—into affordable financing repaid on the property tax bill. The program supports community‑wide uptake, connects homeowners with qualified contractors, and reduces long‑term utility costs by making comprehensive retrofits accessible to younger and cost‑burdened households.

solutions.text: Shared Workspaces, Maker Spaces and Equipment Libraries: Create affordable co‑working spaces, maker labs, and tool libraries that lower overhead for freelancers, creatives, and small business founders.

resources.name: Volta Coworking & Innovation Hub
resources.description: Volta is Atlantic Canada's largest innovation hub, offering affordable coworking desks, private offices, meeting rooms, and shared amenities for startups and solo founders in downtown Halifax. By centralizing space, internet, and equipment under flexible memberships, it reduces overhead for entrepreneurs and freelancers and connects them to mentorship, programming, and community.

resources.name: COVE Shared Labs and Workshops
resources.organization: COVE | Centre for Ocean Ventures & Entrepreneurship
resources.description: COVE provides shared offices, labs, workshops, and prototyping facilities for ocean-technology companies and makers on the Dartmouth waterfront. Its memberships give startups and small firms affordable access to specialized equipment, fabrication space, and dockside testing, lowering capital costs while fostering collaboration and business growth.

resources.name: Lou Duggan Creative Studio (Makerspace)
resources.description: The Lou Duggan Creative Studio at Halifax Central Library is a free public makerspace with 3D printers, sewing machines, Cricut cutters, and media tools, plus staff support and workshops. By offering no‑cost access to equipment and creative workspace, it enables students, artists, and early‑stage entrepreneurs to prototype, learn, and create without having to purchase costly tools.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: CO3 Coworking Community
resources.description: CO3 is a community coworking space in downtown Bridgewater that offers hot desks, dedicated desks, meeting rooms, and shared amenities for freelancers, small business owners, and remote workers. Flexible membership options provide professional workspace and equipment at a fraction of the cost of leasing an office, alongside networking and peer support that help founders get started locally.

solutions.text: Local Transit and Active Transport Improvements: Advocate for improved bus routes, fare reductions for students and young workers, and safe cycling infrastructure to reduce transportation costs and expand employment access.

resources.name: Affordable Access Transit Pass
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Affordable Access Program offers a 50% discount on Halifax Transit monthly passes for eligible low-income residents, including students and young workers. By lowering fare costs, the program makes daily commuting to work, classes, and training more affordable and supports broader access to employment opportunities.

resources.name: Blue Route (Provincial Cycling Network)
resources.description: Cycling Nova Scotia’s Blue Route is a province-wide initiative that builds safer cycling connections through paved-shoulder projects, bike lanes, and wayfinding, in partnership with municipalities and the Nova Scotia Department of Public Works. By expanding safe, connected cycling infrastructure, it provides a low-cost, reliable way for youth and workers to reach jobs, schools, and services while reducing transportation costs.
resources.address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

resources.name: Transportation & Active Transportation (EAC)
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre’s Transportation team advances active transportation across Nova Scotia through policy advocacy, complete streets guidance, and programs like Making Tracks that teach safe walking and cycling skills. Their work helps municipalities plan and implement safer cycling and walking infrastructure, reducing dependence on cars and cutting commuting costs for students and young workers.

resources.name: Cape Breton University U-Pass
resources.organization: Cape Breton University (in partnership with Transit Cape Breton and the CBU Students’ Union)
resources.description: CBU’s U-Pass provides eligible full-time students with unlimited access to Transit Cape Breton through a universal transit pass. This lowers transportation costs for students and improves access to jobs, co-ops, and services along transit routes, supporting affordable mobility across the Sydney area.
resources.address: 1250 Grand Lake Road, Sydney, NS B1P 6L2

resources.name: Halifax Rapid Transit Strategy
resources.description: HRM’s Halifax Rapid Transit Strategy is an active initiative to implement fast, frequent bus rapid transit lines and expanded ferry service connecting key employment and education hubs. By improving route frequency and reliability, it shortens commutes and broadens job access, making transit a more attractive, lower-cost option for students and young workers.

solutions.text: Cooperative Business Development Support: Provide training, incubation, and seed financing for worker‑owned cooperatives so young workers can build businesses with shared risk and local wealth retention.

resources.name: International Centre for Co-operative Management (ICCM)
resources.organization: Sobey School of Business, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: ICCM at Saint Mary’s University delivers specialized training, certificates, and graduate programs focused on co-operative and credit union management, including governance, finance, and strategy relevant to worker-owned co-ops. By equipping emerging leaders and young workers with practical co-op management skills and sector networks, ICCM directly supports the training component needed to launch and sustain worker-owned enterprises that keep wealth in local communities.

resources.name: Coady Institute – Community-Based Enterprise and Co-operative Development
resources.description: Coady Institute provides education and applied learning on community-based enterprise, co-operative development, and asset-based community development, building skills for groups to start and manage co-ops. Through coaching, peer learning, and connections to regional partners, the institute helps young people and community groups incubate worker-owned co-operatives that share risk and retain wealth locally.

resources.name: Small Business Loan Guarantee Program (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Delivered through credit unions like East Coast Credit Union, this program provides seed and early-stage financing for startups and growing businesses, including co-operatives and social enterprises. By reducing lender risk and pairing financing with advisory support, it enables young worker-owners to capitalize their co-ops, create quality jobs, and keep profits circulating in their communities.

resources.name: New Dawn Community Investment Fund (CEDIF)
resources.description: New Dawn raises local capital and provides patient financing to community-rooted enterprises across Cape Breton, with eligibility that includes co-operatives and worker-led ventures. Coupled with mentoring and collaborative space through New Dawn’s community hubs, the fund functions as seed financing and light incubation that helps new worker-owned co-ops start up and build long-term, locally retained wealth.

solutions.text: Peer Mentorship, Networking Circles and Alumni Return Programs: Organize mentorship networks linking recent grads and young professionals with established local leaders, and create ‘return-home’ incentives and alumni programming to attract former residents back.

resources.name: Professional Mentorship Program
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS pairs internationally trained graduates and young professionals with established Nova Scotia mentors in their field for one-on-one guidance, networking, and career navigation. The program facilitates informational interviews, industry connections, and local credential insights that accelerate job entry and income growth—helping reduce the burden of student debt and cost-of-living challenges through stronger networks.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 1020, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Connector Program
resources.description: The Halifax Partnership’s Connector Program links recent graduates and young professionals with senior business and community leaders (“Connectors”) for structured networking introductions. By creating warm referrals and circles of contacts, it helps participants find meaningful local employment and build careers in Nova Scotia—key steps in managing debt loads and making it easier to stay or return home.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Dal Alumni Link
resources.description: Dal Alumni Link is an alumni-to-student/young grad mentoring platform that matches emerging talent with experienced Dalhousie alumni for career conversations, advice, and networking. In addition to one-on-one mentorship, Dal’s alumni programming and Nova Scotia-based events encourage graduates who have left to reconnect with local employers and opportunities—supporting return-home pathways and stronger professional networks.
resources.address: Henry Hicks Building, 6299 South Street, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2

resources.name: SMU Mentors (Ten Thousand Coffees)
resources.description: Saint Mary’s University’s SMU Mentors program uses the Ten Thousand Coffees platform to connect students and recent graduates with alumni mentors for career guidance, informational interviews, and networking. The university’s alumni engagement and homecoming activities in Halifax strengthen ties to the local job market and community, encouraging alumni to return and helping young professionals build the networks needed to manage living costs and launch careers.

solutions.text: Financial Literacy, Budgeting and Credit Clinics: Run community workshops on budgeting, loan consolidation, student loan repayment strategies, and credit rebuilding, delivered through libraries, schools, and financial cooperatives.

resources.name: Financial Literacy Workshops
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries runs recurring, free workshops and information sessions on budgeting, managing debt, understanding credit scores, and student loan repayment options, often in partnership with community credit counsellors and government agencies. Sessions are delivered in-branch (including Central Library) and online, making them accessible to youth, students, and newcomers. This directly implements budgeting and credit clinics by providing practical tools for consolidating debt, rebuilding credit, and planning repayments.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Financial Literacy for Newcomers
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS delivers newcomer-focused financial literacy classes and coaching covering budgeting in Canada, banking, credit building, borrowing options, and student loan repayment information. Workshops are offered at ISANS offices and through community partners (including libraries and schools), with one-on-one settlement counselling and referrals to trusted consolidation and credit-rebuilding supports. This implements the solution by equipping participants with budgeting tools, credit education, and repayment strategies to reduce cost-of-living pressures.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Financial Literacy Workshops
resources.description: East Coast Credit Union offers free community seminars and one-on-one coaching on budgeting, credit rebuilding, debt consolidation options, and student loan repayment strategies across its branches and with local schools and community groups. As a financial cooperative, staff help participants build budgets, understand credit reports and scores, and compare consolidation and repayment pathways. These clinics directly address living costs and debt burdens by improving financial capability and access to responsible credit solutions.

resources.name: Financial Literacy Sessions
resources.description: Valley Credit Union hosts free seminars and personalized financial reviews focused on budgeting, managing and consolidating debt, rebuilding credit, and understanding student loan repayment options. Sessions are delivered at branches and in partnership with local libraries, schools, and employment centres, and include practical tools like budgeting templates and credit check guidance. This fulfills the solution by providing accessible, community-based budgeting and credit clinics that help people stabilize finances and plan for home ownership or entrepreneurship.

resources.name: Financial Literacy Programs
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Library hosts free financial literacy programs at branches such as McConnell Library, featuring sessions on budgeting, credit scores, debt management, student loans, and fraud prevention, often delivered with community partners. Workshops include take-home budgeting tools and referrals to reputable credit counselling and consolidation supports. These library-based clinics implement the solution by making practical money management and credit education accessible to youth, students, and families.

solutions.text: Tax/Benefits Navigation and Emergency Income Smoothing: Offer local clinics and small crisis‑grant programs (via community foundations) to help young people access tax credits, benefits, and short‑term relief to avoid high‑cost debt.

resources.name: Income Tax Program & Benevolent Fund
resources.description: Brunswick Street Mission operates one of Halifax’s largest Community Volunteer Income Tax Program (CVITP) clinics, helping low‑income residents file taxes so they can access refundable credits and benefits like the GST/HST credit, Canada Child Benefit, and provincial rebates. Its Benevolent Fund provides small, rapid‑response grants for urgent needs such as rent, utilities, prescriptions, or work gear, smoothing short‑term income shocks. Together, these services help young people avoid high‑cost debt by unlocking benefits and offering immediate crisis relief.

resources.name: Free Income Tax Clinics (CVITP) – Halifax Central Library
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries hosts free CVITP tax clinics each tax season, including at Halifax Central Library, where trained volunteers file simple tax returns and help patrons access federal and provincial benefits and credits. Filing returns ensures young adults receive refunds and income‑tested supports, improving cash flow. Library staff also connect clients with local emergency assistance programs when needed.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Free Income Tax Clinic (CVITP) – Spryfield
resources.description: Chebucto Connections runs an annual CVITP clinic that assists residents in filing taxes and screening for benefits and credits, helping unlock refunds and supports like the Canada Child Benefit and provincial affordability rebates. Staff offer one‑on‑one navigation and referrals to community resources, including emergency assistance for essentials such as utilities or food. This combination of benefit access and crisis referral helps young people bridge shortfalls without turning to high‑cost lenders.
resources.address: 531 Herring Cove Road, Halifax, NS B3R 1X3

resources.name: Utility and Emergency Assistance Program
resources.description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank provides small, one‑time grants and in‑kind support to households facing financial crises, including assistance with power bills, heating fuel, and essential needs to prevent service cut‑offs or eviction. Staff help clients understand and apply for available government benefits and rebates, and refer to free tax clinics so eligible young people can claim refundable credits. These supports smooth income during emergencies and reduce reliance on payday loans or other high‑cost debt.

obstacles.title: Climate Risks and Community Resilience
obstacles.description: Coastal erosion, storms, and flooding raise insurance and infrastructure costs; slow progress on green job transitions.

solutions.text: Community-led Living Shoreline and Dune Restoration: Volunteer and contractor teams restore and stabilize eroding coastlines using native grasses, dune rebuilding, cobble berms and other nature-based measures to reduce erosion, buffer storms and create habitat. Projects can be phased, documented, and used to attract provincial or federal grants.

resources.name: Coastal Adaptation Program
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre’s Coastal Adaptation Program leads community-led dune and living shoreline restoration across Nova Scotia. They organize volunteer plantings of native marram grass, install sand fencing and biodegradable coir logs, and work with municipalities and provincial parks to rebuild dunes and stabilize eroding beaches, buffering storms while creating wildlife habitat. Staff and partners monitor sites and publish results that communities can use to leverage provincial and federal climate adaptation grants.

resources.name: Coastal Restoration Program – Living Shorelines
resources.description: Coastal Action designs and delivers nature-based shoreline stabilization projects in Lunenburg County and beyond. Working with volunteers, contractors, and waterfront landowners, the team installs hybrid measures such as cobble berms, coir-based erosion controls, and native saltmarsh and dune vegetation to reduce erosion and improve habitat. They document project performance and engage local residents, helping municipalities and community groups secure funding for phased restoration.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations – Living Shorelines and Nature-based Coastal Solutions
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations provides technical leadership and on-the-ground implementation of living shoreline and other nature-based coastal solutions in Nova Scotia. The centre trains community groups, hosts volunteer planting events, and partners with contractors to build hybrid shorelines (e.g., coir-stabilized edges, cobble berms, and salt marsh plantings) that attenuate waves and rebuild dunes. Through monitoring, guidance documents, and project reports, they help communities plan phased projects and access provincial and federal resilience grants.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Living Shoreline Project
resources.description: The Town of Mahone Bay’s Living Shoreline Project protects vulnerable waterfront along the harbour using nature-based infrastructure. In partnership with experts and volunteers, the town installed a cobble berm and planted native saltmarsh and dune species to stabilize the shoreline, reduce storm surge impacts, and enhance habitat along Edgewater Street. The municipality monitors the site and uses the documented results to support phased work and to leverage provincial and federal climate-resilience funding.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Atlantic Piping Plover Conservation Program – Nova Scotia
resources.organization: Nature Conservancy of Canada – Atlantic Region
resources.description: The Nature Conservancy of Canada runs ongoing coastal dune restoration and piping plover stewardship projects at protected beaches in Nova Scotia. Staff and volunteers rebuild degraded dunes by installing sand fencing, regrading blowouts, and planting native marram grass, improving habitat while naturally buffering storm waves and trapping sand. NCC documents restoration outcomes and works with local partners to sequence projects and secure grants that support community-led coastal resilience.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 120, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

solutions.text: Youth Climate Corps for Restoration and Resilience: A local paid program employing young people to do coastal restoration, tree planting, marsh enhancement, stormwater infrastructure installs and retrofits — providing green job experience, certifications, and pathways to trades and environmental careers.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Youth Conservation Corps (NSYCC)
resources.description: NSYCC is a paid summer employment program that places youth (ages 15–30) on crews and with host organizations across Nova Scotia to complete hands-on environmental projects. Participants carry out coastal and riparian restoration, tree planting, wetland and salt marsh enhancement, and small-scale green stormwater infrastructure like rain gardens and bioswales. The program provides training and certifications (e.g., First Aid/CPR, WHMIS, field safety) and mentorship that build pathways into environmental trades, municipal operations, and conservation careers.

resources.name: Clean Leadership Summer Internship Program
resources.description: This paid internship program matches young people with municipalities, Mi’kmaw organizations, NGOs, and businesses across Nova Scotia to work on climate adaptation and resilience projects. Interns support coastal restoration and living shoreline plans, tree and riparian planting, flood-mitigation and stormwater retrofit projects, and nature-based solutions in communities. The program includes professional development, safety training, and career coaching that connect interns to long-term opportunities in environmental services and skilled trades.

resources.name: Coastal and Water Program – Living Shorelines and Green Infrastructure
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre employs paid co-op students and early-career staff to design and implement living shorelines, dune and salt marsh restoration, riparian plantings, and community rain gardens that reduce flood and erosion risk in Nova Scotia. Teams work with municipalities and communities on stormwater retrofits, shoreline stabilization, and habitat enhancement while gaining field skills and certifications. These placements provide on-the-job training and a pathway into environmental consulting, conservation NGOs, and municipal green infrastructure roles.

solutions.text: Community Solar and Microgrid Co‑ops: Form a cooperative to deploy rooftop and ground-mount solar plus community battery storage to increase local energy resilience during storms, lower long-term energy costs, and create installation and maintenance jobs for residents.

resources.name: Berwick Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Berwick Electric Commission / Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA)
resources.description: The Town of Berwick Electric Commission, through the Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA), operates a subscriber-based community solar garden that lets residents and businesses purchase or lease shares in a local ground‑mount array and receive on‑bill credits. By pooling investment in a community-owned utility model, the program lowers barriers to solar, builds local installation and maintenance employment, and distributes generation across the town’s grid to enhance resilience; the utility has designed the project to be compatible with future community battery storage for storm readiness.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility / Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA)
resources.description: Mahone Bay’s municipal electric utility, in partnership with the Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA), runs a community solar garden that allows households and businesses to subscribe to shares in a local array and receive credits on their electric bills. This community-scale deployment aggregates demand, supports local solar and electrical trades jobs, and improves community resilience by adding distributed generation on the town’s network, with the utility planning for compatibility with community battery storage to provide backup during severe storms.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Antigonish Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Antigonish Electric Utility / Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA)
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish Electric Utility, working with the Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA), offers a community solar garden where residents and businesses can buy or lease panel shares and receive on‑bill credits tied to local generation. This shared model reduces upfront costs, keeps energy dollars in the community through local installers and operations staff, and lays the groundwork for pairing community solar with battery storage to bolster resilience during outages caused by coastal storms.

resources.name: Smart Grid Nova Scotia (Battery Storage and Community Resilience Pilot)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s Smart Grid Nova Scotia initiative pilots distributed solar integration, smart inverters, and community/behind‑the‑meter battery storage to improve reliability and enable microgrid capabilities during storms. By coordinating rooftop PV with battery systems and utility controls, the project demonstrates how neighborhoods can maintain critical services through islanding, reduce long‑term energy costs via peak shaving, and create skilled jobs for local electricians, solar installers, and technicians.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

solutions.text: Bulk Home Retrofit and Retrofit Training Program: Organize neighborhood bulk-purchase campaigns for insulation, heat pumps, windows and flood-proofing paired with local training courses (community colleges, tradespeople) so residents save money and local contractors gain steady green retrofit work.

resources.name: Residential Energy Efficiency Programs (Home Energy Assessment and Rebates)
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia delivers province-wide home energy assessments and rebates for insulation, cold-climate heat pumps, and high-efficiency windows/doors, helping households lower bills and emissions. The program aggregates homeowner demand and coordinates an approved Trade Network, while sponsoring and partnering on installer and energy advisor training to expand local retrofit capacity—directly aligning with bulk retrofit delivery and workforce upskilling.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: HomeWarming
resources.organization: Clean Foundation and Efficiency Nova Scotia
resources.description: HomeWarming provides no-cost home energy assessments and installs measures like insulation and air sealing for income-qualified Nova Scotians, improving comfort and resilience while cutting energy use. The initiative coordinates local contractors through centralized procurement and neighborhood scheduling, creating steady retrofit work and linking participants to complementary offerings (such as heat pump rebates) to multiply savings.

resources.name: Neighbourhood Efficiency Nova Scotia (NENS)
resources.description: NENS runs neighborhood-based outreach and in-home visits that install energy-saving devices, provide tailored retrofit guidance, and connect residents with contractors and rebate programs for deeper upgrades. By organizing work at the community scale and coordinating follow-up retrofits with local trades, the program achieves bulk uptake that lowers costs while building community resilience and green job opportunities.

resources.name: Heat Pump Installer and Building Science Training (Continuing Education)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) — Akerley Campus
resources.description: NSCC offers short courses and micro-credentials in residential heat pump installation, HVAC fundamentals, and building envelope retrofit practices, providing hands-on labs aligned with industry standards. These programs upskill apprentices and working tradespeople across Nova Scotia, supplying the trained workforce needed to deliver large-scale, neighborhood retrofit campaigns efficiently and safely.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) Program
resources.description: Bridgewater’s PACE program enables homeowners to bundle retrofits—such as insulation, windows, and cold-climate heat pumps—and repay through property taxes, removing upfront cost barriers. The municipality pre-qualifies contractors and coordinates projects at community scale, effectively aggregating demand to lower prices and provide steady local work in green home retrofits.

solutions.text: Community Flood Response Hubs and Volunteer Teams: Set up neighborhood emergency hubs stocked with pumps, sandbags, communications gear and trained volunteers who can respond rapidly to flooding events, coordinate evacuations and support recovery, reducing damage and cost.

resources.name: Joint Emergency Management (JEM) Program
resources.description: Halifax’s JEM program organizes neighborhood-based volunteer teams that set up community emergency hubs and comfort centres during storms and flooding. Volunteers are trained in basic incident coordination, radio communications, and door‑to‑door wellness checks, and the hubs keep supplies such as sandbags, first aid, and communications gear for rapid deployment. This directly implements the solution by enabling rapid local flood response, coordinating evacuations, and supporting recovery alongside HRM’s Emergency Management and Fire services.

resources.name: Canadian Red Cross Disaster Management – Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Canadian Red Cross recruits and trains volunteer disaster response teams across Nova Scotia, prepositions emergency supplies, and deploys during floods to support evacuations and open community reception centres. Teams bring portable communications kits, manage registration and reunification, and coordinate with municipal EMOs to augment community hubs with staffing, supplies, and recovery services like clean‑up kits and emergency financial assistance. This strengthens community flood readiness and reduces damage by accelerating coordinated, on‑the‑ground support.

resources.name: Kings County Regional Emergency Management Organization (REMO)
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
resources.description: Kings REMO designates and equips community comfort centres and emergency hubs across the county, maintains caches of sandbags and emergency communications equipment, and trains local volunteers to staff them. During coastal storms and river flooding, these volunteer teams activate hubs to share situational updates, coordinate evacuations and wellness checks, and work with fire departments and Public Works on sandbagging and pump‑outs. The program builds localized capacity to mitigate flood damage and speed recovery.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: Lunenburg County Regional Emergency Management Organization (REMO)
resources.organization: Lunenburg County Regional Emergency Management Organization (REMO)
resources.description: Lunenburg County REMO coordinates a network of designated comfort centres and community emergency hubs, equips them with communications gear and essential supplies, and trains volunteers to operate them during severe weather and floods. When flooding occurs, volunteers help with information sharing, wellness checks, and evacuation support, and coordinate with municipal crews and local fire departments to distribute sandbags and assist with water management. This community-based approach reduces damage and speeds recovery through rapid, organized local response.

solutions.text: Citizen Science Shoreline Monitoring Network: Train and coordinate volunteers to collect regular shoreline, dune and marsh condition data (photos, transects, erosion markers). Local data supports grant applications, municipal planning and insurance risk assessments.

resources.name: Coastal Restoration Program – Dune Restoration & Monitoring
resources.description: Coastal Action trains and coordinates local volunteers to monitor South Shore beaches and dunes using standardized photo-points, simple cross-dune transects, and erosion stakes to track storm impacts and shoreline change. The collected data is shared with municipalities and partners to guide living shoreline projects, support grant applications, and inform coastal risk and infrastructure planning.
resources.address: 37 Tannery Road, Unit 3, Lunenburg, NS B0J 2C0

resources.name: Bras d’Or Watch
resources.organization: Unama’ki Institute of Natural Resources (in partnership with Bras d’Or Lake Biosphere Region Association)
resources.description: Bras d’Or Watch engages and trains community volunteers around the Bras d’Or Lake Biosphere Region to collect shoreline observations, site photos, and nearshore measurements (e.g., water levels, temperature, salinity, eelgrass and shoreline habitat condition) during coordinated monitoring days. Results are used by Indigenous guardians, local municipalities, and partners to prioritize restoration, strengthen funding proposals, and plan for coastal risks from storms and sea-level rise.

resources.name: Stewardship Volunteer Program
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Nature Trust trains volunteer stewards to conduct annual monitoring on protected coastal properties, using fixed photo stations, GPS-referenced transects, and standardized condition forms to document dune erosion, salt marsh changes, and storm damage. These citizen-science records inform site management plans and are shared with municipal and provincial partners to support conservation grants, land-use planning, and risk assessments.
resources.address: 81 Prince Albert Road, Unit M, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1M1

resources.name: Community-Based Monitoring for Nature-Based Shorelines
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions (Saint Mary’s University)
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations equips community groups, students, and municipal partners to monitor dunes, beaches, and salt marsh ‘living shoreline’ projects using standardized photo posts, cross-shore transects, vegetation plots, and erosion pins/markers. The data are integrated into project evaluations and shared with municipalities and insurers to guide coastal adaptation planning, demonstrate risk reduction, and strengthen funding applications for resilience projects.

solutions.text: Nature-Based Stormwater Management Projects: Install rain gardens, bioswales, permeable pavements and expanded urban tree canopy in partnership with schools and community groups to reduce runoff, improve infiltration and reduce downstream flood impacts.

resources.name: Depave Paradise (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Clean Foundation delivers Green Communities Canada’s Depave Paradise program across Nova Scotia, working with schools, businesses, and neighbourhood volunteers to remove sections of unnecessary asphalt and replace them with native-plant rain gardens, bioswales, and other permeable landscaping. These community build days increase infiltration, filter pollutants, and reduce peak runoff, directly lowering local flood risk while creating hands-on learning opportunities for youth.

resources.name: Urban Forest Master Plan (UFMP) Implementation
resources.description: HRM’s UFMP guides the annual planting and stewardship of thousands of street and park trees, often in partnership with schools, community groups, and neighbourhood associations. By expanding the urban canopy and integrating soil cells, structural soils, and planted boulevards, the program intercepts rainfall, enhances infiltration, and reduces stormwater runoff and downstream flood impacts across Halifax communities.

resources.name: Sawmill River Daylighting and Naturalization Project
resources.description: Halifax Water is replacing a failing culvert in Dartmouth by daylighting and naturalizing Sawmill River with an open, vegetated channel, floodplain benches, and native plantings. This nature-based stormwater design increases storage and infiltration, reduces neighbourhood flood risk, improves water quality, and creates a community asset that supports education and stewardship around green infrastructure.
resources.address: 450 Cowie Hill Road, Halifax, NS B3P 2V3

solutions.text: Local Green Business Incubator and Microgrant Fund: Create a small local incubator offering mentorship, workspace and microgrants for startups in renewable energy services, sustainable fisheries, circular-economy crafts and other green enterprises to grow local employment.

resources.name: Start-Up Yard at COVE
resources.organization: COVE (Centre for Ocean Ventures and Entrepreneurship)
resources.description: Start-Up Yard is a specialized incubator that provides ocean-focused startups with waterfront workspace, shared labs, on-water testing access, and hands-on mentorship from industry experts. By helping companies developing sustainable fisheries tech, marine renewable solutions, and coastal resilience tools, it directly grows green enterprises and jobs. The program also connects founders to non-dilutive funding opportunities and partner challenges that function like microgrants to accelerate early-stage development.

resources.name: Ocean Startup Project
resources.description: The Ocean Startup Project runs training, mentorship, and funding programs (including non-dilutive awards through the Ocean Startup Challenge) for early-stage ocean technology companies. These supports help founders building solutions in sustainable fisheries, marine renewables, and coastal climate resilience to validate ideas and scale. By pairing expert mentorship with microgrant-style awards, the project embodies a practical incubator-plus-funding model that grows local green employment.

resources.name: Emera ideaHUB
resources.description: Emera ideaHUB is Dalhousie University’s hardware venture incubator that offers entrepreneurs prototyping labs, engineering mentorship, and collaborative workspace to build physical products, including cleantech and circular-economy solutions. Startups receive tailored coaching on design-for-manufacture, testing, and market entry while being connected to partner funding streams and challenge programs. This creates a local pipeline for green enterprises to move from concept to job-creating companies.

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic Innovation Hubs
resources.description: IGNITE operates rural innovation hubs that provide entrepreneurs with mentorship, programming, and co-working/maker spaces in Western and Northern Nova Scotia. The hubs support startups working in clean technology, sustainable resource sectors, and circular economy products, and help founders access regional microgrant competitions and challenge funds (e.g., Spark Nova Scotia) to de-risk early development. This place-based incubator model builds local green businesses and employment outside major urban centres.

resources.name: Community Grants for Waste Diversion
resources.description: Divert NS provides small, non-repayable grants to support community groups and emerging enterprises piloting waste-reduction, reuse, and recycling initiatives that advance the circular economy. Funding is paired with educational resources and connections to municipal partners, enabling new green products and services to be tested and scaled locally. These microgrants directly catalyze circular-economy ventures and green jobs across Nova Scotia communities.
resources.address: 35 Commercial Street, Suite 400, Truro, NS B2N 3H9

solutions.text: Apprenticeship and Re-Skilling Pathways with Community Colleges: Partner with regional colleges and employers to create accelerated apprenticeships in green trades (heat pump technicians, solar installers, coastal engineers) and offer placements prioritized for local youth and displaced workers.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Program
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Program administers work-integrated apprenticeship pathways in trades that are central to the green transition—such as Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Mechanic (heat pumps), Construction Electrician (solar PV), and Sheet Metal Worker. The Agency partners with Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) to deliver in-school technical training and with employers across the province to register and place apprentices; incentives like Apprenticeship START help employers hire local youth and displaced workers into accelerated earn-and-learn roles.

resources.name: Ductless Heat Pump Installer (Microcredential)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) – Akerley Campus
resources.description: This short, hands-on microcredential provides accelerated training for entry-level technicians to install and commission ductless mini-split heat pumps to code and manufacturer standards. Developed with input from local HVAC employers and aligned with Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency pathways, it helps graduates transition into Refrigeration & Air Conditioning Mechanic apprenticeships; NSCC connects learners to employer placements and prioritizes local youth and career-changers through Nova Scotia Works referrals.

resources.name: Marine Geomatics (Advanced Diploma, Co-op)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) – Centre of Geographic Sciences (COGS)
resources.description: NSCC’s Marine Geomatics program prepares technologists for coastal engineering and climate-resilience work, training students in shoreline mapping, hydrography, and geospatial analysis that inform coastal protection and flood planning. The program includes a co-op/internship that places students with Nova Scotia employers—municipalities, engineering consultancies, and environmental organizations—creating direct work-integrated pathways for local youth into coastal resilience careers.

resources.name: Efficiency Preferred Partner (EPP) Network and Contractor Training
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia’s EPP Network upskills and supports contractors delivering energy-efficiency services (e.g., heat pump installation, energy auditing) and connects them to funded projects through provincial rebate programs. Working with NSCC and HRAI to offer local training, the network helps member employers recruit apprentices and entry-level installers—creating placement and re-skilling pathways for Nova Scotian youth and displaced workers entering green trades such as heat pumps and solar-related electrical work.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

solutions.text: Community Resilience Bonds and Pooled Risk Funds: Establish a local pooled fund or resilience bond mechanism to finance community infrastructure upgrades (seawalls, dykes, drainage) and offer lower insurance costs for members by spreading risk and funding preventive measures.

resources.name: Halifax Water Stormwater Credits Program
resources.description: Halifax Water operates a stormwater utility that pools funding from all ratepayers to finance community-scale drainage upgrades (culverts, storm sewers, channels) that reduce flooding and coastal storm impacts. Its Stormwater Credits Program incentivizes on‑site preventive measures (e.g., rain gardens, permeable surfaces), effectively using a pooled fund to finance risk‑reducing infrastructure while rewarding members who lower collective risk—aligning with the community resilience bond/pooled fund model to cut future losses and potential insurance claims.
resources.address: 450 Cowie Hill Road, Halifax, NS B3P 2V3

resources.name: New Dawn Community Investment Fund (CEDIF)
resources.description: New Dawn’s provincially registered Community Economic Development Investment Fund pools capital from local residents—functioning like a community bond—to finance community infrastructure and resilience projects in Cape Breton (e.g., energy retrofits for community buildings and housing, local enterprise development). By mobilizing local investment for preventive upgrades and resilience‑oriented projects, the fund spreads financial risk across community investors, strengthens critical infrastructure, and supports green job creation that helps young people remain in Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Antigonish Farmers’ Mutual Insurance (Member-Owned Risk Pool)
resources.description: As a member‑owned mutual insurer, Antigonish Farmers’ Mutual pools risk among Nova Scotian policyholders to provide property and related coverages, often offering credits and guidance for loss‑prevention measures (e.g., sump pumps, backwater valves, wind and water protections). This pooled risk model stabilizes and can lower insurance costs for members while encouraging preventive upgrades that reduce community‑wide losses from storms and flooding—core to the pooled risk fund aspect of the resilience solution.

solutions.text: Managed Retreat Community Planning and Land Stewardship: Facilitate inclusive local planning for strategic retreat where needed: identify risk zones, create land-swap or buyout proposals, repurpose vulnerable properties for public buffers and habitat, and develop workforce roles in relocation and landscape restoration.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-based Solutions
resources.description: Based at Saint Mary’s University, this centre partners with municipalities, Mi’kmaw communities, and landowners across Nova Scotia to plan for sea‑level rise and storm surge, map high‑risk zones, and design nature‑based adaptation including living shorelines and salt marsh restoration. Their work supports managed retreat by helping communities identify properties that should transition out of development, guiding voluntary land transitions into public buffers and habitat, and training local workforces in restoration, monitoring, and relocation-support roles.

resources.name: HalifACT: Acting on Climate Together
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s climate action plan includes a major adaptation and resilience stream that maps flood and coastal hazard zones, guides development restrictions and setback policies, and plans community-scale adaptation for neighbourhoods most at risk. The program advances managed retreat by engaging residents in planning for relocation where necessary, exploring voluntary property acquisition and land re-use as coastal buffers and parks, and investing in natural infrastructure and restoration projects that create skilled green jobs.

resources.name: Coastal Adaptation (Climate Program)
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre works with coastal communities and municipalities across Nova Scotia to assess risks from erosion, storm surge, and flooding, and to co-develop adaptation pathways that include setbacks, nature-based defenses, and strategic retreat where appropriate. The initiative supports managed retreat by facilitating inclusive planning, helping identify properties for voluntary transition into public buffers or restored habitat, and building local capacity through training for youth and workers in shoreline restoration and land stewardship.

resources.name: Climate Change Program
resources.description: Coastal Action collaborates with Lunenburg County communities and municipalities to conduct climate vulnerability assessments, flood-risk and coastal hazard mapping, and community engagement to plan adaptation options, including strategic retreat from the most exposed sites. The program advances managed retreat by helping identify high-risk properties for voluntary transition and by piloting living shorelines and wetland restoration that repurpose vulnerable lands into protective buffers, while training and employing local crews in restoration and monitoring.
resources.address: 37 Tannery Road, Unit 3, Lunenburg, NS B0J 2C0

resources.name: Saving Our Coasts
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Nature Trust acquires and protects vulnerable coastal properties and conservation easements from willing landowners, converting at-risk parcels into protected buffers that allow shoreline and habitat migration as seas rise. This initiative implements managed retreat by facilitating voluntary land transitions, stewarding and restoring conserved shorelines for public and ecological benefit, and engaging local volunteers and contractors in on-the-ground restoration and stewardship work.
resources.address: 81 Prince Albert Road, Unit 7, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1N3

solutions.text: Indigenous-Led Knowledge Partnerships: Build partnerships with local Indigenous communities to integrate traditional coastal stewardship practices—salt marsh management, species-based indicators and place-based planning—into resilience projects and training programs.

resources.name: Collaborative Environmental Planning Initiative (CEPI) for the Bras d’Or Lakes
resources.organization: Unama’ki Institute of Natural Resources (Secretariat for CEPI)
resources.description: CEPI brings Mi’kmaq Elders, communities, scientists, governments, and NGOs together to steward the Bras d’Or Lakes using Etuaptmumk/Two-Eyed Seeing. The initiative integrates Mi’kmaw ecological knowledge, species-based indicators, and place-based planning into coastal resilience strategies, and delivers community engagement and youth training that guide habitat restoration and shoreline management across the watershed.

resources.name: Unama’ki Guardians Program
resources.description: The Unama’ki Guardians are Indigenous land-and-water stewards who apply Mi’kmaw ecological knowledge alongside science to monitor coastal ecosystems, including eelgrass beds, shellfish, and shoreline wetlands. The program trains Mi’kmaw youth and community members in field monitoring, restoration, and safety, and supports place-based planning and climate resilience actions such as marsh and shoreline stewardship throughout Unama’ki (Cape Breton).

resources.name: Mi’kmaw Conservation Group – Coastal Restoration and Living Shorelines
resources.description: The Mi’kmaw Conservation Group partners with Mi’kmaw communities across mainland Nova Scotia to restore tidal wetlands and salt marshes, monitor culturally significant species, and incorporate Mi’kmaw ecological knowledge into coastal adaptation and planning. Through hands-on restoration projects and training for community members and Guardians, the program advances nature-based shoreline protection and species-based indicators that inform local resilience decisions.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations – Centre for Nature-Based Solutions (Two-Eyed Seeing Partnerships)
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations at Saint Mary’s University collaborates with Mi’kmaw Elders and First Nation communities to co-develop living shorelines and salt marsh restoration that blend traditional stewardship with coastal engineering. The centre delivers practitioner training and workshops that embed Etuaptmumk/Two-Eyed Seeing and place-based planning, preparing youth and professionals to implement culturally grounded, nature-based coastal resilience projects across Nova Scotia.

solutions.text: Local Insurance and Preparedness Advisory Coalition: Form a community group that works with insurers and municipalities to co-develop affordable risk-reducing measures, advocate for subsidized retrofits, and educate homeowners on cost-effective flood-proofing and claims preparedness.

resources.name: Stormwater Right-of-Way Charge Credits Program
resources.description: Halifax Water provides financial credits to properties that implement stormwater best management practices such as rain gardens, infiltration and detention systems, and green roofs. By incentivizing affordable, risk-reducing retrofits and offering technical guidance, the utility works with the municipality and property owners to reduce overland flooding and sewer backup risks, indirectly lowering insurance losses.
