resources.organization: Town of New Glasgow (on behalf of Pictou County municipalities)
resources.description: Pictou County Transit provides scheduled, inter-community routes linking the Towns of New Glasgow, Stellarton, Westville, Trenton, and the Municipality of Pictou County to key destinations such as Aberdeen Hospital, NSCC Pictou Campus, and major retail/industrial employment areas. The service is jointly funded by multiple local governments across Pictou County, and routes/timetables are designed to connect communities with regional employment centers and campuses around typical shift and class start/end times.
resources.address: 111 Provost Street, New Glasgow, NS B2H 5E1

resources.name: Transit Cape Breton
resources.description: Transit Cape Breton operates scheduled buses connecting multiple communities within the Cape Breton Regional Municipality—such as Glace Bay, New Waterford, North Sydney, and Sydney Mines—to regional anchors including downtown Sydney, Cape Breton University, and Cape Breton Regional Hospital. The service is municipally led and supported by provincial transit funding and institutional partnerships (e.g., CBU U‑Pass), with routes and frequencies adjusted to match class schedules and hospital/industrial shifts, thereby improving inter-community commuter access to jobs, education, and services.

solutions.text: Shared community EV carshare and charging network: A locally governed electric carshare fleet with charging installed at community centers and libraries, easing car access for those without vehicles and accelerating local EV adoption.

resources.name: Communauto Atlantic – Halifax EV Carshare
resources.description: Communauto Atlantic operates a carshare service across Halifax with a growing fleet that includes electric and plug‑in hybrid vehicles, placing cars at community hubs such as libraries, municipal lots, and campuses. Stations like the Halifax Central Library provide convenient, transit‑adjacent access to shared EVs and on‑site charging, making car access feasible for residents who don’t own a vehicle and accelerating local EV adoption.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality – EV Charging at Community Facilities
resources.description: HRM has deployed Level 2 and DC fast chargers at public libraries, recreation centres, park-and-ride lots, and other municipal sites to build a reliable community charging network. By placing chargers at accessible civic locations, the program supports shared EV fleets (including carshare vehicles) and enables residents without home charging to conveniently power electric cars.

resources.name: Charge Up Nova Scotia (Community EV Charging Grants)
resources.description: Charge Up NS provides funding and technical support to install Level 2 charging stations at publicly accessible locations such as libraries, community centres, town halls, and workplaces across Nova Scotia. By seeding chargers at community hubs, the program enables municipalities and nonprofits to host shared EVs and carshare vehicles, expanding access for people who don’t own cars and encouraging EV adoption.

resources.name: Plug In Nova Scotia – Public EV Charging Network and Map
resources.description: Plug In NS supports the development and visibility of Nova Scotia’s public EV charging network, working with municipalities and partners to deploy chargers at libraries, community centres, and other public destinations. Its tools and programs make chargers easy to find and use for shared EV fleets and community members, helping carshare services operate reliably outside of private home charging.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Energize Bridgewater – Public EV Charging at Community Hubs
resources.description: Energize Bridgewater has installed public EV chargers at key community locations, including the Lunenburg County Lifestyle Centre (home of the public library), town hall, and downtown parking areas. By concentrating charging at civic facilities, the initiative enables future and current shared EV use—such as community carshare vehicles—while giving residents without home chargers equitable access to electric mobility.

solutions.text: Use of school buses and facilities for community transit: Coordinate after‑hours use of existing school buses and facilities to run community routes or evening services, increasing mobility without large new capital investment.

resources.name: CCRCE School Bus Charter Services
resources.description: Chignecto-Central Regional Centre for Education makes its school bus fleet available for after-hours charter by municipalities, community groups, and non-profits. By coordinating evening and weekend charters and using school sites as pickup hubs, CCRCE enables temporary community routes and shuttles to jobs, training, and events without requiring new capital vehicles, directly aligning with the solution of leveraging school buses and facilities for community transit.

resources.name: HRCE Community Use of Schools & After-Hours Transportation Coordination
resources.description: Halifax Regional Centre for Education provides facility rentals for after-hours community use and coordinates with contracted student transportation providers to support community shuttle needs when requested. Schools serve as accessible pickup/drop-off locations and staging areas, and available school buses can be chartered for evening or event-based routes, expanding mobility for youth and residents without new capital investment.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

resources.name: CSAP Transport Scolaire – Location d’autobus (Bus Charter)
resources.description: Conseil scolaire acadien provincial offers after-hours chartering of its school buses to community partners in Acadian and Francophone regions of Nova Scotia. By opening its existing fleet and school facilities for community pickup points, CSAP enables evening shuttles and special community routes that increase mobility for residents in rural areas without purchasing new vehicles.

solutions.text: Community broadband co‑operative and demand aggregation: Form a cooperative to aggregate local demand, negotiate bulk deals with ISPs or build community-owned fibre/wireless infrastructure so residents and businesses get affordable, high-speed service.

resources.name: Chebucto Community Net
resources.description: Chebucto Community Net is a member-supported, volunteer-driven community internet provider that offers low-cost internet access, email, and hosting services to residents and organizations in Halifax and surrounding areas. By aggregating local demand through memberships and community partners, Chebucto purchases bandwidth in bulk and operates community-owned access services to keep prices affordable and inclusive. This community-network model directly implements the solution by providing an alternative, locally controlled ISP option that expands affordable connectivity.
resources.address: Room 006, Chase Building, Dalhousie University, 6136 University Avenue, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2

resources.name: Internet for Lunenburg County
resources.organization: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
resources.description: The Municipality of the District of Lunenburg leads a county-wide broadband initiative that maps demand, aggregates resident and business interest, and negotiates multi-year build agreements with ISPs to extend fibre and fixed wireless to underserved areas. The municipality uses bulk procurement, co-funding, and access to municipal infrastructure to secure better coverage and pricing, effectively acting as a community aggregator on behalf of residents. This implements the solution by coordinating community demand and leveraging public assets to deliver affordable, high-speed service across rural communities.

resources.name: East Hants Rural High-Speed Internet Project
resources.description: The Municipality of East Hants runs a rural broadband program that surveys households and businesses to aggregate demand, then partners with ISPs through competitive procurements to extend fibre and fixed wireless coverage. By negotiating area-wide builds and coordinating sign-ups, the municipality helps create the economies of scale needed to serve low-density communities at reasonable prices. This demand-aggregation approach implements the solution by securing bulk deals and accelerating community broadband buildouts.

resources.name: Cumberland Rural Internet Improvement Program
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Cumberland
resources.description: The Municipality of the County of Cumberland coordinates broadband expansion by identifying underserved areas, aggregating local demand, and partnering with multiple ISPs to build new fibre and fixed wireless infrastructure. The municipality contributes funding and access to public assets, enabling bulk procurement and negotiated service commitments that reduce costs for residents and businesses. This directly implements the solution by using a community-led approach to organize demand and deliver affordable, high-speed connectivity across rural Cumberland.
resources.address: 1395 Blair Lake Road, Upper Nappan, NS B4H 3Y4

solutions.text: Public Wi‑Fi access points and transit hub hotspots: Install centrally managed Wi‑Fi at libraries, community halls, transit stops and parking lots so residents can connect for job searches, telework and learning while commuting or waiting for transport.

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries — Free Wi‑Fi
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries provides free, centrally managed Wi‑Fi at all branches, including strong outdoor coverage that reaches many plazas and parking areas so people can connect after hours. At Halifax Central Library, which sits beside the Spring Garden Road transit hub, riders can use library Wi‑Fi while waiting for buses to search for jobs, access telework tools, and participate in online learning.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Cape Breton Regional Library — Free Public Wi‑Fi
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Library operates free Wi‑Fi at its branches, including the McConnell Library in downtown Sydney, with signal coverage that extends into the parking lot and adjacent public seating. The centrally managed network enables residents to connect on personal devices for job searches, telehealth, and coursework, and its location near Transit Cape Breton stops allows riders to get online while waiting for transport.

resources.name: Pictou-Antigonish Regional Library — Library Wi‑Fi (People’s Place)
resources.description: People’s Place Library in Antigonish offers free, centrally managed Wi‑Fi throughout the building and outside in its plaza and parking areas, available beyond regular hours. The service supports residents and youth with reliable connectivity for employment searches, remote work, and online education, and its Main Street location near local transit stops lets riders connect while waiting.

resources.name: Downtown Bridgewater Free Public Wi‑Fi
resources.description: The Town of Bridgewater operates free public Wi‑Fi across parts of the downtown core (including sections of King Street and adjacent public spaces), providing always-on connectivity in outdoor areas and near parking. This municipal hotspot network helps residents and commuters get online for job applications, telework, and learning while moving through downtown and waiting at nearby Bridgewater Transit stops.

solutions.text: Local telework / coworking hubs ('digital village' spaces): Create supervised coworking spaces in existing community buildings with reliable high-speed internet, meeting rooms and mentorship programs to support remote work, entrepreneurship and study.

resources.name: CO3
resources.description: CO3 is a community-focused coworking hub offering high-speed internet, flexible desks, private offices, and bookable meeting rooms to support remote workers, students, and entrepreneurs on the South Shore. Staff coordinate events, peer networking, and business support programming, enabling people to work and learn locally and reducing the need to commute long distances for reliable connectivity and professional space.

resources.name: Navigate Startup House
resources.organization: Navigate (Cape Breton University & Cape Breton Partnership)
resources.description: Navigate provides a supervised coworking space with high-speed internet, meeting rooms, and offices for startups, students, and remote workers in Cape Breton. Through mentorship, workshops, and connections to advisors and funding, it enables local entrepreneurship and telework, helping residents access opportunities without leaving their community.

resources.name: Volta
resources.description: Volta operates one of Atlantic Canada’s largest innovation hubs, providing coworking memberships, dedicated offices, high-speed internet, meeting rooms, and event space in downtown Halifax. Its structured mentorship, accelerator-style programming, and community events support remote work and entrepreneurship, giving young people access to resources and professional networks without needing to relocate.

resources.name: Spaces – Purdy’s Wharf
resources.description: Spaces at Purdy’s Wharf offers modern coworking facilities with reliable high-speed internet, shared lounges, private offices, and bookable meeting rooms on Halifax’s waterfront. The professionally managed environment enables teleworkers, freelancers, and students to access infrastructure and collaboration space locally, helping overcome connectivity and workspace barriers.
resources.address: 1959 Upper Water Street, Suite 1300, Halifax, NS B3J 3N2

resources.name: The Kube Workspace – Dartmouth
resources.description: The Kube provides supervised coworking space with fast internet, phone booths, offices, and meeting rooms in Dartmouth Crossing, serving remote employees, entrepreneurs, and students. By offering a professional, well-equipped workspace close to where people live, it reduces commuting burdens and supports productive telework and study.

solutions.text: Device lending and mobile hotspot library: Libraries or community centres lend laptops, tablets and portable hotspots on short-term loans, paired with basic technical support to ensure residents can access online education and work.

resources.name: Mobile WiFi Hotspot Lending
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries lends portable WiFi hotspots that patrons can borrow for short periods, allowing households without reliable broadband to get online for school, work, and services. Library staff provide basic setup help and digital literacy support, ensuring users can connect their devices and access essential online tools.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Borrow a WiFi Hub
resources.description: South Shore Public Libraries circulates mobile WiFi hubs (hotspots) and lends Chromebooks to cardholders, enabling residents to get internet access and a working device at home for coursework, job searches, telehealth, or remote work. Staff offer basic technical support and guidance on using the equipment, lowering barriers for users with limited connectivity or transportation.
resources.address: 135 North Park Street, Bridgewater, NS B4V 9B3

resources.name: Borrow the Internet (Hotspot Lending)
resources.description: Pictou-Antigonish Regional Library lends mobile WiFi hotspots to patrons so they can bring internet access home for online learning, employment tasks, and essential services. The library’s staff provide basic tech help to get patrons connected and troubleshoot common issues, supporting rural residents with limited broadband.
resources.address: 182 Dalhousie Street, New Glasgow, NS B2H 4M7

resources.name: Borrow the Internet (WiFi Hotspots)
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Library offers lendable WiFi hotspots that patrons can sign out to access the internet from home or on the go, supporting remote education, job applications, and community services access. Library staff provide introductory assistance and troubleshooting, helping users set up devices and connect safely.

resources.name: WiFi to Go (Hotspot Lending)
resources.description: Annapolis Valley Regional Library circulates WiFi hubs and other tech kits so residents can temporarily access reliable internet and devices for school assignments, job searches, and teleconferencing. Staff provide basic technical support and device setup assistance, bridging gaps in rural connectivity and transportation.

solutions.text: Community-hosted cell tower and infrastructure agreements: Form landowner and municipal partnerships to host shared cell towers and small cells, enabling communities to negotiate coverage, maintenance and revenue-sharing with carriers.

resources.name: Colchester County Rural Internet Project
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Colchester
resources.description: The Municipality of the County of Colchester financed and sited a network of community‑hosted towers on municipal properties and willing private land, then executed access and lease agreements with carriers/ISPs (e.g., Xplornet) to mount LTE/fixed‑wireless equipment. These multi-tenant sites are positioned to close rural coverage gaps, with contracts specifying coverage targets, maintenance obligations, and lease revenue that flows back to the municipality to sustain the infrastructure.

resources.name: Pictou County Rural Internet Project
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Pictou
resources.description: The Municipality of the County of Pictou aggregates municipal rooftops and parcels to host shared wireless towers and small-cell sites under structured hosting and lease agreements with providers such as Xplornet and Eastlink. The municipality negotiates service levels, coverage milestones, maintenance responsibilities, and revenue-sharing through tower/site leases, enabling community-controlled expansion of coverage into rural areas.

resources.name: Guysborough County Regional Broadband Network (GCRBN)
resources.organization: Municipality of the District of Guysborough
resources.description: Led by the Municipality of the District of Guysborough, GCRBN combines municipally enabled tower sites on public and private lands with fiber backhaul, operated via long-term agreements with Seaside Communications. The community hosts and leases tower infrastructure to the carrier, defining maintenance and performance terms and generating lease revenues, which expands wireless/LTE broadband coverage across dispersed coastal and inland communities.

resources.name: Cumberland County Rural Internet Initiative
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Cumberland
resources.description: The Municipality of the County of Cumberland identifies strategic tower locations and partners with ISPs/carriers through hosting and lease agreements to place shared wireless/LTE equipment on municipally controlled and volunteer landowner sites. Agreements set coverage and uptime requirements, spell out maintenance responsibilities, and return lease revenue to the community, directly aligning with community-hosted tower infrastructure and negotiated service expansion.
resources.address: 1395 Blair Lake Road, Upper Nappan, NS B4H 3Y4

solutions.text: Unified regional mobility platform (Mobility‑as‑a‑Service): Develop a single booking/payment platform that integrates microtransit, buses, bike shares and carshare options so users — especially youth — can plan and pay for multi‑modal trips easily.

resources.name: Halifax Transit – Official Transit App Partnership
resources.description: Halifax Transit designates the Transit app as its official trip-planning platform, giving riders a single interface to plan end‑to‑end journeys using real‑time bus data, walking, and cycling options. In Halifax, the app also surfaces nearby Communauto Atlantic carshare locations with deep links to reserve, helping users—especially youth—mix bus and carshare in one planning flow and move toward a unified Mobility‑as‑a‑Service experience that simplifies multimodal travel and payment handoffs.

resources.name: Communauto Atlantic – Carshare integrated with regional trip-planning
resources.description: Communauto Atlantic operates a station‑based carshare across Halifax and integrates with the Transit app so users can see nearby vehicles from within a multimodal trip plan and seamlessly jump to booking. This linkage allows youth and other riders to combine transit and carshare in a single digital journey, advancing the Mobility‑as‑a‑Service model by connecting planning, booking, and payment across modes within one cohesive user experience.

resources.name: Kings Transit – HotSpot Mobile Ticketing and Trip Tools
resources.description: Kings Transit provides regional bus service in the Annapolis Valley and uses the HotSpot platform to let riders purchase and use mobile fares from a single app. By pairing mobile payments with integrated trip tools and connections to other regional services that also use HotSpot, the system moves toward a unified Mobility‑as‑a‑Service experience that simplifies planning and paying for multimodal trips across rural and small‑town communities.
resources.address: 29 Crescent Drive, New Minas, NS B4N 3G7

solutions.text: Parcel lockers and community logistics hub: Install secure parcel lockers at central community locations and coordinate local pickup/delivery windows to improve e-commerce access for residents without reliable delivery addresses.

resources.name: Maritime Bus Parcel Express – Halifax Terminal
resources.description: Maritime Bus runs a region-wide parcel service that lets customers ship to and pick up packages at its bus terminals and community agent locations on scheduled routes. The Halifax terminal functions as a community logistics hub with set pickup windows, providing reliable access for residents who lack a dependable delivery address and improving last‑mile access between rural communities and urban retailers.

resources.name: FedEx Ship Centre – Hold at Location (Halifax/Dartmouth)
resources.description: FedEx’s Hold at Location option allows customers to have e‑commerce orders shipped directly to the Dartmouth Ship Centre for secure storage and pickup during extended hours. This acts as a community logistics hub, giving people without stable delivery addresses a dependable pickup window and reducing failed deliveries in areas with address or connectivity challenges.

resources.name: UPS Customer Center Will Call – Dartmouth
resources.description: UPS’s Customer Center in Dartmouth offers will‑call parcel pickup, allowing shipments to be held securely for recipients to collect at defined hours. This provides a centralized logistics hub for residents who cannot receive deliveries at home, improving e‑commerce access by coordinating local pickup windows and reducing missed deliveries.

resources.name: Canada Post FlexDelivery – Halifax Shopping Centre Postal Outlet
resources.description: Canada Post’s FlexDelivery service lets customers route online purchases to a selected post office for secure pickup, rather than to a residential address. The Halifax Shopping Centre outlet serves as a community logistics hub with staffed pickup windows and secure holding (including PO Boxes), supporting residents who lack reliable delivery addresses or face connectivity issues in rural and suburban areas.

obstacles.title: Systemic inequities and discrimination
obstacles.description: Persistent barriers faced by Mi'kmaq and African Nova Scotians, newcomers, people with disabilities, and 2SLGBTQIA+ youth limit inclusion, advancement, and community trust.

solutions.text: Indigenous-led employment pathways: Partner with Mi'kmaq leadership and local employers to co-design culturally safe apprenticeship, internship, and hiring programs that include cultural mentorship, land-based training options, and targets for Mi'kmaq youth participation.

resources.name: Employment & Training Services (Indigenous Skills and Employment Training Program)
resources.description: The Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre’s Employment & Training Services co-design training, apprenticeship, and hiring pathways with local employers and Nova Scotia Community College to support urban Mi’kmaw and other Indigenous jobseekers. The program provides culturally safe wraparound supports, including Elders/Knowledge Keeper mentorship, cultural programming, and job coaching, and it brokers paid work placements and apprenticeships with partner employers who commit to inclusive hiring and retention practices for Mi’kmaw youth.

resources.name: Indigenous Skills and Employment Training (ISET) Program
resources.description: NCNS delivers ISET services that create apprenticeship, internship, and direct-to-hire opportunities co-developed with Nova Scotia employers for off-reserve Mi’kmaq and other Indigenous people. The program includes individualized employment plans, cultural mentorship, and employer engagement to build culturally safe worksites, while prioritizing Mi’kmaw youth participation and supporting completion of Red Seal and other trade pathways.
resources.address: 129 Truro Heights Road, Truro Heights, NS B6L 1X1

resources.name: Employment & Training Services
resources.description: Mi’kmaw Kina’matnewey partners with Mi’kmaw leadership, NSCC, the Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency, and local employers to design Indigenous cohorts in trades and technology, paid work placements, and apprenticeship pathways for Mi’kmaw youth from Unama’ki communities. Services integrate Mi’kmaw language and cultural mentorship and, where relevant, land-based learning components that connect students to careers in natural resources, environmental stewardship, and community infrastructure.

resources.name: Youth Internships and Land-Based Training (Guardians and Natural Resources Programs)
resources.description: UINR collaborates with Mi’kmaw communities and employers such as Parks Canada and provincial resource departments to create land-based training, seasonal employment, and internships that build Indigenous career pathways in conservation, fisheries, and forestry. Programs pair Mi’kmaw youth with Elders/Knowledge Keepers and technical mentors, applying Two-Eyed Seeing to develop culturally safe, place-based skills that lead to long-term hiring and apprenticeship opportunities in environmental and resource sectors.

solutions.text: Community anti-racism and inclusion training: Offer ongoing, locally delivered workshops and coaching for schools, businesses, and community groups led by Black, Mi'kmaq, disability, and 2SLGBTQIA+ trainers that include practical anti-bias tools and accountability steps.

resources.name: Workshops & Professional Development
resources.description: The Youth Project delivers ongoing, locally facilitated 2SLGBTQIA+ inclusion workshops and coaching for schools, youth-serving agencies, and workplaces across Nova Scotia. Sessions are led by 2SLGBTQIA+ educators and provide practical anti-bias tools such as inclusive language practices, bystander interventions, safer space guidelines, and policy review checklists with follow-up steps for accountability.

resources.name: Disability Inclusion & Employer Training
resources.description: reachAbility Association offers interactive disability inclusion and anti-ableism training to businesses, public sector teams, and community groups throughout Nova Scotia. Led by trainers with lived experience of disability, workshops include practical tools like accessible service checklists, inclusive hiring templates, and action-planning with measurable accountability steps to sustain change.
resources.address: 311-3845 Joseph Howe Drive, Halifax, NS B3L 4H9

resources.name: Workplace Culture Program
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS’ Workplace Culture Program provides anti-racism, intercultural competency, and bias-reduction training and coaching for employers, educators, and service providers across Nova Scotia. Facilitated by immigrant and racialized trainers, the program equips teams with practical anti-bias tools—such as bias interrupters, inclusive recruitment audits, and equity action plans—with structured follow-up to support accountability.
resources.address: Suite 2120, 6960 Mumford Road, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Anti-Black Racism Education & Cultural Competency Workshops
resources.organization: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia delivers community and workplace workshops led by African Nova Scotian educators that address the history of systemic racism, everyday bias, and strategies for building inclusive environments. Programs provide practical tools—resource guides, anti-bias checklists, and policy-review coaching—along with planning supports to help schools and organizations set and track accountability commitments.
resources.address: 10 Cherry Brook Road, Cherry Brook, NS B2Z 1A8

resources.name: Mi'kmaq Cultural Awareness Training
resources.description: Membertou Heritage Park offers in-person cultural awareness training for schools, businesses, and public sector teams, facilitated by Mi'kmaq knowledge keepers and educators. Workshops cover Mi'kmaq history, treaties, and cultural safety, and include practical anti-bias reflection tools, guidance for respectful engagement, and support to define clear organizational commitments and accountability steps.

solutions.text: Accessible public spaces and transit improvements: Create a community accessibility fund to audit and retrofit public buildings, recreation sites, and transit stops for universal access and implement prioritized short-term fixes recommended by people with disabilities.

resources.name: Community ACCESS-Ability Program (CAAP)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Department of Communities, Culture, Tourism and Heritage
resources.description: A provincial grant program that funds audits and capital upgrades to make community-owned public buildings and recreation facilities accessible (e.g., ramps, power door operators, accessible washrooms, signage, and paths of travel). The program prioritizes projects identified by local accessibility advisory committees and people with disabilities, enabling quick, high-impact retrofits that remove barriers and advance universal access across Nova Scotia communities.

resources.name: HRM Community Grants Program – Access Improvements
resources.description: Halifax’s annual Community Grants Program includes an Access Improvements category that funds non-profit organizations to audit and retrofit public-serving spaces (community halls, museums, recreation facilities) for accessibility. Grants support short-term fixes and barrier-removal projects—such as ramps, door operators, accessible washrooms, and signage—often prioritized through engagement with persons with disabilities and municipal accessibility advisors.

resources.name: Halifax Transit – Bus Stop Accessibility Improvements and Access-A-Bus
resources.description: Halifax Transit runs an ongoing program to audit and upgrade bus stops and terminals with accessible landing pads, curb ramps, shelters, and clear wayfinding, guided by user feedback and accessibility standards. Alongside its Access-A-Bus service, the program prioritizes short-term fixes identified by riders with disabilities and the municipal Accessibility Advisory Committee to ensure safer, more inclusive public transit access.

resources.name: Town of Wolfville Accessibility Plan Implementation
resources.description: Wolfville implements its municipal Accessibility Plan by auditing town-owned buildings, parks, and sidewalks and completing priority retrofits such as curb cuts, accessible entrances, and paths of travel. Guided by its Accessibility Advisory Committee—which includes people with disabilities—the town advances short-term, high-impact fixes and longer-term projects to make civic spaces and routes to transit stops more universally accessible.

solutions.text: Mentorship and sponsorship program for marginalized youth: Connect Mi'kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability-identified, and 2SLGBTQIA+ youth with mentors in trades, tech, arts and business; include sponsored placements, employer commitments, and peer cohorts.

resources.name: Clean Leadership Summer Internship Program
resources.description: Clean Foundation’s paid summer internships place equity-deserving youth in environmental and clean-economy roles with Nova Scotia employers, pairing each participant with a workplace supervisor and sector mentors. The program intentionally recruits Mi'kmaq and other Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability-identified, and 2SLGBTQIA+ youth, delivers cohort-based training, and provides wraparound coaching. Host employers commit to sponsored placements and on-the-job learning, giving participants real work experience in tech, trades-adjacent fieldwork, business operations, and green-sector projects.

resources.name: Pathways to Shipbuilding (African Nova Scotian and Indigenous Cohorts)
resources.organization: Irving Shipbuilding Inc. in partnership with Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) and community partners
resources.description: Pathways to Shipbuilding is a cohort-based initiative that prepares African Nova Scotian and Mi’kmaq/Indigenous youth for skilled trades careers at the Halifax Shipyard through NSCC programs. Participants receive sponsored tuition, dedicated academic and cultural supports, and mentorship from journeypersons, with Irving Shipbuilding committing to work terms and apprenticeship opportunities. The model combines peer cohorts, employer-backed placements, and industry mentorship to remove systemic barriers and support long-term advancement in the trades.

resources.name: BIPOC and Newcomer Film Initiatives (e.g., Newcomer Film Program; Black & Indigenous Filmmaker Residency)
resources.description: AFCOOP runs targeted mentorship and training streams for underrepresented creators—including African Nova Scotian, Indigenous (Mi’kmaq), newcomer, and 2SLGBTQIA+ youth—through cohort-based programs that pair participants with established film professionals. Participants receive intensive workshops, production mentorship, and supported project budgets, and are connected to local crews and companies for on-set experiences. This sponsorship-and-mentorship approach opens pathways into arts careers and creative entrepreneurship while building peer networks in Nova Scotia’s screen sector.

resources.name: WorkBridge: Employment Services for Persons with Disabilities
resources.description: WorkBridge provides individualized employment coaching and employer connections for youth and adults with disabilities, including mentorship, job development, and ongoing on-the-job support. The program partners with businesses across sectors (trades, tech, arts, and office/admin) and coordinates sponsored placements or wage-subsidy opportunities when eligible, securing employer commitments to accessible, mentored roles. Group workshops and job clubs create peer cohorts that build confidence, networks, and long-term inclusion in the workforce.

resources.name: Youth Employment and Skills Strategy (YESS)
resources.description: NCNS’s YESS program supports off-reserve Indigenous (including Mi’kmaq) youth ages 15–30 with paid work experience, mentorship, and skills training across Nova Scotia. The program brokers sponsored placements and wage subsidies with employer partners who commit to coaching and culturally safe workplaces, while staff provide ongoing mentoring and case management. Cohort-based workshops and peer supports help participants build networks and transition into trades, tech, arts, and business roles.
resources.address: 129 Truro Heights Road, Truro Heights, NS B6L 1N5

solutions.text: Microgrants and community incubators for diverse entrepreneurs: Establish small, rapid-access grants and a local incubator offering business coaching, wraparound supports (childcare, translation, accessibility), and networking aimed at underrepresented entrepreneurs.

resources.name: ISANS Business Development Services
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS provides newcomer entrepreneurs with one-on-one business advising, training workshops, market research support, and networking that connects them to lenders, buyers, and mentors. As a community incubator for immigrants, it offers wraparound supports such as interpretation/translation, language support, and childminding for eligible program participants, reducing key barriers to participation. This directly advances inclusive entrepreneurship in Nova Scotia by helping underrepresented newcomers start and grow viable businesses.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Black Business Initiative – Business Development Services
resources.description: BBI offers tailored business training, advisory services, and mentorship to African Nova Scotian and Black entrepreneurs, along with support navigating financing and procurement opportunities. Acting as a community hub and incubator, BBI provides culturally responsive programming, networking, and connections to funding partners that reduce systemic barriers and build business capacity. These services create inclusive pathways for Black founders to start and scale enterprises in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 1660 Hollis Street, Suite 1201, Halifax, NS B3J 1V7

resources.name: Hope Blooms Community Youth Micro-Grants
resources.description: Hope Blooms awards small, rapid-access microgrants that help youth—many from African Nova Scotian and newcomer communities—launch social enterprises and community projects. The program pairs funding with wraparound supports such as mentorship, safe workspace (kitchen/greenhouse), tutoring, and food security, functioning as a community incubator that nurtures skills and confidence. This combination of microgrants and holistic support directly tackles systemic barriers and builds pathways to entrepreneurship for underrepresented youth.

resources.name: CEED Entrepreneurship Programs and Incubator
resources.organization: Centre for Entrepreneurship Education and Development (CEED)
resources.description: CEED operates an entrepreneurship hub that delivers cohort programs, one-on-one coaching, and practical training for early-stage and growth-oriented founders, with access to co-working space and an active mentor network. Programming emphasizes inclusive participation and reduces barriers through flexible delivery and tailored supports, while connecting entrepreneurs to partner funding opportunities and local business networks. This incubator model strengthens the ecosystem for diverse founders to start and grow businesses in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 225, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

solutions.text: Inclusive municipal procurement and supplier development: Adopt local procurement policies that prioritize contracts for Indigenous, Black, newcomer, disability-owned, and 2SLGBTQIA+ businesses and provide supplier-development workshops to help them qualify.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Social Procurement and Supplier Diversity
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality (HRM) embeds social and supplier diversity objectives into its procurement, using evaluation criteria that encourage participation from Indigenous, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability-owned, and 2SLGBTQIA+ suppliers. HRM’s Corporate Procurement team also hosts “Doing Business with HRM” information sessions and outreach with community partners to help diverse suppliers understand requirements, register as vendors, and qualify for municipal tenders.

resources.name: Procurement Readiness and Supplier Diversity Support
resources.description: BBI provides hands-on procurement readiness advising, bid preparation training, and meet-the-buyer events that help Black-owned businesses in Nova Scotia qualify for public-sector contracts. The organization collaborates with municipal and other public buyers to expand opportunities for Black suppliers and supports certification and capacity-building aligned with inclusive procurement goals.
resources.address: 1660 Hollis Street, Suite 1101, Halifax, NS B3J 1V7

resources.name: Business Services – Procurement and Tendering Workshops
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS delivers workshops and one-on-one advising that help immigrant-owned small businesses understand certifications, vendor registration, and tendering processes used by municipalities and other public buyers. By building capacity and connecting newcomer entrepreneurs to buyers and competitions, ISANS supports inclusive supplier development that enables diverse firms to qualify for and win public contracts.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Supplier Diversity and Public Procurement Readiness
resources.organization: Centre for Women in Business (Mount Saint Vincent University)
resources.description: The Centre for Women in Business helps women-owned companies pursue public-sector opportunities by offering training on selling to government, guidance on bid responses, and support to obtain supplier diversity certifications (e.g., WBE). It also facilitates connections between certified women-owned suppliers and public buyers, advancing inclusive procurement outcomes.

resources.name: Port of Halifax Supplier Diversity
resources.description: The Halifax Port Authority integrates supplier diversity commitments into its procurement practices to increase opportunities for Indigenous, Black, women, newcomer, disability-owned, and 2SLGBTQIA+ suppliers. Through vendor information sessions and a transparent supplier registration process, the Port helps diverse businesses understand requirements and qualify to compete for contracts.

solutions.text: Community-led data and accountability dashboard: Collect and publish disaggregated, community-run data on employment, education, housing, and service access, with community targets and regular public progress reports co-managed with representatives of affected groups.

resources.name: Road to Economic Prosperity (REP) for African Nova Scotians
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality – African Nova Scotian Affairs Integration Office (ANSAIO) and Halifax Partnership
resources.description: A community-driven economic development plan co-created by African Nova Scotian leaders, the Halifax Regional Municipality, and the Halifax Partnership. It sets measurable targets on employment, entrepreneurship, education pathways, and land/housing and publishes public progress reports overseen by an implementation table of African Nova Scotian representatives—functioning as a community accountability dashboard that tracks and reports outcomes over time.

resources.name: Centre for Employment Innovation – Nova Scotia Works Shared Measurement
resources.organization: Centre for Employment Innovation, St. Francis Xavier University (StFX) Extension Department
resources.description: CEI co-designs and maintains shared measurement and data systems for the Nova Scotia Works employment services network with community partners, collecting disaggregated data on jobseeker demographics, program access, and employment outcomes. Insights are shared through public reports and tools that set equity targets and track progress, with advisory groups including Mi’kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability, and 2SLGBTQIA+ representatives guiding governance and accountability.

resources.name: ISANS Research & Evaluation
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS collects and publishes community-led data on newcomer employment, credential recognition, entrepreneurship, housing stability, and access to settlement services in Nova Scotia. Through data briefs, public reports, and interactive resources co-developed with newcomer advisory councils, ISANS sets community-informed targets and tracks progress to improve system accountability and outcomes for immigrants and refugee youth and families.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Halifax Quality of Life Survey and Results Dashboard
resources.description: HRM’s Quality of Life initiative gathers and publishes disaggregated survey data on housing affordability, transportation, belonging, safety, employment, and access to services across neighbourhoods. Results are released via an online dashboard and public reports, co-managed with community partners (including United Way Halifax and public health and equity organizations) to support community-set targets and regular progress monitoring.

solutions.text: Safe-space drop-in hubs and peer support networks: Fund local drop-in centres offering culturally relevant mental-health supports, legal navigation, settlement assistance, and peer-run groups specifically for Mi'kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability, and 2SLGBTQIA+ youth.

resources.name: The Youth Project
resources.description: The Youth Project is a province-wide safe-space hub for 2SLGBTQIA+ youth (ages 25 and under) that offers peer-led support groups, drop-in programming, and one-on-one navigation. Staff and trained peer facilitators provide mental-health support, workshops, and referrals, and help youth navigate legal name/gender-marker changes and access affirming health and community services. This directly implements the solution by offering a culturally relevant, youth-run peer network and welcoming drop-in environment for 2SLGBTQIA+ young people.

resources.name: ISANS Youth Settlement Services
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS provides newcomer youth with a welcoming drop-in environment, settlement advising, and navigation support for housing, education, employment, and immigration processes. The program runs youth peer groups, mentorship circles, and mental-health information sessions, and connects clients to legal supports (including immigration law navigation) and community resources. This implements the solution by combining culturally responsive settlement assistance with peer-led networks and safe spaces for newcomer youth.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre
resources.description: The Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre offers an urban Indigenous safe-space hub with cultural programming, youth activities, housing and justice navigation, and wellness supports. Elders, Knowledge Keepers, and staff provide culturally grounded mental-health support and peer circles, alongside practical help accessing IDs, benefits, and community services. This directly implements the solution by providing a drop-in, culturally relevant environment and peer-supported networks specifically for Mi'kmaq and other Indigenous youth in Halifax.

resources.name: Phoenix Centre for Youth
resources.description: Phoenix Centre for Youth is a low-barrier, walk-in hub for young people that offers basic needs support, mental-health counselling, case management, and system navigation (including legal, income, and housing services). The centre hosts peer-led groups and inclusive programming for diverse youth, including 2SLGBTQIA+ and newcomer youth, creating a consistent safe space and community network. This implements the solution by combining a drop-in model with wraparound, youth-centered supports and peer connection.

resources.name: Independent Living Nova Scotia (ILNS) – Peer Support & Navigation
resources.description: ILNS runs peer-led groups and one-to-one navigation for youth and adults with disabilities, offering an accessible drop-in resource centre, independent living skills training, and community connection. Staff support legal-rights and systems navigation (e.g., accommodations, income supports, housing), and facilitate peer mentoring by people with lived experience. This implements the solution by providing a safe, disability-centered hub with culturally relevant, peer-run supports and practical navigation assistance.

solutions.text: Cultural competency and inclusive curriculum in schools: Work with Mi'kmaq knowledge keepers and Black and newcomer educators to integrate local Indigenous and African Nova Scotian histories, anti-racism materials, and disability and LGBTQ+ inclusion into K–12 programming and extracurriculars.

resources.name: Africentric Educational Resources and Teacher Professional Development
resources.description: The Delmore "Buddy" Daye Learning Institute (DBDLI) creates Africentric, curriculum-aligned teaching resources that embed African Nova Scotian histories, local community narratives, and anti-racism frameworks into K–12 classrooms. The institute also delivers professional learning and mentorship for educators and supports school-based and extracurricular initiatives (e.g., African Heritage Month projects) to strengthen culturally responsive pedagogy and student belonging.

resources.name: Cultural Education and School Outreach
resources.description: The Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre engages Elders and knowledge keepers to deliver in-school cultural programming—such as drumming, song, language, storytelling, and treaty teachings—along with guidance on respectful protocols and land-based learning. The centre partners with teachers to integrate Mi'kmaw perspectives into curriculum and supports extracurricular activities that deepen students’ understanding of local Indigenous histories and contemporary life in Mi’kma’ki.

resources.name: Equity and Inclusive Education (K–12)
resources.description: HRCE’s Equity and Inclusive Education services coordinate African Nova Scotian and Mi’kmaq/Indigenous Student Support Workers, RCH (Race Relations, Cross-Cultural Understanding and Human Rights) advisors, and SOGI leads to embed anti-racism, 2SLGBTQIA+ inclusion, and disability-inclusive practices across K–12. The team co-develops curriculum resources, provides educator professional development, and supports school clubs like GSAs and cultural groups, connecting schools with community partners and knowledge keepers.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

resources.name: School Programs and Educator Resources
resources.organization: Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21
resources.description: The Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21 offers curriculum-linked school programs and digital lesson plans that centre newcomer stories, immigration histories, and anti-racism learning for grades K–12. Educator workshops and classroom resources help teachers integrate inclusive narratives and critical thinking about human rights, diversity, and belonging into social studies, language arts, and project-based learning.

resources.name: Education and Workshops (Schools and GSAs)
resources.description: The Youth Project provides 2SLGBTQIA+ education and workshops for students and staff, guidance for inclusive school policies, and support for Gay–Straight Alliances and other student-led groups. By delivering age-appropriate, curriculum-connected sessions on sexual orientation, gender identity, and intersectional anti-discrimination, the program helps K–12 schools build safer classrooms and extracurricular spaces for all students.

solutions.text: Free legal and employment rights clinics: Operate community legal clinics and employment-advice clinics that provide pro bono support for discrimination complaints, workplace accommodations, immigration questions, and settlement-related barriers.

resources.name: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service – Community Legal Clinic
resources.organization: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service (Schulich School of Law, Dalhousie University)
resources.description: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service operates a community legal clinic that provides free legal help to low-income residents, including summary advice and representation on human rights/discrimination, social justice, housing, income supports, and certain employment-related matters (e.g., EI and workplace accommodation issues). The clinic helps clients file complaints, negotiate accommodations, and navigate tribunals, implementing free legal and employment-rights support that addresses systemic inequities facing equity-seeking communities.

resources.name: reachLegal Free Legal Clinics
resources.description: reachAbility Association runs free legal advice clinics where volunteer lawyers provide no-cost, 30-minute consultations focused on disability and human rights law. The clinics support clients with discrimination complaints, workplace accommodation issues, and employment standards questions, reducing legal barriers for people with disabilities and other equity-deserving groups.
resources.address: 3845 Joseph Howe Drive, Suite 201, Halifax, NS B3L 4H9

resources.name: ISANS Pro Bono Immigration and Legal Clinics
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS hosts pro bono legal clinics and workshops in partnership with volunteer lawyers and law firms to provide newcomers with free advice on immigration status, work permits, and settlement-related legal questions. These sessions also cover employment rights, workplace discrimination/harassment, and navigating complaints processes, helping newcomers overcome legal barriers to equitable participation in the workforce.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

solutions.text: Restorative justice and community healing circles: Use restorative practices and Indigenous-led healing circles to respond to local incidents of discrimination and to rebuild trust, involving affected youth, families, elders, and community mediators.

resources.name: Indigenous Justice Program (IJP)
resources.description: The Indigenous Justice Program at the Native Council of Nova Scotia provides community-based restorative justice for off-reserve Mi'kmaq/Indigenous people, using healing, sentencing, and community circles guided by Elders and cultural advisors. The program addresses harms including incidents rooted in racism and discrimination by facilitating dialogue among affected youth, families, and community members to repair relationships, promote accountability, and rebuild trust.
resources.address: 129 Truro Heights Road, Truro Heights, NS B6L 1X1

resources.name: Wagmatcook First Nation Healing to Wellness Court
resources.organization: Courts of Nova Scotia – Provincial Court (Wagmatcook)
resources.description: This specialized Provincial Court integrates Mi’kmaw restorative practices—such as healing circles with Elders, community supports, and culturally grounded wellness plans—to address the underlying causes of harm. It provides a collaborative, circle-based response for Indigenous people impacted by colonial harms and discrimination, engaging youth, families, Elders, and community mediators to promote repair, accountability, and community healing.

resources.name: Restorative Approaches in Schools (HRCE)
resources.description: The Halifax Regional Centre for Education implements restorative approaches across schools, using proactive community- and healing-circle practices to respond to incidents of harm, including bullying, racism, homophobia/transphobia, and ableism. Trained facilitators bring together affected students, families, staff, and community partners to acknowledge impact, rebuild trust, and co-create agreements that repair relationships and strengthen inclusion.
resources.address: 33 Spectacle Lake Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1X7

solutions.text: Public storytelling and empathy campaigns: Run community media projects that amplify lived experiences of Mi'kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability, and 2SLGBTQIA+ youth — arts projects, podcasts, murals and events that reduce stigma and build connections.

resources.name: Pier 21 Oral History and Youth Storytelling Programs
resources.organization: Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21
resources.description: The Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21 collects and shares oral histories and youth-centered stories from immigrants and refugees through exhibits, live programs, and digital media. By equipping newcomer youth to record and publicly present their lived experiences, the museum runs empathy-building storytelling initiatives that reduce stigma and foster connections across communities in Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia – Community Exhibits and Youth Storytelling
resources.organization: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Centre preserves and amplifies African Nova Scotian history and contemporary voices through exhibits, oral history projects, youth workshops, and public events. Its programs invite young people to create and share art, media, and performances that reflect their lived experiences, building understanding and reducing stigma across Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 10 Cherry Brook Road, Cherry Brook, NS B2Z 1A8

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op – Community Storytelling and Creator Supports
resources.description: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op provides an accessible, community-run venue and training supports where emerging and marginalized youth develop and present original work—storytelling nights, theatre, podcasts, film screenings, and multidisciplinary arts. Programming and partnerships regularly feature Mi’kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability, and 2SLGBTQIA+ creators, using public art and events to foster empathy and inclusion.

resources.name: Media Studio at Halifax Central Library
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries’ Media Studio offers free recording, editing, and production space with staff-led workshops that help youth create podcasts, videos, zines, and digital stories. The library also hosts youth showcases and community storytelling series that center Mi’kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability, and 2SLGBTQIA+ perspectives—publicly sharing lived experiences to reduce stigma and build community connections.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: CKDU 88.1 FM Community Radio – Youth and Community Programming
resources.description: CKDU is a campus–community radio station that trains and supports youth and community members to produce shows and podcasts, offering open access to broadcast tools and mentorship. Regular programming and special series highlight stories from Mi’kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability, and 2SLGBTQIA+ communities, using public airwaves to amplify lived experiences and cultivate empathy province-wide.

solutions.text: Targeted affordable housing initiatives for youth: Create community land trusts, co-op housing, and rent-subsidy programs prioritizing marginalized youth transitioning from care, newcomers, or those facing discrimination to stabilize pathways to education and work.

resources.name: Phoenix Youth Housing (PYH)
resources.description: Phoenix Youth Housing provides safe, affordable apartments with rent subsidies and wraparound supports for youth ages 16–24, including those exiting care, 2SLGBTQIA+ youth, and those facing systemic barriers. Case managers help tenants stabilize housing, continue education or training, and connect to employment, addressing inequities that keep marginalized youth out of stable housing and work. The program uses scattered-site units and landlord partnerships to increase access to long‑term, affordable housing for vulnerable youth.

resources.name: Supportive Housing for Young Mothers (SHYM)
resources.description: SHYM offers subsidized, supportive housing for young mothers aged 16–24, many of whom are transitioning from care or have experienced discrimination and housing instability. Residents receive on-site support, life-skills development, and connections to childcare, education, and employment, helping them maintain stable, affordable housing while building sustainable futures. The program directly targets a marginalized youth population with rent‑subsidy and supportive housing to remove barriers to participation in school and work.
resources.address: 358 Herring Cove Road, Halifax, NS B3R 1V8

resources.name: Housing Support Program (Housing First for Indigenous Youth)
resources.description: The Mi’kmaw Native Friendship Centre’s Housing Support Program uses a Housing First approach to secure and maintain affordable rentals for Indigenous youth, including those exiting care or experiencing homelessness. Staff provide cultural, trauma‑informed case management, landlord mediation, and access to rent supplements and benefits, helping youth stabilize housing so they can engage in education, training, and employment. The program explicitly prioritizes urban Indigenous youth facing systemic inequities and discrimination.

resources.name: Housing Support Program for Youth
resources.description: The Portal’s Housing Support Program helps youth ages 16–24 across the Annapolis Valley secure and retain affordable rentals through landlord partnerships, rent‑subsidy navigation, and supportive case management. The program prioritizes youth facing homelessness, discrimination, or transition from care, and provides ongoing support to keep them in school, training, or work. Shared‑housing options and tailored plans reduce barriers and stabilize pathways to education and employment.

solutions.text: Assistive technology and adaptive equipment lending library: Develop a local lending library for assistive devices, adaptive tech and workplace modifications, paired with training and rapid loan programs to remove immediate employment and education barriers.

resources.name: Health Equipment Loan Program (HELP) – Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Canadian Red Cross HELP program provides short‑term loans of assistive and adaptive equipment such as wheelchairs, walkers, crutches, bath aids, and other mobility/support devices through depots across Nova Scotia. Staff and volunteers offer fitting guidance and safe‑use instruction, enabling rapid access to essential equipment that helps people return to work or school and navigate daily life while longer‑term solutions are arranged.

resources.name: Equipment Loan Program
resources.organization: ALS Society of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia
resources.description: ALS NB & NS maintains a lending library of mobility, communication, and accessibility devices (e.g., wheelchairs, speech‑generating devices, environmental controls) provided at no cost to people living with ALS. The organization arranges quick delivery, setup, and user training, helping clients maintain employment, education, and community participation by removing immediate equipment and accessibility barriers.

resources.name: Assistive Technology (AT) Services
resources.description: APSEA provides assistive technology assessments, device loans, and training for students who are blind/low vision or deaf/hard of hearing across Nova Scotia and the Atlantic region. Through its lending pool (e.g., braille displays, screen readers, magnification tools, FM/DM systems) and educator-led training for students, families, and school teams, APSEA rapidly deploys tools that remove learning barriers and support future success in post‑secondary education and employment.

resources.name: Accessibility Services – Assistive Technology Lending
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries lends assistive devices such as DAISY/Victor Reader players, magnifiers, adaptive keyboards/mice, and other accessibility tools to cardholders, with staff offering orientation and one‑on‑one support. This community lending model provides quick, no‑cost access to adaptive technology for learning, job search, and daily independence, reducing immediate barriers for users with print and other disabilities.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

solutions.text: Youth advisory council with representative seats: Form a municipal/regional youth advisory council with reserved seats for Mi'kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability-identified, and 2SLGBTQIA+ youth to influence planning, budgeting, and service design.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Youth Advisory Committee
resources.description: The HRM Youth Advisory Committee is a municipal body that provides Regional Council and staff with advice on policies, planning, programs, and budgeting that affect young people across the municipality. Its membership structure is designed to include designated representation from equity-deserving youth, including Mi’kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability-identified, and 2SLGBTQIA+ youth, ensuring those perspectives directly inform municipal decision-making and service design.

resources.name: IWK Health Centre Youth Advisory Council
resources.description: The IWK Youth Advisory Council is a standing council of diverse youth who co-design, review, and advise on programs, services, and policies affecting young people receiving care at the IWK and in the region. The council intentionally recruits members from Mi’kmaq, African Nova Scotian, newcomer, disability-identified, and 2SLGBTQIA+ communities so these lived experiences shape planning priorities, patient experience improvements, and resource decisions within the health system.

obstacles.title: Cost-of-living pressures, wage stagnation, and student debt
obstacles.description: Rising prices outpace earnings in many sectors; debt burdens delay milestones like home formation, entrepreneurship, and family planning.

solutions.text: Community Living-Wage Employer Network: Form a local coalition of businesses, non-profits and municipalities that adopt a living-wage pledge, share best practices, and publicize certified employers to encourage higher pay and retain local talent.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Living Wage Employer Program
resources.organization: Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives – Nova Scotia (CCPA–NS)
resources.description: This program certifies employers in Nova Scotia that commit to paying at least the locally calculated living wage and sign a living-wage pledge. It maintains a public directory of certified employers, provides implementation tools, and convenes information-sharing so businesses, non-profits, and municipalities can adopt and sustain living-wage practices—directly building the coalition and visibility the solution calls for.

resources.name: United Way Halifax Living Wage Initiative
resources.description: United Way Halifax partners with CCPA–NS to promote and expand the Living Wage Employer Program, recruiting employers and supporting them through certification and implementation. Through outreach, storytelling, and recognition campaigns that highlight certified employers and share best practices, it strengthens the local coalition and normalizes living-wage commitments to help retain and attract talent.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Living Wage Requirement for Service Contracts
resources.description: HRM has adopted a living-wage standard for many contracted services, requiring vendors to meet or exceed the local living wage in order to do business with the municipality. By embedding the living-wage pledge into procurement and publicly communicating the policy, HRM extends the living-wage network into its supply chain, encourages higher pay among local employers, and aligns with community partners’ living-wage efforts.

resources.name: Certified Living Wage Employer (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre is a certified Living Wage Employer in Nova Scotia, demonstrating adoption of the living-wage pledge and transparent decent-work practices. By publicly sharing its commitment and HR approaches with peer organizations and being listed in the provincial living-wage employer directory, it helps publicize and normalize the standard across sectors—supporting the broader coalition envisioned in the solution.

solutions.text: Community Land Trusts and Affordable Housing Co-ops: Create community-owned land trusts or housing co-ops that remove land from the speculative market, keep rental and ownership costs affordable long-term, and prioritize residents with local ties.

resources.name: Community Housing Acquisition Program (CHAP)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Department of Municipal Affairs and Housing (Housing Nova Scotia)
resources.description: CHAP provides financing to eligible non-profits and housing co-operatives to purchase existing rental properties in Nova Scotia, taking them out of the speculative market and preserving affordability over the long term. By enabling community ownership with affordability requirements, the program helps stabilize rents, protect tenants, and supports the growth of co-operative and land-trust style stewardship that prioritizes local residents.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, 2nd Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: Co-operative Development Services (Housing Co-ops)
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Co-operative Council helps communities form and expand housing co-operatives by providing technical assistance, incorporation support, governance training, and access to financing. This hands-on development support enables resident-owned co-ops to acquire and steward land and buildings collectively, keeping homes affordable over the long term and prioritizing people with strong local ties.
resources.address: 90 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

resources.name: Member Services and Sector Development for Nova Scotia Housing Co-ops
resources.organization: Co-operative Housing Federation of Canada (CHF Canada)
resources.description: CHF Canada provides governance training, refinancing and asset management guidance, and development support to housing co-operatives across Nova Scotia, strengthening member-controlled ownership and long-term affordability. By helping co-ops maintain and expand their housing, CHF Canada ensures homes remain outside the speculative market and accessible to residents connected to their communities.

solutions.text: Shared-Equity Homeownership Programs: Develop local shared-equity models where community organizations or municipalities co-invest in homes to lower down-payment needs and preserve affordability when properties are resold.

resources.name: Affordable Homeownership Program
resources.description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia partners with lower- to moderate-income families to purchase homes through an affordable, geared-to-income mortgage and a no-interest second mortgage that represents Habitat’s equity stake. This shared-equity structure lowers or eliminates the need for a large down payment and, through resale covenants and right-of-first-refusal provisions, preserves affordability when the property is resold. By co-investing alongside families, the program directly implements a local shared-equity model that builds stability and reduces cost-of-living pressures for first-time buyers.

resources.name: Indigenous Housing Partnership (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: As the local implementation of Habitat for Humanity’s Indigenous Housing Partnership, Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia co-invests with Mi’kmaw and other Indigenous families in Nova Scotia using the same shared-equity model of an affordable first mortgage paired with a no-interest second mortgage held by Habitat. This reduces upfront cash requirements, supports culturally appropriate pathways to ownership, and includes resale conditions that help keep homes affordable over time. The program advances equitable access to homeownership while preserving long-term affordability in participating communities.

solutions.text: Local Student Debt Clinics and Refinancing Workshops: Host regular clinics with financial counsellors and legal aid to guide graduates on repayment options, refinancing, loan forgiveness programs, and budgeting strategies to reduce debt burdens.

resources.name: Financial Literacy Workshops at Halifax Public Libraries
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries regularly hosts free financial literacy clinics and workshops in partnership with expert facilitators (e.g., CPA volunteers and accredited credit counsellors). Sessions cover student loan repayment options, consolidation/refinancing, budgeting, and how to navigate federal/provincial repayment assistance and forgiveness programs—directly aligning with local student debt clinics and refinancing workshops.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Money Matters and Financial Literacy Workshops
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS offers group workshops and one-on-one financial coaching for newcomers, including internationally educated graduates, on budgeting, credit, and managing debt. These sessions provide guidance on student loan repayment options, consolidation/refinancing pathways, and accessing repayment assistance or forgiveness programs—functioning as practical, local debt clinics for recent graduates.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Debt & Consumer Law Clinics and Public Legal Education
resources.organization: Legal Information Society of Nova Scotia
resources.description: LISNS delivers public legal education sessions and clinics focused on consumer debt, credit, collections, and small claims, helping individuals understand their rights and options. Programming includes information relevant to student debt—such as repayment options, hardship relief, bankruptcy considerations, and how to deal with collectors—often paired with referrals to legal aid and reputable credit counsellors, mirroring the solution’s legal-aid-supported debt clinics.

resources.name: Student Loan Repayment and Budgeting Workshops
resources.description: Saint Mary’s University’s Financial Aid & Awards office provides workshops and one-on-one advising that help students and recent graduates understand Canada and Nova Scotia Student Loans repayment, consolidation/refinancing options, and the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP). Sessions also include practical budgeting strategies and connections to resources that reduce debt burdens, effectively operating as student debt clinics on campus.

resources.name: Loan Repayment Advising and Financial Literacy Sessions
resources.description: MSVU’s Financial Aid office offers advising and periodic workshops that guide students and graduates through student loan repayment timelines, RAP/interest relief, and consolidation/refinancing, alongside core budgeting and credit-management skills. These services function as localized debt clinics that connect attendees with practical tools and official programs to manage and reduce student debt.

solutions.text: Microgrants, Matched-Savings and Seed Funds for Entrepreneurs: Operate community microgrant programs and matched-savings schemes for young entrepreneurs and small startups to lower the financial barrier to launching local businesses.

resources.name: Volta Cohort
resources.description: Volta Cohort awards non-dilutive micro-seed funding (typically $25,000) plus mentorship and resources to early-stage startups, helping them build prototypes and validate markets. By providing cash awards without taking equity, the program lowers the financial barrier for young and first-time founders to launch and grow companies in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: Spark Nova Scotia
resources.description: Spark Nova Scotia is a provincial startup competition that provides non-dilutive seed grants (often in the $10,000–$50,000 range) and mentorship to founders with early-stage, high-potential ideas. The cash awards act as microgrants to cover early costs like prototyping, customer discovery, and initial marketing, reducing the up-front capital hurdles for new entrepreneurs.

resources.name: Invest Nova Scotia Accelerate Program
resources.description: Accelerate provides non-dilutive seed funding (commonly around $40,000 per company), coaching, and incubation to help Nova Scotia tech startups validate problem–solution fit and reach early customers. This grant-style funding directly implements microgrant/seed support by covering critical early expenses that often prevent young entrepreneurs from launching.

resources.name: BioInnovation Challenge
resources.organization: BioNova (Nova Scotia’s Life Sciences Industry Association)
resources.description: The BioInnovation Challenge is an annual pitch competition that awards non-dilutive cash prizes and in-kind services to early-stage life sciences and health startups in Nova Scotia. These seed funds function as microgrants that help founders advance commercialization, develop prototypes, and validate their business models without taking on debt or giving up equity.
resources.address: 1344 Summer Street, Suite 208, Halifax, NS B3H 0A8

solutions.text: Childcare Cooperatives and Sliding-Scale Childcare: Organize parent-led childcare co-ops and support sliding-scale community childcare options to reduce childcare costs that delay workforce participation and family formation.

resources.name: Aboriginal Head Start (Urban and Northern Communities) – Halifax
resources.description: A culture-based early childhood program that provides no-cost preschool and family supports for Indigenous children ages 3–5. Parents are expected to participate in program activities and decision-making, fostering a cooperative, parent-led model; the free care and wraparound supports directly reduce childcare expenses so caregivers can pursue work or education.

resources.name: YMCA Child Care and Financial Assistance
resources.description: The YMCA operates licensed infant, toddler, preschool, and school-age child care across HRM and provides income-based financial assistance while also accepting the provincial Child Care Subsidy. This creates sliding-scale fees that lower out-of-pocket costs, enabling parents to return to work, education, or training sooner.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Child Care Subsidy Program
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Department of Education and Early Childhood Development
resources.description: An income-tested subsidy that reduces child care fees for eligible families using licensed centres and family homes across Nova Scotia. By scaling family contributions to income and paying the remainder directly to providers, it enables community child care to operate on a sliding-scale basis and eases cost pressures that delay workforce participation and family formation.

resources.name: NSCECE Lab School Child Care Centres
resources.organization: Nova Scotia College of Early Childhood Education (NSCECE)
resources.description: Non-profit lab school centres that provide licensed infant, toddler, and preschool care while serving as practicum sites for early childhood education students. They accept the provincial Child Care Subsidy and operate as community-based programs, expanding access to affordable, sliding-scale child care for families in Halifax.
