resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Urban Forestry Program implements the Urban Forest Master Plan by planting and maintaining thousands of street and park trees each year, prioritizing neighbourhoods with low canopy cover and higher heat-vulnerability. The program organizes community tree-planting events and expands shade in parks, pathways, and school-adjacent spaces to reduce urban heat exposure for residents, including seniors and youth, while improving overall neighbourhood livability.

resources.name: Halifax Transit Bus Stop Improvements Program
resources.description: Halifax Transit expands and upgrades bus stop shelters and seating across the municipality, installing covered shelters that provide shade and weather protection at high-ridership and priority locations. These shaded shelters reduce extreme-heat exposure for transit users—particularly seniors, youth, and riders with mobility needs—while improving overall comfort and accessibility at bus stops.

resources.name: Stormwater Credits Program (Green Roof and Onsite Management Incentives)
resources.description: Halifax Water’s Stormwater Credits Program provides financial credits on stormwater charges to property owners who install onsite stormwater management features such as green roofs, cisterns, and permeable surfaces. By incentivizing green roofs—which cool buildings and reduce roof surface temperatures—the program supports ‘cool roof’ outcomes that mitigate urban heat islands while also managing runoff and improving climate resilience.
resources.address: 450 Cowie Hill Road, Halifax, NS B3R 1Y6

solutions.text: Voluntary managed retreat frameworks and land swaps: Community-led planning for phased, voluntary relocation from the highest-risk shorelines — including land-swap mechanisms, buyouts, and local housing placement strategies to keep people in the community while reducing exposure.

resources.name: 2016 Flood Recovery – Voluntary Home Buyout Program
resources.description: Following the October 2016 flood in Sydney and surrounding communities, CBRM implemented a voluntary home buyout program in partnership with Nova Scotia’s Disaster Financial Assistance to reduce future flood losses. The municipality acquired high-risk residential properties in mapped floodways (e.g., along Wash Brook), removed structures, and reserved the land as open floodplain, thereby lowering exposure. Staff worked case-by-case with homeowners to support relocation within CBRM where possible, helping residents stay in their communities while moving out of harm’s way.

resources.name: Truro Flood Mitigation Program – Property Acquisition and Voluntary Buyouts
resources.description: After repeated flooding of the Salmon River floodplain (notably in 2012), the Town of Truro integrated a voluntary property acquisition/buyout component into its broader flood protection program. Using provincial and federal recovery/mitigation funds, the Town purchases homes and lots in the highest-risk floodway, removes structures, and converts the land to green space and flood storage to reduce future damages. The program works with affected residents on relocation options within Truro, aligning with managed-retreat principles that keep people in the community while reducing exposure.

solutions.text: Climate‑resilient trades and workforce training: Local training programs and apprenticeships in resilient construction, floodproofing, shoreline restoration and renewable energy to create jobs for youth and retain talent in the region.

resources.name: Clean Leadership Summer Internship
resources.description: Clean Foundation’s paid summer internship program places youth (15–30) with host employers across Nova Scotia to work on real projects in energy efficiency, coastal and shoreline restoration, climate adaptation planning, and sustainable construction. Interns receive job-readiness training and mentorship while building hands-on skills that align with climate-resilient trades and workforce needs, directly creating a pipeline of local talent for employers working on floodproofing, habitat restoration, and renewable energy initiatives.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations – Living Shorelines Program
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-based Solutions, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations at Saint Mary’s University delivers training and hands-on projects that teach contractors, municipal staff, and community groups how to design and install nature-based shoreline protection (e.g., living shorelines, salt marsh restoration) to reduce storm surge and erosion. Through workshops, field demonstrations, and collaborative builds, the program develops a local workforce skilled in coastal resilience techniques that protect infrastructure and support long-term community stability.

resources.name: Efficiency Preferred Partner (EPP) Network and Contractor Training
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia’s EPP Network provides training, technical resources, and market access for local contractors and trades involved in heat pumps, insulation, building envelope upgrades, and energy auditing. By upskilling installers and builders to deliver energy-efficient, code-compliant, and climate-resilient retrofits, the program strengthens the clean energy workforce and creates ongoing employment opportunities in communities across the province.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Building Futures for Youth (BFY)
resources.organization: Construction Association of Nova Scotia (CANS), in partnership with the Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency and industry
resources.description: BFY places Nova Scotia high school students in paid summer positions with construction employers, providing safety training, mentoring, and exposure to in-demand trades that increasingly include energy-efficient and climate-resilient building practices. The program builds a direct pathway into apprenticeship and long-term careers, helping retain young talent in sectors that deliver resilient housing, infrastructure, and community facilities.
resources.address: 134 Eileen Stubbs Avenue, Unit 301, Dartmouth, NS B3B 2C8

resources.name: Powerline Technician (PLT) Apprenticeship Program
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s PLT apprenticeship trains new entrants to build, maintain, and harden the electrical grid, including storm response, pole-line construction, and integration of distributed renewable energy. The program combines classroom and field-based learning to grow a skilled workforce that enhances community resilience to extreme weather and supports the clean energy transition.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

solutions.text: Support for adaptation in coastal industries: Community business hubs that help fishers, aquaculture operators and tourism businesses diversify markets, adopt resilient infrastructure (e.g., mobile docks), and access funding for climate-ready operations.

resources.name: The PIER (Port Innovation, Engagement and Research)
resources.description: The PIER is an innovation hub at the Halifax Seaport that convenes ocean-sector companies, researchers, and government to co-develop and pilot solutions for resilient coastal operations. Through living-lab demonstrations and partnerships, it helps seafood logistics firms, fishers, aquaculture operators, and marine tourism businesses test and adopt weather-resilient infrastructure and technologies, and connect to funding and market partners to scale climate-ready operations.

resources.name: Centre for Ocean Ventures and Entrepreneurship (COVE)
resources.description: COVE is a coastal industry hub providing shared waterfront facilities, on-water testing, and commercialization support for ocean technologies that improve resilience in fisheries, aquaculture, and marine tourism. It accelerates adoption of tools such as storm-hardened platforms, sensors, and mobile infrastructure, while connecting businesses with investors and public programs (e.g., ACOA, provincial funds) to finance climate-ready upgrades and diversify products and markets.

resources.name: Perennia Aquaculture Development & Seafood Market Services
resources.description: Perennia provides technical and business advisory support to aquaculture producers and seafood processors, helping them improve gear and infrastructure resilience, product quality, and operational safety in a changing climate. Their specialists assist with market diversification, export readiness, and navigating funding programs for equipment and infrastructure upgrades, enabling coastal businesses to stabilize revenues and grow in climate-impacted conditions.
resources.address: 199 Innovation Drive, Suite 110, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2H5

resources.name: Working Waterfronts Program
resources.description: Build Nova Scotia’s Working Waterfronts initiative plans, builds, and manages resilient coastal infrastructure—such as floating and modular docks, seasonal berthing, and accessible shore services—used by fishers, tour operators, and other marine businesses. By providing storm-ready, maintainable, and adaptable facilities across key waterfronts, the program reduces climate risk exposure and enables operators to sustain and expand market offerings in coastal communities.
resources.address: 1875 Upper Water Street, Suite 301, Halifax, NS B3J 1S9

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic Rural Innovation Hub (Yarmouth)
resources.description: IGNITE’s rural hub supports coastal entrepreneurs—including fishers, aquaculture startups, and marine tourism operators—with mentorship, workshops, and hands-on help to adopt resilient equipment, modernize operations, and diversify into new markets (e-commerce, value-added products, year-round experiences). Staff also guide businesses to grants and loans for climate-ready infrastructure and facilitate pilot projects with technology partners to reduce downtime from storms and flooding.

solutions.text: Local land‑use policy and coastal setback advocacy: Mobilize community input to update municipal planning bylaws, enforce coastal setbacks, require flood-resilient building standards and protect natural buffers to reduce future exposure.

resources.name: One City, One Plan — Halifax Regional Plan Review
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s comprehensive plan review is updating the Regional Plan and land-use by-laws with climate-resilient policies, including coastal flood hazard mapping, minimum building elevation requirements, and strengthened coastal buffers. The process features extensive public engagement to shape enforceable coastal setbacks, integrate flood-resilient building standards, and protect natural buffers (dunes, marshes) across HRM’s coastline.

resources.name: Coastal Adaptation
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre’s Coastal Adaptation program mobilizes residents and community groups to advocate for stronger coastal protections in municipal planning, including coastal setbacks, no-build buffers, and flood-resilient standards. The team provides policy guidance, hosts public workshops, and advances nature-based solutions like living shorelines that municipalities can embed in land-use by-laws to reduce storm surge and erosion risks.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations partners with Nova Scotia municipalities and communities to design living shorelines and protect natural buffers such as salt marshes and dunes, then helps translate these practices into local land-use policy. Through technical guidance, policy templates, and community engagement, the centre supports adoption of coastal setback requirements and flood-resilient building standards that reduce exposure to storm surge and sea-level rise.

resources.name: Coastal & Marine Program
resources.description: Coastal Action’s Coastal & Marine Program works with South Shore municipalities and residents to assess coastal hazards, facilitate community input, and implement living shoreline and wetland restoration projects. Their technical support and engagement inform updates to municipal planning strategies and by-laws, embedding coastal setbacks, buffer protections, and flood-resilient requirements to safeguard people and infrastructure.
resources.address: 37 Tannery Road, Unit 1, Lunenburg, NS B0J 2C0

resources.name: Municipal Climate Adaptation
resources.description: Clean Foundation supports Nova Scotia municipalities with flood and coastal risk assessments, public engagement, and policy recommendations that feed directly into Municipal Planning Strategies and Land-Use By-laws. Their services help communities adopt coastal setback policies, floodproofing standards, and natural buffer protections to reduce future exposure and insurance pressures.

solutions.text: Community resilience finance tools: Create local revolving loan funds, resilience bonds or grant-matching pools to finance small-scale adaptation projects, home retrofits and restoration work with community oversight and accessible terms.

resources.name: Solar City (Property Assessed Clean Energy Financing)
resources.description: Halifax’s Solar City program provides Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) financing that allows homeowners to install rooftop solar and repay the cost through their property tax bill over time at accessible, fixed terms. By lowering upfront costs and using a revolving, municipality-managed fund, the program enables home energy retrofits that improve resilience to heat and power disruptions and reduce energy burdens in the face of climate risks.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing Program (PACE) – Town of Bridgewater
resources.description: Bridgewater’s Clean Energy Financing Program is a municipal PACE initiative that provides low-interest, long-term financing for home energy retrofits such as heat pumps, insulation, and solar, with repayment collected via property tax. This revolving loan model reduces upfront barriers and channels community-governed capital into small-scale resilience upgrades that help residents adapt to heat, storms, and energy cost volatility.

resources.name: HomeWarming (Free Home Energy Upgrades for Eligible Households)
resources.organization: HomeWarming (delivered by Clean Foundation and Efficiency Nova Scotia)
resources.description: HomeWarming funds no-cost home energy retrofits—such as insulation, air sealing, and other efficiency measures—for income-qualified Nova Scotians, reducing exposure to extreme heat/cold and lowering energy bills. As a grant-based program delivered by community partners, it functions as an accessible resilience finance tool that supports small-scale, household-level adaptations across the province.

solutions.text: Indigenous partnership and traditional stewardship integration: Work with Mi'kmaq and other Indigenous knowledge holders to co-design shoreline management, incorporate Traditional Ecological Knowledge in restoration, and support Indigenous-led adaptation initiatives.

resources.name: Bras d’Or Lakes Collaborative Environmental Planning Initiative (CEPI)
resources.description: CEPI brings Mi’kmaq Elders, communities, governments, and scientists together to steward the Bras d’Or Lakes and connected shorelines using Two-Eyed Seeing (Etuaptmumk) and Netukulimk principles. It co-designs shoreline and coastal habitat management plans, integrates Mi’kmaq Traditional Ecological Knowledge into restoration and monitoring, and advances climate adaptation actions that reduce storm surge and flooding risks for communities around the Lakes.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions
resources.description: Based at Saint Mary’s University, TransCoastal Adaptations partners with Mi’kmaq communities and organizations to co-design and implement living shorelines and salt marsh restoration projects across Nova Scotia. The centre weaves Mi’kmaq Traditional Ecological Knowledge with coastal engineering and ecology, builds Indigenous guardian and youth capacity, and supports Indigenous-led adaptation planning to protect homes and infrastructure from storm surge and flooding.

resources.name: Kejimkujik Cooperative Management Board
resources.organization: Parks Canada – Kejimkujik National Park and National Historic Site
resources.description: Parks Canada and the Mi’kmaq of Kespukwitk co-manage Kejimkujik, including the coastal Kejimkujik Seaside unit, integrating Mi’kmaw Traditional Ecological Knowledge in stewardship and restoration. The board guides shoreline habitat management for dunes, beaches, and salt marshes, co-develops climate adaptation measures for coastal species at risk, and supports Indigenous-led stewardship and interpretation to address rising seas and storm impacts.
resources.address: 3005 Kejimkujik Main Parkway, Maitland Bridge, NS B0T 1B0

resources.name: Ecology Action Centre – Coastal Adaptation Program
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre works with Mi’kmaq communities and partners to plan and deliver nature-based shoreline management solutions, such as living shorelines and salt marsh restoration, using a Two-Eyed Seeing approach. The program integrates Mi’kmaw Traditional Ecological Knowledge in site selection, design, and monitoring, and provides capacity-building and policy support that enables Indigenous-led climate adaptation along Nova Scotia’s coasts.

solutions.text: Citizen science monitoring network: Organize volunteer programs to monitor shoreline erosion, tide heights, storm damage and heat islands, creating local datasets to inform planning, insurance discussions and grant applications.

resources.name: Community Shoreline Monitoring Program
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: TransCoastal Adaptations trains community volunteers to document coastal change at living shoreline and salt marsh restoration sites across Nova Scotia. Volunteers use standardized photo-monitoring stations, simple beach/dune profiling, and water-level loggers to capture storm tides and post-storm damage, generating local datasets that inform municipal adaptation planning, insurance conversations, and grant applications.

resources.name: Coastal & Marine Community Monitoring
resources.description: Coastal Action engages trained volunteers along Nova Scotia’s South Shore to monitor shoreline change using photo-points and beach/dune profiles, and to document king tide and storm surge flooding after major weather events. The program also tracks coastal water temperatures and habitat indicators, producing community datasets that support municipal coastal planning, resilience projects, and funding proposals.

resources.name: Atlantic Water Network – Community-Based Monitoring Program
resources.description: Atlantic Water Network equips and trains community groups across Nova Scotia to run volunteer monitoring of streams, estuaries, and coastal inlets, including installing staff gauges and loggers for water levels, temperature, and salinity, and conducting post-storm site assessments. AWN provides standardized methods and a data platform so local results feed into Atlantic DataStream and are used for flood risk mapping, coastal planning, and grant applications.

resources.name: Community-Based Environmental Monitoring Program
resources.description: Clean Annapolis River Project coordinates volunteers to monitor the Annapolis River and Basin, including tidal tributaries and shorelines, by deploying temperature and water-level loggers, tracking erosion sites, and documenting high-water marks and storm damage. The resulting datasets support municipal decision-making around dikes, causeways, and coastal assets, and strengthen insurance discussions and funding applications for nature-based adaptation.
resources.address: 314 St. George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

resources.name: Volunteer Property Guardians
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Nature Trust’s trained volunteer guardians regularly visit protected coastal properties to record shoreline erosion, storm impacts, and high-tide encroachment using GPS-referenced photos and standardized checklists. These citizen-science observations inform stewardship and risk reduction on conservation lands and are shared with partners to support local planning, insurance considerations, and grant proposals for restoration and resilience.
resources.address: 81 Prince Albert Road, Unit M, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1M1

obstacles.title: Fragile arts, culture, and creative sector
obstacles.description: Precarious funding, venue shortages, and limited career ladders push artists and cultural workers to larger markets, weakening a key quality-of-life driver.

solutions.text: Community Microgrant Fund for Artists: A locally governed pool of small, fast-turnaround grants funded by residents, businesses, and crowdfunding to cover project costs, materials, and short-term living support so artists can start or sustain work without relocating.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Program
resources.description: Gritty to Pretty provides small, fast-turnaround grants to artists and community groups to create murals, public art, and placemaking projects in downtown Halifax. Funded by local businesses through the business improvement district levy and sponsorships, the program covers artist fees, materials, and project costs, directly enabling artists to initiate work and earn income without leaving the province.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 2A2

resources.name: Community Access Fund
resources.description: The Community Access Fund offers micro-grants in the form of subsidized or fully covered venue rental for artists and grassroots groups at the Bus Stop Theatre, reducing core project costs like space, tech, and materials. Supported by donations from residents, local businesses, and partners, this locally governed fund helps artists quickly mount shows and develop new work while receiving honoraria and retaining earnings that support short-term living needs.

resources.name: Placemaking Grants
resources.description: Placemaking Grants provide small project funds to artists and community partners to produce murals, installations, and creative activations in downtown Dartmouth. Financed by member businesses and sponsors of the Business Improvement District, these quick-to-apply grants cover artist fees and materials, helping creators launch visible projects and earn income locally rather than relocating.

solutions.text: Shared Creative Hubs and Maker Spaces: Convert vacant storefronts, church basements, or school rooms into affordable co-op studios, rehearsal rooms, and maker spaces managed by artists and neighbours to reduce venue shortages and build cross-discipline collaboration.

resources.name: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: A member-owned, artist-run performance venue and community arts hub that offers affordable rehearsal, production, and presentation space for theatre, music, dance, film, and community groups. By pooling resources to operate a shared stage, studios, and equipment, the co-op reduces venue shortages and fosters cross-disciplinary collaboration among local artists and neighbours.

resources.name: RadStorm Halifax
resources.description: An artist-run, volunteer-operated creative hub that combines an all-ages arts venue with Ink Storm Screenprinting Studio, SADRAD Music, and the Anchor Archive Zine Library. It provides sliding-scale rehearsal rooms, a community print shop, and shared resources in a repurposed commercial space, enabling low-cost, cross-disciplinary collaboration and skill-sharing.

resources.name: Halifax Makerspace
resources.description: A non-profit, member-run workshop offering shared access to tools such as 3D printers, laser cutters, electronics benches, and wood/metalworking equipment. Through affordable memberships, peer-led workshops, and open community nights, it functions as a collaborative maker hub that addresses space and equipment barriers for artists, tinkerers, and entrepreneurs.

resources.name: Eltuek Arts Centre
resources.description: A multi-tenant creative hub in a repurposed former convent that offers affordable artist studios, galleries, shared meeting rooms, and a digital access lab. By co-locating artists and cultural organizations with community programming, it provides shared, low-cost space that strengthens collaboration and addresses the scarcity of creative facilities in Cape Breton.

resources.name: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts (Two Planks and a Passion Theatre Society)
resources.description: A rural arts centre providing studios, rehearsal spaces, and interdisciplinary workshops for visual artists, performers, and community members. Through shared facilities, residencies, and artist-led programs, it offers accessible space and resources that build collaboration and mitigate venue shortages in the region.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

solutions.text: Artist Mentorship and Apprenticeship Network: A community-run directory and matching program where established local artists mentor emerging creators and offer paid apprenticeships, creating clearer career ladders and hands-on skill building.

resources.name: VANS Mentorship Program
resources.description: Visual Arts Nova Scotia’s Mentorship Program pairs emerging visual artists with established, locally based mentors for several months of one-on-one guidance, studio visits, and professional development. The program actively matches artists by discipline and goals, offers mentor honoraria and exhibition/artist fees, and culminates in a public showcase—creating hands-on, paid learning and clearer career steps that help retain artists in the province.

resources.name: Alistair MacLeod Mentorship Program
resources.description: The Writers’ Federation of Nova Scotia matches emerging writers with established authors for an intensive multi-month, one-on-one mentorship focused on craft development, industry knowledge, and professional practices. Mentors are paid honoraria and participants receive structured milestones and a final public reading, creating a clear ladder from emerging to professional and building networks that keep literary talent thriving in Nova Scotia.

resources.name: FILM 5
resources.description: AFCOOP’s FILM 5 is an intensive training and production program that pairs emerging directors, writers, and producers with seasoned film professionals for workshops, project development, and on‑set mentorship. Participants move through a structured pathway to produce a short film, with crew attachments and mentor-led guidance that function as apprenticeship-style, hands-on learning—building practical skills and industry connections within Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Media Art Scholarship (MAS)
resources.description: The Centre for Art Tapes’ Media Art Scholarship pairs emerging media artists with experienced mentors and staff support over an extended period, providing equipment access, workshops, and artist fees/stipends. Through individualized matching, hands-on production, and a culminating public screening, the program creates a structured, paid pathway for emerging creators to gain professional skills and enter Nova Scotia’s media arts sector.

solutions.text: Pop-up Performance and Exhibition Series: Organize regular pop-up shows, readings, and galleries in nontraditional venues (cafés, parks, transit hubs) using volunteer event teams and local business partnerships to increase visibility and income for creators.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Program
resources.description: This Downtown Halifax Business Commission program funds and coordinates pop-up art, storefront installations, and small performance activations in vacant shops, alleys, plazas, and other nontraditional spaces. It pairs artists with local property owners and businesses, and mobilizes volunteer support to deliver temporary shows and exhibitions that increase artists’ visibility and create paid opportunities, while animating the downtown for residents and visitors.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 2A2

resources.name: Halifax Fringe Festival
resources.description: The Halifax Fringe Festival presents hundreds of performances each year in bars, cafés, galleries, storefronts, and pop-up spaces across Halifax and Dartmouth. By activating nontraditional venues through partnerships with local businesses and relying on volunteer teams and coordinators, Fringe creates accessible, low-cost performance opportunities that increase exposure and income for emerging and established creators.

resources.name: Portland Street Night Market
resources.description: This recurring open-street event turns Portland Street into a pedestrian zone featuring pop-up stages, buskers, art installations, and vendor booths inside and outside local shops and cafés. Organized by the Downtown Dartmouth Business Commission with volunteer event teams and strong retailer participation, the market gives artists and makers direct sales and performance opportunities while drawing new audiences to independent businesses.

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries – Arts & Culture Pop-up Programming
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries regularly hosts pop-up readings, concerts, exhibitions, and workshops in branch atriums, outdoor plazas, and community rooms—spaces not traditionally dedicated to the arts. Working with local creators, arts groups, and nearby businesses, and supported by staff and volunteers, these free-to-attend events amplify artists’ visibility, provide honoraria and merch sales opportunities, and bring arts programming into everyday community settings.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

solutions.text: Arts-to-Business Sponsorship Consortium: A cooperative of small businesses that pool sponsorship dollars, in-kind services, and promotional space to support local productions and cultural programming, creating sustained private-sector backing.

resources.name: Corporate Partnerships
resources.description: Neptune Theatre’s Corporate Partnerships program convenes many local small and mid-sized businesses to co-sponsor mainstage productions, youth theatre, and community outreach. Partners contribute cash, in-kind services (such as printing, hospitality, and media), and shared promotional placements, creating a sustained private-sector consortium that underwrites local theatre and keeps programming accessible.

resources.name: Sponsorship & Fringe Benefits Partner Program
resources.description: Halifax Fringe organizes restaurants, retailers, and service businesses to collectively sponsor the festival while offering in-kind perks—like discounts, space, and materials—to artists and audiences through its Fringe Benefits partner network. By pooling many small business contributions and promotional channels, the program sustains independent productions and amplifies cultural programming across the city.

resources.name: HAT Business Club
resources.description: The Highland Arts Theatre Business Club invites local enterprises to commit monthly or annual contributions alongside in-kind goods and advertising inventory to support year-round productions, artist development, and community events. This standing network functions as a consortium of private backers, stabilizing revenues and exchanging cross-promotion between member businesses and the theatre’s programming.

resources.name: Corporate Sponsorship Program
resources.description: Chester Playhouse coordinates a portfolio of local business sponsors who collectively fund performances, festivals, and community arts programming. Sponsors contribute cash support, in-kind services (hospitality, printing, technical), and collaborative marketing, pooling private-sector resources to ensure sustained cultural activity in the region.

solutions.text: Local Arts Marketplace and Online Platform: A community-managed website and periodic market that helps artists sell work, book gigs, and list services, combined with digital training to expand markets beyond the region while keeping revenue local.

resources.name: Designer Craft Shop (in-person and online)
resources.organization: Craft Nova Scotia (Centre for Craft Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Craft Nova Scotia operates the Designer Craft Shop as a year-round retail gallery and e-commerce site showcasing juried work by Nova Scotia artisans, helping makers sell locally and beyond the region. They also run periodic juried markets (e.g., Summer and Christmas craft shows) that create in-person sales opportunities, and offer professional development workshops on e-commerce, product photography, and digital marketing so artists can expand markets while keeping revenue local.
resources.address: 1061 Marginal Road, Suite 140, Halifax, NS B3H 4P7

resources.name: CBCCD Gallery Shop & Online Store
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: The Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design runs a curated Gallery Shop and online store that sell work from Cape Breton artisans, alongside seasonal markets and exhibitions that provide recurring, local sales opportunities. Through its business training (e.g., Craft Business Skills for Success) and digital marketing workshops, CBCCD equips artists with the skills to list services, improve online sales, and reach customers beyond the island while anchoring earnings in the local economy.

resources.name: NGFM Market to Go
resources.description: Market to Go is the New Glasgow Farmers Market’s weekly online marketplace that features local food and artisan goods, paired with the Saturday in-person market to create steady sales channels for makers. The co-operative helps vendors set up digital storefronts and improve product listings (photography, descriptions, pricing) and periodically offers vendor training, enabling artisans to grow e-commerce capacity, reach new customers, and keep revenue circulating in Pictou County.
resources.address: 620 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3S2

resources.name: CBMIC Membership, Artist Directory & Training
resources.description: CBMIC maintains an online member directory that connects Cape Breton musicians and industry professionals with bookers and clients, supporting gig bookings and service listings. It complements this platform with regular professional development—covering digital distribution, marketing, grant writing, and business skills—and showcases that create live performance opportunities, helping artists build sustainable careers from Nova Scotia while growing audiences beyond the region.

solutions.text: Culture Incubator and Business-Training Workshops: Volunteer-led workshops and short incubator programs teaching budgeting, grantwriting, marketing, and contract negotiation tailored to creative careers, run in partnership with libraries, colleges, and business volunteers.

resources.name: Professional Development Workshops
resources.description: Visual Arts Nova Scotia (VANS) runs ongoing professional development workshops and info sessions for artists across the province, covering grant writing, budgeting and pricing, contracts, marketing, and career planning. Delivered with practicing artists and community partners, these sessions equip creatives with concrete business skills to build sustainable careers in the cultural sector.
resources.address: 1113 Marginal Road, Suite 201, Halifax, NS B3H 4P7

resources.name: Professional Development Workshops (Business of Writing)
resources.description: The Writers’ Federation of Nova Scotia offers regular workshops and webinars on the business side of a writing career, including grant application strategy, project budgeting, publishing contracts, marketing, and author branding. Programs connect emerging and established writers with industry professionals and mentors, directly supporting the development of sustainable creative livelihoods.
resources.address: 1113 Marginal Road, Suite 201, Halifax, NS B3H 4P7

resources.name: Industry Education & Professional Development
resources.description: Music Nova Scotia delivers year-round training, bootcamps, and mentorship for artists and music entrepreneurs on funding applications, tour and project budgeting, marketing and release planning, and contract basics. Drawing on industry volunteers and partners, these workshops provide targeted business skills that help musicians grow viable careers in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 2169 Gottingen Street, Suite 202, Halifax, NS B3K 3B5

resources.name: Craft Business Skills Workshops
resources.organization: Craft Nova Scotia (Centre for Craft Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Craft Nova Scotia’s Centre for Craft hosts recurring professional development sessions focused on the business of craft, including budgeting and pricing, grant and proposal writing, marketing, and navigating wholesale/retail contracts. Led by practicing craftspeople and guest business mentors, these workshops help artisans translate creative practice into sustainable enterprises.

resources.name: Creative Entrepreneurship & Business Skills
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: The Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design offers creative entrepreneurship training and business-skills workshops for artisans and designers, covering topics like pricing, budgeting, grant writing, marketing, and sales planning. Programs pair participants with local mentors and partner organizations to incubate craft-based ventures and strengthen the island’s creative economy.

solutions.text: Neighbourhood Public Art & Place-making Projects: Community-driven murals, sculptures, and performance trails that use local artists, students, and volunteers to animate public space, attract visitors, and demonstrate the social value of arts investments.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Program
resources.description: Downtown Halifax Business Commission’s Gritty to Pretty funds and produces community-led murals, artist-designed installations, and public-space activations across downtown. The program hires local artists, partners with property owners, and involves volunteers to transform laneways and facades, attracting visitors and demonstrating the economic and social value of arts investment.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 3X7

resources.name: Downtown Dartmouth Mural Project
resources.description: The Downtown Dartmouth Business Commission commissions large-scale murals and street art that engage local artists, schools, and neighbourhood volunteers to enliven walls and laneways. The project creates a walkable outdoor gallery that draws foot traffic and visitors to small businesses, showing how public art investment strengthens community identity and the local economy.

resources.name: Kentville Pumpkin People
resources.description: Each October, the Town of Kentville produces a town-wide trail of whimsical pumpkin-figure sculptures created with local businesses, students, and community volunteers. The installations animate parks and storefronts, attract thousands of visitors, and showcase how creative, community-built public art energizes public spaces and supports the local economy.

resources.name: Art in the Landscape
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts curates a seasonal outdoor sculpture and installations trail on its grounds, created by Nova Scotian artists alongside youth and community participants in hands-on workshops. The program pairs public art with guided walks and community events, animating a rural cultural hub and demonstrating the social value of investing in place-based arts.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

solutions.text: Cooperative Gallery and Touring Network: An artist-run cooperative that shares gallery space, curatorial costs, and a mobile touring program that rotates exhibits and performances through nearby towns to expand audiences and revenue streams.

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: A member-owned, artist-run co-operative venue in Halifax that pools resources like gallery/performance space, technical gear, and administrative support so independent artists can share exhibition and curatorial costs. Through co-productions and partnerships with presenters across Nova Scotia, the co-op regularly hosts and routes touring theatre, music, and interdisciplinary performances, rotating shows through nearby towns to grow audiences and earned revenue for artists.

resources.name: Art 1274 Hollis Cooperative Gallery
resources.description: An artist-run cooperative gallery where member artists collectively manage the space, share rent and staffing, and co-curate rotating exhibitions and sales events. The co-op also collaborates on pop-up displays and off-site showcases with partner venues and festivals around Nova Scotia, effectively taking members’ work on tour to broaden audiences and sales opportunities.

resources.name: ViewPoint Gallery (Artist-Run Cooperative)
resources.description: A photographer-run cooperative gallery whose members jointly manage the exhibition program and share operating and curatorial costs, presenting ongoing group and solo shows. ViewPoint partners with other galleries and community venues to organize exchange and pop-up photography exhibitions and artist talks across Nova Scotia, rotating displays to reach new audiences and revenue streams for members.

resources.name: Ross Creek Outreach and Touring Programs
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: A rural arts initiative that shares gallery and production resources with artists through residencies and co-presentations at the Ross Creek Centre, reducing individual costs while building collective capacity. Its outreach and touring activities take exhibitions, performances, and workshops to neighbouring Valley communities and schools, rotating programming in partnership with local venues to expand access and audiences across the region.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

solutions.text: Volunteer Arts Advocacy Coalition: A grassroots group of artists, residents, and business owners that organizes petitions, meets with municipal leaders, and campaigns for stable municipal/ provincial support and affordable cultural zoning.

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: An artist- and community-run theatre that has led grassroots advocacy to secure affordable cultural space on Halifax’s Gottingen Street. The co-op has organized petitions, deputed to Halifax Regional Council, and worked directly with municipal and provincial leaders to obtain stable operating and capital support, protecting a vital, low-cost venue for artists and community groups.

resources.name: Craft Nova Scotia
resources.description: The provincial craft sector association convenes artists, studios, and craft businesses to advocate for sustainable public investment and policies that protect and grow cultural spaces. Through member mobilization, budget submissions, and regular meetings with municipal and provincial officials, it campaigns for stable funding and affordable studio, retail, and exhibition zoning, particularly around the Halifax Seaport creative district.
resources.address: 1061 Marginal Road, Suite 140, Halifax, NS B3H 4P7

resources.name: Writers’ Federation of Nova Scotia
resources.description: A province-wide membership organization that mobilizes writers and allies to advocate for stable arts funding and policies that sustain affordable creative workspaces. It coordinates letter-writing campaigns and petitions, prepares policy submissions, and meets with municipal and provincial leaders to strengthen cultural infrastructure and protect cultural zoning that benefits literary artists.

resources.name: Neptune Theatre
resources.description: Halifax’s flagship theatre engages artists, local businesses, and audiences in advocacy for stable municipal and provincial support and for zoning that preserves downtown performance venues. Through public campaigns, coalition-building across the arts and hospitality sectors, and direct meetings with HRM and provincial officials, it advances policies that keep cultural spaces accessible and sustainable.

solutions.text: Youth Creative Career Pathways Program: Local schools, colleges, and arts organizations collaborate on work-integrated learning, summer placements, and entrepreneurship projects so young people can see viable creative career options at home.

resources.name: NSCAD University Co-op Education Program
resources.description: NSCAD’s Co-op Education places art, design, and media students in paid, credit-earning work terms with local studios, galleries, game/animation shops, and cultural organizations across Nova Scotia. By coordinating summer and semester-long placements and employer partnerships, the program provides real-world creative work experience and helps students see viable career paths in the province.

resources.name: NSCC Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) and Co-op Education
resources.description: NSCC integrates co-ops, internships, and applied projects into creative programs such as Screen Arts, Music Arts, Graphic & Print Production, and Photography, matching students with Nova Scotian employers for semester and summer placements. These partnerships with studios, festivals, theatres, and design firms give youth hands-on experience, industry mentorship, and entrepreneurship exposure so they can build creative careers at home.

resources.name: Neptune Theatre School and Apprenticeships
resources.description: Neptune offers youth training, teen companies, and technical/theatre apprenticeships that place learners alongside professional artists and crews on mainstage and studio productions. Through school-year intensives, summer programs, and internships, participants gain practical credits, mentorship, and paid early-career opportunities that build a local pathway into Nova Scotia’s performing arts sector.

resources.name: FILM 5 Training & Production Program
resources.description: AFCOOP’s FILM 5 is a rigorous, multi-month program where emerging filmmakers receive industry training, mentorship, and hands-on production experience to create short films with professional crews. By partnering with local mentors, post-secondary graduates, and screen-sector employers, the program functions like work-integrated learning—building portfolios, on-set networks, and pathways to paid roles in Nova Scotia’s film industry.
resources.address: 5663 Nora Bernard Street, Suite 101, Halifax, NS B3K 1B6

resources.name: Production Assistant (PA) and Crew Training
resources.description: Screen Nova Scotia delivers industry-led PA and crew training that prepares new entrants—including youth and recent grads—for immediate, paid placements on local film and TV productions. Working with unions, colleges, and production companies, the program links training to real jobs, strengthens local hiring pipelines, and demonstrates clear, homegrown career pathways in the creative screen sector.
resources.address: 1800 Argyle Street, Suite 802, Halifax, NS B3J 3N8

solutions.text: Time-Banking and Skill-Share for Cultural Workers: A local time-bank where artists trade skills (e.g., web design for poster printing) and volunteers donate hours to events, reducing costs and strengthening community reciprocity around cultural production.

resources.name: AFCOOP Co-op Credits (Volunteer Program)
resources.description: Atlantic Filmmakers Cooperative (AFCOOP) runs a volunteer credit system where members earn “Co-op Credits” by donating time to productions, workshops, and events, which can be redeemed for discounted equipment rentals, post-production access, and training. This effectively time-banks labour and skills within the film community and enables artists to trade expertise (e.g., crew work or workshop facilitation) for tangible production resources, reducing costs and strengthening peer-to-peer reciprocity.
resources.address: 5663 Nora Bernard Street, Suite 101, Halifax, NS B3K 1B6

resources.name: Halifax Tool Library
resources.description: The Halifax Tool Library provides shared access to tools and offers member-led workshops, enabling artists and cultural workers to develop and exchange practical skills for set-building, installations, and fabrication. Members can offset fees through volunteer shifts and teaching, creating a time-banking dynamic where labour and knowledge translate into access to equipment and training—reducing project costs and fostering community reciprocity.

resources.name: Radstorm Halifax
resources.description: Radstorm is a collectively run arts space (including music venue and screen-print studio) where members exchange volunteer hours for access to facilities, training, and events. Through regular skill-shares and collaborative projects (e.g., trading web help for print access or event support), artists time-bank their labour to reduce production costs and build a reciprocal, peer-supported cultural ecosystem.

resources.name: The Deanery Project
resources.description: The Deanery Project hosts community arts workshops, residencies, and maker activities where participants frequently exchange volunteer time for discounted access and share skills in areas like printmaking, natural dyes, woodworking, and event production. This work-trade and skill-sharing model functions as a local time-bank, lowering barriers for cultural producers and strengthening rural creative networks in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

obstacles.title: Rural service erosion and community capacity constraints
obstacles.description: Aging populations, volunteer burnout, and loss of local services reduce vibrancy and make it harder for young people to stay in or move to smaller communities.

solutions.text: Community Volunteer Hub: Create a local volunteer coordination hub (physical or online) that matches volunteers to short- and long-term opportunities, manages schedules to avoid burnout, and offers onboarding and recognition to sustain engagement.

resources.name: Volunteer Nova Scotia
resources.organization: Community Sector Council of Nova Scotia (CSCNS)
resources.description: Volunteer Nova Scotia is a province-wide online hub that connects individuals with short- and long-term volunteer opportunities across communities and sectors in Nova Scotia. The platform helps organizations post roles, match with interested volunteers, and use built-in tools for scheduling and communications, supporting better workload balance and reducing burnout. It also provides resources for onboarding and recognition, helping groups welcome, train, and retain volunteers.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 201, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries Volunteer Program
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries operates a coordinated volunteer program across multiple branches, matching volunteers to roles like programming support, homework help, English conversation groups, and events. Staff manage schedules and shift rotations to balance commitments, and provide orientation, training, and ongoing supervision so volunteers are set up for success. The system includes regular recognition and appreciation activities to sustain engagement over time.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: QEII Health Sciences Centre Volunteer Services
resources.description: QEII’s Volunteer Services matches community members to a range of hospital-based opportunities—such as patient support, information desks, and wayfinding—based on interests, availability, and skills. The program handles screening, onboarding, and training, and uses shift scheduling to balance time commitments and prevent volunteer burnout. Volunteers are recognized through appreciation events and ongoing support to encourage long-term engagement.
resources.address: 1276 South Park Street, Halifax, NS B3H 2Y9

resources.name: Feed Nova Scotia Volunteer Program
resources.description: Feed Nova Scotia coordinates volunteers for warehouse operations, deliveries, special events, and office support, matching people to short- and long-term roles that fit their schedules. The team provides safety orientation and role-specific training, and uses scheduling tools to distribute shifts fairly and reduce burnout. Regular recognition and appreciation help retain volunteers and sustain a reliable community-wide support network.

solutions.text: Intergenerational Mentorship Programs: Pair older residents with young people for skills transfer (trades, crafts, storytelling) and companionship, creating purposeful roles for seniors while giving youth real-world learning and community ties.

resources.name: 4-H Nova Scotia
resources.description: Across rural Nova Scotia, adult volunteer leaders—often older farmers, tradespeople, and crafts mentors—guide youth ages 7–21 through 4-H clubs. Weekly meetings and project work in agriculture, woodworking, sewing, mechanics, public speaking, and community service create sustained, intergenerational mentorship and companionship. This hands-on skills transfer helps young people build confidence and roots in their communities.
resources.address: 60 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

resources.name: Youth Program
resources.description: MNFC’s Youth Program connects Indigenous youth with Elders and Knowledge Keepers for cultural mentorship in Mi’kmaw language, drumming, crafting, and land-based learning. Regular circles, storytelling, and workshops create meaningful relationships where older community members pass on skills, teachings, and support. The intergenerational approach strengthens identity and community ties that help youth thrive in Halifax and beyond.

resources.name: The Deanery Project
resources.description: The Deanery Project hosts intergenerational workshops and community build projects in sustainable building, woodworking, boatbuilding, fibre arts, and music. Retired tradespeople, artisans, and knowledge holders mentor youth and students through hands-on projects and storytelling events, transferring practical skills and local knowledge. These relationships foster belonging and create purposeful roles for seniors while giving young people real-world learning in a rural setting.
resources.address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

resources.name: Intergenerational Programs
resources.description: Northwood’s intergenerational programs bring seniors in long-term care together with local students and youth volunteers for shared activities like reading circles, arts and crafts, music, gardening, and technology help. Residents share life experience, stories, and practical skills with young people in recurring visits that build companionship and mutual learning. The model creates purposeful engagement for older adults while strengthening youth connections to community.

resources.name: Community Kitchen & Garden
resources.description: The North Grove’s Community Kitchen & Garden intentionally brings seniors and youth together to cook, preserve food, garden, and share stories. Experienced older volunteers mentor young participants in practical food and life skills while youth reciprocate with tech help and community projects. These sustained, hands-on sessions create intergenerational bonds and real-world learning that supports community resilience in Dartmouth North.

solutions.text: Time-Banking and Skill-Swap Networks: Launch a community time-bank where residents trade hours of service (childcare, gardening, IT help), building mutual support without financial strain and reducing reliance on volunteers doing repeated unpaid tasks.

resources.name: Halifax Tool Library
resources.description: A community-run lending library for tools that also hosts repair cafés and peer-led workshops where members trade time and skills (e.g., sharpening, bike repair, basic carpentry). Members can contribute volunteer hours to staff shifts or teach skills in exchange for borrowing privileges and learning from others, creating a practical, hour-for-hour skill-swap network that lowers costs and spreads effort across many participants.

resources.name: Library of Things and Community Skill-Share & Repair Programs
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries facilitates community-led skill-shares and recurring fix-it/repair events where residents offer and receive help repairing household items, learning digital skills, or sharing childcare and gardening tips in workshop formats. By encouraging participants to return as volunteer mentors or event helpers, the library helps build a time-based reciprocity loop that reduces financial barriers and distributes the workload across a broad network of neighbours.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Community Repair Cafés and Skill-Swap Events
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre partners with local groups to run repair cafés and hands-on skill-sharing sessions where community members exchange time and know-how to fix clothing, appliances, and bikes, and to learn maintenance skills. These events foster a mutual-aid network that mirrors time-banking principles—participants contribute volunteer hours as hosts or fixers and, in turn, receive help and training—reducing costs and preventing burnout among a small core of volunteers.

solutions.text: Shared-Service Cooperatives: Form cooperatives to jointly operate essential services (grocery, laundry, childcare, transportation) so costs and responsibilities are distributed across members, keeping services locally available.

resources.name: MusGo Rider Cooperative Ltd.
resources.description: MusGo Rider is a community-owned rural transportation cooperative that provides door-to-door rides for residents along Nova Scotia’s Eastern Shore, sharing costs and governance among member-users. By pooling vehicles, dispatch, and volunteer/paid driver capacity, the co-op keeps essential transportation locally available for work, medical appointments, shopping, and social needs—directly addressing rural service erosion and enabling people (including youth and families) to live and work in their communities.

resources.name: Truro Farmers’ Market Cooperative
resources.description: The Truro Farmers’ Market is a vendor-owned cooperative that jointly operates year-round access to groceries and essentials from local producers. By sharing facility costs, marketing, scheduling, and governance among member vendors, the co-op sustains a reliable, community-rooted food service in a regional hub—keeping healthy, affordable food nearby and supporting young and established entrepreneurs in rural Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Antigonish Farmers’ Market Co-operative
resources.description: The Antigonish Farmers’ Market is a co-operative that brings together dozens of food and craft producers to operate a shared retail marketplace for local groceries and household essentials. Members collectively manage space, operations, and outreach, lowering costs and stabilizing access to fresh food for the town and surrounding rural areas—helping maintain local services and create opportunities that encourage young people to stay or return.

solutions.text: Microgrants for Local Initiatives: Establish small, accessible community microgrants to seed youth-led projects, pop-up services, or volunteer relief efforts, lowering barriers for new ideas and encouraging young people to lead.

resources.name: Community Health Boards Wellness Funds
resources.description: Nova Scotia Health’s Community Health Boards award small, accessible grants (often in the $1,000–$10,000 range) to seed local projects that improve community well-being. Funds frequently support youth-led initiatives, pop-up programs, and volunteer-driven activities across rural and urban communities, lowering barriers for first-time applicants and strengthening local capacity where services are limited.
resources.address: 90 Lovett Lake Court, Halifax, NS B3S 0H6

resources.name: Neighbourhood Grants
resources.description: United Way Halifax provides microgrants to resident- and youth-led projects that build connection and well-being in local communities, from pop-up events and mini-programs to mutual-aid and volunteer initiatives. The streamlined application and coaching support reduce barriers so young people and grassroots groups can test new ideas and strengthen neighbourhood vibrancy.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Grants
resources.description: This program includes a micro-grants stream that funds quick, low-cost placemaking and public art projects, enabling youth and community members to launch pop-ups, activations, and small-scale improvements in public spaces. By covering materials and modest stipends with a light application process, it lowers barriers for new ideas and supports volunteer-led efforts to animate downtown.

solutions.text: Flexible and Micro-Volunteering Opportunities: Design volunteer roles that fit varied schedules and energy levels (one-off events, seasonal tasks, micro-shifts) to attract younger people and prevent burnout among long-term volunteers.

resources.name: Warehouse and Events Volunteer Program
resources.description: Feed Nova Scotia offers flexible 2–3 hour ‘sort and pack’ warehouse shifts and one-off event roles that volunteers can book as their schedules allow. Seasonal campaigns (like holiday hamper packing and food drives) add short-term opportunities that attract students and young professionals, spreading tasks across many helpers to reduce burnout among core, long-term volunteers.

resources.name: ReStore and Build-Day Volunteers
resources.description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia provides micro-shifts at the ReStore (merchandising, customer service, donations sorting) that can be scheduled in short blocks, as well as one-day ‘build’ and event roles. This mix of drop-in friendly and seasonal tasks accommodates varied energy levels and schedules, engaging younger volunteers and preventing burnout by rotating responsibilities.

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries Volunteer Program
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries offers flexible, low-commitment roles such as event support, one-time tech help pop-ups, and short-term projects (e.g., book sale setup and community program assistance). Teen and adult opportunities are designed with micro-shifts and seasonal commitments, making it easy for busy or first-time volunteers to contribute without long-term pressure.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Community Meals and Urban Garden Volunteer Program
resources.description: The North Grove schedules short kitchen shifts for community meals and seasonal garden ‘work parties’ that volunteers can join as available. These micro-volunteering and drop-in style roles lower barriers for youth and working families, distributing tasks across many people to support continuity and reduce strain on long-time volunteers.

resources.name: Action Teams and Event-Day Volunteers
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre organizes one-off environmental actions—such as shoreline cleanups, tree plantings, citizen-science counts, and event-day support—often in 1–3 hour blocks. These bite-sized, seasonal opportunities are designed for flexible participation, engaging younger volunteers while distributing workloads to avoid burnout among core organizers.

solutions.text: Community Skills and Entrepreneurship Workshops: Offer regular local workshops on business basics, digital skills, grant writing, and trades entrepreneurship to help young people start local enterprises and to upskill residents to run community services.

resources.name: CEED Workshops & Training
resources.organization: Centre for Entrepreneurship Education and Development (CEED)
resources.description: CEED delivers regular, practical workshops on starting and growing a business—covering business planning, bookkeeping, pricing, marketing, and digital tools—alongside youth-focused entrepreneurship programs. By bringing hands-on training and mentorship to aspiring and existing entrepreneurs across Nova Scotia, CEED helps young people launch local enterprises and equips residents with skills to operate and sustain community services.

resources.name: Community Entrepreneurship Training & Workshops
resources.description: Acadia Entrepreneurship Centre offers community-based entrepreneurship training and advisory workshops for entrepreneurs, nonprofits, and social enterprises, including business planning, financial management, marketing, and grant-writing. Working with municipalities and rural groups across the Annapolis Valley and beyond, AEC builds local capacity so youth and residents can create and grow community-serving ventures and essential services.

resources.name: Navigate Startup House Programs & Workshops
resources.organization: Navigate Startup Ecosystem (Cape Breton Partnership & Cape Breton University)
resources.description: Navigate hosts free and low-cost startup workshops, lunch-and-learns, mentorship sessions, and digital skills events for entrepreneurs in Cape Breton. Its programming helps youth and community members validate ideas, learn business fundamentals, and access tools to start enterprises that fill local service gaps and strengthen rural communities.

resources.name: Training & Development Programs
resources.organization: Centre for Women in Business, Mount Saint Vincent University
resources.description: The Centre for Women in Business provides ongoing training and development workshops—business fundamentals, digital marketing, financials, exporting, and leadership—tailored to women and gender-diverse entrepreneurs, including those in rural Nova Scotia. These sessions build practical skills, confidence, and networks to launch or expand community-focused enterprises and services that keep local economies vibrant.
resources.address: 166 Bedford Highway, 3rd Floor, McCain Centre, Halifax, NS B3M 2J6

resources.name: Business Development Workshops
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS offers recurring workshops on starting a business in Nova Scotia, business planning, market research, financial literacy, and using digital platforms, designed for newcomers and youth. By providing step-by-step training, coaching, and connections to funding and supports, ISANS enables residents to launch local businesses and social enterprises that enhance community services in both urban and rural areas.

solutions.text: Local Youth Advisory Councils: Create youth councils that advise the municipality and community organizations, give young people decision-making power, and develop projects that respond to their needs and attract peers to stay or return.

resources.name: Halifax Youth Advisory Committee (HYAC)
resources.description: HYAC is a formal advisory committee of Halifax Regional Council that brings youth perspectives into municipal decision-making on policies, programs, and services that affect young people. Members identify priorities, recommend actions to Council and staff, and collaborate on youth-led initiatives—strengthening civic engagement and helping make HRM more attractive for youth to stay or return.

resources.name: Bridgewater Youth Action Council (YAC)
resources.description: YAC is a youth-led council supported by the Town of Bridgewater that advises municipal staff and Council on youth issues and leads community projects and events. Members co-design local initiatives, inform municipal planning for youth-friendly spaces and services, and champion projects that build community capacity and encourage young people to remain in or return to Bridgewater.

resources.name: Mayor’s Youth Advisory Committee (MYAC) – Town of Yarmouth
resources.description: MYAC convenes local youth to provide direct advice to the Mayor and Town Council on decisions and priorities that impact young residents. Through regular meetings and youth-driven projects, MYAC elevates youth voices in municipal policy and programming and creates opportunities and activities that help young people feel welcomed and invested in staying in Yarmouth.

resources.name: Teen Advisory Groups (TAG)
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries’ Teen Advisory Groups give youth a structured voice to shape library programs, services, and spaces across branches. Participants co-create events, advise on collections and policies relevant to teens, and lead volunteer initiatives—demonstrating how a community organization uses a youth council model to increase youth decision-making and strengthen local engagement.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

solutions.text: Succession Planning for Community Organizations: Encourage clubs and nonprofits to document roles, create co-lead positions, and train successors to avoid service gaps when volunteers retire and to welcome younger leaders into governance.

resources.name: Club Development and Governance Workshops
resources.description: Sport Nova Scotia provides training and advisory support to community sport clubs on board governance, volunteer management, and succession planning. Workshops and templates help clubs document executive roles, adopt co-coach or co-chair models, and build onboarding plans so new and younger volunteers can step into leadership without service gaps.
resources.address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

resources.name: Volunteer Leadership and Board Development
resources.description: Recreation Nova Scotia supports volunteer-led recreation groups and nonprofits with training on board roles, governance policies, and succession planning. Their resources and sessions guide organizations to formalize role descriptions, create co-lead or co-chair positions, and mentor new leaders—especially youth—so organizations remain strong as long-time volunteers retire.
resources.address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

resources.name: Club Executive Training and Leaders-in-Training (LIT)
resources.description: 4-H Nova Scotia equips youth-run clubs across rural communities with structured officer training, clear executive role descriptions, and adult-youth co-leadership. Annual officer and LIT training prepares successors for roles like president, treasurer, and project leader, ensuring smooth transitions and welcoming younger members into governance as older volunteers step back.
resources.address: 90 Research Drive, Suite 122, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

solutions.text: Community Transport Solutions: Coordinate community-run ride-shares, pooled taxis, or volunteer driver programs to address mobility for seniors and youth, improving access to jobs, services, and social opportunities.

resources.name: BayRides Community Transit
resources.description: BayRides is a community-run, door-to-door transit service that coordinates shared rides for residents of St. Margarets Bay and surrounding rural communities. By pooling trips and scheduling pick-ups in advance, it increases mobility for seniors and youth to reach jobs, school, healthcare, and social activities, directly addressing gaps where fixed-route transit is limited.
resources.address: 5288 St. Margarets Bay Road, Upper Tantallon, NS B3Z 2H5

resources.name: MusGo Rider Eastern Shore
resources.description: MusGo Rider Eastern Shore is a community transportation co-operative offering pre-booked, shared rides and door-to-door service across the Eastern Shore. Using a volunteer-driven, community-governed model, it pools trips for seniors, youth, and workers to improve access to employment, healthcare, education, and community life in areas with limited public transit.

resources.name: Kings Point-to-Point Transit
resources.description: Kings Point-to-Point Transit provides demand-responsive, shared rides throughout Kings County, coordinating trips so multiple passengers can travel together to work, school, medical appointments, and community services. The non-profit model supports seniors and youth in rural areas by filling service gaps with affordable, community-based transportation.
resources.address: 14 Crescent Drive, New Minas, NS B4N 3G7

solutions.text: Shared Workspaces and Remote Work Support: Develop affordable co-working hubs with reliable internet, meeting rooms, and business support to retain and attract remote workers and young entrepreneurs to the community.

resources.name: The HUB South Shore
resources.description: The HUB South Shore is a community coworking space offering affordable desks, meeting rooms, and reliable high-speed internet for freelancers, remote workers, and startups. It hosts events, peer meetups, and mentorship opportunities that connect entrepreneurs with local resources and networks. By reducing overhead and providing business supports in Bridgewater, it helps retain and attract young professionals to the South Shore.

resources.name: WorkEvolved Antigonish
resources.description: WorkEvolved provides flexible coworking memberships, private offices, and bookable meeting rooms with fast internet for remote workers and entrepreneurs in northeastern Nova Scotia. It offers programming such as workshops, networking, and business support connections that help founders grow locally. The space enables young professionals to live and work in Antigonish while accessing professional infrastructure and community.

resources.name: COVE (Centre for Ocean Ventures & Entrepreneurship)
resources.description: COVE operates a collaborative waterfront campus with shared offices, coworking areas, labs, and meeting facilities supported by robust internet connectivity for ocean-tech companies and remote teams. It delivers business supports—mentorship, workshops, and industry networking—that help startups and mobile professionals build careers in Nova Scotia’s blue economy. This shared workspace model anchors talent in the region by pairing infrastructure with community and commercialization support.

resources.name: The Commons Halifax
resources.description: The Commons is a flexible coworking hub with hot desks, private offices, meeting rooms, and 24/7 access backed by reliable high-speed internet. It supports a diverse community of freelancers, remote workers, and early-stage entrepreneurs through events, peer networks, and business resources. By lowering barriers to professional space and connection, it helps young people establish and grow their work lives in Nova Scotia.

solutions.text: Pop-up and Mobile Services: Organize rotating pop-up clinics, markets, library stands, and professional services using community spaces or mobile units to keep services accessible while longer-term solutions are developed.

resources.name: Mobile Primary Care Clinics
resources.description: Nova Scotia Health operates rotating pop-up primary care clinics that set up in community spaces across the province to provide same-day care, prescriptions, and referrals for people without timely access to a family practitioner. These mobile clinics bring services to rural and underserviced areas, maintaining access while longer-term primary care solutions are developed.
resources.address: 1276 South Park Street, Halifax, NS B3H 2Y9

resources.name: Mobile Outreach Street Health (MOSH)
resources.description: MOSH is a mobile health service that travels by van and sets up pop-up clinics in shelters, encampments, and community hubs to deliver primary care, nursing, harm reduction, and social supports to people facing barriers to traditional care. By bringing professionals directly into neighborhoods, MOSH keeps essential services accessible and responsive while broader community health infrastructure is strengthened.

resources.name: Pop-Up Library and Community Outreach
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries runs pop-up library stands at community centres, markets, shelters, and rural gathering places, offering on-the-spot library cards, book borrowing, Wi‑Fi hotspots, and program sign-ups. These mobile and temporary setups keep cultural, learning, and digital services within reach for communities experiencing service erosion, helping residents—especially youth—stay connected.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Pop-Up Library Outreach
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Library deploys pop-up libraries at festivals, community halls, and rural hubs across the island, providing borrowing, library cards, program registration, and digital literacy support. This mobile outreach model sustains access to information and services in smaller communities, complementing branch services and reducing travel barriers.

solutions.text: Local Hiring and Youth Apprenticeships: Partner businesses and community organizations to create paid local apprenticeships, internships, and entry-level positions for youth, linking training to local job pathways.

resources.name: Clean Leadership Summer Internship Program
resources.description: Clean Foundation’s Clean Leadership program places high school, college, and university-age youth in paid summer internships with municipalities, Indigenous communities, nonprofits, and local businesses across Nova Scotia. The program provides training and mentorship and partners directly with local host organizations so interns build skills and transition into environmental and clean-economy job pathways in their home communities.

resources.name: Pathways to Shipbuilding
resources.description: Pathways to Shipbuilding recruits and trains cohorts of youth from underrepresented communities to enter marine trades through NSCC classroom learning linked to paid, entry-level positions and Red Seal apprenticeships at the Halifax Shipyard. The initiative is a partnership among Irving Shipbuilding, Nova Scotia Community College, and community organizations, ensuring training directly feeds into local, long-term careers in Nova Scotia’s shipbuilding sector.

resources.name: NSCC Co-operative Education and Work-Integrated Learning
resources.description: Nova Scotia Community College coordinates paid co-ops, practicums, and apprenticeship-aligned work experiences with employers in communities across the province. By matching students in trades, IT, business, health, and community services with local businesses, municipalities, and nonprofits, NSCC links education to clear local job pathways that often lead to ongoing employment where students study and live.

resources.name: Acadia Co-operative Education Program
resources.description: Acadia’s Co-op program partners with employers throughout Nova Scotia to create paid, discipline-related work terms for undergraduate students in fields such as business, computer science, community development, and the sciences. Students receive job-readiness training and are placed with local businesses and organizations—including in rural towns—so that work terms build experience and frequently convert into permanent roles in the region.
