solutions.text: Cultural Venue Cooperative Ownership: Support cooperative ownership models where local artists, audiences, and businesses buy membership shares to collectively own and run small performance venues or galleries, ensuring democratic governance and affordable programming.

resources.name: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op is a member-owned performing arts venue where artists, audiences, and local businesses buy memberships/shares to collectively own and democratically govern a black-box theatre. The co-op acquired and operates its building, keeping rental rates and technical support affordable for independent producers, festivals, and emerging artists, and programming is shaped by member vote and community needs. This cooperative ownership stabilizes cultural space on the Halifax Peninsula and ensures accessible, year-round performance opportunities.

resources.name: Acadia Cinema Cooperative – Al Whittle Theatre
resources.description: Formed by community members, students, artists, and local businesses, the Acadia Cinema Cooperative Ltd. raised community shares to purchase and operate the historic Al Whittle Theatre in downtown Wolfville. As a co-op with one-member-one-vote governance, it collectively runs a small cinema and performance venue, offering affordable rentals and community-driven film, music, theatre, and arts programming. This cooperative ownership model preserves cultural infrastructure while keeping access and prices within reach for local creators and audiences.

resources.name: ViewPoint Gallery Photography Cooperative
resources.description: ViewPoint Gallery is a member-owned photographers’ cooperative that collectively operates a dedicated exhibition space in Halifax. Artist-members purchase memberships, share governance and staffing, and set policies that keep exhibition fees and public events—talks, openings, portfolio reviews—affordable and community-focused. The co-op model ensures democratic control of the gallery and sustains an accessible cultural venue for both creators and audiences.

resources.name: ART1274 Hollis Cooperative Gallery
resources.description: ART1274 Hollis is an artist-run cooperative where member artists collectively own and govern the gallery operation, sharing costs and decisions to maintain an accessible exhibition venue in downtown Halifax. Through its co-op structure, members curate shows, staff the space, and offer workshops and events at community-friendly prices, ensuring affordable cultural programming and sustainable gallery space for local creators. Supporters and patrons engage directly with the co-op, reinforcing a community-rooted model for cultural venue stewardship.

solutions.text: Pop-Up Festivals and Night Markets: Organize regular, low-cost pop-up festivals and night markets that prioritize local musicians, makers, and food vendors. Use public parks, waterfronts, and closed streets to create recurring opportunities for creatives to earn income and build audiences.

resources.name: Kentville Night Market
resources.description: The Town of Kentville runs a recurring summer Night Market series that animates Centre Square and nearby closed streets with Nova Scotian artisans, food trucks, and live music. By activating public space in the evening with affordable vendor fees and performance slots, the market creates low-barrier, pop-up earning opportunities for local makers and musicians while helping them build audiences.

resources.name: New Glasgow Riverfront Night Market
resources.organization: Glasgow Square Theatre (Town of New Glasgow)
resources.description: Hosted along the waterfront at Glasgow Square, this recurring evening market features dozens of local makers, food vendors, and live music. It transforms public riverfront space into a low-cost pop-up venue, giving creative entrepreneurs and musicians consistent opportunities to earn income and reach new audiences in northern Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 155 Riverside Parkway, New Glasgow, NS B2H 5E8

resources.name: Wolfville Farmers’ Market: Night Markets
resources.description: The Wolfville Farmers’ Market periodically hosts Night Markets and after-hours pop-ups that turn the market hall and outdoor space into an evening showcase of local food, craft, and live music. These events offer affordable tables for vendors and programmed performance slots, creating recurring opportunities for creatives to generate income and grow their followings.

resources.name: Lunenburg Night Market
resources.description: This summertime evening street market brings together local artists, makers, food vendors, and performers along Lunenburg’s historic waterfront and downtown streets. Organized with the business community, the series closes streets to traffic and provides affordable vendor space, creating pop-up opportunities for creatives to sell their work and perform for residents and visitors.
resources.address: 11 Blockhouse Hill Road, Lunenburg, NS B0J 2C0

solutions.text: Business-Artist Partnership Program: Facilitate partnerships between local businesses and artists for storefront activations, commissioned public art, in-store performances, and event sponsorships. Offer incentives to businesses (promotion, recognition, tax guidance) to lower barriers to collaboration.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Grant Program
resources.description: Gritty to Pretty provides grants and coordination for murals, storefront/window art, public installations, and placemaking projects on or adjacent to local businesses in Downtown Halifax. The program actively matches property and business owners with artists, supports permitting and production, and promotes completed works, lowering barriers to collaboration while delivering high-visibility activations and commissions that benefit both businesses and artists.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 2A2

resources.name: Evergreen Festival
resources.description: Evergreen Festival is a multi-week winter celebration that animates business districts in Halifax with light installations, window displays, pop-up markets, and a program of live performances. The festival facilitates partnerships by placing artists in and around storefronts, coordinating sponsored stages and events with local businesses, and delivering extensive marketing and recognition that incentivize business participation while creating paid opportunities for artists.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 300, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Downtown Truro Mural Program
resources.description: The Downtown Truro Mural Program commissions and curates murals and public art installations on privately owned business facades, alleys, and public-facing walls in the downtown core. Downtown Truro Partnership facilitates calls for artists, coordinates with property and business owners, secures sponsorships, and promotes completed works—creating direct business-artist partnerships that activate storefronts and draw visitors to local shops and services.

resources.name: Public Art Program (Sydney Mural Project)
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design’s Public Art Program commissions murals and installations throughout downtown Sydney in collaboration with business and property owners. The Centre manages artist selection, contracting, and project delivery, and works with local partners to provide funding and promotion—enabling businesses to host commissioned public art that enhances storefronts, increases foot traffic, and creates paid opportunities for artists.

solutions.text: Placemaking and Public Art Projects: Develop a public art strategy with small-scale, community-led placemaking projects (murals, installations, performance stages) that improve public spaces, give artists paid work, and attract residents and visitors. Use community workshops to guide selections and ensure local relevance.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty Placemaking Program
resources.description: Run by the downtown business association, Gritty to Pretty provides grants to create murals, installations, lighting, and small-scale public realm improvements that animate streets and plazas. The program pays local artists and collaborates with property owners and community groups, using a juried process and community input to ensure projects reflect local culture and improve public spaces to attract residents and visitors.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 3X7

resources.name: Beautification and Placemaking Grant
resources.description: This grant supports community-led public art and placemaking projects in downtown Dartmouth, including murals, street installations, and enhancements to small public spaces. It commissions and pays artists while encouraging proposals from local businesses and community groups, with DDBC staff facilitating permissions and engagement so projects are locally relevant and help draw people to the area.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Public Art Program
resources.description: HRM’s Public Art Program commissions and supports temporary and permanent artworks in public spaces across the municipality, including murals, installations, and performance infrastructure. Through open calls, artist fees, and community consultation, the program ensures projects reflect local stories and Mi’kma’ki context while enhancing public spaces to increase vibrancy and visitation.

resources.name: Downtown Truro Public Art Program
resources.description: Downtown Truro Partnership coordinates murals, sculptures, and other public art projects that activate streetscapes and laneways in the town core. The initiative pays artists, partners with property owners and the municipality, and engages local stakeholders to select sites and themes, creating welcoming spaces that attract residents and visitors year-round.
resources.address: 605 Prince Street, Suite 203, Truro, NS B2N 1G2

solutions.text: Creative Skills and Mentorship Network: Build a volunteer-run network connecting established artists and tradespeople with emerging creatives for mentorship, portfolio reviews, and skills-sharing sessions (technical production, grant writing, marketing) to help young artists build sustainable careers.

resources.name: VANS Mentorship Program
resources.description: Visual Arts Nova Scotia pairs emerging visual artists with established professional artists for multi-month, one-on-one mentorships focused on portfolio development, critique, and career planning. The program also offers professional practice workshops and resources on grant writing, marketing, and exhibiting, creating a skills-sharing network that helps artists build sustainable careers in the province.

resources.name: Alistair MacLeod Mentorship Program
resources.description: The Writers’ Federation of Nova Scotia’s flagship mentorship pairs emerging writers with seasoned, award-winning authors for an intensive, months-long process of editorial feedback, career guidance, and industry navigation. Participants also access professional development on grant applications, networking, and marketing, connecting them to a province-wide community of mentors who volunteer expertise to support sustainable literary careers.

resources.name: Neptune Theatre Chrysalis Project
resources.description: Neptune’s Chrysalis Project supports early-career theatre artists by pairing them with experienced directors, designers, dramaturgs, and producers for mentorship, portfolio-building opportunities, and hands-on production experience. The program includes skills-sharing sessions on auditioning, producing, grant writing, and marketing, helping emerging creatives transition into sustainable professional practice in Nova Scotia’s performing arts sector.

resources.name: Playwrights Unit
resources.description: Eastern Front Theatre’s Playwrights Unit brings together emerging playwrights with established dramaturgs and theatre professionals for regular feedback, script development, and portfolio reviews. Participants take part in professional workshops covering topics like grant writing, producing, and marketing, building a mentorship network that connects new voices with the practical skills and relationships needed for long-term careers.

solutions.text: Local Digital Platform and Marketplace: Create a community-run online platform that lists local events, venues, artist profiles, opportunities, and sells digital tickets/works. Offer integrated promotion for member artists and a low-fee marketplace to expand audiences beyond the town and generate income.

resources.name: Shop Craft Nova Scotia (Online Store)
resources.organization: Craft Nova Scotia (Centre for Craft Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Craft Nova Scotia operates a member-based online marketplace that showcases Nova Scotian craft artists, featuring artisan profiles and selling their works directly through e-commerce. The platform also promotes exhibitions, markets, and learning opportunities, helping artists reach audiences beyond their local communities and generate income through digital sales.

resources.name: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design Online Store
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: This community-run platform features an online shop and artisan directory, highlighting Cape Breton craftspeople with artist profiles and selling their work to buyers locally and beyond. It integrates promotion through exhibitions, events, and training opportunities listed on the site, expanding audiences and creating revenue pathways for creative workers.

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co-op Events Calendar & Ticketing
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op maintains an online calendar and show pages for community-produced performances, with integrated links for digital ticket sales and artist/company information. As a cooperative, it promotes member artists and provides a centralized venue and digital presence that aggregates events and opportunities, helping creators market their work and reach wider audiences.

resources.name: Highland Arts Theatre Online Box Office
resources.description: Highland Arts Theatre runs a robust online platform listing shows, casts, and local creative talent, selling digital tickets and passes for year-round community productions. The site and its communications promote artists and events across Cape Breton, providing a digital marketplace and promotional hub that supports local performers and grows audiences.

resources.name: Argyle Fine Art Online Gallery & Shop
resources.description: Argyle Fine Art offers an online gallery with artist profiles and an e-commerce shop that sells works by Nova Scotia artists to buyers across Canada and beyond. Through curated exhibitions, event listings, newsletters, and social promotion, the platform provides integrated visibility and a digital sales channel that helps artists generate income outside in-person visits.

solutions.text: Policy Toolkit and Advocacy Coalition: Form a community advocacy coalition to work with municipal government on zoning flexibility for mixed-use artistic spaces, temporary-use permits for events, tax relief or incentives for cultural landlords, and inclusion of arts in economic development plans.

resources.name: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: An artist-run cooperative that operates a mixed-use performance venue and leads local advocacy for sustainable cultural space in Halifax’s North End. The co-op regularly collaborates with Halifax Regional Municipality (HRM) on planning consultations, zoning flexibility for artist-run spaces, and streamlined temporary-use permits for festivals and community events, while championing long-term policy tools and incentives that keep cultural landlords and venues viable. By convening artists, residents, and partners, it advances inclusion of arts infrastructure in municipal economic development and community plans.

resources.name: Music Nova Scotia – Industry Advocacy and Venue Coalition
resources.description: Music Nova Scotia convenes artists, venue operators, and promoters to advocate with municipal and provincial governments on policies that affect live music, including zoning and noise by-laws, all-ages access, and simplified temporary-use permitting for events. It advances measures that reduce costs and risk for cultural landlords and small venues (e.g., property and business tax considerations, regulatory clarity) and promotes the inclusion of music and the wider creative economy in economic development strategies across Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 2169 Gottingen Street, Suite 101, Halifax, NS B3K 3B5

resources.name: Screen Nova Scotia – Policy and Municipal Liaison Program
resources.description: Screen Nova Scotia represents the film, television, and digital media sector and works with municipalities (including HRM) on filming permits, location access, and zoning that enables adaptive reuse of warehouses and mixed-use spaces for studios and creative production. The association advocates for tax credits and incentives that anchor cultural landlords and screen-based businesses, and partners with economic development agencies to embed the screen sector within regional growth plans and workforce strategies that attract and retain young talent.
resources.address: 1800 Argyle Street, Suite 802, Halifax, NS B3J 3N8

resources.name: Eyelevel – Off-site and Temporary Use Program
resources.description: Eyelevel is an artist-run centre that programs exhibitions and events in non-traditional and vacant spaces, coordinating with landlords and HRM to secure temporary-use permits and short-term licenses that activate underused properties for the arts. Through these projects and policy consultations, Eyelevel demonstrates mixed-use models for cultural space, advocates for flexible zoning and low-barrier permitting, and contributes to municipal cultural planning that integrates the arts into neighbourhood revitalization and economic development.

solutions.text: Youth Arts Council and Grant Review Panel: Establish a youth-led arts council that advises on funding priorities, curates programs, and sits on grant review panels to ensure youth needs shape cultural offerings, create leadership pathways, and improve retention of young creatives.

resources.name: Halifax Central Library Teen Advisory Group (TAG)
resources.description: TAG is a youth-led council at Halifax Central Library that collaborates with staff to set priorities for teen arts and culture programming, plan events, and curate showcases such as zines, exhibitions, and open mics. Members advise how small program budgets are spent and take part in selection panels for teen-led displays and performances, ensuring that youth voices shape cultural offerings and build leadership pathways.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: FIN Kids Youth Jury
resources.description: Part of FIN Atlantic International Film Festival, the FIN Kids Youth Jury is composed of young people who watch, deliberate, and award films in the youth program, directly influencing which works are elevated and celebrated. By placing youth on adjudication panels and involving them in programming decisions, the initiative builds leadership experience and ensures festival content reflects youth interests and perspectives.

resources.name: Community Access Program (Venue Subsidy) Jury
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op’s Community Access Program provides in-kind grants (space subsidies) to community groups, with applications reviewed by a volunteer jury that includes artists and community members, often prioritizing youth-led and all-ages projects. Involving young creatives in selection and curation helps direct limited cultural resources (affordable venue time) toward youth needs while developing leadership and governance experience.

resources.name: Teen Arts Council
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: Ross Creek’s Teen Arts Council engages youth (typically ages 14–19) to co-design programming, curate youth-focused arts events, and advise staff on priorities that make the centre’s offerings more responsive to young people. Council members also help review proposals for youth showcases and initiatives, creating leadership pathways and ensuring that programming and limited resources reflect youth perspectives.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

obstacles.title: Climate Risks and Coastal Vulnerability
obstacles.description: Storms, sea-level rise, floods, and wildfires threaten homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods. Insurance costs and uncertainty deter investment and long-term settlement in vulnerable areas.

solutions.text: Living shorelines and salt-marsh restoration: Community-led projects to restore marshes, eelgrass beds, and create living shorelines that absorb wave energy and reduce erosion, protecting homes and fisheries while providing local stewardship and seasonal jobs.

resources.name: TransCoastal Adaptations: Living Shorelines Program
resources.organization: TransCoastal Adaptations: Centre for Nature-Based Solutions, Saint Mary’s University
resources.description: Based at Saint Mary’s University, TransCoastal Adaptations designs and delivers living shorelines and salt-marsh restoration projects at priority coastal sites across Nova Scotia. Working with municipalities, Mi’kmaq communities, and local volunteers, they install nature-based features (e.g., rock and coir log sills, native salt-marsh plantings, and tidal flow restoration) that absorb wave energy, curb erosion, and protect nearby homes and roads while training and hiring seasonal field crews for planting and monitoring.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Living Shoreline Project
resources.description: This project created a nature-based shoreline along Edgewater Street in Mahone Bay using offshore rock sills, coir logs, and native marsh and dune vegetation to dissipate waves, reduce erosion, and protect municipal roads and adjacent homes. Coastal Action engages local residents, schools, and volunteers in stewardship, and employs seasonal technicians to plant, maintain, and monitor the site, enhancing fish habitat and coastal resilience.
resources.address: 37 Tannery Road, Unit 2, Lunenburg, NS B0J 2C0

resources.name: Bras d’Or Lakes Eelgrass Restoration
resources.description: UINR partners with Mi’kmaq communities, fishers, and researchers to restore and transplant eelgrass beds in the Bras d’Or Lakes, stabilizing sediments, improving water quality, and providing nursery habitat for culturally and economically important fisheries like lobster. The program blends community science and hands-on restoration, engaging local volunteers and hiring Mi’kmaq youth as seasonal field staff for mapping, planting, and monitoring.

resources.name: Coastal Adaptation: Living Shorelines and Salt-Marsh Stewardship
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre supports community-led living shoreline designs and salt-marsh restoration across Nova Scotia, applying native plantings, biodegradable stabilization, and dune/marsh creation to absorb wave energy and reduce flooding and erosion. EAC mobilizes volunteers, provides training, and creates seasonal opportunities for youth to implement and monitor projects that protect homes and working waterfronts while enhancing fish and wildlife habitat.

resources.name: Saint Mary’s Boat Club Living Shoreline
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality replaced a deteriorating seawall at the Saint Mary’s Boat Club on the Northwest Arm with a living shoreline that uses rock sills, coir logs, and native salt-marsh vegetation to reduce wave energy, control erosion, and improve intertidal habitat. The site serves as a public demonstration of nature-based coastal protection and involves local stewardship and seasonal maintenance and monitoring activities.

solutions.text: Community flood mapping and risk communication: Volunteer-driven mapping of high-risk streets, basements and access routes combined with clear, locally distributed guidance so residents, prospective homebuyers and insurers understand true risk and adaptation options.

resources.name: Coastal Adaptation Program
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre’s Coastal Adaptation Program works with Nova Scotia communities to identify and map local flooding hotspots—such as repeatedly flooded streets, basements, and at-risk access routes—through resident walkabouts, surveys, and community mapping sessions. The program translates technical sea-level-rise and flood data into easy-to-read neighbourhood maps and distributes homeowner guides, insurance and retrofit checklists, and emergency route information online and in print so residents, prospective buyers, and insurers can understand location-specific risk and adaptation options.

resources.name: Stormwater and Coastal Flood Resilience Initiatives (including Adopt-A-Drain Lunenburg County)
resources.description: Coastal Action mobilizes volunteers to survey and map flooding hotspots across Lunenburg County—documenting flooded basements, blocked culverts, vulnerable streets, and critical access routes—through initiatives like Adopt‑A‑Drain and community flood‑watch activities. The organization compiles these observations into GIS layers and public story maps, and delivers workshops, flyers, and business/homeowner toolkits that explain localized flood risks, detour routes, and practical property-level adaptations that residents, realtors, and insurers can use to make informed decisions.

resources.name: Applied Geomatics Research Group (AGRG) – Coastal Flood Risk Mapping
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College – Centre of Geographic Sciences (COGS), Applied Geomatics Research Group
resources.description: NSCC’s AGRG collaborates with municipalities and communities across Nova Scotia to produce neighbourhood-scale coastal flood and storm-surge maps, integrating LiDAR and modelling with resident ground‑truthing (e.g., photo-logs and walkabouts of nuisance flooding on streets and basements). They co-create accessible map products, high‑water mark signage, and property‑owner guidance documents that are shared locally and online so homeowners, prospective buyers, and insurers can clearly understand true flood risk and available adaptation options.

resources.name: Flood Risk Mapping & Public Education
resources.description: The Town of Truro maintains Salmon River floodplain maps and an online viewer and augments them with resident-reported flooding hotspots gathered through public meetings and service requests to identify high‑risk streets, basements, and access routes. The Town provides printed and online homeowner guides, development checklists, and emergency detour information so residents, prospective homebuyers, and insurers can assess parcel‑level flood risk and understand mitigation and adaptation measures.

solutions.text: Neighborhood resilience hubs: Convert trusted local buildings (libraries, community centres, fire halls) into hubs with backup power, emergency supplies, WIFI and warming/cooling spaces to support residents during storms and to coordinate recovery.

resources.name: HRM Comfort Centres and Warming Centres
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality pre-identifies and equips trusted local buildings—such as community centres, libraries, and fire halls—to operate as Comfort Centres and Warming Centres during severe weather and extended outages. These hubs provide generator-backed power, WiFi and device charging, potable water, washrooms, and safe warming/cooling spaces, and are used to share situational updates and coordinate recovery with residents and partner agencies.

resources.name: Halifax Public Libraries – Libraries as Community Resilience Hubs
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries activates branches like Halifax Central Library and other generator-equipped locations as community resilience hubs during storms and outages. These libraries offer public WiFi, device charging, accessible washrooms, and safe warming/cooling spaces, and collaborate with HRM Emergency Management and community partners to share information, host briefings, and support supply distribution and recovery activities.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: CBRM Comfort Centres Network
resources.organization: Cape Breton Regional Municipality Emergency Management
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Municipality maintains a network of designated comfort centres in trusted local buildings such as community halls and volunteer fire stations, many with backup generators and connectivity. When activated for hurricanes, winter storms, or wildfires, these hubs provide heat/cooling, WiFi, device charging, basic supplies, and coordinated recovery information, managed through CBRM’s Emergency Management Office and community volunteers.

resources.name: Town of Lunenburg – Emergency Warming & Comfort Centre (Lunenburg Community Centre)
resources.description: The Town of Lunenburg designates the Lunenburg Community Centre as an emergency warming/comfort centre, leveraging backup power, public WiFi, showers, and kitchen facilities to support residents during storms and extended outages. Municipal staff and EMO partners use the site to provide safe warming/cooling spaces, device charging, and to coordinate information sharing and recovery assistance for the community.

solutions.text: Home retrofit and elevation co-op: A community co-op that helps pool labour, tool lending, group purchasing and technical advice for flood-proofing, elevating homes and installing sump pumps to lower repair costs and insurance claims.

resources.name: Halifax Tool Library
resources.description: A community tool-lending library that provides affordable access to tools and DIY training so residents can complete home flood-resilience projects such as improving drainage, sealing foundations, and installing/maintaining sump pumps and backwater valves. By sharing tools and skills, it pools community labour and reduces individual costs, enabling group work days and neighbour-to-neighbour assistance after flood events. This directly supports the co-op model of tool lending, collective effort, and practical technical advice for home retrofits.

resources.name: Stormwater Management and Rainscaping
resources.description: Coastal Action works with homeowners and communities on the South Shore to reduce overland flooding through site assessments, rain gardens, downspout reconfiguration, grading, and other lot-level measures. They coordinate volunteer work bees and bulk purchasing of materials and native plants, lowering costs for residents undertaking flood-proofing retrofits. Staff provide technical advice that helps households plan and implement practical measures like sump pump maintenance, backflow prevention, and elevating utilities above expected flood levels.

resources.name: Rainscaping and Stormwater Management
resources.description: Clean Annapolis River Project supports property-level flood resilience across the Annapolis Valley by advising on rain gardens, permeable landscaping, downspout disconnects, and other stormwater controls. They organize community volunteer builds and coordinate bulk buys of rain barrels and materials, pooling labour and purchasing power to reduce retrofit costs. Staff provide practical guidance to homeowners on sump pump use, drainage improvements, and protecting basements from infiltration, aligning with the co‑op style of shared effort and technical support.
resources.address: 314 St. George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

resources.name: Emergency Repair Program (ERP)
resources.organization: Housing Nova Scotia (Department of Municipal Affairs and Housing)
resources.description: Housing Nova Scotia’s ERP provides grants to low-income homeowners for urgent health and safety repairs, which can include foundation and drainage work, backwater valves, and sump pump installation or replacement to reduce flood damage risk. The program lowers out-of-pocket costs and can be combined with community volunteer labour or group purchasing to stretch funds further. By enabling critical flood-proofing retrofits, ERP directly reduces repair costs and future insurance claims for vulnerable households.

solutions.text: Community emergency response teams (CERT): Train local volunteers in search-and-rescue, first aid, sandbagging and incident coordination so neighbourhoods can respond faster during storms and wildfires while building social cohesion.

resources.name: Emergency Response Team (ERT) – Nova Scotia
resources.description: The Canadian Red Cross ERT program recruits and trains local volunteers across Nova Scotia in disaster response, including first aid, shelter/reception centre operations, logistics, and emergency social services. During floods, storms, and wildfires, ERT volunteers assist municipalities with sandbagging, evacuations, and incident coordination at community sites—accelerating on-the-ground response while strengthening neighbourhood ties through volunteer engagement and preparedness workshops.

resources.name: Joint Emergency Management (JEM) Program
resources.description: Halifax’s JEM program forms neighbourhood-based volunteer teams that receive training in emergency preparedness, comfort centre operations, damage assessment, wellness checks, and community-level coordination. These teams mobilize during severe storms and wildfires to support sandbagging, information sharing, and incident coordination alongside Halifax Regional Fire & Emergency—providing CERT-style capacity that speeds local response and builds social cohesion.

resources.name: Medical First Responder (MFR) – Nova Scotia
resources.organization: St. John Ambulance Nova Scotia/Prince Edward Island Council
resources.description: St. John Ambulance’s MFR program trains community volunteers in advanced first aid, patient assessment, and incident support, and deploys units to assist during emergencies, evacuations, and reception centre operations. In severe weather and wildfire events, MFR volunteers integrate with municipal emergency management to provide on-site first aid, triage, and support for evacuees—complementing local CERT-style efforts and reinforcing community resilience.
resources.address: 72 Highfield Park Drive, Dartmouth, NS B3A 4X2

solutions.text: Community land trust for safe, affordable housing: Acquire and hold land on higher ground to develop permanently affordable, climate-resilient housing that keeps young families local and reduces pressure to occupy high-risk coastal properties.

resources.name: Affordable Homeownership Program
resources.description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia acquires land and builds energy-efficient starter homes, then stewards long-term affordability through zero- or low-interest mortgages and resale/affordability covenants. By selecting sites away from flood- and storm-surge zones and building to modern efficiency standards, the program creates climate-resilient, permanently affordable homes that help young families remain in their communities instead of seeking housing on more vulnerable coastal properties.
resources.address: 81 Wright Avenue, Unit 12, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1H4

resources.name: New Dawn Rental Properties
resources.description: New Dawn Enterprises acquires, develops, and holds residential properties in Cape Breton as community assets, keeping them off the speculative market and maintaining below-market rents over the long term. Projects are sited inland and incorporate efficiency upgrades to reduce climate risks and operating costs, providing stable, affordable, and resilient housing that helps young workers and families stay local and avoid pressure to occupy high‑risk coastal areas.

solutions.text: Green jobs and trades training in climate adaptation: Local apprenticeship and short-course programs (shoreline restoration, resilient construction, wildfire mitigation, renewable energy) to equip young people with in-demand skills and anchor work locally.

resources.name: Clean Leadership Internship Program
resources.description: Clean Leadership provides paid summer and year-round internships that place Nova Scotia youth (ages 15–30) with host employers to work on climate adaptation and clean economy projects. Interns receive training, mentorship, and certifications while contributing to shoreline restoration, stormwater management, wildfire preparedness planning, and energy-efficiency/renewable energy projects across the province—building practical, in-demand skills and connecting them to local employers.

resources.name: Trade Network and Energy Advisor Training
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia recruits, trains, and supports Energy Advisors and trade contractors through short courses, NRCan exam preparation, and ongoing professional development focused on energy-efficient and resilient building upgrades (insulation, air sealing, heat pumps, and building envelope improvements). By connecting trainees to its province-wide contractor network and rebate programs, it anchors steady local work in retrofits and new builds that lower emissions and improve climate resilience.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Energy Sustainability Engineering Technology (ESET)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) – Ivany Campus
resources.description: NSCC’s ESET diploma trains technologists in renewable energy systems, energy auditing, and sustainable design, with hands-on labs and co-op placements that connect students to Nova Scotian employers. Graduates gain practical skills for solar PV, wind, and energy-efficiency projects that support climate adaptation and resilience in buildings and infrastructure, and NSCC also offers related short courses and microcredentials through Continuing Education to quickly upskill tradespeople.

resources.name: Unama’ki Guardian Program
resources.description: UINR’s Guardian Program trains Mi’kmaq youth and community members in environmental monitoring and habitat restoration, including shoreline and stream restoration, invasive species control, and coastal resilience projects throughout Cape Breton (Unama’ki). Participants receive field certifications and practical experience that translate to local jobs in conservation, climate adaptation, and land stewardship, and collaborate with provincial partners on wildfire awareness and community preparedness.

resources.name: CHBA Net Zero Builder and Renovator Training (delivered by NSHBA)
resources.description: NSHBA delivers short courses and certifications such as CHBA Net Zero Builder/Renovator training, building science, and code-compliance workshops that equip carpenters, electricians, and renovators to construct resilient, low-energy homes. These credentials align with Nova Scotia’s climate goals by preparing local trades to implement deep-energy retrofits, high-performance envelopes, and heat pump-ready systems—creating steady, in-demand green jobs across the province.
resources.address: 124 Chain Lake Drive, Halifax, NS B3S 1A2

solutions.text: Community-owned microgrids and resilient energy: Install community solar, battery storage and microgrids to keep critical services running during outages, reduce recovery costs, and make neighbourhoods more attractive to residents and businesses.

resources.name: Smart Grid Nova Scotia
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s Smart Grid Nova Scotia is an ongoing initiative that deploys distributed energy resources like residential batteries, smart thermostats, EV chargers, and controllable water heaters to create a virtual power plant. By aggregating customer-sited storage and solar, the program improves grid resilience during storms, supports critical loads by shortening outages and smoothing restoration, and lowers recovery costs—making communities more attractive for residents and businesses.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Antigonish Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Antigonish Electric Utility (with Alternative Resource Energy Authority)
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish Electric Utility, working with the Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA), operates a community solar garden that lets residents and businesses subscribe to locally generated solar power. As community-owned generation on a locally managed distribution grid, it strengthens energy resilience, can be paired with battery storage to keep essential services powered in outages, and stabilizes energy costs, helping attract and retain people and employers.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility (with Alternative Resource Energy Authority)
resources.description: Mahone Bay’s municipal electric utility, in partnership with AREA, operates a subscriber-based community solar garden that feeds clean power into the town’s locally owned grid. This community-owned resource reduces reliance on distant infrastructure, can integrate with battery storage and smart controls to keep priority facilities running during storms, and enhances local energy self-reliance—supporting quality of life and economic vitality.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Berwick Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Berwick Electric Commission (with Alternative Resource Energy Authority)
resources.description: The Berwick Electric Commission, collaborating with AREA, delivers a community solar garden that residents and businesses can subscribe to through the local municipal utility. By producing power close to where it’s used and enabling future coupling with battery storage and microgrid controls, the project improves outage resilience for municipal services and the wider community while lowering long-term energy costs and enhancing the town’s appeal.

solutions.text: Community insurance pools and group purchasing: Organize voluntary local insurance or re-insurance pools and negotiate group rates with insurers to lower premiums and create clearer claims processes for small communities.

resources.name: Halifax Water – Service Line Warranties of Canada Program
resources.organization: Halifax Water (in partnership with Service Line Warranties of Canada)
resources.description: Halifax Water partners with Service Line Warranties of Canada (SLWC) to offer optional water and sewer service line repair and interior plumbing protection plans to Halifax homeowners at negotiated group rates. This municipal-led group purchasing arrangement pools local demand to secure lower premiums and standardizes claims handling through SLWC, giving residents a clear, 24/7 claims process for breaks and failures often exacerbated by climate-related freeze/thaw cycles and flooding.
resources.address: 450 Cowie Hill Road, Halifax, NS B3P 2V3

resources.name: Healthcare Insurance Reciprocal of Canada (HIROC) – Nova Scotia Subscribers
resources.description: HIROC is a subscriber-owned insurance reciprocal that pools the risks of healthcare organizations across Canada, including Nova Scotia Health, IWK Health, and community care providers in Nova Scotia. By aggregating members’ exposure and negotiating reinsurance on their behalf, HIROC stabilizes premiums and delivers consistent, transparent claims management and risk advisory services—functioning as a community-style pool that helps institutions manage climate and disaster-related property and business interruption risks.
resources.address: 4711 Yonge Street, Suite 1600, Toronto, ON M2N 6K8

solutions.text: Planned buyouts and voluntary managed retreat program: A locally managed, transparent program offering fair purchase or relocation support for repeatedly damaged properties, converting vulnerable land to public green space or coastal buffers.

resources.name: Disaster Financial Assistance Program (DFA) – Voluntary Buyout and Relocation Option
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Department of Municipal Affairs and Housing / Nova Scotia Emergency Management Office
resources.description: Nova Scotia’s DFA provides post-disaster support that has included voluntary residential buyouts and relocation assistance for properties repeatedly damaged by floods and extreme weather (e.g., after the 2016 Cape Breton floods and subsequent events). The program works with homeowners and municipalities to purchase high-risk properties at fair value and retire them from development, allowing municipalities to clear structures and convert floodways to open space or green buffers that reduce future damage.

resources.name: Green Network Plan – Land Acquisition for Coastal and Flood Resilience
resources.description: HRM’s Green Network Plan guides targeted, voluntary land acquisition and easements in areas that provide climate resilience, including floodplains, riparian corridors, and vulnerable coasts. By purchasing at-risk parcels or accepting dedications and converting them to parks, trails, and natural buffers, HRM implements a form of managed retreat that limits redevelopment in hazard-prone locations and creates public green space that absorbs storm surge and overland flooding.

resources.name: Coastal Land Acquisition and Protection Program
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Nature Trust acquires vulnerable coastal properties from willing sellers and places them under permanent protection, preventing redevelopment in high-risk locations. These voluntary purchases convert shorelines into conserved natural buffers that absorb storm impacts and sea-level rise while providing public ecological benefits—an on-the-ground, managed-retreat approach that reduces future property loss and insurance risk.
resources.address: 81 Prince Albert Road, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1M1

resources.name: Oxford Sinkhole Property Acquisition and Risk Reduction Initiative
resources.description: Following the emergence of an expanding karst sinkhole that threatens adjacent properties and public spaces, the Town of Oxford has pursued voluntary acquisitions of high-risk parcels and established no-build buffer zones. By purchasing and retiring vulnerable land and converting it to green space, the municipality is implementing a locally managed, transparent retreat strategy that reduces danger to residents and prevents future losses.
resources.address: 105 Lower Main Street, Oxford, NS B0M 1P0

solutions.text: Urban tree canopy and community wildfire plans: Neighbourhood tree planting, defensible-space programs and fuel-reduction volunteer crews in interface areas to reduce wildfire spread and heat-related risks in towns.

resources.name: Halifax Urban Forest Master Plan (UFMP) & Street Tree Planting
resources.description: Halifax’s UFMP guides long-term expansion and care of the urban tree canopy through annual street and park tree planting, species diversification, and maintenance in neighbourhoods across the municipality. The program prioritizes shade in heat-vulnerable areas and engages residents and community groups in local planting and stewardship, directly reducing urban heat risks while improving resilience to storms and flooding.

resources.name: Town of Truro Urban Forestry Program
resources.description: Truro’s urban forestry program maintains and expands the town’s street and park tree canopy, including annual planting, inventory, and care of municipal trees. By growing canopy cover and focusing plantings in residential neighbourhoods and public spaces, the program mitigates urban heat, provides shade, and supports storm resilience for residents.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Fire & Emergency – Wildfire Risk Reduction and FireSmart Outreach
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Fire & Emergency (Halifax Regional Municipality)
resources.description: HRFE delivers FireSmart education and neighbourhood outreach in wildland–urban interface areas like Hammonds Plains and Upper Tantallon, helping residents create defensible space around homes and outbuildings. The program coordinates community clean‑ups and brush disposal/chipping events with local volunteers and fire stations to reduce hazardous fuels and lower the risk of wildfire spread into towns and subdivisions.

resources.name: MODL FireSmart Community Chipping Program
resources.organization: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
resources.description: The Municipality of the District of Lunenburg runs seasonal FireSmart community chipping and brush disposal to help households clear ladder fuels and vegetation near buildings. Working with local volunteer fire departments and residents, the program supports defensible‑space practices and neighbourhood fuel‑reduction work parties in interface communities, lowering wildfire ignition potential and spread.

resources.name: Kejimkujik FireSmart and Fuel-Management Program
resources.organization: Parks Canada – Kejimkujik National Park and National Historic Site
resources.description: Parks Canada implements FireSmart landscaping and targeted fuel‑management around facilities, campgrounds, and trailheads at Kejimkujik, and collaborates with nearby communities on preparedness and homeowner guidance. Volunteer events and outreach help reduce surface fuels and tidy interface areas, supporting defensible space and lowering the chance of wildfire spread into neighbouring settlements.
resources.address: 3005 Kejimkujik Main Parkway, Maitland Bridge, NS B0T 1B0

solutions.text: Local zoning advocacy and climate-informed bylaws: Community coalitions work with municipal councils to update setback rules, floodplain development standards and building codes so new development avoids high-risk areas.

resources.name: Regional Plan Review (RP+10): Coastal Resilience and Floodplain Policies
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s ongoing Regional Plan Review introduces climate-informed zoning tools such as coastal elevation and floodplain overlays that limit or condition new development in areas vulnerable to sea-level rise, storm surge, and riverine flooding. The initiative updates land-use by-laws to require setbacks, elevation standards, and floodproofing in high-risk areas, developed through consultation with residents, developers, and council to keep growth out of hazard zones.

resources.name: Coastal and Water Program – Municipal Coastal Policy Support
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre works with coastal communities and municipal councils to integrate sea-level rise and storm-surge science into Municipal Planning Strategies and Land-Use By-laws. Through technical submissions, public workshops, and coalition-building, the program advocates for stronger setback rules, floodplain development standards, and climate-informed zoning that steer new development away from high-risk areas.

resources.name: Climate-Resilient Land-Use By-law Updates for Member Municipalities
resources.description: The Eastern District Planning Commission drafts and updates Municipal Planning Strategies and Land-Use By-laws for its member municipalities, embedding floodplain overlays, coastal erosion setbacks, and storm-surge standards based on current hazard mapping. The commission facilitates council and community engagement to align zoning with climate risks so new development avoids flood- and surge-prone areas.
resources.address: 606 Reeves Street, Unit 3, Port Hawkesbury, NS B9A 2R7

resources.name: Land Use By-law Flood Risk Overlay and Climate Adaptation Integration
resources.description: The Town of Mahone Bay implements a Flood Risk Overlay in its Land Use By-law that restricts or conditions development in areas exposed to storm surge and sea-level rise, including setbacks and minimum elevation requirements. The town coordinates with residents, provincial partners, and local NGOs to keep zoning aligned with updated risk maps so new construction avoids high-hazard coastal areas.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Inundation and Flood Risk Policies in Municipal Planning Strategy and Land-Use By-law
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
resources.description: The Municipality of the County of Kings incorporates climate risk mapping into its Municipal Planning Strategy and Land-Use By-law through floodplain and coastal inundation policies that set development setbacks, require raised floor elevations, and limit new construction in high-risk zones. Planning staff regularly engage council, developers, and the public to maintain climate-informed standards that direct growth to safer areas.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

solutions.text: Resilience financing: local funds, levies and green bonds: Create community resilience funds (seeded by grants, municipal levies or green bonds) to finance home retrofits, buyouts, natural infrastructure and local adaptation businesses.

resources.name: Sustainable Communities Challenge Fund (SCCF)
resources.organization: Clean Foundation (on behalf of the Province of Nova Scotia)
resources.description: The Sustainable Communities Challenge Fund provides multi-year grants to municipalities, Mi’kmaw communities, and non-profits across Nova Scotia for climate adaptation projects such as coastal flood protection, living shorelines, and community resilience planning. By seeding local projects with provincial grant funding administered by Clean Foundation, the SCCF functions as a community resilience fund that leverages additional municipal and federal dollars to finance natural infrastructure and support local adaptation-focused businesses and retrofits.

resources.name: Solar City Program (Local Improvement Charge Financing)
resources.description: Halifax’s Solar City program offers no-money-down, low-interest financing for residential solar and efficiency upgrades using a Local Improvement Charge (LIC) repaid via property tax bills. This levy-based mechanism creates a revolving municipal fund that finances home retrofits and distributed resilience assets, lowering risk for homeowners and scaling local clean energy and adaptation-related services.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) Program
resources.description: Bridgewater’s Clean Energy Financing program uses Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) via Local Improvement Charges to cover up-front costs for home retrofits like insulation, heat pumps, and solar, with repayment attached to the property tax bill. The revolving fund structure leverages municipal debentures and grants to finance resilience-improving home upgrades while growing local trades and clean-technology businesses.

resources.name: Stormwater Service and Right-of-Way (ROW) Charge
resources.description: Halifax Water’s stormwater service charge and ROW charge generate dedicated, levy-based revenue to design, build, and maintain stormwater and flood-mitigation infrastructure, including green infrastructure retrofits and natural channels. This financing model directly funds local adaptation projects that reduce flooding and sea-level rise impacts, with credit programs that encourage property-level resilience measures.
resources.address: 450 Cowie Hill Road, Halifax, NS B3P 2V3

solutions.text: Youth-led climate entrepreneurship incubator: An incubator that supports young entrepreneurs building climate-resilient businesses (e.g., restoration services, climate-smart tourism, resilient construction) with mentoring and seed grants.

resources.name: Start-Up Yard at COVE
resources.description: Start-Up Yard at COVE is an incubator for early-stage ocean technology companies in Nova Scotia. It equips youth and student-led teams with workspace, technical mentorship, testing infrastructure on Halifax Harbour, and business coaching to build solutions such as coastal monitoring tools, resilient marine infrastructure, and climate-smart tourism services. The program also connects founders to non-dilutive seed funding and pilot opportunities through the Ocean Startup Project and industry partners, accelerating climate-resilient businesses in coastal communities.

resources.name: Ocean Startup Project
resources.description: The Ocean Startup Project is a pan-Atlantic initiative headquartered in Nova Scotia that helps new ocean-focused companies get started and grow. Through its Ocean Startup Challenge and year-round programming, it provides non-dilutive seed funding, intensive mentorship, and market validation to student- and youth-led ventures working on coastal resilience, marine restoration, and other climate-adaptation products and services. By lowering risk and providing capital and coaching, it advances youth climate entrepreneurship that strengthens Nova Scotia’s coastal economy.

resources.name: Cleantech Scale-Up Platform
resources.organization: Verschuren Centre for Sustainability in Energy and the Environment
resources.description: The Verschuren Centre at Cape Breton University operates a cleantech scale-up platform that incubates startups developing decarbonization, bioeconomy, and sustainable materials solutions relevant to climate resilience. Founders, including recent graduates and young entrepreneurs, access pilot-scale facilities, expert mentors, and commercialization coaching, along with connections to investors and public seed funding programs. This hands-on support helps youth-led businesses de-risk climate technologies and bring them to market in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 1250 Grand Lake Road, Sydney, NS B1M 1A2

resources.name: Innovation Fund
resources.description: Divert NS’s Innovation Fund supports entrepreneurs advancing circular-economy and waste-reduction solutions that cut emissions, conserve resources, and improve community resilience. The program provides seed funding, guidance, and industry connections that help youth-led and early-stage ventures validate and commercialize climate-positive products and services (e.g., recycled building materials, repair/refurbish models). By backing Nova Scotia founders with capital and mentorship, it functions as an incubator for climate-smart businesses that create local jobs.
resources.address: 35 Commercial Street, Suite 400, Truro, NS B2N 3H9

solutions.text: Nature-based stormwater and flood storage: Community projects to build wetlands, retention ponds, permeable parking and rain gardens that reduce flood peaks, recharge groundwater and create recreational green space.

resources.name: Depave Paradise – Nova Scotia
resources.description: Clean Foundation delivers the Depave Paradise program across Nova Scotia, mobilizing volunteers to remove unnecessary asphalt from schoolyards, church lots, and community spaces and replace it with rain gardens and permeable landscaping. These nature-based retrofits infiltrate stormwater, reduce runoff and localized flooding, recharge groundwater, and add accessible green space in urban areas.

resources.name: Depave Paradise – Halifax Region
resources.description: The Ecology Action Centre hosts Depave Paradise events in the Halifax region to remove impermeable pavement and install native plant rain gardens and other permeable features at community sites. By capturing and infiltrating runoff where it falls, these projects lower flood peaks, improve water quality, recharge groundwater, and create attractive, usable green spaces.

resources.name: Miners Marsh Conservation Area Wetland Restoration
resources.organization: Town of Kentville (in partnership with Ducks Unlimited Canada)
resources.description: The Town of Kentville, in partnership with Ducks Unlimited Canada, restored and manages the Miners Marsh wetland complex adjacent to the Cornwallis River to provide natural floodwater storage and peak-flow attenuation. The constructed and enhanced wetlands slow and store stormwater, support groundwater recharge, improve habitat, and offer trails and viewing platforms that serve as community recreational green space.

resources.name: Halifax Water Stormwater Services – Green Infrastructure and Ponds
resources.description: Halifax Water designs, operates, and maintains stormwater infrastructure that integrates nature-based features such as constructed wetlands, retention/detention ponds, bioswales, and vegetated channels in new developments and retrofits. These installations store and slowly release runoff to reduce flood peaks, promote infiltration and groundwater recharge, and, where possible, provide naturalized community spaces.
resources.address: 450 Cowie Hill Road, Halifax, NS B3R 1A1

solutions.text: Local monitoring network and data sharing: Volunteer-operated sensors and shoreline change monitoring with open data dashboards to inform local planning, insurance underwriting and timely warnings for residents.

resources.name: Equipment Hub and Atlantic DataStream
resources.description: Atlantic Water Network equips and trains community and Indigenous volunteers across Nova Scotia to deploy low-cost water quality and water-level sensors, plus conduct shoreline and stream monitoring. Data are published openly through Atlantic DataStream’s interactive maps and dashboards, giving municipalities, planners, and insurers access to standardized datasets that support flood risk assessment, adaptation planning, and timely public advisories.

resources.name: Annapolis River Guardians Community-Based Monitoring
resources.description: Volunteer River Guardians collect water quality, water level, and habitat data throughout the Annapolis River and tidal reaches influenced by the Bay of Fundy, tracking storm impacts and shoreline conditions. Clean Annapolis River Project shares results via open reports and Atlantic DataStream, enabling municipalities and emergency managers to use local evidence for planning, insurance risk discussions, and timely flood and water-quality advisories for residents.
resources.address: 314 St. George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

resources.name: Coastal and Marine Program – Community Monitoring
resources.description: Coastal Action engages local volunteers and partners along Nova Scotia’s South Shore to monitor nearshore water quality, temperature, storm impacts, and shoreline change using sensors and standardized survey methods. The organization publishes geospatial data, dashboards, and technical reports (including contributions to Atlantic DataStream), which inform municipal coastal planning, nature-based adaptation projects, and risk communication to residents.

resources.name: Flood Monitoring and Alerting System
resources.description: The Town of Truro operates a local monitoring network with river stage gauges on the Salmon River and shares real-time levels and flood risk updates through public web dashboards and alerts. This open data helps residents prepare for flood events and supports municipal planning and infrastructure decisions, reducing risk in a community highly exposed to storm-driven flooding.

solutions.text: Business continuity supports for local firms: Peer networks and toolkits that help small businesses prepare continuity plans, access emergency funds and retrofit premises to reduce downtime after events.

resources.name: Emergency Planning for Businesses (HRM EMO)
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality Emergency Management Office
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Emergency Management Office provides guidance, templates, and checklists to help small businesses develop business continuity plans for hazards like storms, floods, and wildfires. It hosts preparedness workshops and coordinates alerts, and directs firms to disaster financial assistance, permitting, and cleanup supports to reduce downtime and speed reopening after events.

resources.name: Small Business Energy Solutions
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia offers on-site energy assessments, rebates, and financing to help small businesses retrofit lighting, HVAC, refrigeration, and controls. These upgrades improve reliability and reduce the risk of equipment failures and power-related downtime during severe weather, helping firms maintain operations and recover more quickly after events.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Emergency Preparedness Planning for Farms
resources.organization: Farm Safety Nova Scotia (Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture)
resources.description: Farm Safety Nova Scotia provides toolkits, templates, and training to help farm businesses build emergency response and business continuity plans for wildfires, floods, storms, and power outages. Workshops and advisory support promote peer learning and practical retrofits (e.g., backup power, infrastructure protection) that reduce downtime and safeguard livelihoods after extreme events.
resources.address: 60 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

resources.name: Business Advisory and Financing Programs
resources.organization: Centre for Entrepreneurship Education and Development (CEED)
resources.description: CEED supports entrepreneurs through peer cohorts, mentorship, and advisory services that include risk assessment and business continuity planning for disruptions like storms and wildfires. It also helps businesses navigate funding and offers microloans that can be used for recovery and resiliency improvements (e.g., space retrofits and equipment upgrades) to reduce future downtime.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 225, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

solutions.text: Community mental-health and relocation supports: Locally organized counselling, peer-support groups and practical relocation assistance to help residents cope with loss, insurance disputes or voluntary moves, preserving social ties.

resources.name: Canadian Red Cross – Emergency Management (Nova Scotia)
resources.description: The Canadian Red Cross provides immediate and longer-term disaster recovery support in Nova Scotia, including case management, psychosocial/psychological first aid, and financial assistance for essentials and temporary lodging. Trained volunteers and staff help residents navigate insurance claims, access government disaster assistance, and plan relocations when homes are unsafe or rebuilding isn’t feasible. Community-based supports, including friendly calls and group information sessions, help people cope with loss while maintaining social connections.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Health – Community Mental Health and Addictions (Bayers Road Clinic)
resources.description: This clinic offers free, community-based counselling, group programs, and peer-support services to help adults manage stress, grief, trauma and anxiety following crises such as floods, wildfires or displacement. Clinicians provide short-term therapy and connect clients to social workers and navigation supports that coordinate with housing and community services when relocation is necessary. The locally delivered, team-based approach preserves social ties by linking people to peer groups and resources in their home communities.

resources.name: Mi'kmaw Native Friendship Centre – Housing Support Program
resources.description: The Centre’s Housing Support Program helps Indigenous and non-Indigenous urban community members secure and stabilize housing, including assistance with searching for rentals, landlord mediation, and navigation of income supports after emergencies. Staff provide culturally grounded peer support circles, Elder-led guidance, and referrals to counselling that address trauma and loss from events like wildfires or flooding. By coordinating practical relocation help and community-based healing, the program supports continuity of social and cultural connections.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Legal Aid – Social Justice (Housing, Income & Insurance) – Halifax Office
resources.description: Nova Scotia Legal Aid provides free legal help for tenants and low-income residents dealing with landlord–tenant issues, insurance disputes, and income supports—common challenges following climate-related damage or voluntary relocation. Lawyers and advocates assist with negotiating insurance claims, enforcing repair or relocation rights, and securing benefits needed to move safely and maintain stability. Their services complement counselling and community supports by resolving legal barriers that can fracture social ties during displacement.
resources.address: 1701 Hollis Street, Suite 920, Halifax, NS B3J 3M8

obstacles.title: Energy and Grid Constraints for Growth
obstacles.description: Grid capacity, interties, and interconnection timelines limit renewable projects and electrification. Energy costs and uncertainty slow growth in clean industries that appeal to young workers.

solutions.text: Community Energy Co‑operatives: Form local co‑ops to develop, own and operate small‑scale renewables (rooftop solar, small wind) and shared battery storage so benefits and revenues stay local while reducing strain on the wider grid.

resources.name: Antigonish Community Solar Garden
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish Electric Utility’s subscriber-based community solar garden lets local residents and businesses buy shares (solar blocks) in a municipally owned array and receive on-bill credits for their portion of the energy produced. This shared-ownership model keeps revenues within the community-owned utility and brings new distributed generation onto the local feeder, easing demand on the wider provincial grid. The program mirrors a co‑op approach by pooling community investment and governance locally and is designed to integrate with demand management and future storage to manage peaks.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Community Solar Garden
resources.description: Mahone Bay’s municipally owned electric utility operates a community solar garden that allows customers to subscribe to panels in a shared array and receive credits on their bills. By pooling local investment and ownership, the initiative keeps benefits and revenues in town while adding distributed renewable capacity that reduces strain on the broader grid. The town’s community energy planning includes evaluating battery storage to pair with the solar garden to further smooth local peaks.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: Berwick Community Solar Garden
resources.description: The Town of Berwick Electric Utility runs a community solar garden where residents and businesses can subscribe to a portion of a town-owned solar array and receive bill credits for the output. This shared, community-led model keeps project value within the municipal utility and adds local renewable generation that can help defer costly grid upgrades by reducing peak imports. It functions much like a co‑op in practice by aggregating community participation and aligning benefits with local ratepayers.

resources.name: AREA Community-Owned Renewables (Ellershouse Wind and Community Solar)
resources.description: The Alternative Resource Energy Authority (AREA)—a joint entity of the municipal utilities of Antigonish, Berwick, and Mahone Bay—develops, owns, and operates community-scale renewables on behalf of local ratepayers, including the Ellershouse Wind Farm and multiple community solar gardens. By aggregating community and municipal ownership across member towns, AREA keeps revenues in local hands, builds distributed generation close to load, and lessens reliance on the provincial grid. Its portfolio approach creates a platform for adding shared battery storage to manage peaks and improve reliability across the member communities.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

solutions.text: Neighbourhood Microgrids and Resilience Hubs: Pilot microgrids that pair solar + batteries + smart controls at community centres or business districts to provide local reliability, reduce peak loads, and demonstrate interconnection pathways for larger projects.

resources.name: Smart Grid Nova Scotia
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s Smart Grid Nova Scotia program pilots distributed solar, battery storage (including behind‑the‑meter and community‑scale systems), and advanced controls across the province. By pairing solar with batteries at customer sites and community facilities and coordinating them with smart grid software, the program reduces local peak loads, provides backup power during outages, and tests interconnection pathways that can be scaled up for larger neighborhood microgrids and resilience hubs.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: The Deanery Project Microgrid & Resilience Hub
resources.description: The Deanery Project operates a community hub powered by an onsite microgrid that integrates solar PV, battery storage, and smart controls to serve multiple buildings in a rural setting. As a living demonstration site, it provides reliable local power during outages, supports community gathering and essential services, and showcases how solar-plus-storage microgrids can strengthen resilience for neighborhood and community facilities elsewhere in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1Y0

solutions.text: Municipal Aggregated Procurement for DERs and EV Chargers: Municipalities or community groups pool demand to negotiate better pricing and faster deployment of rooftop solar, batteries and EV chargers for homes, businesses and public sites, simplifying vendor selection and installation.

resources.name: SolarSwitch Halifax
resources.organization: Halifax Regional Municipality in partnership with iChoosr
resources.description: SolarSwitch Halifax is a group-purchasing program where residents and businesses register interest and a third-party (iChoosr) runs a reverse auction among pre-vetted solar installers to secure volume pricing. The municipality promotes the program and helps standardize the customer journey, while participants receive a single, competitive group rate and turnkey installation, speeding deployment of rooftop solar across the community. This is a direct example of aggregated procurement that simplifies vendor selection and lowers costs for distributed energy resources.

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: Solar City is HRM’s municipal program that aggregates demand for rooftop solar by offering standardized financing (LIC), pre-qualified contractors selected through competitive procurement, and coordinated permitting and installation support. By bundling many small residential and commercial projects under one program with vetted vendors and set terms, it reduces soft costs and accelerates deployment at scale. This simplifies vendor selection for property owners and implements an aggregated procurement model for DERs in the municipality.

resources.name: NSFM–Canoe Procurement Program
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Federation of Municipalities (NSFM) in partnership with Canoe Procurement Group of Canada
resources.description: Through its partnership with the Canoe Procurement Group of Canada, NSFM enables Nova Scotia municipalities to buy EV charging equipment, solar PV systems, and related hardware via pre-tendered, compliant contracts with vetted suppliers. Municipalities leverage aggregated national and regional purchasing volumes to obtain better pricing and faster delivery, while avoiding complex individual RFPs. This group-buy model directly supports rapid deployment of public-site EV chargers and DERs across Nova Scotia communities.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1304, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) – Multi-Municipal Program
resources.description: Administered by Clean Foundation, this Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) program serves multiple Nova Scotia municipalities with shared program administration, centralized contractor pre-qualification, and standardized documentation. By coordinating vendor networks and financing across several communities, it effectively aggregates demand for rooftop solar and other DER upgrades, lowering costs and shortening timelines for homeowners and small businesses. The program simplifies vendor selection and streamlines large-scale DER adoption at the municipal level.

solutions.text: Local Demand‑Response and Time‑of‑Use Programs: Organize community campaigns and incentives to shift discretionary electricity use (water heating, EV charging, appliances) to off‑peak hours using smart timers and price signals, lowering peak stress on the grid.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Power Time-of-Day (TOD) Rate
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power offers a Time-of-Day electricity rate that provides lower prices during off-peak periods (typically nights and weekends), encouraging customers to shift discretionary uses like water heating, EV charging, laundry, and dishwashing to those hours. With smart meters and simple timers or smart plugs, households can automate usage to take advantage of off-peak pricing, reducing demand during system peaks. This shifts load away from critical hours, easing grid constraints and lowering overall system costs.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Nova Scotia Power Interruptible Load Rider
resources.description: For large commercial and industrial customers, Nova Scotia Power provides an interruptible/curtailable service option that offers bill credits in exchange for reducing load when the utility calls peak events. Facilities use building automation, process scheduling, or thermal storage to temporarily curtail demand during the highest-stress hours, responding to clear price signals and event notices. This demand-response program directly lowers peak demand on the provincial grid and complements broader electrification and renewable integration.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Town of Antigonish Electric Utility Time-of-Day Rate and ETS Program
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish Electric Utility offers a Time-of-Day rate and actively promotes Electric Thermal Storage (ETS) space and water heating to shift energy use to overnight off-peak hours. Customers use smart thermostats, ETS controls, and appliance/EV charger timers to preheat or charge when prices are lowest, then rely on stored heat or battery charge during peak times. This community-focused approach reduces peak stress on the local distribution system and supports affordable electrification.

resources.name: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility Time-of-Day Rate
resources.description: Mahone Bay’s municipal electric utility provides a Time-of-Day rate that rewards customers for shifting power use to off-peak periods and promotes technologies like Electric Thermal Storage and smart EV charging. The town shares seasonal peak alerts and encourages residents to delay laundry, dishwashing, and EV charging to evenings or overnight using built-in appliance delays or smart timers. These actions flatten local peaks, improving grid reliability and helping integrate more renewable energy.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

solutions.text: Community Energy Efficiency Retrofits: Coordinate bulk retrofit programs (insulation, heat pumps, LED lighting, smart thermostats) for homes, schools and small businesses to cut electricity demand and reduce the need for new grid capacity.

resources.name: Home Energy Assessment (HEA) and Home Energy Upgrade Rebates
