resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia provides EnerGuide home energy assessments that identify the most impactful upgrades and connect homeowners to rebates for insulation, air sealing, and cold-climate heat pumps. The program coordinates a network of registered contractors and offers incentives that lower upfront costs, enabling bulk, community-scale retrofits that cut electricity use and peak demand—reducing pressure on the grid and deferring new capacity.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Small Business Energy Solutions
resources.description: This direct-install program delivers turnkey retrofits for small businesses, including on-site energy assessments and installation of LED lighting, smart thermostats, and other efficiency measures with substantial incentives. By bundling common upgrades and coordinating qualified contractors, it reduces electricity consumption and peak loads across many small facilities, easing grid constraints while lowering operating costs for local businesses.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: HomeWarming
resources.organization: Clean Foundation and EfficiencyOne (Efficiency Nova Scotia)
resources.description: HomeWarming provides free home energy assessments and fully funded upgrades—such as insulation, draft-proofing, and heat pumps where appropriate—for income-qualified Nova Scotians. Delivered by Clean Foundation and Efficiency Nova Scotia, the program coordinates contractors to complete high-impact retrofits at scale, lowering household electricity demand and helping reduce the need for new grid capacity province-wide.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) – Nova Scotia Municipalities
resources.description: Clean Foundation partners with Nova Scotia municipalities to offer Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) financing that enables homeowners to undertake energy retrofits—such as heat pumps, insulation, windows/doors, and controls—with approved contractors. By spreading costs on the property tax bill and coordinating projects across communities, the program accelerates bulk retrofits that lower electricity demand and peak loads, easing grid constraints while improving home comfort.

solutions.text: Local Battery Banks and Second‑Life EV Storage: Develop community battery projects using new or second‑life EV batteries to store excess local generation, smooth demand, and offer a local resource for outages and peak shaving.

resources.name: Smart Grid Nova Scotia – Community Energy Storage and Residential Battery Pilot
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s Smart Grid Nova Scotia pilot deployed a utility‑side community battery and an aggregated network of customer‑sited batteries (e.g., Tesla Powerwall units) to store excess local generation and discharge during peak times. The community energy storage unit provides localized peak shaving and supports outages by supplying power to the surrounding feeders, while the aggregated residential batteries operate as a virtual power plant to reduce grid constraints. Together, these local battery banks smooth demand, lower curtailment of renewables, and enhance resilience for communities.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Nova Scotia Power Grid-Scale Battery Storage Program (Province-wide BESS Portfolio)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power is deploying multiple grid-scale battery energy storage systems across communities in the province to integrate renewables, provide peak shaving, and offer localized resilience during outages. These distribution- and substation-connected battery banks act as local capacity resources that store wind and solar generation when it’s abundant and discharge during demand peaks or grid contingencies. By siting batteries near communities, the program directly addresses interconnection constraints and improves reliability while enabling growth in clean electricity use.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

solutions.text: Neighborhood EV Charging Hubs with Smart Load Management: Install shared charging hubs in residential areas and workplaces that use smart chargers to manage loads, prioritize queueing, and avoid sudden spikes that stress distribution lines.

resources.name: Halifax Public EV Charging Network
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality operates shared, multi-port EV charging hubs at municipal libraries, arenas, parkades, and other public sites across the city. The networked smart chargers are configured with power management to cap total site demand, dynamically share available power between ports, and use app-based waitlists/notifications to prioritize users and reduce queuing friction. This approach spreads charging demand over time and avoids sudden load spikes that would otherwise stress local distribution lines.

resources.name: Dalhousie University Campus EV Charging Program
resources.description: Dalhousie University provides shared workplace and public EV charging hubs on campus parking lots and parkades using networked Level 2 stations. The chargers employ smart load management—such as circuit sharing and site-level demand limits—and app-based queueing (e.g., waitlists and notifications) to allocate access fairly while keeping the aggregate load within building and feeder constraints. This reduces peak demand charges and prevents sudden spikes on campus distribution infrastructure.

resources.name: Killam Apartment REIT Resident EV Charging
resources.description: Killam Apartment REIT is deploying shared EV charging hubs at multi-unit residential buildings in Halifax and across Nova Scotia. The installations use smart, networked chargers with dynamic load balancing to keep total current within each building’s electrical capacity and to avoid costly service upgrades; residents use an app to manage access and queueing, ensuring fair use of limited ports. By smoothing demand and prioritizing charging, these hubs prevent sudden load spikes on neighborhood distribution lines.
resources.address: 3700 Kempt Road, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3K 4X8

resources.name: Nova Scotia Power EV Smart Charging Pilot
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power runs an EV smart charging initiative that connects networked chargers at homes and workplaces to utility-side demand management. The program throttles and schedules charging across participating hubs to keep aggregate load within feeder and substation limits, while providing prioritization rules so vehicles with urgent needs are served first without creating peak spikes. This coordinated control demonstrates how shared charging can scale without overloading local distribution infrastructure.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

solutions.text: Interconnection Working Group (Community + Utility): Create a local forum of municipalities, developers, utilities and residents to map interconnection pain points, co‑design streamlined processes, and pilot faster approval workflows for small and community projects.

resources.name: Generator Interconnections (Distribution & Transmission)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s interconnection services team runs ongoing stakeholder engagements and technical consultations with municipalities, renewable developers, and customers to identify bottlenecks in connecting distributed and community-scale projects. Through updated standards, pre-application reviews, and streamlined workflows for small generators and net-metered systems, the utility co-designs and pilots faster approval processes that reduce interconnection timelines and clarify requirements for community projects.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: Halifax’s Solar City convenes homeowners, solar installers, municipal permitting staff, and Nova Scotia Power to surface interconnection pain points and standardize the steps for rooftop solar under net metering. The program provides a single point of contact, coordinated permit and utility application support, and batch submissions that pilot quicker approvals—directly implementing a community–utility forum and streamlined workflow for small, distributed projects.

resources.name: Antigonish Community Solar Program
resources.description: The Town of Antigonish Electric Utility organizes public information sessions and works directly with residents, local developers, and utility engineers to design and interconnect its community solar garden and other distributed resources. By coordinating interconnection studies, standardizing technical requirements, and iterating processes with community feedback, the program operates as a local working forum that pilots faster, clearer approvals for community-scale projects.

resources.name: Mahone Bay Community Solar Garden
resources.organization: Town of Mahone Bay Electric Utility
resources.description: Mahone Bay’s municipal electric utility convenes residents, contractors, and utility staff to plan, interconnect, and operate a community solar garden within its local distribution system. The initiative uses regular community–utility meetings to identify interconnection challenges and implement standardized applications and technical reviews, effectively piloting faster approval workflows for small and community projects.
resources.address: 493 Main Street, Mahone Bay, NS B0J 2E0

resources.name: OATT and Interconnection Stakeholder Processes
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Utility and Review Board
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Utility and Review Board (NSUARB) oversees and convenes formal stakeholder processes on Nova Scotia Power’s Open Access Transmission Tariff and Generator Interconnection Procedures. These proceedings bring together the utility, independent power producers, municipalities, and consumer representatives to surface interconnection pain points and co-design rule and process changes that streamline timelines and improve transparency for new community and small-scale projects.
resources.address: 1601 Lower Water Street, 3rd Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 3P6

solutions.text: Streamlined Local Permitting and Siting Guidelines: Municipalities adopt clear, standard permitting checklists and pre‑approved siting templates for rooftop solar, small wind and charging infrastructure to cut delays and uncertainty for community projects.

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: Halifax’s Solar City provides a turnkey pathway for rooftop solar that standardizes site assessments, application documents, and contractor requirements, and coordinates inspections with municipal staff. By using clear checklists and a single point of contact, the program streamlines permitting and siting decisions for residential and community solar projects, cutting delays and uncertainty.

resources.name: Renewable Energy Siting and Permitting (Small Wind and Solar)
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings – Planning & Inspections
resources.description: The Municipality of the County of Kings has embedded clear standards for rooftop solar and small wind in its planning and development process, using defined setbacks, heights, and mounting criteria alongside concise development-permit checklists. These pre-set siting rules and application requirements shorten review timelines and give residents, farms, and community groups predictable pathways to authorize installations.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: Energize Bridgewater – Clean Energy Financing (PACE)
resources.description: Bridgewater’s PACE program standardizes applications and documentation for eligible upgrades like rooftop solar, provides pre-approved contractor pathways, and coordinates required municipal permits and inspections. By offering clear checklists and an end-to-end municipal process, the initiative reduces administrative friction and accelerates siting and approval for local clean energy projects.

solutions.text: Community Green Financing (Local Bonds, PACE, Co‑op Shares): Use community financing tools — municipal green bonds, Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) programs, or cooperative share offerings — to lower capital barriers for clean energy and grid‑supporting projects.

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: Halifax’s Solar City is a Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) program that finances rooftop solar installations through a Local Improvement Charge repaid on the property tax bill, removing upfront cost barriers for homeowners. By enabling distributed solar generation, the program supports grid reliability and reduces peak demand while accelerating clean electrification in the municipality.

resources.name: Switch Bridgewater (PACE Financing)
resources.organization: Town of Bridgewater in partnership with PACE Atlantic C I C
resources.description: Switch Bridgewater provides Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) financing so homeowners can install measures like solar PV, heat pumps, and insulation with repayment attached to the property tax bill. This community-based financing lowers capital barriers, expands distributed energy and efficiency upgrades, and helps reduce local grid stress and energy costs.

resources.name: Switch Wolfville (PACE Financing)
resources.organization: Town of Wolfville in partnership with PACE Atlantic C I C
resources.description: Switch Wolfville delivers PACE financing for residential clean energy and efficiency projects, allowing costs to be repaid via the property tax bill rather than upfront. The program accelerates adoption of rooftop solar and building electrification upgrades, contributing to local grid resilience and lowering long-term energy costs for residents.

resources.name: Switch Colchester (PACE Financing)
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Colchester in partnership with PACE Atlantic C I C
resources.description: Switch Colchester offers Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) financing to county residents for eligible upgrades such as solar PV and high-efficiency heat pumps, with repayment collected on the property tax bill. By removing upfront cost barriers and scaling distributed energy resources, the program supports grid capacity and reliability across the county.

resources.name: Province of Nova Scotia Green Bond Program
resources.organization: Province of Nova Scotia — Department of Finance and Treasury Board
resources.description: Nova Scotia issues Green Bonds to mobilize private capital for eligible climate and clean energy projects, including energy efficiency, clean transportation, and resilient infrastructure that supports the grid. By spreading costs over time and attracting investors, the program lowers financing barriers for public clean-energy initiatives that unlock electrification and grid-supporting improvements.

solutions.text: Local Workforce Training and Apprenticeship Programs: Partner with colleges, unions and employers to create fast‑track training for grid technicians, solar installers, battery specialists and control‑system operators to ensure skilled local labour for growth.

resources.name: Powerline Technician Apprenticeship and Grid Operations Training
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power recruits and trains Powerline Technician (PLT) apprentices and substation technicians to build, maintain, and modernize the provincial grid, including hands-on training with live-line tools, distribution equipment, and substations. The utility also provides in-house training for system/dispatch operators on SCADA and protection-and-control systems, developing local control‑system operators who can integrate renewables and manage reliability. The programs are delivered in partnership with employers, unions, and the Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency to fast‑track skilled local labour for grid growth.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Energy Sustainability Engineering Technology (ESET)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) – Ivany Campus
resources.description: This two‑year NSCC diploma trains technicians in solar PV, energy storage, power electronics, building automation, and grid‑interactive controls through labs and industry projects. The program partners with employers and industry groups for co‑ops and applied learning, producing job‑ready solar installers, battery specialists, and controls technologists. Graduates help accelerate clean‑energy deployment and grid modernization across Nova Scotia.

resources.name: Power Engineering Technology
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) – Marconi Campus
resources.description: NSCC’s Power Engineering Technology program prepares technologists to operate and maintain boilers, turbines, generators, and control systems used in power and industrial energy facilities. With extensive lab time, certifications, and work placements, it develops local talent for plant operations, protection and controls, and grid‑support roles critical to integrating renewables and storage. The apprenticeship‑aligned pathway fast‑tracks skilled workers to support Nova Scotia’s evolving energy system.
resources.address: 1240 Grand Lake Road, Sydney, NS B1P 6J7

resources.name: Clean Energy Workforce Programs (Energy Advisor and Installer Training)
resources.description: Clean Foundation delivers fast‑track training and upskilling for clean‑energy careers, including NRCan Energy Advisor preparation, building science, heat‑pump/EVSE fundamentals, and partnerships that support solar PV and electrification contractors. Programs are run with colleges, utilities, and employers to create local, job‑ready talent for efficiency, distributed energy, and grid‑friendly technologies. This builds the workforce needed to lower demand, integrate renewables, and manage grid growth across communities.

resources.name: Workforce Development and Contractor Training (SolarHomes, Heat Pump Installer, and Trade Network)
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia provides contractor training, accreditation support, and market development for local installers of heat pumps, solar PV (SolarHomes), and other electrification measures that reduce load and enable cleaner grids. By connecting employers with training, quality standards, and incentives, the program fast‑tracks skilled local labour and expands the clean‑energy contractor base. These efforts complement utility and college partnerships to accelerate renewable integration and grid‑supporting technologies in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

solutions.text: District Energy and Heat Collaboration: Pilot community district heating or combined heat and power projects (using waste heat, biomass, or geo‑thermal) that reduce electric heating loads and better integrate thermal and electric planning at local scale.

resources.name: Alderney 5 Trigeneration and District Energy Project
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality operates a combined heat and power system at the Alderney Ferry Terminal/Alderney Gate complex that generates electricity on-site and captures waste heat to supply space and water heating across connected municipal buildings via a shared thermal loop. The project also uses seawater for cooling, which reduces electric cooling loads. By integrating thermal and electric systems at a district scale, it lowers peak demand and demonstrates how CHP and heat recovery can reduce reliance on electric resistance heating.

resources.name: Cogswell District Energy System
resources.description: As part of the Cogswell Redevelopment, HRM is implementing a new district energy/ambient loop system designed to use geoexchange and recoverable waste heat to serve multiple mixed-use buildings in the new downtown district. The system will shift heating and cooling loads off individual electric systems, enabling efficient thermal sharing and lower peak electricity demand. This integrated thermal-electric planning at neighborhood scale will support low-carbon growth in the urban core.

resources.name: Dalhousie Agricultural Campus Biomass District Heating Plant
resources.description: Dalhousie University’s Agricultural Campus operates a central biomass heating plant that uses locally sourced wood chips to produce hot water/steam distributed through a district network to multiple campus buildings in Bible Hill. This system displaces oil and electric heating, cutting peak electricity demand and fuel costs while demonstrating community-scale bioheat. It shows how biomass district energy can integrate local thermal resources with campus energy planning.
resources.address: 62 Cumming Drive, Bible Hill, NS B2N 5E3

resources.name: Point Tupper Biomass Combined Heat and Power
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Power Inc. (in partnership with Port Hawkesbury Paper LP)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power operates a biomass cogeneration facility at Point Tupper that produces electricity for the grid and supplies process steam/heat to Port Hawkesbury Paper. By using forest biomass residues for combined heat and power, the project integrates thermal and electric planning at an industrial district scale and reduces reliance on separate electric heating loads. It demonstrates how CHP can support grid capacity while delivering useful heat to nearby large energy users.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Springhill Mine Water Geothermal District Energy
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Cumberland
resources.description: The Municipality of Cumberland supports a district-scale geothermal system in Springhill that taps warm mine water from abandoned coal workings to provide heating and cooling to multiple commercial and industrial buildings. Shared thermal loops reduce the need for electric resistance heating and lower peak electrical demand. This community energy system showcases integrated thermal-electric planning that leverages local resources to enable low-carbon growth.
resources.address: 1395 Blair Lake Road, Upper Nappan, NS B4H 3Y4

solutions.text: Local Data Sharing and Grid Forecasting Platform: Establish a community data platform (open, privacy‑respecting) to share local generation, load and EV charging patterns with utilities and planners so interconnection and upgrades can be better targeted.

resources.name: Smart Metering (Advanced Metering Infrastructure)
resources.description: Nova Scotia Power’s smart meter program deploys AMI across the province, collecting interval electricity consumption and distributed generation data at the neighbourhood level. The utility aggregates and analyzes this privacy‑protected local load and generation data to improve grid forecasting for EV adoption, target distribution upgrades, and streamline interconnections; customers can also access and share their own interval data to support community energy planning.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Nova Scotia Power OASIS (Open Access Same-Time Information System)
resources.description: NS Power’s OASIS portal openly publishes transmission system information, including available transfer capability, interconnection queue status, and planning studies. By making grid capacity and interconnection data accessible to communities, developers, and planners, it supports forecasting and helps target where upgrades and new DER connections are most feasible in Nova Scotia.
resources.address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

resources.name: Halifax Open Data Portal (Energy and Environment Datasets)
resources.description: The Halifax Regional Municipality publishes open, privacy‑respecting datasets such as municipal EV charging locations/status, solar program installations, and building energy indicators. This community data platform enables utilities, planners, and local groups to analyze local generation and load patterns, improving grid forecasting and informing where EV infrastructure and distribution upgrades should be prioritized within HRM.

resources.name: FORCE Data Centre (Fundy Ocean Research Center for Energy)
resources.organization: Fundy Ocean Research Center for Energy (FORCE)
resources.description: FORCE maintains a public data platform sharing high‑resolution environmental and electrical data from the Minas Passage tidal test site and its grid interconnection in Parrsboro. By openly providing generation resource measurements and interconnection performance data to researchers, utilities, and planners, it supports localized forecasting and guides targeted grid upgrades for marine renewables connecting to Nova Scotia’s system.
resources.address: 1156 West Bay Road, Parrsboro, NS B0M 1S0

solutions.text: Community Advocacy and Regional Coordination: Organize residents and businesses to advocate for prioritized intertie upgrades, fair interconnection fee structures and predictable timelines from provincial and utility authorities, leveraging consolidated local evidence and petitions.

resources.name: Climate & Energy Program
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre’s Climate & Energy Program organizes residents, community groups, and businesses to advocate for a cleaner, more reliable grid in Nova Scotia. The team submits evidence to provincial decision-makers and the Utility and Review Board, mobilizes public campaigns and petitions, and presses for prioritized transmission/intertie upgrades as well as fair, transparent interconnection fees and predictable timelines to enable renewables and electrification.

resources.name: Sustainable Communities Advocacy
resources.description: NSFM coordinates Nova Scotia’s municipalities to present unified advocacy to the Province, Nova Scotia Power, and regulators on energy infrastructure. Through joint resolutions, submissions, and stakeholder roundtables, NSFM advances prioritized transmission and intertie upgrades and calls for standardized, predictable interconnection fees and timelines—backed by evidence gathered from member municipalities, local utilities, and businesses.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1304, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Energy and Green Economy Policy Advocacy
resources.description: The Halifax Chamber of Commerce convenes businesses affected by grid constraints to develop policy positions and submissions to government, Nova Scotia Power, and the Utility and Review Board. Through member surveys, policy papers, and letters, the Chamber advocates for prioritized grid and intertie upgrades and for transparent, fair interconnection fee structures with predictable timelines to unlock clean growth and electrification.

resources.name: Affordable Energy Coalition – UARB Interventions
resources.organization: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service (on behalf of the Affordable Energy Coalition)
resources.description: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service represents the Affordable Energy Coalition in Nova Scotia Utility and Review Board proceedings, coordinating community voices and evidence to improve electricity policy. Their interventions advocate for equitable, transparent fee design (including connection-related charges), consumer protections, and clearer, more predictable utility processes and timelines—supporting fair access to electrification and distributed renewables.

obstacles.title: Governance Fragmentation and Coordination Silos
obstacles.description: Misalignment across municipal, provincial, and federal policies—and between urban and rural priorities—slows execution. Data gaps and short planning horizons hinder evidence-based decisions and accountability.

solutions.text: Local Cross-Sector Coordination Councils: Form neighbourhood or regional councils made up of municipal staff, community organizations, business leaders, post-secondary representatives, Indigenous partners, and youth to meet regularly, align priorities, and coordinate local initiatives so projects move from idea to implementation faster and with shared accountability.

resources.name: Halifax Local Immigration Partnership (HLIP)
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: HLIP convenes a cross-sector council co-led by ISANS and the Halifax Regional Municipality, bringing together municipal staff, settlement and community organizations, employers, post-secondary representatives, health and policing, Indigenous and African Nova Scotian partners, and youth voices. Through standing working groups and regular roundtables, partners align priorities, share local newcomer data, and coordinate initiatives (e.g., employment pathways, inclusive community projects) so ideas move to implementation faster with shared accountability.
resources.address: 6960 Mumford Road, Suite 2120, Halifax, NS B3L 4P1

resources.name: Cape Breton Local Immigration Partnership (CBLIP)
resources.description: CBLIP operates as a cross-sector coordination table hosted by the Cape Breton Partnership, uniting municipal units, settlement agencies, Cape Breton University and NSCC, Indigenous partners, employers, and youth to improve newcomer attraction and retention. Its regular council meetings and thematic working groups align regional priorities, share evidence, and coordinate joint projects—accelerating implementation of community and workforce initiatives with clear roles and shared accountability.

resources.name: Centre for Ocean Ventures & Entrepreneurship (COVE) – Oceans Network and Working Groups
resources.description: COVE convenes industry leaders, municipal/provincial/federal officials, post-secondary researchers (e.g., Dalhousie, NSCC), Indigenous partners, and youth talent through standing councils, working groups, and regular network meetings focused on the ocean economy. These local cross-sector tables align priorities, coordinate pilot projects in Halifax Harbour, and share data and accountability frameworks—moving innovations from idea and R&D to deployment faster and with shared responsibility.

resources.name: ACAP Cape Breton – Community Advisory and Coordination Tables
resources.description: ACAP Cape Breton acts as a coordinating hub that brings together Cape Breton Regional Municipality departments, Indigenous communities, local businesses, post-secondary institutions, and youth and community groups to plan and deliver environmental and community development projects. Through recurring advisory committees and cross-sector roundtables, ACAP aligns priorities (e.g., coastal resilience, green jobs, neighborhood revitalization) and coordinates implementation, ensuring initiatives move quickly from concept to action with shared measurement and accountability.

solutions.text: Community Open Data Hub: Create a locally governed open data portal (hosted by a library, university, or community co-op) that aggregates labour, housing, transportation, and service-access data to inform planning, enable evidence-based decisions, and reduce duplication across jurisdictions.

resources.name: Halifax Open Data
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s open data program publishes machine‑readable datasets on transit (including GTFS), land use and zoning, property, active transportation, recreation facilities, and more. By centralizing municipal datasets and providing APIs and bulk downloads, it enables planners, community groups, and researchers to analyze housing, transportation, and service-access patterns without duplicating data collection. The portal’s standardized formats and metadata support evidence-based decisions and coordination with provincial and federal programs operating in the region.

resources.name: Nova Scotia Open Data Portal
resources.description: The provincial open data portal aggregates datasets across departments on topics such as labour market and economy, housing and property, transportation infrastructure, and community and social services. It provides a single, governed platform with APIs that reduce duplication across municipalities and supports cross-jurisdictional analysis for planning and accountability. Local governments, non-profits, and researchers use these standardized datasets to inform evidence-based strategies that align provincial and municipal priorities.

resources.name: CBRM Open Data
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Municipality’s open data portal consolidates municipal geospatial and tabular data including land use, properties, transportation networks, civic addresses, and community services. By making these datasets publicly accessible and reusable, it supports local planning for housing, mobility, and service access, and allows community groups and institutions to build evidence-based projects without recreating data. The portal helps coordinate work between municipal units and outside partners by using common formats and a shared catalogue.

resources.name: Energize Bridgewater Data Hub
resources.description: As part of its Smart Cities energy poverty initiative, the Town of Bridgewater maintains a public data hub that maps and shares community energy, housing condition, transportation access, and related service information. The platform consolidates local and partner datasets to guide municipal programs and community collaborations, helping target supports, plan transit and active transportation, and improve housing outcomes. By publishing data and indicators in one place, it reduces duplication across agencies and enables residents and organizations to make evidence-based decisions.

solutions.text: Multi-Year Community Development Plans: Develop 3–5 year plans led by communities that set measurable goals for youth retention, skills development, and quality-of-life improvements; these plans include check-in milestones to extend planning horizons beyond election cycles and create continuity across governments.

resources.name: Halifax Economic Growth Plan 2022–27
resources.description: Halifax Partnership leads a five-year, community-driven plan for inclusive growth that sets measurable targets for talent attraction and retention (including youth and recent graduates), skills development, entrepreneurship, and quality-of-life improvements. The plan includes annual scorecards and check-in milestones with cross-sector partners (municipal, provincial, post-secondary, and industry) to extend planning beyond election cycles and maintain continuity across governments.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1201, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Municipality of the County of Kings Strategic Plan 2021–2024
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
resources.description: This multi-year municipal plan sets out specific goals and indicators for population and workforce attraction/retention, recreation and housing, active transportation, and downtown/rural vitality—key quality-of-life and youth retention drivers. Progress is tracked through scheduled reporting to Council and the public, and aligned with long-horizon land-use planning (Kings 2050), creating continuity across political terms and coordinating actions with provincial and community partners.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: Town of Truro Strategic Plan 2023–2026
resources.description: Truro’s four-year strategic plan establishes measurable objectives for workforce and population growth, downtown revitalization, active transportation, recreation, and service improvements that directly support youth retention and quality of life. The town conducts regular progress updates and collaborates with regional partners (e.g., County of Colchester, post-secondary institutions, and the Province) to coordinate implementation beyond election cycles and maintain accountability.

solutions.text: Inter-Municipal Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs): Encourage neighbouring municipalities to sign simple MOUs to share services, coordinate land-use and transit planning, and pool funding for regional priorities, reducing policy fragmentation and improving efficiency for rural-urban linkages.

resources.name: Eastern District Planning Commission (EDPC)
resources.description: EDPC is an inter-municipal planning service created through agreements among several municipalities in eastern Nova Scotia to share land-use planning, development control, and building inspection. By pooling staff, data systems (including GIS), and policy expertise across municipal boundaries, EDPC coordinates municipal planning strategies and by-laws, reducing fragmentation and enabling consistent, regionally aligned decisions that support rural-urban linkages.
resources.address: 606 Reeves Street, Port Hawkesbury, NS B9A 2R7

resources.name: Town and County of Antigonish Joint Planning and Building Services
resources.organization: Town of Antigonish and Municipality of the County of Antigonish
resources.description: Through a shared-services agreement, the Town of Antigonish and the Municipality of the County of Antigonish operate a joint planning and building services team that harmonizes land-use policies, development review, and building inspection across urban and rural areas. The arrangement pools funding and professional capacity, coordinates growth management and active transportation planning, and creates a single interface for developers and residents, directly reducing governance silos.
resources.address: 285 Beech Hill Road, Antigonish, NS B2G 0B4

resources.name: Kings Partnership Steering Committee (KPSC) / Kings 2050 Collaboration
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Kings; Town of Berwick; Town of Kentville; Town of Wolfville
resources.description: KPSC is an inter-municipal forum established by agreement among the County of Kings and the Towns of Berwick, Kentville, and Wolfville to coordinate on shared services and regional planning. Through initiatives such as the Kings 2050 collaboration, partners align municipal planning strategies, coordinate regional transit and solid waste services, and pool resources for cross-boundary priorities, improving efficiency and reducing policy fragmentation across the Annapolis Valley’s rural and urban communities.
resources.address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

resources.name: Transit Lunenburg County (TLC)
resources.organization: Town of Bridgewater (on behalf of municipal partners in Lunenburg County)
resources.description: TLC is a regional transit service delivered through an inter-municipal partnership that includes the Town of Bridgewater and neighboring municipal units, pooling municipal and provincial funding to run coordinated routes serving both urban and rural communities. The partnership aligns service design with land-use and economic nodes across municipal boundaries, creating a unified governance and planning table that reduces fragmentation in mobility planning and strengthens rural-urban connectivity.

solutions.text: Community Data Stewards Program: Train volunteers and staff from local organizations to collect, curate, and interpret community-level data (surveys, vacancy rates, youth employment outcomes) so data gaps shrink and local evidence feeds into higher-level policy conversations.

resources.name: Community-Based Coastal and Freshwater Monitoring
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre trains community volunteers, local organizations, and municipal partners to collect standardized water quality and habitat data in watersheds and along the coast across Nova Scotia. They curate and interpret these community-level datasets, publish accessible reports, and translate findings into briefs and submissions to municipal, provincial, and federal policymakers—shrinking data gaps and ensuring locally gathered evidence informs higher-level decisions.

resources.name: LaHave River Watershed Project (Community-Based Monitoring)
resources.description: Coastal Action trains residents, students, and staff from partner community organizations to collect long-term water quality and habitat data throughout the LaHave River watershed and nearby communities. The organization curates and analyzes the data, shares results with municipalities and provincial regulators, and uses the evidence to guide management actions and policy advocacy—building local data stewardship capacity and feeding community evidence into policy conversations.
resources.address: 37 Tannery Road, Unit 2, Lunenburg, NS B0J 2C0

resources.name: Research, Evaluation, and Data Services
resources.organization: Immigration Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS builds data capacity among staff and community partners by training them to design and run surveys, track employment and settlement outcomes (including youth), and interpret findings for program improvement. The team curates community-level datasets and briefs that are shared with municipal, provincial, and federal stakeholders, reducing data gaps and aligning on-the-ground evidence with policy development.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Community Energy Data & HomeWarming Insights
resources.description: Through programs like HomeWarming, Clean Foundation trains partner organizations’ outreach staff and community ambassadors to gather standardized household data on energy efficiency, housing conditions, and energy affordability across Nova Scotia. Clean curates and analyzes these data to produce community-level insights that are shared with municipalities and the Province, informing housing, climate, and affordability policy while closing data gaps for underserved communities.

solutions.text: Youth-Led Advisory Panels: Establish panels of diverse young residents who co-design local strategies, advise councils, and help monitor progress. Their ongoing input helps align policies with youth priorities and holds decision-makers accountable.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Youth Advisory Committee
resources.description: The HRM Youth Advisory Committee is a panel of diverse residents ages 15–24 that advises Halifax Regional Council and its standing committees on policies, programs, and services that affect youth. Members co-design engagement strategies, bring forward recommendations across departments (e.g., recreation, transit, planning), and review staff follow-ups, creating an ongoing feedback loop that aligns municipal actions with youth priorities and supports accountability for progress.

resources.name: Truro Youth Council
resources.description: The Truro Youth Council brings together secondary and post-secondary youth from across the town to advise the Mayor and Town Council on local priorities such as recreation, downtown vitality, housing, and transportation. Through regular meetings, formal presentations to Council, and participation in municipal projects, the council co-designs strategies and helps track implementation, ensuring decision-makers remain accountable to youth perspectives across departments.

resources.name: Teen Advisory Groups (TAG)
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries hosts Teen Advisory Groups at multiple branches where youth plan programs, advise on services and spaces, and provide feedback on library and community initiatives. These youth-led panels co-design local engagement strategies and report on outcomes with staff, helping a key municipal service align with youth needs and maintain transparency about progress across urban and suburban communities.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: IWK Youth Advisory Council
resources.description: The IWK Youth Advisory Council is made up of youth and young adults who partner with IWK Health leadership to shape policies, care experiences, and quality-improvement projects in pediatric and mental health services. By co-designing initiatives, reviewing patient-experience data, and offering ongoing advice to decision-makers, the council ensures health-system actions reflect youth priorities and that progress is monitored and reported.

solutions.text: Regional Pilot Projects and Learning Labs: Run small, time-bound pilots (affordable housing models, apprenticeship pathways, shared workspace hubs) across municipalities with common evaluation metrics so successful models scale and policy can be adjusted based on local evidence.

resources.name: Downtowns & Main Streets Initiative
resources.description: Build Nova Scotia partners with municipalities across the province to deliver quick, time-bound placemaking pilots—such as pop-up public spaces, active transportation improvements, and storefront activations—with standardized reporting on outcomes like foot traffic, business engagement, and vacancy impacts. The initiative functions as a learning lab model: results and toolkits are shared across participating communities so successful approaches scale to other towns and inform provincial policy and investment decisions.
resources.address: 1875 Upper Water Street, Suite 300, Halifax, NS B3J 1S9

resources.name: Energize Bridgewater
resources.description: The Town of Bridgewater runs data-driven pilot projects to reduce energy poverty and improve housing affordability, including clean energy financing (PACE), retrofit demonstrations, and home energy coaching—each with clear evaluation metrics tied to household savings, emissions, and participation. The program openly shares tools, data, and lessons with other Nova Scotia municipalities and national networks, enabling proven models to scale and informing policy adjustments at the municipal and provincial levels.

resources.name: IGNITE Atlantic – Rural Innovation Hubs and Applied Innovation Pilots
resources.description: IGNITE Atlantic operates collaborative innovation hubs in multiple rural municipalities, running time-bound pilot challenges with local governments, SMEs, and youth founders to test solutions (e.g., ocean, clean tech, agri-tech) in real-world settings. Cohorts use shared KPIs (adoption, jobs/placements, commercialization pathways) and post-pilot reporting, allowing successful pilots to scale across communities and informing municipal and regional policy/practice based on evidence.
resources.address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

resources.name: Nova Scotia Works Innovation Lab
resources.organization: Centre for Employment Innovation (St. Francis Xavier University)
resources.description: Housed at St. Francis Xavier University’s Centre for Employment Innovation, this lab co-designs and evaluates short, place-based pilots with Nova Scotia Works employment service providers across municipalities to improve youth and underrepresented groups’ pathways into training, apprenticeships, and work. Using common evaluation frameworks and developmental evaluation, findings are shared system-wide so effective models scale and inform provincial employment and skills policy.

resources.name: Solar City Program
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality’s Solar City pioneered a municipal PACE financing pilot for residential solar and efficiency upgrades with standardized participation, cost, and performance metrics. The model, data, and procurement templates have been shared widely, enabling other Nova Scotia municipalities to adopt similar programs and informing provincial clean energy and housing affordability policies through evidence gathered locally.

solutions.text: Community Performance Dashboards: Publish simple, accessible dashboards tracking key local indicators (jobs for youth, housing availability, transit access, program take-up) so residents and officials can see progress, compare neighbourhoods, and make data-driven choices.

resources.name: Centre Plan Key Performance Indicator (KPI) Dashboard
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality publishes an online KPI dashboard that tracks development activity, new housing units, density targets, and related planning indicators across the Regional Centre. The dashboard lets residents, councillors, and planners monitor progress by area, compare trends across neighbourhoods, and assess the take-up of planning tools to guide housing and infrastructure decisions. This accessible, regularly updated view supports coordinated, evidence-based choices across municipal and provincial priorities.

resources.name: Halifax Index (Interactive Economic and Community Dashboard)
resources.description: The Halifax Index is an annual, interactive dashboard that consolidates data on labour markets (including youth employment), population, business growth, housing and real estate, transportation, and quality of life. Produced by Halifax Partnership, it enables the public and decision-makers to track performance over time and benchmark Halifax against peer cities, with downloadable data and clear visualizations. By presenting comparable, citywide indicators in one place, it supports data-driven policy alignment and investment decisions across sectors.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1201, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Nova Scotia Open Data Portal (Dashboards and Indicators)
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Open Data Portal centralizes public datasets and interactive visualizations (story dashboards) published by provincial departments, including indicators related to labour markets, housing and construction activity, and transportation and mobility. These dashboards and standardized datasets allow municipalities, community groups, and residents to monitor trends, compare communities, and evaluate program take-up using a shared, authoritative source. The platform reduces information silos and shortens feedback loops for evidence-based decision-making across the province.

resources.name: Energize Bridgewater Community Energy and Emissions Dashboard
resources.description: The Town of Bridgewater’s Energize Bridgewater initiative publishes an online dashboard tracking local energy use, household energy affordability, transportation mode share, and progress on retrofit and clean-energy programs. Residents and officials can view clear, neighborhood-scale indicators and program participation metrics to compare areas, target investments, and measure outcomes over time. This community performance dashboard helps align municipal actions with provincial climate, housing affordability, and equity goals using transparent, shared data.

solutions.text: Joint Funding Consortia: Build coalitions of municipalities, non-profits, businesses, and post-secondary institutions that pool grant-matching funds to co-invest in cross-jurisdictional projects, making it easier to pursue longer-term initiatives that transcend political cycles.

resources.name: Internet for Nova Scotia Initiative (IFNSI)
resources.description: IFNSI is a province-wide broadband build-out led by Build Nova Scotia that pools funding from the Nova Scotia Internet Funding Trust, federal broadband programs, municipalities, and private internet service providers to co-invest in large, multi-year projects. By coordinating cross-municipal builds and aligning public and private matching dollars, the initiative overcomes governance silos and enables long-term infrastructure commitments that extend beyond political cycles.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Ocean Startup Project
resources.organization: Centre for Ocean Ventures and Entrepreneurship (COVE) and partners
resources.description: The Ocean Startup Project is a multi-partner consortium that pools funding from federal (e.g., ACOA), industry (e.g., Canada’s Ocean Supercluster), and provincial partners to co-invest in startup competitions, accelerators, and commercialization supports across Atlantic Canada. Hosted at COVE in Dartmouth, it convenes universities, colleges, industry, and municipalities to match funds and deliver cross-jurisdictional programming that strengthens the ocean economy over multiple years.

resources.name: Ocean Frontier Institute (OFI)
resources.description: OFI is a research consortium led by Dalhousie University that brings together multiple Atlantic universities, federal laboratories, Indigenous and community organizations, and industry to co-fund large-scale ocean research. Using pooled and matched funds from the Canada First Research Excellence Fund and provincial/industry partners, OFI supports multi-year, cross-jurisdictional projects that align policy, science, and industry needs while building shared data and evidence for decision-making.
resources.address: Steele Ocean Sciences Building, 1355 Oxford Street, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2

resources.name: Perennia Collaborative Applied Research and Extension Programs
resources.description: Perennia convenes producers, processors, municipalities, Dalhousie’s Faculty of Agriculture, and provincial/federal funders (e.g., Sustainable Canadian Agricultural Partnership) to pool matching funds for applied research, extension, and pilot projects in agri-food. These consortia-based initiatives operate across rural regions of Nova Scotia, reduce duplication among jurisdictions, and sustain multi-year projects that help align policy, market needs, and community outcomes.
resources.address: 199 Innovation Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2H5

solutions.text: Regular Knowledge-Sharing Forums: Host quarterly forums where municipal staff, community groups, and provincial representatives exchange lessons, harmonize approaches, and create shared toolkits — reducing siloed practice and speeding adoption of proven policies.

resources.name: NSFM Regional Caucus Meetings and Annual Conference
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Federation of Municipalities convenes regular regional caucus meetings (rural, towns, and regional municipalities) and an annual conference that bring together municipal staff, elected officials, and provincial department representatives to exchange lessons and align on priority files. These forums surface common challenges, harmonize approaches across jurisdictions, and generate shared toolkits and templates (e.g., on housing, asset management, and climate adaptation) that reduce siloed practice and speed adoption of proven policies.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1106, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Sustainable Communities Challenge Fund (SCCF) Learning Series
resources.description: As the program administrator for Nova Scotia’s SCCF, Clean Foundation hosts recurring knowledge‑exchange webinars and communities of practice that convene municipal staff, Mi’kmaw communities, nonprofits, and provincial Environment and Climate Change representatives. The sessions share lessons from funded projects, align methodologies, and produce reusable guidance, templates, and case studies—creating shared toolkits that reduce duplication and accelerate community adoption of effective climate and sustainability policies.

resources.name: Physical Activity Leadership (PAL) Network and Provincial–Municipal Recreation Roundtables
resources.description: Recreation Nova Scotia facilitates the PAL Network and regular provincial–municipal recreation leadership roundtables that connect municipal recreation directors, community organizations, and provincial partners from Communities, Culture, Tourism and Heritage and Public Health. Meeting on a recurring (often quarterly) basis, these forums share program models and data, co‑develop practical toolkits and training (e.g., youth engagement, inclusion, active transportation), and help align policy and program delivery across urban and rural communities.
resources.address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

solutions.text: Rural-Urban Liaison Roles: Create volunteer or part-time liaison positions that connect rural communities with urban centres and provincial agencies to ensure priorities, transit links, and workforce pipelines are coordinated and that rural voices are reflected in regional planning.

resources.name: NSFM Rural Caucus
resources.description: The Rural Caucus of the Nova Scotia Federation of Municipalities brings together elected officials from rural municipalities to coordinate priorities and speak with one voice to provincial departments and urban centres. Through policy working groups and regular liaison with the Province, it ensures rural perspectives inform regional planning discussions on issues like transportation connectivity, housing, and workforce development, thereby reducing governance silos and aligning actions across jurisdictions.
resources.address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1304, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

resources.name: Intergovernmental & Rights Implementation
resources.description: This department at The Confederacy of Mainland Mi'kmaq serves as a formal liaison between Mi'kmaw communities (many of them rural) and provincial/federal agencies, ensuring community priorities are reflected in regional policy and planning. By coordinating multi-party tables on infrastructure, transportation access, education/employment pathways, and land-use considerations, it channels rural voices into decision-making and aligns programs that build workforce and service links between communities and urban hubs.
resources.address: 57 Martin Crescent, Truro Heights, NS B6L 1L4

resources.name: Connect2 Active Transportation Program
resources.organization: Clean Foundation (in partnership with the Province of Nova Scotia)
resources.description: Connect2 convenes municipalities, community groups, and the Province to plan and fund active transportation projects that link people to key destinations, often bridging rural communities with urban service centres. Acting as a facilitator and liaison, the program supports evidence-based project selection, provincial-municipal coordination, and integrated mobility planning—strengthening transit links and ensuring local priorities inform regional transportation strategies.

resources.name: Kings Transit Authority (Inter-Municipal Transit Service)
resources.description: Kings Transit Authority operates an inter-municipal transit system across the Annapolis Valley, coordinating with multiple rural municipalities and the Province to align routes, funding, and service standards. By linking smaller communities with urban hubs like Kentville and Wolfville and participating in regional planning forums, KTA functions as a practical liaison for mobility priorities, enabling workforce access, education commutes, and service connectivity across jurisdictions.
resources.address: 29 Crescent Drive, New Minas, NS B4N 3G7

solutions.text: Participatory Budgeting for Youth Priorities: Allocate a portion of municipal or community organization budgets for participatory budgeting processes focused on youth-led projects, increasing transparency, aligning spending with community needs, and fostering sustained civic engagement.

resources.name: District 7 Participatory Budgeting (Halifax South Downtown)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality allocates a portion of the District 7 capital funds to a participatory budgeting process where community members propose and vote on projects. Youth-led and youth-serving groups are explicitly invited to submit ideas (e.g., school clubs, arts, recreation, and community services), and youth residents are encouraged to participate in project selection, aligning spending with youth priorities. This open vote and public reporting increase transparency while cultivating sustained civic engagement among young people.

resources.name: District 8 Participatory Budgeting (Halifax Peninsula North)
resources.description: HRM’s District 8 uses participatory budgeting to direct a share of district capital funds to projects chosen by residents, with outreach that encourages youth-led proposals and youth participation in voting. The process elevates local youth priorities—such as safe spaces, programming, culture, and recreation—through project pitches and public decision-making. By publishing results and funding decisions, it enhances transparency and keeps spending aligned with community needs identified by young people.

resources.name: District 5 Participatory Budgeting (Dartmouth Centre)
resources.description: Through District 5’s participatory budgeting, a defined portion of local capital funds is set aside for community-proposed projects that are selected by resident vote, including youth. Youth organizations and young leaders can submit proposals that respond to local needs—such as arts, recreation, safety, and skills programs—and help decide which initiatives are funded. The process provides clear, public criteria and results, building trust, accountability, and ongoing civic engagement among young people.

resources.name: District 9 Participatory Budgeting (Halifax West Armdale)
resources.description: District 9 runs a participatory budgeting process that dedicates part of its district capital funds to projects prioritized by residents, with targeted outreach to ensure youth-led initiatives are proposed and voted on. By enabling young people to help allocate funds to community improvements—from recreation to cultural programming—the initiative aligns spending with youth priorities while making decisions transparent. This hands-on process strengthens youth civic engagement and builds capacity for collaborative local governance.

obstacles.title: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
obstacles.description: Limited affordable recreation, nightlife, and year-round public spaces—especially in smaller towns—reduce day-to-day quality of life. A lack of ‘third places’ weakens social ties and belonging.

solutions.text: Pop-up events in vacant storefronts: Organize rotating weekend or evening pop-ups (food, craft markets, music, exhibitions) in empty retail spaces. Run by community groups and local entrepreneurs, these activate downtowns, support small vendors, and create low-cost nightlife without long-term commercial leases.

resources.name: Gritty to Pretty: Storefront and Public Space Animation Grants
resources.description: Gritty to Pretty funds short-term activations that turn empty or underused downtown storefronts into pop-up galleries, micro-retail, and performance spaces. By partnering with property owners and local creatives, the program enables evening and weekend pop-ups that animate vacant retail bays, support small vendors and artists, and draw foot traffic to Downtown Halifax without long-term leases.
resources.address: 1546 Barrington Street, Suite 104, Halifax, NS B3J 2A2

resources.name: Downtown Truro Pop-Up Shop Program
resources.description: This initiative matches landlords of vacant storefronts with local makers, food entrepreneurs, and community groups to host short-term retail and cultural pop-ups on weekends and evenings. By lowering barriers to entry and activating empty spaces on Prince Street and nearby blocks, the program creates lively third places, boosts downtown vibrancy, and gives small vendors a low-cost way to test the market.

resources.name: Downtown Sydney Pop-Up Shops
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: Working with property owners and the downtown business district, this program curates rotating artisan and craft pop-ups in temporarily vacant storefronts along Charlotte Street, especially during evenings and weekends. These short-term shops and exhibitions activate idle retail spaces, provide low-cost opportunities for local creatives, and attract residents back to the core with music, markets, and cultural programming.

solutions.text: Shared-use community hubs: Convert underused municipal buildings, libraries, or school gyms into multi-use hubs with scheduled programming (classes, co-working, youth hangouts, evening cafés). Managed by a community board, fees are sliding-scale and hours extend into evenings/weekends.

resources.name: Halifax Central Library
resources.description: Halifax Central Library functions as a shared-use community hub with free co-working-style spaces, bookable meeting rooms, performance venues, and a public rooftop alongside an on-site café. It delivers a full calendar of classes, tech workshops, youth hangouts, and cultural events, and maintains evening and weekend hours; rooms and services are free or low-cost, making it an accessible ‘third place’ managed by a public library board.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: People’s Place: Antigonish Town & County Library
resources.description: People’s Place transforms the town library into a multi-purpose hub with program rooms, a community living room, exhibit space, and a courtyard used for classes, meetups, youth activities, and performances. Operated by the regional library system, it offers evening and weekend hours, free drop-in space and Wi‑Fi, and low-cost room bookings—embodying the ‘third place’ model that strengthens social ties year-round.

resources.name: Eltuek Arts Centre
resources.description: Eltuek Arts Centre repurposes the former Holy Angels school site into a multi-tenant arts and community hub with studios, galleries, shared meeting rooms, and event spaces. Operated by New Dawn, it hosts workshops, exhibitions, youth creative programs, and community gatherings—often in the evenings and on weekends—with accessible, affordable space rentals that enable wide community use.

resources.name: The North Grove (Community Hub)
resources.description: The North Grove operates a shared-use community hub that combines a family resource centre and community food centre with commercial kitchens, classrooms, play spaces, and gardens. It offers scheduled programming such as community meals, after-school youth activities, and skills classes—many offered free or pay-what-you-can—and regularly hosts evening events, creating an inclusive ‘third place’ governed by a community non-profit.

resources.name: The Deanery Project
resources.description: The Deanery Project revitalizes a former church retreat into a rural community hub featuring co-working areas, makerspaces, classrooms, and performance spaces. It runs workshops, artist residencies, film nights, and youth programs—often on a sliding-scale or by-donation basis—and hosts evening and weekend events, demonstrating shared community governance and accessible, year-round use.
resources.address: 37 Deanery Road, Lower Ship Harbour, NS B0J 1W0

solutions.text: Community-run café/co-op as a 'third place': Form a cooperative to open a volunteer-run café or social space offering affordable food, free wifi, meeting rooms, and cultural programming. Profits reinvested in programming and subsidized space rental for local groups.

resources.name: Just Us! Coffeehouse – Wolfville
resources.description: A worker-owned co‑operative café that provides affordable food and fair‑trade coffee, free Wi‑Fi, and a welcoming space for meetups and small gatherings. The Wolfville coffeehouse hosts community events and bookings, and as a co‑op, surplus revenue is reinvested into education, programming, and community initiatives—aligning with the third‑place model that supports local groups.

resources.name: Bus Stop Theatre Co‑op
resources.description: A member‑owned co‑operative arts venue that operates year‑round as a community hub with free Wi‑Fi, accessible gathering space, and diverse cultural programming (theatre, music, film, and community meetings). Revenues are reinvested to maintain programming and offer subsidized rental rates for local groups, delivering a co‑op ‘third place’ that strengthens social ties in Halifax’s North End.

resources.name: The Loaded Ladle (Student‑Run Food Co‑op)
resources.description: A volunteer‑driven, non‑profit food co‑operative that serves free/pay‑what‑you‑can plant‑based meals and hosts workshops and community events in the Dalhousie Student Union Building, creating an inclusive third‑place environment with seating and Wi‑Fi. Funds and donations are reinvested into programming, and the co‑op collaborates with campus and community groups to share space and resources at low or no cost.

resources.name: The North Grove (Community Café & Hub)
resources.description: A community hub in Dartmouth North offering drop‑in community meals, free Wi‑Fi, a welcoming café‑style gathering area, and meeting rooms alongside cooking programs and cultural activities. Supported by volunteers and community partners, revenues and donations are reinvested into programs and free/subsidized space for local groups, functioning as a neighborhood third place year‑round.

solutions.text: Seasonal and winterized public-space activation: Install temporary heated pavilions, skating/hockey rinks, covered market stalls, and lighting to extend outdoor use year-round. Community volunteers help maintain features and programing keeps spaces lively across seasons.

resources.name: Emera Oval (Halifax Common)
resources.description: The Emera Oval is a large, refrigerated outdoor skating rink that operates all winter with free public skating, equipment lending, lighting, and on-site heated facilities, then transitions to inline/roller skating and other activities in warmer seasons. HRM programs lessons, theme skates, and community events that keep the Halifax Common active year-round, extending use of the public space across seasons and improving accessible, affordable recreation.

resources.name: Evergreen Festival / Evergreen Bright
resources.description: Evergreen transforms the Halifax Waterfront into a winter destination with illuminated trails, light art, and a seasonal market using covered vendor huts, wind breaks, outdoor heaters, and cozy gathering spots. Programming includes live music, cultural performances, and family-friendly activities that draw people outdoors in colder months, activating public spaces and waterfront plazas through the season.
resources.address: 1875 Upper Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 1S9

resources.name: Truro Civic Square Skating Oval
resources.organization: Town of Truro Parks, Recreation & Culture
resources.description: Each winter, the Town of Truro installs and maintains a public skating oval in Civic Square with lighting, music, and special-event programming that draws residents downtown. The space also hosts winter festivals and community-led activities, turning the central square into a seasonal hub and extending outdoor use with accessible, low-cost recreation.

resources.name: Downtown Dartmouth Ice Festival
resources.description: This annual winter festival activates public streets and plazas with illuminated ice sculptures, live entertainment, and outdoor programming that encourages people to explore the downtown on foot. Pop-up vendors and sheltered stalls complement the installations, while community volunteers and local businesses help animate and maintain spaces during the cold season.

solutions.text: Evening markets and extended-hours nights: Coordinate monthly evening markets, themed 'night out' events or late-shopping nights with local businesses, street performances, and family-friendly activities to create regular safe nightlife options.

resources.name: Friday Night Market (Annapolis Royal)
resources.description: From late spring through fall, the Town of Annapolis Royal hosts a weekly Friday Night Market that turns St. George Street and Market Square into a pedestrian-friendly evening marketplace. Local artisans, food vendors, and shops stay open late while live music and street performances create a safe, family-friendly ‘night out’ experience that supports downtown businesses and social gathering.
resources.address: 285 St. George Street, Annapolis Royal, NS B0S 1A0

resources.name: Moonlight Madness (Downtown Truro)
resources.description: Downtown Truro Partnership’s Moonlight Madness is a recurring late-shopping night that sees downtown businesses extend their hours into the evening and activate the streets with music, buskers, and pop-up vendors. The event creates a festive, family-friendly nighttime environment and encourages residents to gather in public spaces while supporting local retail and food businesses.
resources.address: 605 Prince Street, Suite 305, Truro, NS B2N 1G2

resources.name: Creamery Square Night Market (Tatamagouche)
resources.description: Held seasonally at the waterfront, the Creamery Square Night Market offers evening shopping with local producers, artisans, and food vendors alongside live entertainment. By programming markets after typical business hours and adding music and family-friendly activities, it provides a safe, social ‘night out’ that strengthens community life and supports small businesses.

resources.name: Food Truck Friday at the Barn (Hubbards)
resources.description: The Hubbards Barn Association runs weekly evening Food Truck Fridays with multiple local vendors, live music, and family-friendly space on the Barn grounds. These extended-hours nights draw residents and visitors for a casual community ‘night out,’ supporting local food entrepreneurs and creating regular, safe nighttime activity in a shared public venue.

resources.name: Riverfront Night Market (New Glasgow)
resources.organization: Town of New Glasgow / Glasgow Square Theatre
resources.description: Hosted at Glasgow Square on the East River, New Glasgow’s Riverfront Night Market features evening vendors, live performances, and food offerings with nearby businesses staying open late. The series transforms the riverfront into a safe, family-friendly nightlife option that blends culture, commerce, and public space activation.
resources.address: 155 Riverside Parkway, New Glasgow, NS B2H 5E8

solutions.text: Community arts incubators and pop-up galleries: Support artist collectives to use empty spaces for studios, shows, and workshops. Low-cost studio share, open-mic nights, and artist-led classes build cultural life and give creatives reasons to stay or return.

resources.name: Eltuek Arts Centre
resources.organization: Eltuek Arts Centre (operated by New Dawn Enterprises)
resources.description: Eltuek Arts Centre repurposes a historic former convent/school into a multidisciplinary arts hub with affordable artist studios, shared workspaces, galleries, and community rooms. They host exhibitions, pop-up shows, workshops, and artist-led programs that activate underused space and create a vibrant third place for Sydney’s creative community, encouraging artists to stay or return.

resources.name: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
resources.description: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design runs community studios (ceramics, metals, textiles, print) with low-cost memberships and day passes, plus artist-led classes and mentorship for all skill levels. Its gallery and seasonal pop-up markets showcase local work, while open studio access functions as a craft incubator that animates downtown Sydney year-round.

resources.name: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
resources.description: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts provides studio and rehearsal spaces, artist residencies, and a robust schedule of artist-led workshops for youth and adults. By combining affordable creation space with public exhibitions and performances—and partnering on pop-up projects—it serves as a rural arts incubator and third place that strengthens community life year-round.
resources.address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

resources.name: Lunenburg School of the Arts
resources.description: Lunenburg School of the Arts offers artist-led workshops and courses throughout the year and converts classrooms into active studio and exhibition spaces. Through accessible programming, visiting artist initiatives, and community events, it gives local creatives a reason to learn, teach, and showcase work in a walkable small-town setting.

resources.name: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op
resources.description: The Bus Stop Theatre Co-op is a cooperatively run performance and arts venue that offers affordable rentals for pop-up shows, readings, screenings, and multidisciplinary events. By hosting open-mic nights, community festivals, and artist-led workshops, it turns a main-street space into a year-round cultural third place that supports emerging creators.

solutions.text: Affordable programming fund and microgrants: Establish a small community fund (crowdfunded + municipal match) to provide microgrants to grassroots organizers for festivals, sports leagues, youth nights, and other low-cost recreation initiatives.

resources.name: Halifax Regional Municipality Community Grants Program
resources.description: HRM’s Community Grants Program provides small project grants to non-profit and volunteer groups to deliver low-cost or free community programming, including local festivals, youth activities, neighborhood sport leagues, and public-space activations. The microgrants help cover modest costs like equipment, venue rentals, permits, and insurance, enabling grassroots organizers to create accessible, year-round recreation and ‘third place’ experiences that strengthen social ties.

resources.name: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg Community Grants
resources.organization: Municipality of the District of Lunenburg
resources.description: MODL offers several small grant streams that provide micro-funding to community halls, recreation associations, and volunteer groups to run festivals, youth nights, and local sport and recreation programs across rural communities. These grants—typically a few thousand dollars—offset equipment, space, and promotion costs so organizers can keep participation fees low or free, building vibrant, inclusive ‘third places’ year-round.

resources.name: Municipality of Colchester Community Grants Program
resources.organization: Municipality of the County of Colchester
resources.description: The County of Colchester provides small project grants to non-profit and volunteer organizations for community development, recreation, and local events throughout the county. Funding helps grassroots organizers cover program delivery costs such as equipment, facility rentals, and insurance, enabling affordable festivals, sport leagues, and youth-oriented activities that activate public spaces and build community belonging.

resources.name: Sport Nova Scotia Sport Fund
resources.description: The Sport Fund offers seed microgrants to community sport organizations across Nova Scotia to start or expand low-cost sport and physical activity programs. Grants typically cover equipment, coaching training, and facility costs, which lowers financial barriers so local groups can deliver affordable leagues, try‑it sessions, and after‑school programs that engage children and youth in accessible recreation.
resources.address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

solutions.text: Community transportation for evening events: Coordinate volunteer-run or subsidized shuttle services and safe-route escorts for teens and seniors to access evening programming, increasing attendance and reducing barriers created by limited transit in smaller towns.

resources.name: Community Wheels
resources.organization: St. Margaret’s Bay Community Transportation Society
resources.description: Community Wheels is a volunteer-driven, door-to-door community transit service serving the rural St. Margaret’s Bay area.
