Participating companies are publicly recognized by the program and industry partners, signaling a youth-friendly workplace and helping them attract emerging talent while enhancing the region’s reputation for career-ready opportunities.
resources.address: 260 Brownlow Avenue, Unit 3, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1V9

resources.name: Clean Leadership Summer Internship Program
resources.description: This province-wide program invites organizations to pledge host roles for youth (ages 15–30) in paid summer internships focused on clean growth, climate action, and community impact, offering real project experience and mentorship. Host employers are profiled as partners and can display program recognition, reinforcing their reputation as youth-friendly and flexible workplaces that contribute to Nova Scotia’s innovative, sustainable economy.

resources.name: Techsploration Employer Partnerships
resources.description: Techsploration engages Nova Scotia employers to commit time and resources to mentor and host young women exploring careers in science, trades, and technology, creating visible pathways from school to skilled careers. Employer partners are publicly recognized by Techsploration and can use partnership branding, signaling a commitment to inclusive youth talent development and helping shift regional perceptions about local opportunities in high-demand fields.
resources.address: 36 Brookshire Court, Suite 210, Bedford, NS B4A 4E9

obstacles.title: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
obstacles.description: Rising costs for food, transportation, utilities, and insurance outpace wage gains. Even with a job, basic affordability challenges constrain lifestyle and savings for young people.

solutions.text: Community Food Co-op and Bulk-Buy Program: A member-run grocery co-op that aggregates bulk purchases from regional suppliers (including Maritime producers) to lower grocery costs, offers sliding-scale memberships for youth, and hosts weekly low-cost pantry staples distribution.

resources.name: Square Roots Bundle Program
resources.description: Square Roots aggregates surplus and locally sourced produce into affordable, pay-what-you-can food bundles that are distributed through community hubs across Nova Scotia. By bulk-purchasing from farms and wholesalers and rescuing excess food, the program lowers grocery costs while offering sliding-scale pricing that is accessible to youth, students, and low-income residents. Regular monthly or biweekly distributions provide consistent access to low-cost pantry staples and fresh items.

resources.name: Affordable Produce Market (Dartmouth North Community Food Centre)
resources.organization: Dartmouth Family Centre & Dartmouth North Community Food Centre
resources.description: The Dartmouth North Community Food Centre runs an affordable produce market that sources food through bulk and wholesale channels to keep prices low for community members. The weekly market prioritizes pantry staples and fresh basics at reduced cost and often incorporates pay-what-you-can or low/no-cost access through community programs, making it youth- and family-friendly. This model mirrors a community bulk-buy approach to lower grocery bills and improve regular access to essentials.

resources.name: Mobile Food Market (Halifax)
resources.organization: Ecology Action Centre (in partnership with Halifax Regional Municipality)
resources.description: The Mobile Food Market partners with local growers and wholesalers to bulk-purchase produce and sell it at pop-up markets in communities across Halifax at reduced prices. By aggregating supply and operating weekly or biweekly markets, it offers affordable produce packs and staples, increasing access to healthy food for youth, seniors, and families facing high grocery costs. The initiative functions like a community buying club on wheels, bringing low-cost essentials directly to neighborhoods.

resources.name: Food Bank and Mobile Food Bank
resources.description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank distributes weekly food hampers with pantry staples and fresh items, combining bulk-purchased and donated foods to reduce costs for clients. Its Mobile Food Bank extends low-cost and no-cost distribution into multiple neighborhoods, improving access for youth and families affected by rising living expenses. The program’s centralized procurement and regular distribution align with a bulk-buy model that keeps staple foods affordable.

solutions.text: Community Gardens, Gleaning Networks and Farm Partnerships: Neighbourhood gardens on municipal or church land, paired with gleaning programs that collect surplus from local farms and distribute it through community hubs, increasing access to fresh produce and reducing grocery bills.

resources.name: Farm Partners and Food Rescue
resources.description: Feed Nova Scotia works directly with Nova Scotia farmers and producers to collect surplus and donated crops—including post-harvest and seasonal excess—and moves that fresh produce through a province-wide network of community food banks, meal programs, and shelters. By coordinating farm partnerships and food rescue (including field gleaning when possible), they increase access to healthy fruits and vegetables at neighborhood hubs and help households reduce grocery costs.

resources.name: Community Gardens & Good Food Market
resources.description: The North Grove operates large community gardens and a greenhouse where local residents grow food, learn gardening skills, and harvest produce for household use. Through partnerships with nearby farms, they stock a low-cost Good Food Market and distribute donated surplus via community meals and a community fridge, increasing access to fresh, local produce and helping families stretch their food budgets.

resources.name: Charity Harvest & Gleaning Days
resources.description: Noggins Corner Farm organizes charity harvest and gleaning days where volunteers help collect surplus produce from their fields for donation to local food programs and food banks. By channeling post-harvest excess to community hubs like Feed Nova Scotia and neighborhood agencies, the farm reduces food waste and expands access to fresh fruits and vegetables for families facing high grocery costs.

resources.name: Community Garden, Greenhouse & Bulk Food Program
resources.description: The New Ross Family Resource Centre maintains on-site community gardens and a teaching greenhouse where residents grow and share produce while learning food skills. They partner with local farms to source seasonal surplus for low- or no-cost community meals and a bulk-buy food program, distributing fresh produce through a trusted community hub to help reduce household food expenses.

solutions.text: Community Kitchens and Shared Meal Programs: Shared commercial kitchen hours, meal prep co-ops, and pay-what-you-can community dinners run by local organizations to lower meal costs, build skills, and reduce food waste.

resources.name: Community Meals and Community Kitchen
resources.description: The North Grove runs pay-what-you-can community suppers and hands-on community kitchen programs in a fully equipped kitchen in Dartmouth North. Participants cook together, learn budgeting and meal-planning skills, and batch-prep affordable meals using rescued and bulk ingredients—lowering food costs and reducing waste.

resources.name: ISANS Community Kitchen
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS brings newcomers together in its commercial training kitchen to co‑cook culturally diverse, low-cost meals and take portions home. By sharing ingredients, kitchen time, and food skills, the program lowers per‑meal costs, builds confidence, and reduces food waste; periodic community dinners are offered free or pay‑what‑you‑can to foster inclusion.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: Community Kitchen & Community Suppers
resources.organization: Chebucto Family Centre (Home of the Guardian Angel)
resources.description: Chebucto Family Centre hosts collective kitchen sessions where participants batch-cook family-sized meals to take home while learning nutrition, budgeting, and safe food handling. The centre also offers free or pay-what-you-can community dinners that use donated and rescued ingredients to stretch budgets and cut food waste.

resources.name: Free Lunch Program
resources.description: The Loaded Ladle serves free or pay-what-you-can vegan lunches for students and community members from a shared campus kitchen at Dalhousie University. Volunteer-led prep shifts teach cooking and organizing skills, while bulk purchasing and donated produce lower costs and help prevent food waste.

resources.name: Community Kitchen Meal Program
resources.description: Loaves and Fishes operates a community kitchen and dining room that serves daily free or very low-cost hot meals in downtown Sydney. Using donated and surplus food and volunteer prep in a commercial kitchen, the program reduces waste, provides shared meals, and offers opportunities to build practical kitchen skills.

solutions.text: Sliding-Scale CSA and Farmers' Market Subsidy: Partnerships between farmers, markets and community groups to offer community-supported agriculture (CSA) shares on a sliding scale, vendor-sponsored discounted produce days, and vouchers for young people.

resources.name: Nourishing Communities Food Coupon Program
resources.description: Wolfville Farmers’ Market partners with community agencies and vendors to provide weekly food coupons that can be redeemed with market vendors for fresh produce and other staples. The coupons are distributed to low-income households, including families with children and young people, effectively subsidizing the cost of healthy food. Vendor and community sponsorships fund the discounts, aligning with the solution’s focus on market subsidies and vouchers.

resources.name: Nourish ‘Food Bucks’ Program
resources.description: The New Glasgow Farmers Market runs a voucher program that distributes ‘Food Bucks’ through local community partners to individuals and families who face barriers to affording fresh food. Recipients use the vouchers directly with market vendors for produce, creating a vendor-supported subsidy that reduces cost at the point of purchase. The program helps young people and families access nutritious food and mirrors the sliding-scale/market subsidy approach.
resources.address: 620 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3S2

resources.name: Community Market and Market Greens Produce Vouchers
resources.description: The North Grove operates a weekly community market with subsidized pricing on fresh produce and pantry staples, making healthy food more affordable. Through the Market Greens produce prescription and related voucher initiatives, eligible residents—especially families with children and young people—receive credits to buy fruits and vegetables. This blends vendor- and donor-supported discounts with vouchers, directly implementing the solution’s market subsidy and youth-focused access.

resources.name: Pay-What-You-Can Produce Bundles & Token Program
resources.description: Square Roots partners with Nova Scotia farmers to assemble 10 lb produce bundles offered on a pay-what-you-can sliding scale, reducing cost barriers while preventing food waste. Community-distributed tokens act as vouchers so young people and low-income residents can access bundles at no cost, with vendor and donor support covering the subsidy. Local chapters across the province collaborate with community groups to ensure broad access to affordable produce.

solutions.text: Volunteer Driver and Community Ride-Share Network: A locally operated app/phone line that coordinates volunteer drivers, carpool matches and low-cost ride-shares for work, school and medical appointments to reduce individual transportation costs.

resources.name: MusGo Rider Community Transportation
resources.description: MusGo Rider is a community, volunteer-driven transportation co-operative serving the Eastern Shore and Musquodoboit Valley, coordinating pre-booked rides by phone and online to get residents to work, school, medical appointments, and daily errands at low, distance-based fares. The service matches riders with vetted volunteer drivers (and community vehicles) to reduce individual transportation costs in rural areas where public transit is limited, effectively operating a community ride-share network.
resources.address: 67 Park Road, Musquodoboit Harbour, NS B0J 2L0

resources.name: Kings Point-to-Point Transit
resources.description: Kings Point-to-Point Transit provides door-to-door, pre-booked community transportation across Kings County for employment, education, medical, and essential trips at affordable fares. Using a dispatch phone line and online booking tools, the service coordinates rides (including with volunteer drivers) to share vehicle capacity and lower per-person travel costs, functioning as a local ride-share/carpool network for residents without reliable transportation.
resources.address: 14 Crescent Drive, New Minas, NS B4N 3G7

resources.name: Wheels of Hope (Transportation Service)
resources.description: Wheels of Hope coordinates volunteer drivers who use their own vehicles to provide low-cost rides for people traveling to cancer-related medical appointments across Nova Scotia. Requests are handled via phone and online, matching riders to nearby volunteers and subsidizing mileage so clients face minimal out-of-pocket costs—directly reducing transportation expenses for essential health trips.

solutions.text: Bike Libraries and Active-Transportation Hubs: Loaner bike programs, community bike repair cafés, and mapped safe routes to encourage cycling as an affordable commute option, paired with group purchasing of helmets and lights.

resources.name: Welcoming Wheels
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: Welcoming Wheels provides refurbished bicycles to newcomers and refugees, paired with traffic-safety training and basic maintenance workshops so riders can commute confidently and affordably. Participants receive essential gear—helmets, lights, and locks—sourced through donations and bulk purchasing to keep upfront costs low. The program also orients riders to safe local routes and community cycling resources to support daily travel by bike.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 2005, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: DSU Bike Centre
resources.description: The DSU Bike Centre operates an on-campus bike library with low-cost semester rentals and a do‑it‑yourself repair shop stocked with tools, parts, and guidance from student mechanics. It runs maintenance clinics and commuting workshops, and connects students with affordable safety gear such as helmets and lights via in‑shop sales or partner discounts. By reducing acquisition and upkeep costs and teaching safe riding skills, it supports cycling as a budget‑friendly way to get to class and work.

resources.name: Halifax Bike Week and Active Transportation Programs
resources.description: HRM’s Active Transportation team publishes the official Halifax Cycling Map and provides route planning and wayfinding that identify safer corridors for daily trips. Through Halifax Bike Week and year‑round pop‑ups with community partners, the municipality supports group rides, repair cafés, and free light/helmet giveaways that help new riders get equipped and comfortable on city streets. Together, mapped routes, education, and equipment access reduce barriers to low‑cost cycling.

resources.name: Child Safety Link Helmet Bulk Purchase Program
resources.organization: IWK Health Centre – Child Safety Link
resources.description: Child Safety Link coordinates a bulk‑purchasing program that enables schools, youth groups, and community agencies to order CSA‑approved bicycle helmets at discounted prices. It also provides fit clinics and safety resources that complement community cycling initiatives and bike libraries, lowering the cost of essential protective gear for riders. This addresses the group‑purchasing component of the solution, making safe, everyday cycling more affordable.

solutions.text: Neighbourhood Car-Share Co-op: Community-owned car-share vehicles with hourly rates and membership discounts for students and entry-level workers, reducing the need for personal car ownership and insurance costs.

resources.name: Communauto Atlantic – Halifax Carsharing
resources.description: Communauto Atlantic operates a network of shared vehicles in Halifax Regional Municipality that members can book by the hour or day, with fuel, insurance, and maintenance included. Flexible plans and a Student plan provide reduced fees and lower-cost access, helping students and entry‑level workers avoid the upfront purchase price, monthly payments, and high insurance costs of owning a personal vehicle. Stations are placed in walkable neighbourhoods to complement transit and cycling, reducing overall transportation expenses.

resources.name: CarShare Atlantic – Student & Community Memberships
resources.description: CarShare Atlantic provides community-based carsharing with neighbourhood vehicles available 24/7 for hourly bookings, bundling insurance, fuel, and maintenance into simple rates. Student and low-cost membership options reduce barriers to access, letting young people and entry‑level workers pay only when they need a vehicle instead of bearing the fixed costs of ownership and insurance. This directly implements a neighbourhood car‑share model that eases cost-of-living pressures beyond housing.

solutions.text: Community Energy Co-operatives and Bulk Heat-Pump Purchases: Local co-ops that develop small renewable projects and organize bulk purchases/installation discounts for heat pumps and energy-efficient appliances to lower utility bills and upfront costs.

resources.name: Heat Pump Rebates and Instant Discounts
resources.description: Efficiency Nova Scotia provides rebates on high-efficiency heat pumps and negotiates province-wide instant discounts with retailers and contractors, reducing upfront costs at the point of purchase. By aggregating demand through a large network of participating suppliers and installers, the program helps households access lower prices and install equipment that cuts monthly utility bills—directly addressing cost-of-living pressures.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) – Nova Scotia Municipalities
resources.description: Clean Foundation administers Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) programs that enable homeowners in participating Nova Scotia municipalities to install heat pumps and energy-efficient upgrades with no upfront payment, repaid on property tax bills. The program pre-qualifies contractors and coordinates multiple projects across communities, creating economies of scale that help secure competitive installation pricing while lowering residents’ utility costs.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing Program (Energize Bridgewater)
resources.description: Bridgewater’s municipal PACE program helps residents install cold-climate heat pumps and other home efficiency measures with zero-upfront-cost financing repaid on their property tax bill. By using approved contractors and coordinated project support, the program reduces barriers to bulk adoption of efficient technologies, delivering lower energy bills and improved affordability for local households.

solutions.text: Volunteer Weatherization and Retrofit Program: Neighbourhood teams trained to do low-cost weatherization (sealing, insulation upgrades, programmable thermostats) for low-income households, coordinated with municipal permit supports and bulk material discounts.

resources.name: HomeWarming
resources.organization: HomeWarming (delivered by Clean Foundation and Efficiency Nova Scotia)
resources.description: HomeWarming provides no-cost home energy assessments and upgrades for income-qualified Nova Scotians, including draft-proofing, insulation, and smart/programmable thermostats to cut heating bills. Delivered by Clean Foundation and Efficiency Nova Scotia, the program coordinates contractors, manages any required permits, and leverages bulk purchasing of materials to reduce costs—directly implementing community-scale weatherization for low-income households.

resources.name: Mi’kmaw Home Energy Efficiency Project (MHEEP)
resources.description: MHEEP partners with Mi’kmaw communities across Nova Scotia to deliver energy assessments and install low-cost weatherization measures—such as air sealing, insulation upgrades, and smart/programmable thermostats—for on-reserve households. The program trains community-based teams and coordinates bulk procurement and contractor support, reducing costs and improving comfort and affordability for low-income families.

resources.name: Clean Energy Financing Program (PACE) – Town of Bridgewater
resources.description: Bridgewater’s PACE program helps homeowners finance energy-efficiency retrofits like insulation, air sealing, and smart thermostats with on-bill repayment, lowering upfront barriers. Municipal staff guide permitting, connect residents with vetted contractors, and use program-scale procurement to drive down costs—supporting neighbourhood-level, low-cost weatherization that reduces utility bills.

resources.name: Affordable Multi-Unit Housing Program
resources.description: This Efficiency Nova Scotia program works with non-profit and co-operative housing providers to assess buildings and implement weatherization upgrades—air sealing, added insulation, and controls—to reduce energy use and costs for low-income tenants. It coordinates contractors, provides incentives, and leverages bulk purchasing to streamline retrofits at scale, aligning with community-focused, low-cost weatherization goals.
resources.address: 230 Brownlow Avenue, Suite 300, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0G5

solutions.text: Group Insurance Pools and Broker Clinics: Local associations (youth chambers, co-ops, freelancer networks) negotiate group rates for auto, renter's and small-business insurance; host clinics with brokers to compare low-cost coverage and claims advice.

resources.name: Chambers of Commerce Group Insurance Plan & Member Insurance Clinics
resources.description: The Halifax Chamber of Commerce aggregates local businesses into the national Chambers of Commerce Group Insurance Plan and partners with local brokers to secure group-rated benefits and small-business insurance. Through member benefits and events, the Chamber also facilitates discounted home and auto options for member employees and hosts broker-led clinics and info sessions where entrepreneurs and young professionals can compare coverage, understand claims processes, and choose low-cost plans.
resources.address: 32 Akerley Boulevard, Unit 100, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1N1

resources.name: NSGEU Group Home, Auto & Tenant Insurance Program
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Government & General Employees Union (NSGEU)
resources.description: NSGEU negotiates preferred group rates on home, auto, and tenant insurance for members through a national insurer partner and local brokers, lowering everyday insurance costs. The union regularly hosts on-site and virtual clinics with insurance representatives to help members compare coverage, access discounts, and receive practical claims advice.
resources.address: 255 John Savage Avenue, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0J3

resources.name: NSNU Member Home & Auto Group Insurance
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Nurses’ Union offers members group-rated home, auto, and tenant insurance through an affinity partnership, using pooled purchasing power to reduce premiums. NSNU complements the discount program with broker/advisor-led information sessions and webinars that walk members through coverage comparisons, savings options, and claims support.

resources.name: SMU Alumni Insurance Program (Home, Auto & Tenant)
resources.description: Saint Mary’s University Alumni Association partners with a national insurer to provide alumni in Nova Scotia with affinity group rates on home, tenant, and auto insurance, helping graduates manage cost-of-living pressures. The alumni office periodically coordinates broker/advisor info sessions and webinars so members can compare policies, understand coverage trade-offs, and get claims guidance.

solutions.text: Cooperative Childcare and Shared Nanny Networks: Parent-run childcare co-ops, shared nanny/childminding networks and time-share childcare arrangements that lower childcare costs and increase flexible, community-based options for working young parents.

resources.name: Family Home Child Care (FHCC) Program
resources.description: The YMCA’s licensed Family Home Child Care program recruits, trains, and supports approved home child care providers and matches them with families seeking small-group care. By enabling multiple families to share a single caregiver in a home setting and to arrange part‑time or non‑standard hours, the network lowers per‑family costs and offers flexible, community‑based options that align with cooperative and shared childminding models for working parents.

resources.name: Care for Newcomer Children (CNC) Childminding
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS provides no‑cost, licensed childminding on site while parents attend employment, language, and settlement programs, creating a shared childminding solution that eases childcare expenses during critical work‑ and training‑related hours. This community‑based model pools resources to offer safe group care, making childcare more accessible and flexible for newcomer families balancing work, study, and resettlement.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

solutions.text: Living-Wage Employer Coalition and Youth Hiring Pledge: A local employer coalition that commits to living wages, predictable scheduling, apprenticeship slots and mentorship for young workers, with public recognition for participating businesses to encourage uptake.

resources.name: Living Wage Requirement for Suppliers (Procurement)
resources.description: Halifax Regional Municipality requires vendors providing certain contracted services to pay at least a locally defined living wage to the workers who deliver those contracts. By embedding living-wage standards into procurement and publicly posting the policy and compliance expectations, HRM creates market recognition for businesses that meet the standard and nudges a coalition of local employers toward better wages and more predictable, decent work for young employees.

resources.name: Building Futures for Youth (BFY)
resources.description: BFY is a province-wide program that places high school students in paid summer work with construction employers, pairing them with trained mentors and exposing them to apprenticeship pathways. Participating employers commit to providing safe, structured, and predictable placements with on-the-job mentorship, and they receive public recognition through the program’s partner listings—creating a visible coalition of youth-friendly, apprenticeship-focused employers.
resources.address: 134 Eileen Stubbs Avenue, Unit 103, Dartmouth, NS B3B 2C4

resources.name: Youth Apprenticeship Pathways and Employer Incentives (START)
resources.description: The Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency supports employers to hire and mentor young workers through registered apprenticeship, offering structured training plans, progressive wage scales, and journeyperson mentorship. Through the START employer incentive and related programs, businesses commit to apprenticeship slots and receive support and public recognition (e.g., awards, success stories), reinforcing a province-wide network of employers offering predictable, skills-building jobs for youth.

solutions.text: Micro-Grants, Incubators and Co‑Working for Young Entrepreneurs: Community-managed micro-grants, low-cost co-working spaces, equipment libraries and mentorship programs that reduce startup costs for small businesses and side hustles.

resources.name: Volta
resources.description: Volta is Atlantic Canada’s largest innovation hub, offering subsidized co-working, meeting rooms, and a community of mentors and experts to help founders launch and grow. Through programs like Volta Cohort (which provides equity-free funding and wraparound support), Volta directly reduces early startup costs for young entrepreneurs and side hustlers while connecting them to investors and talent.
resources.address: 1505 Barrington Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K5

resources.name: CEED (Centre for Entrepreneurship Education & Development)
resources.organization: Centre for Entrepreneurship Education and Development (CEED)
resources.description: CEED provides accessible entrepreneurship training, coaching, and low-cost co-working options alongside micro-financing programs that help cover early business expenses. By pairing mentorship with affordable workspace and access to small-scale capital, CEED lowers barriers for young and first-time founders to test ideas and build sustainable ventures.
resources.address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 225, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

resources.name: CO3 Space
resources.description: CO3 Space is a community-focused co-working hub on the South Shore that offers affordable desks, meeting rooms, and programming for freelancers, startups, and small businesses. Its flexible memberships, peer mentorship, and regular skill-building events help reduce overhead and provide a supportive environment for young entrepreneurs and side hustles.

resources.name: The Spark Zone (Nova Scotia Sandbox)
resources.organization: Saint Mary’s University – The Spark Zone Sandbox
resources.description: The Spark Zone is a university-led incubator that provides free co-working space, mentorship, workshops, and small seed funding to help students and recent graduates validate ideas and build early-stage ventures. By covering essentials like workspace, coaching, and prototype micro-grants, it reduces startup costs and risk for emerging entrepreneurs.

resources.name: ShiftKey Labs (Nova Scotia Sandbox)
resources.description: ShiftKey Labs is a Dalhousie-based technology sandbox offering free co-working, access to prototyping resources, mentorship from industry professionals, and small project funding for student teams. This support lowers the financial barriers to building proofs-of-concept and launching tech side hustles, helping young founders get to market faster and at lower cost.

solutions.text: Community Credit Union Programs and Matched-Savings: Partnerships with local credit unions to offer no-fee accounts, low-interest small loans, matched-savings programs for training or emergencies, and youth-friendly financial products.

resources.name: CUA Microloan Program
resources.description: CUA offers small-dollar, low-interest microloans designed to help individuals cover essential costs such as emergency expenses, car repairs, or utility arrears, with flexible terms that help build or repair credit. As a community credit union, CUA also provides youth-friendly accounts and financial coaching, reducing fees and barriers to everyday banking. This directly supports young people managing cost-of-living pressures by providing affordable credit and accessible, no-fee banking options.
resources.address: 1475 Lower Water Street, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3J 3Z2

resources.name: Student Line of Credit and Youth Accounts
resources.description: Sydney Credit Union provides a Student Line of Credit with competitive rates and interest-only payments while in school, helping students and young workers finance tuition, tools, and training with lower monthly costs. It also offers youth-friendly chequing and savings options with low or no monthly fees, plus digital banking tools and in-branch advice to build financial skills. Together, these products make day-to-day banking more affordable and provide accessible credit to manage rising non-housing living costs.

resources.name: Small Business Loan Guarantee Program (Nova Scotia)
resources.organization: Nova Scotia Co-operative Council (delivered through participating Nova Scotia credit unions)
resources.description: This province-wide program, delivered through local credit unions, offers low-interest loans guaranteed by the Province of Nova Scotia to help entrepreneurs start or grow small businesses. By partnering with credit unions, it increases access to capital for young entrepreneurs who may lack collateral or lengthy credit histories, often with flexible terms and mentorship supports. Access to affordable financing helps stabilize income, offset cost-of-living pressures, and create local employment opportunities.

solutions.text: Time Banks and Skill-Swap Platforms: Local time-banking systems where residents exchange hours of work (childcare, tutoring, repairs) instead of money, building mutual aid networks that cut service costs for young people.

resources.name: Fix-It Fair (Halifax Central Library)
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries hosts recurring Fix-It Fair events where volunteer repairers donate their time to help residents fix household items (small appliances, clothing, electronics) and learn repair skills hands-on. No money changes hands—community members exchange time and know-how, directly cutting repair costs for young people while growing a local mutual-aid network.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Repair Café (Alderney Gate Public Library – Dartmouth)
resources.description: At Alderney Gate Public Library, volunteers with skills in sewing, electronics, and small repairs offer their time to help neighbours troubleshoot and fix broken items. The skill-sharing format functions like a community time exchange—participants receive service and learn skills without fees, reducing everyday costs and strengthening peer-to-peer support.

resources.name: Repair Café (Lunenburg Library)
resources.description: South Shore Public Libraries runs Repair Café events at the Lunenburg Library where local volunteers share their time and expertise to repair clothing, bikes, and household items, and to teach basic maintenance. This skill-swap model lowers out-of-pocket service costs for residents—especially young people—by exchanging volunteer hours and knowledge instead of money.

resources.name: Bike Again! Community Bike Shop (Earn-a-Bike & Skill-Share)
resources.description: Bike Again! is a volunteer-run community bike workshop where residents learn bike maintenance and can contribute volunteer hours to earn bicycles or parts, reducing transportation costs. Through hands-on mentorship and time-for-value exchanges, it operates as a practical skill-swap platform that builds mutual aid and affordable mobility for young people.

solutions.text: Financial Literacy, Benefits Navigation and Tax Clinics: Regular community workshops and drop-in clinics that teach budgeting, debt management, claims for provincial/federal benefits, and how to access eligible subsidies to improve net income.

resources.name: Free Tax Clinics (CVITP) and Financial Literacy Programs
resources.description: Halifax Public Libraries partners with the Community Volunteer Income Tax Program (CVITP) to host free, appointment-based and drop-in tax clinics across branches, helping low- and modest-income residents file taxes and access eligible refunds and benefits. The library also offers regular financial literacy workshops covering budgeting, debt management, and fraud prevention, giving young people practical skills to stretch incomes and reduce costs.
resources.address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

resources.name: Community Tax Clinic and Benefits Navigation
resources.organization: Dartmouth Family Centre & Dartmouth North Community Food Centre
resources.description: Dartmouth Family Centre & Dartmouth North Community Food Centre runs a free Community Tax Clinic that helps individuals file returns and unlock federal/provincial benefits and credits. Staff and volunteers also provide benefits navigation and group sessions on budgeting and credit basics, connecting participants to subsidies and income supports that can improve monthly cash flow.

resources.name: Free Income Tax Clinic and Community Outreach & Navigation
resources.description: Chebucto Connections offers a free income tax clinic through CVITP to help low- and modest-income residents in Spryfield complete returns and receive eligible benefits and credits. Their Community Outreach & Navigation team provides one-on-one support to apply for rebates and subsidies (e.g., utilities, transportation, child benefits) and hosts occasional budgeting and money management workshops to help reduce household costs.
resources.address: 531 Herring Cove Road, Suite 102, Halifax, NS B3R 1X3

resources.name: Income Tax Preparation Program
resources.description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank runs a free income tax preparation program for low-income individuals and families, ensuring clients file accurately and access refundable credits and benefits. The organization also provides drop-in support to review bills and budgets and connects people with subsidies and partner agencies for debt counselling to help stabilize household finances.

resources.name: Free Tax Clinics (CVITP) and Money Matters Workshops
resources.description: Cape Breton Regional Library hosts free CVITP tax clinics at branches like the McConnell Library, helping residents file returns and claim eligible benefits and credits. The library also offers adult learning sessions such as Money Matters financial literacy workshops on budgeting, banking, and credit, giving community members tools to manage expenses and improve net income.

solutions.text: Community Fridges and Food Rescue Partnerships: Neighbourhood fridges, pantry nodes and partnerships with grocery stores, restaurants and campuses to redistribute surplus food to residents, reducing household grocery expense and waste.

resources.name: Retail Food Recovery and Distribution
resources.description: Feed Nova Scotia rescues surplus edible food from grocery retailers, wholesalers, farms, and food distributors and redistributes it through a network of 140+ member agencies across the province. This includes community pantries, meal programs, and food banks that make rescued food available to residents at no cost. By channeling surplus into communities, the program reduces household grocery expenses and prevents good food from going to waste.

resources.name: Food Bank and Fresh Food Rescue Partnerships
resources.description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank operates a community food bank and partners with local grocers, bakeries, farms, and food rescue networks to accept surplus food. Donated and rescued groceries are redistributed to residents through regular food hampers and a pantry model, offering fresh produce, baked goods, and staples. This approach directly lowers grocery costs for households while diverting edible food from landfill.

resources.name: Community Food Centre Market and Pantry
resources.description: The North Grove runs community food access programs that include an affordable market and a pantry-style distribution of donated and rescued foods like produce and bread. Working with local grocers, farms, and provincial food recovery partners, they redistribute surplus foods to Dartmouth North residents. These programs help reduce grocery bills for families and young people while cutting down on food waste.

resources.name: DSU Food Bank
resources.description: The Dalhousie Student Union Food Bank operates a campus pantry that redistributes donated and rescued groceries, including fresh produce and ready-to-eat items from local partners and campus events. Students can access free food on a weekly basis, reducing their out-of-pocket grocery costs. By prioritizing rescued and donated foods, the service also helps minimize food waste.

resources.name: Community Food Room
resources.description: Saint Mary’s University’s Community Food Room is a student-focused pantry that offers free access to fresh and shelf-stable foods sourced through donations and food recovery partners, including surplus from retailers and campus food services. The program reduces grocery expenses for students while ensuring good food is not wasted. Regular distributions and open hours make it a reliable, stigma-reducing access point on campus.

solutions.text: Advocacy Network for Local Cost-of-Living Policies: A community-led coalition that collects lived-experience data and advocates municipal/provincial leaders for targeted supports (transit passes, childcare subsidies, living-wage bylaws), amplifying community-driven policy wins.

resources.name: Transportation & Built Environment Program
resources.description: Ecology Action Centre’s transportation team convenes riders, youth, disability advocates, and low‑income community members to document lived experiences with transit and mobility costs, and turns that evidence into policy briefs and submissions to HRM and the Province. They advocate for targeted supports such as equitable fare policies, low‑income transit passes, safer active transportation options, and investments that reduce household transportation costs, amplifying community voices to secure local policy improvements.

resources.name: Affordable Energy Coalition (Nova Scotia)
resources.organization: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service (representation for the Affordable Energy Coalition)
resources.description: The Affordable Energy Coalition, represented by Dalhousie Legal Aid Service, gathers testimony and data from low‑income ratepayers on energy poverty and presents this lived experience to the Nova Scotia Utility and Review Board. The coalition advocates for targeted utility supports—such as low‑income efficiency programs, bill assistance, and consumer protections—so rising electricity and heating costs don’t outpace wages, directly addressing a core driver of cost‑of‑living pressure.

resources.name: Advocacy
resources.description: Feed Nova Scotia’s advocacy program compiles data and stories from people accessing food support across the province to highlight how food, transportation, and utility costs strain household budgets. Using this lived‑experience evidence, they engage municipal and provincial leaders to push for income‑based solutions—like living‑wage policies, stronger income assistance, and affordable access programs—that reduce cost‑of‑living pressures beyond housing.

resources.name: Poverty Solutions Advisory Committee
resources.description: This United Way Halifax initiative brings together people with lived and living experience of poverty to identify barriers—such as transit fares, childcare costs, and low wages—and co‑develop policy recommendations. The committee engages directly with HRM and Nova Scotia decision‑makers to advocate for targeted supports (e.g., affordable transit programs and childcare subsidies), ensuring community‑driven insights shape local policy change.

resources.name: Policy, Research and Advocacy
resources.organization: Immigrant Services Association of Nova Scotia (ISANS)
resources.description: ISANS consults newcomers and youth to document lived experiences with the cost of transportation, childcare access, credentialing, and workplace barriers, translating these findings into policy briefs and submissions. They work with municipal and provincial leaders to advance targeted supports—such as discounted transit access, childcare subsidies, and fair employment practices—that improve affordability and retention for young people and immigrant families in Nova Scotia.
